speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My family was allocated quarters there because my father was a pilot in the RSAF.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They were happy memories: growing up within my close-knit group of Air Force families and their children, the smell of sea breeze from Changi Beach and the daily chant of "kiri, kiri, kiri, kanan, kiri" of soldiers, both National Servicemen and regulars, who would run through the streets of the airbase.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That daily chant ensured that the whole team of soldiers got to their destinations together, united.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singaporeans voted to give the best chance possible for Singapore in the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singaporean voters placed into our hands that previous ingredient for effective leadership – that of trust.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Being a Member of Parliament is not a job or an appointment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And so, we, the elected few, must respect that trust that has been placed in our hands.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must nurture it and reciprocate it with very hard work; even harder work now for the residents we serve and their families.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But Madam, on this, the first Sitting of Parliament post-GE2015, what will our chant be as a country?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we look into the horizon of the next 50 years, what will our drumbeat be as a people of Singapore to ensure that we stay united and get to our destinations together?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, that we recognise that Singapore is indeed a precious gem – unparalleled in the region, unparalleled globally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, we must realise that while economic accolades are important, these accolades must benefit the very Singaporeans who make up Singapore, her identity and drive.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, we, as a Government, must put on the cloak of humility and realise that there is still a lot more progress and advancement that can be made for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we are to put on such a cloak of humility, we will realise that there are some countries globally that have effective social economic policies that have worked well for their populations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we are humble enough, we will be able to adopt such policies while adapting them and nuancing them to the local context for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, while we put on such a cloak of humility, we should and must retain a deep sense of quiet confidence so that we can likewise recognise countries regionally and globally that have not done so well for their populations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should have that quiet confidence to resist taking on-board short-term economic policies to the long-term detriment of our people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Page: 8 Madam, let me delve into four key policy areas which I feel we need to get right for the continued survival of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A look at the South China Sea will show many competing claims over territory.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Equally, we need the best equipment and infrastructure to ensure that these men and women in uniform are able to fulfil their roles.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A strong defence budget will help ensure this.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, Madam, it is not only sovereignty security that is important, but domestic security too.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A quick look at our neighbours, Malaysia, Indonesia and even ourselves, shows that there are some individuals who become radicalised domestically.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They then take up arms in other countries to support "terrorist causes".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, we need to ensure that we have a strong Home Team budget to ensure that we have a well-equipped Home Team and a proficient Internal Security Department (ISD).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will ensure that we are able to detect and deter threats beyond our shores and to ensure that we have a safe and secure Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Should the threats unfortunately vest in Singapore, we will have a strong team partnering various community organisations to preserve our communal ties and overcome such threats and adversities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important to ensure that our students are given the most number of opportunities available to reach their potential domestically, regionally and globally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because they will be our next generation of Singaporeans, advancing the country's interests and their own in the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to create an education system that provides opportunities for all Singaporeans and that maximises their potential.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I strongly believe that of equal importance is the need to instil character, values and ethics in a child.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To assess a school purely on its academic output is too simplistic.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because the schools with longer histories usually have the ability to set the higher cut-off as the entry criteria into the school.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It therefore follows that at the next major national examination, the school's academic performance would be good, if not better than average.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would have thought a better assessment of the success of a school would be the amount of value-add that the school gives to each individual child.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, I would like to acknowledge the concerted effort of Minister Heng Swee Keat and his team in the Education Ministry in the last Term to instil the importance of character in students.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This policy has gone down well among parents that I have met at school functions, dialogues and community events.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because it recognises the individual talents and gifts of the child, Page: 9 beyond academics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It incentivises the school and prioritises the school's focus to bring out the best in each child, for example, to turn a less confident child into a team player.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I would ask the new leadership team at MOE, namely, the two new Acting Ministers, to advance and consolidate the existing character-, values- and ethics-based education system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My vision is for Singaporean students, when they eventually enter the working world, whether domestically, regionally or globally, to be known for their character, ethics and integrity and that they will make the right decisions and choices in difficult situations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Global MNCs, domestic and regional firms would want to employ Singaporeans because of their character traits and values, in addition to their academic ability and skillset.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If we are able to get this right, then, the brightness of our little red dot will radiate in cities and countries around the world, through our Singaporeans who live and work in them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The third policy area that I wish to speak on, Madam, is the need to create a sustainable and predictable property market.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I raised in this House the possibility of adapting the Australian model to Singapore to deter overly speculative behaviour by foreigners in the market.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In summary, in Australia, foreigners are only allowed to buy new property and only allowed to sell that property back to domestic buyers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This somewhat fetters speculation by foreigners in the Australian property market because these foreigners will not buy property at a price that they do not think they will be able to resell it at to an Australian.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When I first raised this in Parliament, the then Minister for National Development, Mr Khaw Boon Wan, explained that he would much rather adopt a more calibrated and flexible approach to cooling the property market.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By retaining the TDSR, a Singaporean is only going to be allowed a credit line that is within his means.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If this Singaporean is able to afford a second or third property through the TDSR regime, why tax him with an additional buyer's stamp duty?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The fourth policy area, Madam, relates to caring for the marginalised and vulnerable in our society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I strongly believe that one day soon, governments will be assessed also on how they treat the most vulnerable in society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yes, Singapore has altruistic social and economic initiatives and, yes, we have an effective and efficient Government to administer these policies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, some among us face circumstances that we were never able to predict.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And some, through no fault of their own, land in some very dire straits.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, we must have a compassionate and proactive Civil Service that ensures that we partner the vulnerable in Singapore and lift them up again.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is in line with the President's message to care for one another.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, Madam, I would like to talk about four specific vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have worked with shelters that do marvellous work for this vulnerable group.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Among them, Dayspring, which runs a shelter within Holland-Bukit Timah GRC, and the Good Shepherd Sisters which also runs a shelter in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I feel that the Government can do a lot more to partner these groups in three concrete ways.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Page: 10 One, to provide livable long-term shelters.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Three, full-time support in the form of book-keeping and administration.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, would the Government provide, for example, on secondment a civil servant to assist with book-keeping and administration?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is so that the volunteers at such organisations can focus on giving their time and energy to vulnerable women and children, and partnering them out of difficult situations, rather than getting bogged down with administrative matters.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The second vulnerable group are stateless residents of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A common theme often found among these people is that often, it was their parents who did not register them for a birth certificate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As compared to potential new citizens, I would have thought that these stateless people, born and bred in Singapore, are more deserving of consideration for citizenship.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The third group, Madam, is the foreign or migrant workforce and in particular, the migrant workers who may have been duped, cheated or mistreated by their employers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, those that have not been paid their wages, or worse still, have had crimes committed against them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, these people have literally helped to build Singapore and are assisting the state in investigations and the prosecution of errant employers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I think it fair that as a gracious host, Singapore should allow them to earn a wage while they assist the authorities, so that they can pay down their high agency fees.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yes, Yellow Ribbon Project is a worthwhile cause but could we not go further?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe that Singapore has flown its first 50 years well.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yes, we have encountered some turbulence, squalls and weather fronts, but we have pulled through because we stayed united.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we embark on the next leg of our flight together as a nation and look at the horizon of the next 50 years, I humbly say that we are starting from a position of strength.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because on this aircraft of Singapore, we have powerful arsenal, that of meritocracy, that of a Government that has no tolerance for corruption and that of a diligent and courageous people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And if we get our drumbeat as a people right, if we get our chant as a nation right, then I believe, because I choose to believe, that Singapore will survive.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Twenty-fifteen was said to be a watershed year for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We celebrated our nation's 50th anniversary, mourned the passing of our founding father, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, and had the first General Election (GE) since Independence where all parliamentary seats were hotly contested.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The results of 2015 are plain for everyone to see.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It marked a coming together of Singaporeans and their Government, a sense that we are together in this journey.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: After GE 2011, it appeared as though there was a "disconnect" between the Government and the people.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I spoke on the paradigm of "trust" at the Budget debate in 2013.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I appealed to the Government to listen better and communicate more.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I also spoke on the "out of touch" politician at the Budget debate in 2014.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It was not a critique of individuals or the Government.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It was to say, from my heart, what I heard about the perception of "disconnect".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: You should think that I would be a happy man.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Well, I am, but I also feel a much heavier burden.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I feel that I now have the unenviable but proud task of living up to all the expectations and trust that my voters have placed on me.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I am sure that each and every Member of this House feels the same.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But Mdm Speaker, credit must be given where credit is due.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It worked hard at building and rebuilding its relationship with the People.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But more importantly, what enabled the change was not any single national initiative but the entire mindset of the Government.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong led his Ministers and office-holders in cutting through the red tape of bureaucracy and communicating directly with the people.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There was a determined and concerted attempt to get the people to "buy in".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A wave of new initiatives on many fronts for the young and the old were launched.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Unlike many other governments, it "walked the talk", and the people responded.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The GE2015 results speak resoundingly loud and crystal clear.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is, however, just the beginning of a new journey.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A new and fresh journey in which the Government and the people, having come together in 2015, must work even harder and build a future together for our country as we march towards our next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If we fail, we will all go down together.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We do not have natural resources and, as a little red dot, stand exposed to be battered in this global arena of constant calamities.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: All we have are people of true grit, will power and determination.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Page: 12 So, we journey afresh knowing what we have, what we do not have, but stand "always prepared".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We cannot afford to let our guard down.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We must always stay ahead of the game.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If we do, the next 50 years will be better than the last.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Since October 2015, there have been rapid global changes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We head into uncertain times and unchartered waters.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The terrorists have again struck close to our border at our neighbour.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Big developing economies are slowing down and showing signs of distress or are undergoing corrections.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These are really strong ill winds that will have severe repercussions on us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The challenges we face now are not unlike those in 1965.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But we were blessed with strong leaders and a united people who rallied behind their Government.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They were men and women made of steel.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They knew the special characteristics of Singaporeans; penchant for hard work; willingness to cast aside communal and religious divides for the common good; thirst for education and skills; unity to succeed and, above all, resilience in their hearts.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Fifty years of hard work has earned us strong reserves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We have good infrastructure and a modern city.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Naysayers argue that as we grew more affluent as a people, we are no longer as hungry.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They say that we no longer possess that fighting spirit and the desire to succeed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The people I see around me are just as hungry.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Singaporeans in sports and the arts are being groomed to take on and grow with the best around the world.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our goals in life may be different now but I do not think there is less desire to succeed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is true though that the dreams and aspirations of Singaporeans have changed.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is no longer only about three square meals on the table, a roof over the head and good sanitation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They want to be included in discussions and be consulted.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Views are becoming increasingly more diverse as our social fabric becomes more complex.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They have access to the world and, sometimes, want it all.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is to be expected as we grow as a country and as a society.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We are after all, a First World country now.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I spoke on this at the President's Address in 2014.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is what we do and how we adapt that matters, but we must never allow ourselves to lapse into complacency that has befallen other successful First World countries.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Never fall for the seductive nectar of basking in a "Good Life" without hard work and constant striving to improve.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But Mdm Speaker, I look around at my colleagues in this House and Singaporeans at large, and I feel confident of our country's future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I said earlier that, as a country, we have some strong characteristics.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The one that is not commonly applauded is "resilience".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A resilience running through the Government and the people as one.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Page: 13 I believe, Mdm Speaker, that this is what makes us special.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: During tough times, our people rolled up their sleeves, sweat and put their shoulders together with the Government to grind it out and make it work.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We do it on the basis that we will never allow anyone to trod on us or take us for granted simply because of our size.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We need to maintain this core fibre of resilience that made Singapore so successful for the past 50 years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The single-minded desire running through the Government and our people as one to make our little red dot a safe and successful harbour and home for each and every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A place to live and grow old in and see our children grow up and live on.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If we lose this desire, we are but a tray of loose sand and will achieve nothing and most certainly regress from what our forefathers have built for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But, Mdm Speaker, the Government cannot do this on its own.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Former United States President John F Kennedy famously asked of his fellow Americans at his inauguration, "Ask not what your country can do for you – ask what you can do for your country".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We are a different people and these are different times.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Government and people are a partnership and the glue is trust.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Singaporeans need to accept that new times will bring new challenges.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It was not plain sailing for the past 50 years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It will not be plain sailing for the next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There will be times when the very foundations of our country will be severely tested.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The Chinese characters for the word "Country" is 国家. 所谓，先有国才有家.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It means, not literally, that for family units to exist, there must first be a stable country.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, to all Singaporeans, I urge you to back the Government fully.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Our country did not arrive at what it is in 2016 by accident.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It was only through the sheer hard work and commitment of the Government and the people, with and to each other.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We must build on it, people and Government, hand in hand together, in order to ensure that our future generations can enjoy the same fruits that we now enjoy.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: On the other hand, the Government needs to reciprocate and do its utmost to maintain this trust.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: To continue to build and re-build its relationship with the people, as we embark on a journey that is likely to be fraught with difficulties and many unknown challenges.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But more, importantly, not only to concentrate on winning the trust of the people, but also to trust the people.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Trust that the people will fully support the Government even when things are imperfect or when times are difficult.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Page: 14 At the same time, we must put out our hands to the people to travel with us together, as without them, we are nothing and will likely become another footnote in the history books.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore is at a pivotal point in our history.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Over the past year, we reflected on our journey as a nation and celebrated how far we have come along by overcoming the odds.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have also started an important conversation about the next 50 years – will Singapore be around in 50 years, and if so, what will SG100 look like?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An important question was raised by our President, Dr Tony Tan in his Opening Address in Parliament – how do we ensure that our island nation remains a shining Red Dot so that our children and grandchildren will thrive?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The last 50 years have seen Singapore going through a phenomenal transformation which was achieved through the collective efforts of our Pioneer Generation, the Baby Boomers and Generation X.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The next 50 years will be shaped and led by our Gen Y, otherwise known as the "Millennials", who are born between the years 1981 and 2000; and the Gen Z – those born from the year 2000 onwards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of them are at the beginning of their careers, or may be in their second jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Amidst a restructuring and renewing economy, I believe that we are at the inflexion point in our nation's development where we must put in place structures that best allow our Millennials and young Singaporean workers to succeed and shape our nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the Fourth Industrial Revolution, talent, rather than capital, will be the critical factor of production.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is vital to Singapore that we prepare them for this future economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is why I will be focusing on how we can best help our Millennials and young workers to succeed at work, at home and in society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, first, we have to seek to understand the Millennials and young workers and what are their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am not young enough to be a Millennial, yet not too old to be too far from being one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, I spoke to quite a few Millennials and young workers to find out about their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Their answers surprised me because despite the generational differences, they want what many of us in other generations desire: financial and career growth, opportunities for growth and learning, and to be successful, not just at work, but also with their family and socially.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some of them have not thought about jobs or what career paths they would like to pursue.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I do worry for this group of Millennials and young workers because while new opportunities abound, Singapore also faces uncertainty in the economic and geopolitical spaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Preparing early and being ready to adapt quickly to new workplace requirements is more important than ever.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At this point, I must also caution against generalisations about specific generations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Generational differences are often accentuated by experiences and priorities at different life stages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, whether they are generational or life-stage traits at this point, I think, there are several observations that might prove to be useful insights for us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Page: 15 First, young workers aspire to be successful across different facets of their lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We often hear that the younger workers are only concerned about work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But I believe what many meant is, "Not only is career success important, but so are social and family successes." They want latitude in managing their time to explore personal growth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is especially so when they are true digital natives who are comfortable producing work anywhere, not just in the office.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, young workers believe in chasing growth and learning curves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is not uncommon to hear employers lament that young workers just do not stay long enough in their job to learn sufficiently.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: My dialogues with many of the young workers reveal that some left their jobs because they felt that they are not learning much anymore, or when their career paths are not clear, or when they cannot identify with the work of their companies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Third, they learn best when there is a combination of good communications, hands-on work and mentorship.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Technology has allowed them to learn more and better through connecting with people, rather than just mere consumption of information.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The older Millennials have also proven to be resilient as they experienced tough times entering the workforce during the recession due to the 2008 Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If we harness the strengths of our young workers and are willing to look for ways to support them, they can take us boldly and purposefully into SG100.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The challenge is, how do we then continue to provide such opportunities for subsequent generations?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Disruptive innovation has fundamentally changed many industries and the way we work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This has become a "VUCA" world – volatile, uncertain, complex and unpredictable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And to do so, they must learn and apply continuously.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They must learn to integrate information across domains into usable knowledge to be applied at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In a VUCA world, competencies such as lifelong learning and learning agility are key.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The question is: knowing the aspirations and inclinations of our Millennials and young workers, how can we better prepare them to be future ready?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our youths and young workers should be empowered with information to make more informed learning and career choices, but we must pair it with mentors from the working world to cater to the learning preferences of the young people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are important initiatives that can help our youths to chart their learning and career journeys.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must ensure that they are well-synced to avoid duplication and enhance their awareness and usage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Page: 16 Importantly, to scale and enhance the efficacy of such schemes, mentors, both formal and informal, where students can reach out to easily, are critical.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: After all, people connect best to people and not just to technology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Importantly, mentors can share what the real world requirements and conditions are.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have new non-profits, such as The Apprenticeship Collective in Singapore and MENTOR in the United States, seeking to crowd source mentors for the diverse needs of our youths and young workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are many more Singaporeans who are willing to step forward to help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can tap upon the inventiveness and dynamism of the corporate volunteers to better prepare our students for the fast evolving workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I would also encourage the Government agencies to work closely with the Labour Movement's Unions and U Associates for access to networks and mentorship.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can allow for faster scaling, leveraging on existing resources.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For instance, NTUC has the Young Engineers Leadership Programme where young engineers can attend talks and network with senior professionals in their fields.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Young NTUC holds its CrossRoads programmes to link students and young working adults to industry captains.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To prepare our youths and young workers, we must also ensure a tight nexus between learning and job requirements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must ensure that this is not merely a paper chase but we add real value to their professional development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I came across young working adults who found that their private degrees did not significantly improve career and job prospects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many employers have also found new entrants from schools under-prepared for the workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This nexus is also tightened when learning is current.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This then requires the deeper involvement of the private sector in shaping curriculum.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In a casual conversation that I had with Dr Robert Yap, President of SNEF, one comment struck me.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Employers are key to helping our young workers to be future-ready.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An employer that can best tap on the strengths of our Millennials would need to, one, constantly scan the business environment to calibrate and develop skill requirements and career ladders; and two, adopt progressive workplace practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our young workers aspire to chase growth and learning curves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Employers can help to keep Millennials relevant and help them to grow through market-calibrated and well-defined skills and career ladders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many companies, especially the SMEs find it difficult to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I encourage Government to consider further measures to help these SMEs, especially in enhancing their HR capabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are many established workplace practices but we shall examine two that best cater to the work inclinations and aspirations of our young people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, employers can better help young workers achieve work-life balance and pursue success in different domains by, one, adopting outcome-based mindsets; and two, allowing for flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Trusting them to manage their targets while mentoring them provides for a nurturing work environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: More can be done to allow employees to do telecommuting, have flexible work schedules or staggered working hours.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Diversity of work arrangements can play to the strengths of our young workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Page: 17 We have established earlier that our young Millennials want to succeed not only in their careers but also in raising families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The question is how we can better support them to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One immediate group of workers who can benefit further from a more progressive attitude towards work is new mothers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Often, new mothers who have to return to full-time work after 16 weeks of maternity leave, feel anxious and have difficulties adjusting back to work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Anxiety from being apart from her child and establishing a new work and family routine requires transition time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are indeed many different ways, avenues and facets to helping our Millennials and young workers to be future-ready – more than what my speech today can do to do justice to the topic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On this note, Mdm Speaker, I support the Motion of Thanks to the President.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: I will cover two main topics in my speech today.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: First, true security requires external and internal borders.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This is achieved through the unity of hearts, minds and wills.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Second, a prosperous, harmonious society must ensure social mobility.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: From our early days, we got our fundamentals right.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The late President Yusof Ishak said in his speech in 1965 at the Opening of the First Parliament of sovereign Singapore: "An industrious and talented people striving to secure their future will surge forward to prosperity and strength if they are given honest administration and effective leadership".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Here we are 51 years later, an industrious and talented people united behind a Government with the people, for the people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We have exciting plans for the future, charting our course for the next five years and laying foundations for SG100.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Our plans for the future require stability and good economic growth.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We are facing the future from a position of strength – with a strong military and Home Team, a dynamic economy and cohesive people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: But for all our progress in the last 50 years, many daunting challenges remain.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We remain a small state with a multiracial and religious people in a turbulent world.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Our stability is the result of our unity amidst our diversity of racial and religious backgrounds.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: It is a continuing and necessary work-in-progress, a responsibility we all share.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: I was happy to hear in President Tony Tan's Address a call for us to stay strong and united especially when others seek to sow fear and create division.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Divisive forces that threaten Singapore are not new.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: In 1965, President Yusof Ishak spoke about a potent, disruptive group – the Communists who played on communal heart strings.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Today, we face another potent, disruptive group – extremists and terrorists motivated by religious extremism.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: They seek to spread their twisted ideologies and ferment chaos by exploiting our diversity, and sow fear and discord.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Internally, we have to strengthen our mental and emotional borders to ensure they are impenetrable to invidious elements.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The key entry points that can tear our social fabric are our hearts and minds.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: If we learned anything from how we fought the communists in the 1960s, it is that legislation, policies and weapons alone are not enough.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We have to involve the community; we have to win hearts and minds; we have to stand as one united people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: In 11 September 2001, I was in New York as an exchange student at Columbia University.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: That fateful day, I remember the devastating terrorist attack on The World Trade Center.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: I remember the horror and shock everyone felt, standing on the streets.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: But more than that, I remember the amazing generosity and rich spirit of Americans who came together to comfort one another.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Americans who stood shoulder-to-shoulder on the streets to cheer the first responders and the tribute sites which sprang all over America.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: I also remember the sense of fear, people running out of subways and buildings due to false alarms, people exacting revenge on Muslim Americans and those who resemble Muslims, in particular the Sikhs who wear turbans, and vandalism of Muslim-owned shops.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Even with our best efforts, there is no guarantee that they will never succeed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We have to get it right every single time, all the time.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: While the terrorists only have to get through once, at any time.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Our security agencies will step up their readiness and responses to prevent, deter and deal with an attack.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We will work closely with private and public building owners to strengthen the protection of our hard and soft targets.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: But, at the very heart of it, is the community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We have to involve every single one of us, our people, in our efforts to better protect ourselves from a terrorist attack and its aftermath.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Should the unthinkable happen and a terrorist attack happens, we have to make absolutely sure that the terrorists' agenda to create chaos and sow discord does not prevail.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Brick and mortar Page: 19 can be repaired and rebuilt easily.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Fractures in our community cannot be fixed so readily.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The bleak, dark message of extremists contrasts markedly with a vision of our Singapore, a sunny island by the sea, a land of opportunity, a beacon of hope, a magnet for promise and a caring, compassionate society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: But so can success, if the fruits of success are not equally accessible to all.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Where we start in life does not dictate where we will end up.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: It is our task to ensure that our society provides opportunities for upward mobility.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Our people must know that the stars they strive for are within reach.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: And if they need a little boost to help cover that extra bit of distance, there is help given.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Rich or poor, strong or weak, academically inclined or not, no one gets left behind.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: An African proverb says, "If you want to go fast, go alone.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: If you want to go far, go together." This is not a sprint.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This is a marathon, and we are in it for the long haul, together, as one united Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We saw how Singaporeans came together this past year in happiness and in sorrow.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We mourned for our late Mr Lee Kuan Yew and celebrated our nation's success at SG50 celebrations, SEA Games and ASEAN Para Games.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Crisis after crisis, generations of Singaporeans stood as one people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We built this country together, we will keep it thriving together and we will continue standing as one people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: (In Malay):   Recently, I met students from the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) and the Singapore Polytechnic for a discussion.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: I am proud of their maturity and confidence in expressing their views on many issues – from housing, employment to national security.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The courses that they are studying are interesting – for instance, infrastructural engineering, information technology and communications, aerospace systems, electronic games design and chemical engineering.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Our community's future is bright with such a wide range of educational opportunities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: He received the Outstanding Student Award from 4PM.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Fahmy initially did not do well in school, but he turned over a new leaf while doing National Service and, after National Service, Fahmy resumed his studies in the ITE.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Initially, Fahmy told me that he felt awkward because many of his ITE schoolmates were younger than him.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: But Fahmy's determination and resolve to study was strong.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: He is now studying Marine Engineering at Singapore Polytechnic.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Another example from our community is Captain Muhammad Azhar Said, 37 years old.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: He is an officer from the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF).

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: He was named as the best cadet at the commander's course.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Fahmy and Azhar's road to success showed their resolve, determination and desire for lifelong learning and continuous upgrading.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This is the indomitable spirit of our young Malays.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We are now hearing more and more about young Malays achieving excellent results, from PSLE, up to degrees and PhDs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This fighting spirit is not only evident in the academic field, but also in sports and the arts.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: These excellent results proved that we can stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the rest.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Our young talents are not only shining brightly in Singapore, but in other countries too.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Sufie Rashid was crowned champion of Akademi Fantasia in Malaysia.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: During the finals, he had fever with a temperature of 39 degree Celsius.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Nonetheless, Sufie managed to give a sizzling hot performance.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This is a good example of our young Malays who are confident, able to compete on the international stage and brought honour to our community and nation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: In sports, I still remember Nur Alfian who won gold in the silat event at the SEA Games.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Although his foot was injured, he never gave up and soldiered on.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The sight of him in tears while the National Anthem was playing was touching.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The determination to work hard and the Singapore spirit is alive and well in our community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Yes, we are sons and daughters of Singapore!

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This success comes from our hard work and the community's strong support for Government policies that provide opportunities and ensure security, prosperity, harmony and progress for the nation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Our community's solidarity cannot be taken for granted.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We are able to perform our obligations as Muslims peacefully without any interference from anyone.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This is in contrast to certain countries where members of the Muslim population were harassed by neighbours or colleagues, just because they are Muslims.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This situation is worsened by the ideologies of terrorists who mis-use the holy name of Islam to create havoc in their countries.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We must protect our country from such a situation by having a moderate stance, in line with a multi-racial and multi-religious Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We must help to spread the message of compassion, peace, and respect for one another, regardless of religion or race.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: There are still many challenges facing our community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We can overcome these problems and challenges together.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Every member of the community, working hand in hand with the Government.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: But as they say, Malays never fear from facing challenges head on.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Today's battlefield is in the economic arena, in educational institutes, in sporting arenas and in the artistic stage.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The competition is fierce, but we are not easily cowered.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Today, we are equipped with better education and better skills so that we can address future challenges wisely and stoically.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Page: 21 Our Malay community is well known for our polite demeanour, our elegant language and our immense fighting spirit.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This generation will ensure that our community will stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the other communities in Singapore and in the world.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: With one voice, the Malay community will be united, with a noble and new spirit, together we proclaim – Majulah Singapura!

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, Singapore is never resting on its laurels.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: A people moving ahead with determination to claim our place in history, to build a truly remarkable Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: President Tony Tan's Address echoes a familiar call – a call to action for Singaporeans to unite and renew our hopes for a brighter Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This is a call familiar to generations of Singaporeans across time.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: From the Samsui women and the dock-side coolies who toiled under the sun, to our tireless Pioneers who built this nation; from our children in schools and madrasahs; our men and women defending our nation; to leaders, the likes of Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Generation after generation, year after year, there was never a doubt – "Singapore will survive".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we deliberate our next 50 years together, I think it worthwhile if we think about who we are as a people, the values that define us and what we want in our society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From the time we struggled to make ends meet, to now where we have an opportunity to shape the future Singapore for our children, where we can be aspirational, to become a great nation and a great people.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Straits Times is running a nomination for the Singaporean of the Year.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She said, "I will always make time for them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can I not?" The Singapore Story has often been told in terms of an economic success.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But it is also a story of human spirit.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After 50 years, through our repeated choices of what we want and what we reject, we have distilled and created something – the spirit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The broad social mobility, social cohesion and racial harmony that we enjoy now are a function of the generosity Page: 22 that we show each other.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We curbed our individual tribal instincts so as to grow a greater common area and we balanced the needs of everyone in our society because we celebrate our success together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the first 50 years, we created more by sharing what little we had.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In our next 50 years together, we will have to nurture and grow this generosity of spirit, for it will allow us to go beyond ourselves, beyond current possibilities, beyond our shores, and set us on the path to becoming a great nation and a great people.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the President's words, "Ours should be... a society consisting of generous hearts who treat one another with warmth and dignity".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, as our needs, interests and perspectives become more diverse, how do we go beyond ourselves and beyond narrow self-interest?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Einstein once said, "A man starts to live when he can live outside himself".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We see issues through the lenses of our own backgrounds and experiences.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When there are differences, can we look beyond our own perspectives and find the generosity to love and accept another human being, to go pass all that divides us and believe in a common humanity and a shared destiny as Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the example of Mdm Noriza has shown us, we can.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She helped a stranger, not of the same race, not of the same religion, someone who is elderly and vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Her personal act of generosity shows us how as individuals we can epitomise our values of social and racial harmony.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should also exercise generosity in our worldviews and the way we see each other.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As our young aspire to take different routes to success, can we stand by their choices and not let our pre-conceived biases tie them down?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we as a society be less judgmental when others take a less well-trodden route to success?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And as representatives of the people, while we fight for the interests of our constituents, can we strive to promote an uplifting politics of constructive criticism and discourage the politics of division?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the President highlighted, "Our system discourages narrow interest-based politics".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Generosity does not mean that we are indiscriminate about what we accept.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, as we are undergoing economic transformation, how do we go beyond current possibilities?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The new economy brings challenges in terms of new technologies, new skills to master and new ways of working.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Often times, we know what we must do, but our human psychology trips us up.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, where a new technology emerges, are industry incumbents generous enough to embrace it knowing it may displace legacy assets?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Or where there is a need for us to relearn skills or work with others in an interdisciplinary way, are we able to put our egos aside to form new collaborations and break new ground?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We will need a generosity of spirit to embrace the changes which will lead to long-term benefits for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We welcome people with ideas and energy who share our values and aspirations and want to help make Singapore a success.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have always been an international hub, since our days as a free trade harbour.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we continue to keep that openness and generosity Page: 23 of spirit so that Singapore can continue to achieve success as a hub for people; and ideas and help to power and shape the region and the world?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore, as we have created it, is a function of our thinking.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We cannot change it without first changing our thinking.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To go beyond what we have now, requires us to find the generosity within us to accommodate differences, accept changes, care for our community and become a hub for people, activities and ideas.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, how do we strengthen this generosity of spirit?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: People to people, people to Government, people to social organisations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to first communicate to understand each other's perspective and then only can we resolve to respect differences and be generous in accommodating each other.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, the way we bring up our children is important.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we teach them to be self-centred, to be close-minded, or do we encourage them to be considerate, to be team players, to try varied experiences, to explore and to be curious.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our media can also contribute to a positive culture by showcasing admirable qualities in the human condition and promoting the generosity inherent in our national psyche.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to set in motion a virtuous cycle of imbuing generosity into our lives.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But just like the late Minister Mentor Lee once said in 1965, "10 years from now, this will be a metropolis – never fear!" We believed, we aspired and we achieved.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the next 50 years, let us aspire to greatness.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And that starts with each and every one of us.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are made a kinder and a greater people for it.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would now like to say a few words in Chinese.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   Looking back at the 50 years of nation-building of Singapore, perhaps, the most outstanding feature is our economic success.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, what has guided us in our action and led to our success, is the spirit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Singapore Spirit is not based on a single race, language or religion, instead, it encompasses the spirit of every Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is based on something that we can all identify with, that lies deeper within, and that is – the spirit of inclusiveness and humanity.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Inclusiveness and humanity are part and parcel of Singapore's development as a fair and harmonious society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Inclusiveness and humanity is crucial as Singaporeans stand united to weather difficult times together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Inclusiveness and humanity are also intrinsically linked to Singapore's role as a bridge to the world.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is the spirit that uplifts the individual and it is also the spirit that makes a nation great.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For Singapore to progress from prosperity to greatness, not only do we need material wealth, but also great spiritual strength.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: First and foremost, this requires understanding and tolerance between people.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In our pursuit of personal happiness, we must also be tolerant and care for others, especially those who need help.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As Singapore becomes an ageing society, we need to establish, more than ever, a society that respects the elderly and care for the young, where people care for each other and is full of human kindness.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Likewise, to develop the new economy and utilise new technologies also require an open mind and an inclusive attitude.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: New models may disrupt old business chains and impact traditional trades.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can our Government, businesses and individuals accept new technologies and new models that will bring long-term benefits with an open mind and inclusive attitude, while taking care of each individual's interests?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During my Secondary school years, I attended CHIJ St Nicholas Girls' School.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That was a period of my life where I received the most warmth and was most confident.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Two weeks ago, when I met my principal Mrs Lee Poh See again after many years, I finally realised why I felt so.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On that day, there was an alumnae event where we gathered to watch a documentary about xinyao (新谣).

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was directed by alumna Eva Tang (Deng Bao Cui).

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After the documentary screening ended, we took a photograph together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mrs Lee led us to shout, "Bao Cui, we will always support you!" Mrs Lee is already more than 70 years old and her legs are not working well, but still, she raised her arms and hugged all of us.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And once again, we felt the same warmth that we experienced back in our Secondary school years.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I remember back then, the school organised many extra-curricular activities, every student had a chance to shine in her own field.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It did not matter if your results were good or not, Mrs Lee had encouragement for every student.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Now, I finally understood that good education has to be inclusive, and requires love and the ability to embrace the individuality of every student, to unearth their potential and to enable them to progress to the next stage of life with confidence. "The ocean can hold water from thousands of rivers, it is great because it embraces all." Our success depends on how big-hearted we are.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Previously, we came from different backgrounds, speaking different languages and had different beliefs.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On this island that was almost overlooked, we overcame difficulties and created a miracle, all because we respected and embraced one another, all because we respected and embraced the world. "Be strict with oneself, but forgiving towards others".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In an unpredictable and ever-changing world, Singapore, the little red dot, shall forever be a shining light for humanity in the history of mankind.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Twenty-fifteen also saw the passing of our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Mr Lee is widely regarded as an exceptional man, but to be an exceptional nation takes more than an exceptional leader.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Any organisation that cannot sustain its performance after the departure of a particular CEO, cannot call itself a great organisation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The current economic climate seems dire, with analysts predicting that it would deteriorate further and hoping it would not be as bad as the post-Lehman period of 2008.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The region's stock markets continue to dive, including the STI.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: China's growth has slowed down, affecting many countries, especially Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Worldwide, jobs are being cut, with Singapore as no exception.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is weak demand for office space, with vacancy rates here expected to be in the double digits this year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Amidst this climate, what does it take to be an exceptional nation?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government has laid out its Addenda to the President's Address, setting out in broad strokes some of its plans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We need to debate them in the coming days.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For my speech today, I would like to focus on the role of the people of Singapore in building an exceptional nation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of course, this aggregated figure at the national level is no measure of wealth distribution amongst citizens and no indication of inequalities that exist.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have spoken in the past about the inadequacies of GDP as a measure of the people's well-being and I believe that is clearly accepted in many developed countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Neither is a high GDP per capita a measure of how committed a population is to the country.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my past teaching career and travels, I have encountered people from countries far less wealthy than ours, countries whose GDP per capita is about US$1,000 or less.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What strikes me is that even though the international community may laugh at them or even use their countries as negative case studies, the people have a strong commitment and passion to their home.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When natural disaster strikes, the people use their own resources and energy to help each other, knowing that they have to take the initiative.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Should there be a border incursion by a neighbouring country, the people are up in arms and willing to fight with whatever outdated weapons and ammunition they have to ensure that not one inch of their soil is given up.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To me, these are exceptional displays of love of country, of passion for their country that money cannot buy.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Fundamentally, these citizens strongly believe in their ability to make a difference and that it is up to them to make their country stronger.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: About 20 years ago, in a speech to the Singapore Press Club, Mr Lee Kuan Yew expressed sadness that a young Singaporean had considered emigration because she could not fulfil her dream of owning a house and a car. "Man does not live by bread alone," he said, quoting that famous biblical phrase.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He recalled that when he first set out as a young man, he had a Singapore dream, a dream that Singapore would be a democratic society, keen and vibrant, a united people.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Its people should have dreams for the country, a vision of what the country should be and the gumption to go out and realise that vision.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We must believe that they are the ones who can move the country higher and be unafraid to take Page: 26 risks even if they should fail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: An exceptional nation should have a people whose DNA is being unafraid to fail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What then can be done to unleash Singaporeans' potential to dream and be agents of change?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To foster a climate that supports dreaming big would require a thorough examination of Singapore's life cycle: how children are brought up, what role models society celebrates, safety nets for failure and the extent of citizen empowerment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, I would like to touch on just two areas that I believe are worth looking into: one, aspects of our education system; and two, scaling back Government in non-core government functions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over the years, our education system has been a social leveller and a key to social mobility.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is important for us to ensure that students from poorer backgrounds continue to have equal access to education opportunities in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government has stated that it is making efforts to ensure that our students' experience is holistic.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Parents will have to pressure children to achieve academic scores over and above all else.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Students will be hard pressed to spend more time to pursue other interests against society's pressures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To ensure the message is not diluted, such an approach should not be just in one or two subjects, but be a pervasive and consistent theme throughout our education and assessment system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Granted – each subject is different and what is possible would vary from subject to subject.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is the surest way to discourage creative thinking.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
