text: As dreams also carry the risk of failure, students should also learn that some things may be worth doing even if one fails.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The school syllabus should highlight case studies of persons who failed to achieve what they set out to do, to appreciate why certain endeavours are important even if the outcome is uncertain.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If we believe we need a different mould of Singaporeans to face the future, compared to the past, our education system must support these goals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, scaling back Government in non-core government functions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our Civil Service has known no other governing party.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over these five decades, the governing party has established strong connections within the public sector and outside.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government's presence is Page: 27 felt in practically every aspect of life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, even the Government understands that there must be stabilisers and checks and balances in the system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is not sufficient to talk about letting alternative views be articulated and taken into consideration.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans must feel that they can make a difference.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In other words, all citizens should be free to have a vision for Singapore and to be a mover to achieve that vision.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To truly empower citizens, there must be real power centres outside the Government – in local enterprises, in the private sector, in civil society, in the people sector – so as to effectively check and work with the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Lately, the Government has been using the phrase "collaborative governance", referring to a collaboration between the public sector and the private and people sectors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For true collaboration, no partner should be dominant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government needs to let go and devolve more power first, so that there is real and meaningful collaborative partnership among equals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans should be given more voice and more say in the running of their lives and society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For a start, a lot of Government nominees are on the boards of professional bodies and sports groups.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While in the past, we could get far while being technically competent and hardworking, today's ever-changing world requires a people who are visionary, adaptable, resilient and empowered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is our home and Singaporeans must take ownership of it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Empowered Singaporeans will not blame others when the going gets tough but will face difficulties squarely, with an unwavering faith that they can be overcome.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We need Singaporeans who will stick by Singapore through thick and thin because that is what an exceptional nation is all about.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have heard questions of exceptionalism, of the exceptional.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And the exceptional is also about imagining what exceptional challenges lie before us and how we may meet them, no matter what form they come in.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Science fiction writer Iain M Banks described what he called an "Outside Context Problem", where a society encounters an existential challenge which it did not foresee.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we must always be ready as one people to confront the unexpected.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because only by imagining the unthinkable, can we be ready to survive whatever the future may bring.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: History has shown that perfect storms and black swans are not that rare.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If I may, let me highlight four areas where exceptional circumstances might happen and then look at how we may survive together these challenges.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Page: 28 Four areas: international relations; the global economy; our social fabric; our politics.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Four areas where a few or all of these factors could come together as a perfect storm.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: An established superpower, with another great power rising: building its own blue water fleet; land-based and maritime Silk Roads; an additional set of institutions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And today, globalisation connects countries, economies and people.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, there can be a healthy accommodation between these powers that will benefit the world and Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Of course, there may yet be a miscalculation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A junior officer may set off a skirmish: sink a boat, or shoot down a plane.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is unlikely, but we must be prepared in case the exceptional occurs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Non-state actors are a very real challenge, Mdm Speaker.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: ISIS, as fellow Members of this House have pointed out, can poison a young mind from thousands of miles away.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens if they establish a wilayat, a province of their Caliphate in Southeast Asia?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our ASEAN neighbours are doing more to tackle terrorism, but the problem has been growing for some time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We see the challenges in Jakarta, recent arrests in Kuala Lumpur and the arrest of the radicalised Bangladeshi migrant workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have to do all we can to prevent an attack on Singapore soil.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But it is possible that such an attack might happen, and in the event it happens, we must be resilient and make sure that it does not break our society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The global economy, Mdm Speaker, is another situation where the exceptional may occur – the exceptionally challenging.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If it slows more sharply, it would affect our tourism, our SMEs, our exports.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The US recovery, some green shoots, but it may yet run out of steam.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And both great economies have limited short-term policy options for stimulus.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At home, big challenges for us as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If we do not restructure fast enough, we could be in a trap of a high-cost environment, but not creating high enough value to compete with the top tier of global cities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have to beware of stagnation and inflation at the same time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What other exceptional challenges might we face in our society?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have pledged ourselves as one united people.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But the Pioneers who were present at the creation, who lived through our first foundation, that first forging of our Singapore identity – they are growing old, dwindling in number, fading into history.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, each generation must pledge itself anew and re-forge that unity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Independent schools charging more, which can discourage students who are afraid that they might not qualify for a full fee scholarship.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Belief systems and values from faraway lands, very different to Singapore, coming to our island.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Foreigners and locals, old Singaporeans, new Singaporeans – as some choose to call it.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I will not pollute this House by naming specific websites or their supporters, but we know who they are.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We know which websites they are and can guess much money they make from advertising, while trying to teach Singaporeans how to hate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And the risk, Mdm Speaker, is exceptional when multiple fault lines come together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our local politics, Mdm Speaker, could turn divisive.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens if a campaign is waged with negative, destructive emotions?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It could be a General Election, a Presidential Election.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The politics of protest, of tearing down – we have seen what it can do in the traditional mature democracies.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Gridlock in some of the major democracies in the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Anti-immigrant UKIP in the UK, Syriza in Greece, AfD (Alternative fÃ¼r Deutschland) in Germany, a far right party.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And such parties need not do exceptionally well to win, Mdm Speaker.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And then having to face a major crisis – a terrorist attack on Singapore soil, a pandemic, or a regional conflict where old friends ask us to choose between them.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, how do we get Singapore ready to survive an exceptional Perfect Storm?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If I may suggest, not even the PAP.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: No matter how many seats we have in Parliament, no matter how strong our mandate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In this, we all have a role to play: Government, politics, citizens.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I do not think the answer is less Government involvement.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I do not think the answer is politicians' stepping back.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I do not believe the answer lies in citizens becoming disengaged, disillusioned and disenchanted by rhetoric that is negative and destructive.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Government, Politics, Citizens – there is all a role in building this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But it is cohesion that keeps a family at home at the dinner table, talking to each other, having a shared sense of purpose.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And Government has a role here, shaping social norms, shaping values.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A school system that brings students together from different backgrounds.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Housing estates bringing residents together: shared spaces, hawker centres, green gardens, even void decks, they Page: 30 make a difference.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The tone of our politics and our culture, bringing people together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The marketplace of ideas can be a powerful, positive, progressive force: the wisdom of crowds, the energy of the new, working together with experts and expertise.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But as we have seen elsewhere, there can be market failure in the marketplace of ideas.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We would not accept laissez-faire economics in this decade.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The lessons of the past 20 years have suggested otherwise.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I do not believe in laissez-faire politics either.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Open politics, so you know where the other person is coming from, what they stand for, their views on major issues of the day.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not just the easy issues, but the challenging issues.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Where you need not be a millionaire or have the right friends to step into the ring.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: People having the courage of convictions, standing up for what they believe in, but at the end of the day, always remembering that we are Singaporean brothers and sisters with a shared future.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The poison of money politics, where political parties feel they have to reward their supporters with kickbacks, favours and contracts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The poison of anger, envy and hate – where politicians encourage voters to destroy what has been built over decades and generations, tearing down institutions, tearing down ideas, without a vision for what comes the day after.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Telling people to vote for something, without saying how they will get you there.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The risks and benefits, the side effects, the journey.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But above all, Mdm Speaker, we, the citizens of Singapore, have a responsibility.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must keep on building a sense of fellowship.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Understanding our brothers and sisters, our different faiths, our different cultures.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Through seeing the people next to us, seeing through their eyes, seeing how they see us, we learn to see better, to understand, to grow together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Every individual's actions can make that difference, make our society stronger.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Whether it is giving up a seat on the MRT train to someone who needs it more, or giving your time and energy to help fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Page: 31 In Clementi, where I serve, we have a voluntary welfare organisation (VWO) – Bringing Love to Every Single Soul.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Young Singaporeans reading together with children, children of all races from our rental flats.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Young Singaporeans, helping children who start with less.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Its founder, Ms Francesca Wah, is a Primary school teacher – a very busy job, but she makes time to give back from the heart.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In Jurong, we have the Fei Yue Early Intervention Programme for Infants and Children (EIPIC) with special needs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Fei Yue had three students with many illnesses and difficulties with mobility.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The fundraising lead was Mr Lim Der Shing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He is a successful entrepreneur, the founder of JobsCentral.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He has done well, yet Der Shing uses his skills, networks and resources to help the community.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That spirit of an activist community of volunteerism, people stepping forward, is very much alive.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And Government and politicians partnering with that can make it even stronger.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we must always be a fair and just society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Regardless of your background, where you start in life, or how much you start with.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Yesterday's Pioneers, today's Singaporeans, tomorrow's children, who will inherit the risks and rewards of what we decide today.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And that culture of responsibility, those values of fairness, equitability, social cohesion – they are the ultimate safeguard to ensure good politics as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: By becoming a stronger, more resilient, more cohesive Greater Society, we will be ready to see SG100 – as One United People.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a new Member of the House, I seek your guidance as I embark on my journey as a parliamentarian.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SG51 to SG100 will, however, be very different in terms of our external circumstances, in terms of our domestic situation, in terms of the outlook of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, the eyes of our people are upon us, the Government.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are jointly committed to the next phase of nation building.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some principles – integrity, meritocracy, open to the world – we must steadfastly hold on to them, while other things must evolve to suit new circumstances.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, I would like to talk about three aspects that we may have to evolve.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I choose the word "may", because the process will never be straightforward, certainly not sudden, and always a gradual, progressive evolution, fraught with tensions even at times.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But this process of evolution is absolutely necessary because no city stays successful by standing still.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Page: 32 Animals – they develop sharper claws, harder shells, longer beaks in order to survive.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The three aspects of evolution that I would like to talk about today are: faster legs, stronger hearts and wiser minds.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, faster legs, which means how we make a living.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The global economic system was then emerging from the old world of colonialism, where country-to-country relationships were hierarchical and benefits unbalanced.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was changing to a new global order based on market forces.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our economy strategy of attracting FDI was conceived in this era of receding colonialism.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the next 50 years will be different.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: US, Europe and Japan will continue to be major players and important investors in Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we are also in the midst of the making of an Asian century.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: China is a major part of that equation.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We need to look at China's trajectory beyond the current stock market sell down, beyond the current pessimistic talk about hard and soft landing.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: China's economic transformation has moved on from growth to addressing the quality of growth.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Low value-added activities are no longer the China Dream, 中国梦.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The major change is that the Chinese economy will be more discerning in allocating capital to more productive uses, it will move up the value added ladder and with greater discipline in allocating capital to production capacity, consumption accounts for a higher proportion of China's growth and investments today.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Consumption is not just of goods, but also of services.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why services are generating more jobs than manufacturing in China today.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With that, ASEAN no longer serves as the major component supplier for China.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: China now produces those components, assembles them into final products and ships them globally, including to ASEAN.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because of that, our trade surplus in ASEAN that we used to experience in the early 2000s, has now flipped into a deficit now.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: India may also feature prominently in our economic fate.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is the fastest growing developing country in Asia.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Outside of Asia, Africa's demographic momentum will be of tremendous global impact.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Africa will be a major part of the global equation on growth as well as climate change and even international migration.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: FDI has many more places to go to.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We cannot look at the value chain of China and try to fit ourselves in, as we did when we outsourced more labour intensive activities to China.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must now look at China as a tremendous business and consumer space that we can tap into.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many Asian economies are facing headwinds, not because there is slower growth in China but that a new division of labour is emerging in the world, in Asia, and every country and every economy is finding its footing in this new configuration.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Page: 33 For Singapore, I think we must know the markets around us intimately – traditions, customs, taste, language, habits, psychology.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We used to encourage Singaporeans to anchor in Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With a stronger anchor now planted, it is now necessary to seek our fortunes out in the region.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: President Tony Tan has warned that, "We cannot expect an easy journey ahead".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is why Institutes of Higher Education are encouraging overseas internships for their students.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must be able to understand, bridge and operate across different cultures.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must have depth in our know-how, in our skills, so that wherever we go, our expertise is valued and can be put to good use.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Most of all, as Mr Christopher de Souza said, we must always be grounded in values, character and ethics.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This refers to our resolve to define Singapore and our national identity.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the beginning, Singapore was regarded as special because we resolved to move ahead together.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fifty years later, one of the greatest achievements arising from that resolve is to have built a national self-consciousness, an emerging, unique Singapore identity, from a diverse immigrant society with hardly any common ground to stand on.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But this is a process that will take further decades and centuries.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we look around us, China and India – they are civilisations.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That will be our moment for the next 50 years.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But our identity is not merely derived by a legal fiat that pronounces that everyone is "Singaporean".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is richness in the identity, drawn from our diversity, ancestry and cultural origins.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is derived from that inclusive, generous spirit, as Ms Sun Xueling has mentioned.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is why it is critical that we make, and continue to make, great effort in living together, side by side, appreciate each other, understand each other, and build even larger common spaces.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As Members of Parliament, we knock on the doors of many HDB units in many HDB blocks.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Just within one block, I have stood before homes with Quran verses, crucifixes, joss stick urns, statues of Ganesh, fixed around and at the side of their front doors.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Nowhere in the world can we find this.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think our HDB flats, maybe, also deserve UNESCO recognition, not that we have applied.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The President has said that, "To remain special, we must first resolve to move ahead together".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: While we do that, I say – let us not be afraid of the old – things of old are part of history and part of our soul.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even as we continue to develop physically, we must take pride and care to preserve special buildings, our art pieces, historical artefacts, and our beautiful old trees that provide glimpses into our soul.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: More young Singaporeans are now curious about the paths we have travelled, interested in our history and proud of it.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We should celebrate this because this is a new generation trying to discover their sense of self.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Like the National Gallery and Botanic Gardens, as we preserve them we also modernise them and take a leap forward.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our national journey is not measured in artificial laps of decades, 50 years or 100 years, but it is a continuous chain and cycle of preservation and renewal, of understanding history and inventing the future.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have vivid memories of conversations in my family when I was a child and we were living in our little flat in Bukit Ho Swee.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At that time, getting demerit points for bad driving or a red summons for not paying your PUB bills were major family affairs involving family conferences.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Often, we would gather around Page: 34 and the adults would always discuss whether we should appeal to the authorities to waive that red summons.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But inevitably, some aunty of mine would say that it was no point appealing because "Government operates law by law".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a kid, who hardly knew any English, even I knew that that made no grammatical sense, but gradually, I realised this means that rules are transparent, consistently applied, with no quarter given.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Similarly, throughout the Government administrative system, decisions are often made by strict adherence to rules and criteria, or comparing scores and numbers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We allocate – and we are quite used to this – school places by PSLE T-scores and aggregate scores, and award tenders by the lowest price if we are buying, or the highest price if we are selling.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At a time where our nation was nascent, certainty of rules and consistency in application were critical.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is an approach that leaves little or no room for personal favours and, hence, no scope for corruption.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is because the world is now too complex to be reduced to rule and numbers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Rules are made for man, not man for rules.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Abiding by the rules is part of standard operating procedure, but so too, must be the exercise of judgement.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singapore is successful today partly because at the crossroads of our nation's history, our founding fathers and Pioneer leaders made important and the right judgement calls.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In time to come, robots and computers will take over many, many human functions.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But, I always believe one thing they can never overtake is the ability of humans to make and exercise judgement.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is also the risk that we excessively view ourselves in numerical terms – whether it is scores or rankings.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What we need is a clear focus on what truly matters – the worth of an individual, the standing of institutions, people and country, which can only be captured in part by numbers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Indeed, we are already seeing greater exercise of judgement today.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They have rules and criteria, but, on the ground, lots of qualitative assessment and judgement are taking place.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because, who is to say a person earning $2,500 with two aged and sick parents to support is less deserving than somebody, a single man, with $1,500 of income?

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Similarly, in many public tenders now, the consideration is no longer just price, but how compelling and attractive the entire proposal is.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such contests can only be decided through judgement.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All the qualities, attributes, interests, achievements and moral grounding of a person cannot possibly be expressed in one metric.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A well-calibrated, greater exercise of judgement must permeate throughout our system.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Page: 35 Exercising human judgement does not mean we simply use our gut, or to bend rules willy-nilly.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is far more difficult, but far more superior, than simply sticking to rules and numbers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This involves courage, heart, purity of intentions and a very human touch.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The President has said that ours should be "a society where the bonds of kinship run deep and people look out for one another".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, and in this House, we must answer the President's call to continue to improve ourselves, to develop faster legs, stronger hearts, wiser minds, and to renew our resolve to march towards our common destinies.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.05 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.42 pm until 4.05 pm.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will be speaking on two themes in the President's Address.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first is keeping Singapore safe and secure, and the second is renewing our economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the first theme, keeping Singapore safe and secure, as a National Serviceman, I have seen the growth of Singapore's Armed Forces, even in the short span of my own lifetime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When I first started National Service, I remember the weapon of choice was the M16.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On a good day, I will be able to pass my shooting test by hitting one out of every two shots.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: During reservist, I was introduced to a new weapon.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do not believe this is a military secret.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With the aid of this new weapon, I was able to get a marksman at my first range – not on any improvement on my account but purely because of better technology.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This growth in the Singapore's Armed Forces is probably seen in many different areas.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I think one of the important things about Singapore's Armed Forces is that it is one of the most respected in the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Whenever I meet counterparts in other countries, they are always grateful for the Singapore Armed Forces, sometimes because they provided them with help in times of need.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our Indonesian counterparts are grateful for the help we rendered in Aceh.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And when I visited New Zealand, they still remember the assistance we provided Page: 36 when the Christchurch earthquake hit.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, Singapore's Armed Forces is respected in the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it has been an important part of the lives of many people in this House.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The question is what role would the Armed Forces play and what are the upcoming security issues we face in the foreseeable future?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I see at least three sources of security concerns.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it is important to have a strong Armed Forces to deal with all three.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is one of the oldest causes of conflict and it has been there since time immemorial.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Whenever countries feel the need to rally themselves together or to divert attention away from domestic issues, they sometimes raise concerns with neighbours, they try to unify the country against someone else.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: You see this in many areas, not all of them focused on Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The tension between North and South Korea often sees a very strong assertion of identity on both parts of the divide.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Differences between China and Taiwan often have a strong nationalistic streak, notwithstanding the strong economic ties between the countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are all examples of how neighbouring countries or countries around the region may decide to assert a strong nationalist identity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Nationalism, if it does not result in anything else, does not really mean very much.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, nationalism or rising nationalism is often the first step towards the building of hostilities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The strong assertion of a national identity, if it ultimately needs to express itself in territorial expansion, would be one of the major sources of security concerns.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This brings me now to the second point, which is closely related, the hunger for resources.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The hunger for resources has also been a very old cause of war from time immemorial.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When a country is growing, it needs more resources.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A simple way of doing it is to march across to its neighbour and take over, especially if your army is stronger.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The post-World War II era has made this a lot more difficult because of the strong network of international law, and a willingness to enforce that by the major powers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But these two need to go hand in hand; international law in itself is not enough.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This hunger for resources manifests itself in some disputes that are even closer to home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But it is not really the pieces of stone they are fighting over but the large economic zones that come with them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is an expression of the hunger for resources.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As these countries grow, they are hungry for resources and they will grab on to anything they can legitimately grab.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is in this light that we find ourselves in the middle of disputes that we may have no personal stake in but which will, nonetheless, affect us very profoundly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The South China Sea dispute, for example, includes many of our ASEAN neighbours as well as China, all of whom are countries we have very close ties with, and navigating these straits is not going to be easy for us, literally.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The third source of threat is, perhaps, the most insidious, and this is terrorism.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Terrorism is a little bit different from the first two because it originates from non-state actors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The origins of ISIS come from the Middle East, and the battles that they are most concerned with are the Syrian conflict and Page: 37 the Iraqi conflict.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, the expression of terrorism and its manifestation has gone far and wide.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Terrorist attacks in Paris, Ankara and Jakarta have all been linked to ISIS.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, the threats are, in fact, very close to home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We are dealing with a non-state actor but they penetrate through boundaries, and they may express themselves in countries that are very far away – so certainly not something that we can rest easily with.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our Armed Forces have joined the coalition against ISIS together with about 39 other countries but, of course, helping in the way it can within the limited resources that it has.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it is important for Singapore to continue to express its strong stand against terrorism even as we take domestic measures to fight and weed out the threats from within.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second broad area I wish to deal with, and this actually links up a little bit to the first as well, is in renewing our economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The ASEAN Economic Community has a great deal of promise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Economic integration is a very important means of preventing other types of hostilities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if the economic destinies of the ASEAN countries are more closely integrated, that would hopefully allow ASEAN to provide a united front in other aspects as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Europe has been at it for the last 30 years and it is not easy to find the right balance.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The easiest of the forms of integration is to get rid of trade barriers and that has already been done effectively.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, it is quite easy for goods to move between ASEAN countries without tariffs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, more challenges come when we talk about other aspects of integration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When we talk about movement of services or investment and capital, this is much more difficult.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are many prohibitions in individual countries relating to shares that foreign investors can have in domestic companies and land that can be owned by foreign investors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, if we have the free movement of capital between countries, I think it would benefit all ASEAN nations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, many of our ASEAN counterparts are rich in resources and have large populations with unemployment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, we have a lot of capital, we are short of labour, we have a much older population.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In that sense, there is ample scope for win-win solutions if capital is allowed to flow to other countries, but this needs to be supported by the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, it would be ideal if the flow of capital is supported by investment treaties and, hopefully, aspirationally, also a dispute resolution mechanism.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the best case scenario, investment disputes should be able to resolve themselves privately without having to involve state actors at all stages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It would be quite unwieldy if every investment dispute needed to have diplomatic relations involved to resolve it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My hope is that at some point, there will be a dispute resolution forum as well for the ASEAN region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While I am a strong supporter of the free movement of goods and the free movement of capital, I would be a little more hesitant when it comes to the free movement of labour.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this respect, I am glad to note that the integration process is also a lot more measured.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is important to understand the differences between the ASEAN region and Europe in this respect.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When the European Union, or the European Community first formed and subsequently became the European Union, it was a group of economies of about equal standing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I say "about" – Page: 38 but all of them would have been what was traditionally known as the First World.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Given the constraints Singapore is already facing with the inflow of foreign workers and foreign talents, we would be under even more pressure if such a measure were part of the ASEAN integration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, many of our ASEAN counterparts would benefit from having skilled labour from Singapore move over there to help build up economies, build up cities, build up industries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, in this sense, my hope is that ASEAN counterparts would be amenable to more nuanced labour movement rules, ones that allow the appropriate talent to move between countries without opening the flood gates that would cause a brain drain from one way and a flood of talent in the other.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I also think it is important to look at the AEC in the context of the larger global economic malaise that some of my colleagues have mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The reality is that the economy looks like it is going to slow.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Stock markets have been falling all across the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But what is important is that even in the face of a global economic slowdown, if we can find discrete economic opportunities, there will a chance for us to continue growing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The same way in 2008, when the Lehman Crisis hit, by nuancing our economic policies, we were able to benefit from the flight for safety to bring capital into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, likewise I believe, that if we can open a new market into ASEAN at the same time, as the global economies slow, this could provide a promising platform for Singapore businesses to find growth even in difficult economic climate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   In the President's Address, I was heartened to hear the Government's commitment that Singapore will continue to be a place where children can "chase rainbows and fulfil aspirations".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This includes investing in education, from pre-school to lifelong learning with SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would encourage all members of our community to take full advantage of the opportunities on offer.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These were more likely to be children from low-income families whose parents had less education.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: SINDA had put in place a wide range of programmes to address this concern, including a preschool bursary for low-income families.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My hope is that with additional Government support, all parents, particularly those from lower-income groups, would realise that preschool education is within their reach and that it is important for their child's future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The theme of the President's speech before this House – "Renewing Our Commitment to a Better Singapore" – is also at the heart of what Singapore's Labour Movement strives to do day in, day out for all collars, all ages and all nationalities of workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this regard, I would like to devote my maiden speech to tripartism in Singapore and what it holds for us.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore's 50th birthday last year triggered a reflection on the attributing factors that have transformed our nation remarkably from a Third World to a First World country.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One key, but often overlooked factor to the success story of Singapore is our tripartite system.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Tripartism was born at the time in our early years when there was a great need to move away from confrontational labour-management relations to strive for industrial peace with a common mission to making progress as one nation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our dynamic brand of tripartism has been tested and put into action over the past decades, and more recently, during the 2009 global economic downturn.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Then, while many countries were cutting jobs to save costs, the tripartite partners in Singapore had a different approach.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The concerted efforts by the tripartite partners enabled Singapore to upturn the downturn in a swift manner.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This year, the slowing of the economy and tightening of the labour market are major concerns for the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Labour Movement will continue to work closely with our tripartite partners to ensure that our workers are taken care of and not left behind.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We simply have to imagine what it would be without tripartism to understand its importance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government would possibly plan and implement policies based on empirical studies and technical data, without proper ground sensing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employers would resort to actions that are beneficial to its businesses, possibly at the expense of the workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And the unions would fight for the welfare of the workers, without considered thoughts for the business climate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Each party would do things according to its own, sometimes mutually-exclusive interests, in a silo manner.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Needless to say, the result would be a lose-lose for Page: 40 all parties.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For tripartism to be successful, there must be mutual trust and a "give and take" understanding between Government, trade unions and employers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Each partner must also be strong and representative of its constituents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, tripartism at our national level is strong.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MOM works closely and works well with NTUC and the employers to roll out effective measures for the benefit of our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, going forward, with different industrial needs and challenges, a one-size-fits-all approach at the national level may no longer fully address the issues faced by the respective industries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sectoral tripartism is not a new concept and it has been practised in certain industries for specific purposes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe sectoral tripartism strengthens our national tripartism and we need to do more to entrench the tripartite spirit at the sectoral level.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In any economic cycle, different industries would likely be impacted at varying degrees.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: National tripartism must provide the key direction and guidance, while sectoral tripartism can tailor measures according to the respective industries' needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As new technology develops and we continue to restructure our economy, there is also an urgent need to optimise our workforce for the future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some industries will need more manpower, some will require manpower with new skills, while others may need to shed manpower through automation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sectoral tripartism would play an important role to help our workers enhance their employability through continuous learning.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Employers, too, can leverage on sectoral collaboration to create higher value-added jobs and better paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the new bus contracting model was first mooted, our transport workers were very concerned with job security and staff welfare.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would they lose their staff benefits in a new company?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Gathering these ground feedback, the National Transport Workers' Union highlighted these concerns to the Public Transport Tripartite Committee.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The PTTC includes representatives from the union, LTA and the public transport operators.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All bus operators would have to factor these guidelines into their tender proposals accordingly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such tripartite outcome is probably not seen in any other parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: More needs to be done to enhance our sectoral tripartism.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government, Labour Movement and employers would each have to stand strong in its own ways.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For matters on industrial relations, MOM has traditionally been the main representative of the Government.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, at the sectoral level, the Government is represented by various Ministries and Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We require these Government agencies to be aligned to tripartism as well.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It works closely with the transport workers' union and the public transport operators, and adopts a partnership approach to achieve a win-win-win outcome for all Page: 41 parties.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As for the Labour Movement, we would have to reach out to more workers and expand our membership in the different industries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With a changing workforce demographic, the Labour Movement has to cater to a more mature workforce, an increasing number of PMEs and a growing economy of freelancers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the case of PTTC, the main public transport operators are the sectoral employer representatives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, for some other industries, there can be many companies with possibly a wide range of different concerns.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Employers' Federation has to expand its membership so that it is able to have a pervasive presence across industries and provide strong sectoral representatives at the industry level.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would our tripartism stay strong as it is forever?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The lifespan of tripartism depends on whether the strong tripartite relationships are sustained.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The current tripartite leaders have built up the reservoir of trust over a period of time, from working with one another, through good and bad times.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We cannot assume future generations of tripartite leaders would automatically have the same strong bonds.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the President said, our economy requires an upgrade to meet tomorrow's challenges; so does our tripartism.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If it is left on auto-pilot, if complacency sets in, the strong tripartism that we had yesterday and working today would easily be no more tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a powerful weapon in our economic defence.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Following the President's speech on our Government's priorities, our Ministries had announced a series of policy outlines and measures to support these goals.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of the schemes will require substantial investment and expenditure.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am very grateful that we have the resources Page: 42 to implement them.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our predecessors had accumulated significant assets through sacrifice, hard work and discipline.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Building a nation from almost nothing – not even water – they had not only survived but thrived, raised children and grandchildren, and left us something extra.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is how we celebrated our 50th National Day in style and substance last year.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Let us work even harder to ensure that we get ahead for our future generations, just like what our forefathers and the Pioneer Generation have done for us.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A growing economy generates good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It will also help retain the talented and our young who are mobile and attractive to other competing economies.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Historically, our growing economy has created wealth through asset ownership, which helps to build retirement security, especially with new HDB schemes.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If this form of wealth preservation for retirement purposes is no longer viable in the absence of similar rates of growth as in the past, how do we ensure Singaporeans are well-prepared for retirement as leasehold assets would generally depreciate over time?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is wisdom in the continual pursuit of economic growth and wealth.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is needed to generate sufficient revenue to defend our shores, build infrastructure and help the disadvantaged and underprivileged amongst us, and even build surpluses so that future generations will not have to shoulder our debts.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The world economy is increasingly difficult to forecast.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over and above market forces, frequent government interventions have contributed to the volatility and uncertainty of global markets.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The world is expected to be in a prolonged low growth environment.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can Singapore achieve moderate growth in this environment?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: An advanced economy like ours has the advantage of a more educated and skilled workforce but we also have a higher cost environment and an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government has emphasised the focus on higher value-added and less labour intensive sectors, more productive industries and in particular, those where we have a comparative advantage, such as services.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Investments and projects in these fields should be further strengthened and built upon.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am glad that the Committee on the Future Economy, headed by our Finance Minister, will be looking into five key areas essential to our economic growth.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We all know that it takes many years, lots of resources and efforts to build up skillsets, talents and capacity.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At this juncture, perhaps we should critically re-examine our divestment policies to ensure that the divested entities are indeed past its relevance to our economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, we face mounting challenges on many fronts.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Rapid developments in many sectors have brought about shorter business cycles.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The relentless pace of change can be intimidating and disconcerting, even for those who are prepared.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is not just the older employees who are under Page: 43 pressure to upgrade constantly and face the threat of redundancy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even younger ones are subject to similar stresses.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, staying relevant and competitive is increasingly difficult.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, if we can take advantage of developments in technology and R&D, Singapore is in good shape and well-placed to seize these opportunities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have a well-educated workforce with a "can-do" spirit.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Through SkillsFuture, the Government is helping Singaporeans equip themselves with the skills to elevate their relevance in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the same time, we need to think ahead.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the plans to diversify drivers and industries of growth so as to satisfy the aspirations of the greater proportion of skilled workers who as individuals would have different aspirations, interests, expertise and goals?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Clearly, we are in the process of transiting to a higher-value economy and innovative society.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: An innovative economy will provide more jobs, better pay and longer employment security.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are aware that growth and transitions can put a strain on existing capacities and disrupt the status quo.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unfortunately, investments and projects do not come in neat packages at desired intervals.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have to adapt to their schedules instead.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Human capital is critical to the success of our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must help young Singaporeans see their own potential to grow with promising SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should also give recognition to successful executives in growing SMEs, so that the younger generation can see joining SMEs as an exciting career path where they can make a significant and different contribution building an international company with Singapore DNA.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: SME bosses must be open-minded and offer attractive remuneration packages when they hire professionals.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They should also set up human resource management systems that are transparent and consistent, to show their staff that the company's promotion and leadership prospects are based on performance, not personal or family ties.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Undoubtedly, SMEs will continue to play a critical role in our economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, the Government must do more to develop our SMEs and help them grow as regional or international headquarters, for example, provide incentives that are similar to those given to MNCs that set up headquarters in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are many schemes to assist our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The amount of the assistance funds which have been tapped would probably vary from scheme to scheme.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the draw-down rate is low, the Government must rethink and review to see if the reason for the low drawdown is due to the qualifying criteria or if there is a mismatch between the definition of the schemes and the needs of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Time to market is of the essence in particular for innovative industries.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Prime Minister Lee mentioned in 2008 that about 25% of the top A-level students who had gone abroad to study or work did not return.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must do what we can to provide the most attractive work and living environments so that we can retain as many talents that we have nurtured as possible.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the past two years, I have met many management level executives in the course of my work who have been retrenched.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are mid to senior managers in their 30s and 40s, who are unable to find a job for many months.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are at the stage in their lives when they have young children and old parents to provide for and mortgages to pay.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During the period of unemployment, some even have to pretend to go to work so as not to pass on their worries to their family members.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They suffered a big blow to their ego and confidence.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are many reasons for this unemployment, one of which is lack of matching of skills; another is their reluctance to lower their expectation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The latter attitude could be attributed to their faith in the Government to lead the economy out of this low growth situation and the return of good jobs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the current economic conditions, I believe many more companies are looking to trim headcount and the situation would likely worsen.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government needs to do more to help these groups of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the ways would be to provide more publicity and create greater awareness for our National Jobs Bank and CaliberLink, which provides training advisory and employment assistance for our local Professionals, Managers and Executives (PMEs).

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Both are set up and administered by the Workforce Development Agency (WDA).

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe that many of these jobs could be filled by Singaporeans but why are there so many vacancies not taken up on the website?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How long do these listings remain, on average?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Traditionally, PMETs go to placement agencies and head-hunting firms for jobs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can more be done to make JobsBank the go-to site for those seeking employment?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps more frequent advertisements on our free-to-air channels and newspapers will be helpful.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a society we must respect all jobs and take pride in all occupations, "敬业乐业" as we say in Chinese, which means to take pride and derive joy from one's chosen vocation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is still a general perception in Singapore that jobs that require abstract thinking – "using brains" – are superior to jobs requiring skills – "using hands".

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such an unjustified and unfounded preference is undesirable and will have severe repercussions on our economy and social make-up.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Together, let us create an environment that will boost the confidence of every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One would feel safe in the knowledge that no one will be left behind.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With peace of mind and confidence in the future, we can be free to pursue our dreams and soar.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I Page: 45 support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   First of all, I would like to take this opportunity to put on record my thanks to the voters of Aljunied GRC who gave me and my colleagues the trust for the second time to be their voice in this House.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I agree with the objectives that were outlined.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In this speech, I would like to focus on the objective of "Creating a More Graceful and Caring Society".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I will be focusing on this specifically because I am of the belief that it is the primary objective that will give us the basic factors for achieving the other objectives.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A society that is gracious and caring by nature is a society that will have mutual trust and will help each other even though it may consist of various ethnic groups, religious beliefs and backgrounds, just like Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These characters will create closer ties between the different races and hence, there will be solidarity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Solidarity is necessary for us to achieve whatever are our desired objectives.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: So, what are the factors that will result in creating a gracious and caring society?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Undoubtedly, political philosophy and the administrative principles of a government is one of the basic factors.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because the political philosophy and principles of a government is an important thrust in the formulation of policies and schemes that will be applied by the government administration.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The policies and schemes implemented by the government have an effect on the creation of the society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is like the nature and circumstances of a family, which is formed, whether for better or for worse, through the methods of the head of the family in leading the family.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It was also in the Twelfth Parliament that there was a shift of the Government's perspective on meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: He said that the word "compassionate meritocracy" was first used by the Emeritus Senior Minister Mr Goh Chok Tong who said that compassionate meritocracy is a concept where those who are successful help those who are still looking for success.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Changes in terms of philosophy and principles have led to the Government giving more focus to social policies and channelling more social support and assistance than before.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Financial assistance, such as ComCare has also been extended so that more of the needy could receive necessary help.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: What could have triggered this shift by the Government?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In my view, it is the people's voice.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is the people's voice expressed through the ballot papers in the 2011 General Elections and the by-elections of 2012 and 2013.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, he also reminded us to tread with caution so that the social assistance programmes are not implemented excessively, as has frequently happened in advanced countries that resulted in complications for the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party agrees with the reminder given by the President.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
