text: The Workers' Party supports Government's measures to enhance social assistance but at the same time, we also acknowledge we have to be cautious so that there will be no adverse effects.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In this consideration, I would like to once again propose that we have a monitoring system for the social assistance schemes that we have presently.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have put across this proposal during the debate at the Opening of the Second Session of the Twelfth Parliament.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: With this monitoring system, we will know the effectiveness of the assistance schemes and will be able to take the necessary measures to improve them.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In the previous term of Parliament, the Government had also widened its perspective in the education sector.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: MOE which has been maintaining that the Edusave Scheme can only be offered to students in the national schools, has changed its position so that more Singaporean students can benefit from Edusave.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The launching of ASPIRE in 2013 has given better recognition and support to ITE and Polytechnic students and graduates in the effort to improve their skills and enhance their careers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is a change on the part of the Government which usually gives more encouragement to students to pursue University level education as a way to achieve success and progress in their careers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Although many improvements and changes have been made to Government policies and schemes, efforts to raise the standards of living of the people of Singapore needs continuous effort.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Currently, there are many things that could be improved and implemented.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some of the existing Government policies and schemes will still need to be reviewed so that they remain relevant to ever changing and challenging circumstances, especially since these policies and schemes could impact the well-being and lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In my observation, there are still some segments of Singaporeans who need public rental housing due to their financial and family situation that are becoming increasingly challenging.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, these groups are not eligible for the Public Rental Scheme because they do not meet the stipulated criteria.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a result, many of them are forced to rent rooms in the open market and continue to remain in an unstable financial and family situation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because they have to set aside a large portion of their monthly income to pay for the room rental and they also suffer psychological stress due to the lack of space.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For those who cannot afford to rent from the open market and have no means for other alternatives, public areas such as void decks and beaches become their residence.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I cite these above examples because I would like to paint a picture of a situation where there are still Singaporeans who face difficulties and pressures as a result of side effects of existing Government schemes and policies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These pressures occur because these policies have an impact on the individual's effort to fulfil basic needs such as shelter, a source of income and maintaining family ties.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And as a result, Singaporeans who are affected feel like they are shunted out because it looks like their basic needs seemed to receive no attention from the Government.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Based on what I have shared, I feel that it is necessary for these measures to be reviewed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These are good measures which have been well-received by the people, including us, the Workers' Party Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because the objective is in line with the main vision of the Workers' Party that was stated since it was set up in 1957, which is "Towards a Caring Society".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is our philosophy that every policy measure outlined and implemented by the Government must take into account and emphasise human needs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Only through these measures, inclusiveness, graciousness and care will remain alive in the hearts of the people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Hence, this would drive the people to contribute their best towards national building.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: MCCY talked about the SGfuture engagement that functions as a platform for conversation towards achieving a shared future.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I support the good intentions behind the idea of SGfuture engagement in providing space and opportunities for the multiracial people of Singapore with different backgrounds and religions to express, listen to one another and exchange ideas sincerely and openly.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such a conversation would be positive because it would create discussion that can be scrutinised and understood in the best way possible.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The understanding and clarity that will be obtained from these sessions will result in consensus if there is a meeting of perspectives.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, if there are differences that cannot be resolved.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This holistic conversation can produce mutual respect between one another – as we say in English, "Agree to disagree".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In this respect, I would like to suggest that current issues that have impact on the general public could be discussed on the SGfuture engagement platform, for example, current issues that are being hotly debated such as the threat of radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A dialogue session held in this way will open the opportunities for multilateral discussions as it will allow the perspectives and ideas from all parties to be presented openly and sincerely.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This will also enable all parties involved to understand one another's perspectives and, in this way, find the best resolution.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I feel that such a holistic dialogue will be more positive, constructive and inclusive in our effort to find collective consensus on an Page: 48 issue.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In the end, this will generate mutual respect and caring amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Today, we have heard from several Members on their concerns about the threat of terrorism and the ISIS – a force that is insidious and growing, but not insurmountable.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: If we stand back-to-back, join hands, hearts and minds, together, we can collectively fight the battle to win this war.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Each of us – from the doorman, to the clerk, lawyer, teacher or firefighter – has a responsibility for our collective security.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The Government can be our bulwark, but each Singaporean is needed to prevent terrorism from splintering our society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is a fight that calls on all Singaporeans to play a part in defending and protecting our home, people and land from the terrorist threat.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is a battle beyond border controls, guns or law.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We are waging a war for hearts and minds.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The forces of terrorism capture the thoughts and desires of individuals and lead them to destroy their country, loved ones and home.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Cyberspace spreads dissatisfactions, feelings of injustice and anger.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In an economic downturn, it is even easier for terrorism to play the card of race and religion to divide us.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Potential fault lines like a wrong understanding of Islam, racial stereotyping or weak national identity can threaten us from within.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Therefore, as one people, we must close ranks to build a fair, caring, cohesive and inclusive Singapore that leaves no space for the weeds of terrorism to grow.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Please allow me to elaborate on "I" – Inclusive society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In President Tony Tan's Address to the Thirteenth Parliament, he urged us to build a caring and inclusive Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Building an inclusive society is our ultimate defence against terrorism for when members of a society care for one another in unity, divisive elements find it hard to take root.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Home-grown terrorism tends to be driven by disaffection, anger and the search for significance.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Potential ISIS recruits are attracted by false sense of idealism and the promise of being able to change the world.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: By strengthening our community bonds, and building trust across races, we weave a tight network against this warped ideologies.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: By caring for the marginalised and weaker members of our community, an inclusive society is able to desist the lies of radicals like the ISIS seeking to lure the disenfranchised. "C" – Community involvement and all hands on deck.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The fight against terrorism belongs to us all, each and every Singaporean.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Only a whole-of-society response can nullify this clear and present danger.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To do this, we need all hands on deck – community involvement from self-help groups like the CDAC, Mendaki, SINDA, Eurasian Association and bodies like the inter-religious organisations (IROs), People's Association as well as voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) and Page: 49 non-governmental organisations (NGOs).

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Together, we must continue to make social harmony a priority, for without it, Singapore would not be where it is today nor can we progress.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: At every level of our society, we must strive to foster mutual understanding, tolerance and respect, and enable Singaporeans, regardless of race, language or religion, to flourish in diversity and harmony.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Social harmony and inclusiveness promote trust across religions and strengthen community bonds.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To this end, inter-faith dialogues and initiatives must continue to play a part in uniting Singaporeans and fostering mutual understanding, multi-racialism and multi-culturalism.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: By safeguarding and upholding religious and social harmony, we are each doing our part to boost our strategy of Total Defence that comprises military, civil, economic, social and psychological defence.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The community can give early warning signs for the Police and intelligence services.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Social workers and family members can work upstream to prevent potential ISIS recruits from being radicalised.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Together, we can work to prevent potential fall-out from social disenfranchisement by strengthening families and marriages, keeping open communication lines between races and educating the public on the role in our collective fight against terrorism.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Singaporeans have also stepped up in support too, through social entrepreneurship and charity giving.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Most importantly, an inclusive Singapore will unite Singaporeans and counter potential fractures of marginalisation and disaffection that could make us vulnerable.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We have to continue to work hard at it, and it takes time.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In addition, radicalisation is not limited to those on the fringe.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: A Quebec University psychology professor who has studied hundreds of terrorism examples, Mr Jocelyn Bélanger, suggests that radicalisations stem from the fundamental and universal human quest for significance.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: He found proof that "feeling humiliated and ashamed were predictors of radicalisation and willingness to die for a cause." He further explained that "Neuroscientific evidence shows that the part of brain associated with social exclusion and physical pain is the same".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It means that when you are being ostracised and excluded, you are physically hurt.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Therefore, inclusion is vital and education is key to guiding this fundamental human drive.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Through education in the public sphere and in schools, we can promote the right understanding of Islam, encourage Singaporeans to be inclusive, show respect and tolerance, prevent marginalisation and uphold our nation's founding principles of justice, equality and meritocracy. "A" – Advance our goals of meritocracy, equality and opportunities for all.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: By upholding and advancing these inclusive values, we can snuff out the warped ideology behind terrorism.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our pledge of "being one united people, regardless of race, language or religion, based on justice and equality" keeps our nation united as we defend and uphold it across all sectors of our society, be it in education, the economy or social sector, Singaporeans must safeguard, live up and hold fast to these principles.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our diversity in higher education makes for an inclusive Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: There will be no let-up in our efforts to improve healthcare, transport and infrastructure.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As the economy re-structures, we continue to strive to create opportunities for all.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As we reaffirm our fundamental values, we value our people and, ultimately, protect ourselves from terrorism. "N" – A strong National identity.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As a form of defence, may I suggest, Mdm Speaker, that we take a fresh look at how we can fortify our Singapore identity and national pride.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The love for our nation is preventive medicine to the toxins of ISIS.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Nationalism and positive fervour for our country is counter-defence against the emotional pull of radicalised terrorists, who are, sadly, ready to even give up their lives for a broken ideology.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Having a strong national identity gives us rootedness, connections and a deep sense of belonging to one other and our homeland.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: One year after our SG50, the time is now – to fortify, to validate and to let our Singapore pride shine.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: During the Jubilee year, we shared a sense of unity and national pride like never before.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We saw a glimpse of this fierce and protective love expressed during the passing of the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Singaporeans of different races, ages and beliefs were united in grief.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Under the blanket of mourning, a special sense of togetherness, a special sense of kindness and, I will say, a special sense of Singaporean-ness emerged during that one week.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As we waved the Singapore flags to bid Mr Lee goodbye, there came a realisation of what our little red dot has achieved, encapsulated in the life of our late Founding Father.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This emerging honest and fierce pride can defend us against the threat of terrorism.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In an interview by The New Yorker, a young French Socialist politician Nicolas Cadene shared that one of the reasons for the rise of extremism in France was because it had failed to create a national story that included all its citizens.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, what is our Singapore narrative today, one year after SG50?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: What are our guiding principles that we want enshrined − old and new − that will lead us towards SG100?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: While the SGfuture dialogues will help us answer some of these questions, we need to waste no time in forging a strong post-SG50 Singapore identity that can withstand the onslaught of globalised terrorism and its insidious penetration.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And, indeed, our common Singapore identity, values, dreams will give us the rootedness and strong ground from where we can stand to fend off the enemy's aims to alienate and divide us.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It may sound antithetical, but celebrating our Singapore culture, identity and uniqueness is really the soft power to fight the harsh and cruel sting of terrorism.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our collective identity, values and aspirations and inclusive Singapore narrative rise up to form a formidable psychological defence.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We are to always be alert but not afraid.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Like fighting a virus, the harder we fight, the stronger we get.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: On this note, Mdm Speaker, please allow me to continue in Mandarin.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, last year we just celebrated SG50.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Within a generation, Singapore has transformed itself from a Third World country to a developed nation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We achieved this not only because of the wisdom of our Pioneer leaders and the hard work of our people, but also one very important factor, that is, peace and stability – the peace Page: 51 and stability of the region, our country as well as our society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With peace and stability, we will have progress and development.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With peace and stability, all that we have achieved with hard work can be sustained.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With peace and stability, our next generation can stay healthy and strong under a favourable environment.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Therefore, we must continue to work hard to defend our peace and stability and not let terrorism destroy all that we have carefully nurtured.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It means frankness and open discussion on difficult issues we face, the concerns we have and the consequences we fear.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We are a multiracial, multicultural and multi-religious society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Only by open discussion and sharing, can different races deepen our understanding and discover that, after all, we are all worried about the same thing − the future of our country.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And what we treasure are also the same things, which are the prosperity and stability of our society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It is only by confronting the issues frankly, can we be fully prepared for the future.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It is not easy to build but can be easily destroyed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: If we run away, we will be more likely to become a target sooner.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: But if we do not take it seriously, should an attack occur, we will be caught unprepared.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Therefore, we must be well prepared and face the risk with courage.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Regardless we are Chinese, Malay or Indian, all that we Singaporeans have are one another.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, we must be loyal to our country, loyal to Singapore and defend the home that we have built together.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In our Chinese culture and also in our Southeast Asian traditional values, harmony is a common core value.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: First, in our dealings with one another, it is best to have peace in our heart and a calm tone, so that a big issue will become a small issue and a small issue a non-issue.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Second, we say that "the family will do well when there is harmony".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: A family must be in peace and harmony for it to prosper.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Similarly, a country will prosper and grow if it can maintain peace and harmony.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Third, between people, we must put a premium on harmony.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This follows the same logic as "the family will do well when there is harmony".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: What I understand is that in Arabic and in Islam, harmony is also a core value.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We know that when Muslims meet one another, they will say, "As-salamu alaykum".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In English, it means, "May peace be upon you".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We can see that in our heart of hearts, what we are looking for is the same, and that is peace, harmony and happiness.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Therefore, we must treasure what we have today in Singapore − the peace, harmony and happiness.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Acting Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Let us take these traditional values as our nutrients, stay firmly grounded and work together to create a peaceful, stable and prosperous Singapore for the next generation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Collaboration essentially means to work with a person or with a group in order to achieve something, to cooperate or to work jointly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There is no mention − and this is according to Webster's dictionary − of equal contributions, equal partnership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In collaborative leadership as well, there is no mention of equality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, I am happy to stand before the House and state that I am a strong proponent of collaboration and collaborative culture, collaborative leadership, collaborative effort and collaborative everything, if it will deliver whatever desired outcome I want.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I would also be glad to say that I will contribute more than my fair share if I can, if I know how to and if I am capable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: However, I would like to ask what has he got to come up with?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):    What substantial suggestions does the Opposition have for Singaporeans?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They are the alternative voice in Parliament but we have never heard this alternative voice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Their job is not only to question the Government's schemes but also to step forward with new ideas that are substantial and practical for Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For his information, the schemes that he mentioned and wanted to know whether they are monitored; we, in the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC), always give our feedback and monitor these schemes, and hence changes are made to the schemes, and that is how the changes have been made for our people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, thank you for allowing me to join the debate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We thank the President for setting the strategic thrust for us moving into the coming years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: President Obama, in his final State of the Union Address recently, made a very impassioned call for real changes in the "nuts and bolts of American politics".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: He also said: "We need to fix our Page: 53 politics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If we want better politics, it is not enough to just change a Congressman, a Congress woman or even a senator or the President.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We have to change the system to reflect ourselves better".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, rather aligned with the call by President Tony Tan for a "refreshed system".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Many described our political system as that of a socialist democracy, perhaps now drifting a little towards liberalism, what with the majority of the electorate now born post-Independence and desiring more political diversity, competition and democratic openness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They have to be, in order to accommodate the changing nature of human societies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The political system of the day that we have must be able to safeguard the rights of our people and sort out social and political issues facing the nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Good women and men in leadership, coupled with a rigorous and robust system of checks and balances, will enhance our system of Government and governance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Whatever changes and migration we have in our political system, the following tenets must be upheld.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One, a strong, effective, accountable and clean government after every election, to develop, align and deliver on sound policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Two, ensuring diversity in the representation, and this is really moving away from what our President called the narrow interest-based politics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The two groups of changes that we may see may include amendments, that is, making needed changes in the current system whilst keeping the basic nature of the system intact, or to changes that may change the whole basic structure or nature of the system that would be a serious or major shift.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Politics is not an exclusive club for ambitious members, but more a general membership organisation that gets better and stronger the more people join and buy in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Politics is the lubricant that helps grease the government machinery to make it responsive to human and population needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Politics is the adhesive that holds a diverse society, like ours, together, by involving individuals and groups, such as Our Singapore Conversation, Our SG Future, focused group discussions and many, many more to come.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But we also realise that good policies may not necessarily get the credit they deserve from the public sometimes, depending on a variety of factors, of course.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, what are some of the changes I would hope to see?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore, I feel, must offer and help create an environment where the bright and talented young people with leadership qualities can bloom and be groomed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Their strength and mettle will be proven when they fight their electoral battles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We owe it to ourselves and our future generations to make the positive changes and evolve the system further, and inclusivity is the correct starting point, I feel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The French novelist Marcel Proust said: "The real act of discovery consist not in finding new land but in seeing with new eyes".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our engagements will have to be even more multifaceted and deep.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For the masses − for the aunties and the uncles who do not routinely read the newspapers; for the quiet and silent voices who need more personalised approach; the Government, leadership and society partnership must continue to be strengthened, and this is what all of us are doing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This will, of course, cause some conflicting interests or issues to arise, as we access greater needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But it will be useful to find means to understand, embrace and, maybe, include and accept some of these.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In order not to widen fault lines in society, we can seal these up through common needs and aspirations through some of our dialogues and conversations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is what we want – equal opportunities, where we can manage and practice our worldly and religious activities, and showcase the abilities of our present and future generations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our community is unique, different from other Malay communities in our neighbouring countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is because we are comfortable with life and the interactions within a plural society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, this strengthens us and our commitment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our Malay/Muslim community can work with other communities in many activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They understand that this is important and this enables them to progress quicker and further together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They generously share the common spaces instead of arguing about their own rights like in other countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: During the dialogue sessions, Madam, we heard "The Aspirations of our Malay Community", which I have mentioned before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We organised these dialogue sessions because we wanted to know what the community wants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thirdly, they want Singapore to continue succeeding and be able to overcome all global challenges that we are facing now and in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They definitely have other aspirations, but these are the most obvious ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I am heartened to hear these because it is the correct direction for our community, for us, for Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our grassroots leaders and Inter-Racial and Religious Confidence Circles (IRCC) members have worked hard to provide clarifications to the other communities about the true nature of Islam and correct all the misperceptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: There were also innocent women and children who were affected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Among them, the terrorists used ball bearings, or tiny pieces of metal balls, in their bombs and explosive devices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These flew into the bodies, organs and bones of these casualties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Islam has never condoned such actions, and in fact, condemns them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is the global situation now – more complex, ever changing and unstable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It will be with us for years to come.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, we should take care of ourselves, our families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Every Singaporean plays an important role – take care of our family members, neighbours, friends and every Singaporean.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Correct all the misperceptions in our plural society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Every Singaporean plays an important role in our country's Total Defence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): Madam, we are all against this war on terrorism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Separation, division and hatred will only tear us apart and break our will together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The Paris attack, for example, demonstrated multi-site attacks happening simultaneously, and the intricacies and complexities of the minds of the terrorists that we are dealing with today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It was planned both within and outside France, involving foreigners as well as French nationals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It commenced with an explosion in a packed stadium and it was followed within 20 minutes by shootings which happened at four different sites and also explosions at three other sites, and not forgetting, hostage-takers set to action in a concert hall.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: All these were planned to simultaneously deplete or overwhelm the resources of a nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Knowing this calls upon us to review our strengths, strategies and intelligence of the relevant agencies and resources that we have in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But we Page: 56 are a small country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This was also the first time that the authorities in France activated their "White Plan", which has been around for some 20 years, but has been well exercised and tested.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, frequent exercises have proven beneficial for them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This time round, the coordination between the pre-hospital and the hospital care was very good, and has come forth in many publications as excellent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These are also issues for Singapore to think about.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Dr Robert Massey of the Royal Astronomical Society calls it: "The dance of the planets." Our own Dr Cindy Ng from NUS calls it a "special event", one that is well worth to get out and have a look.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Both are saying that the stars have all aligned.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, over 50 years ago, the stars perhaps did not quite align – no celestial night show, no astronomical extravaganza – something quite terrestrial happened, however, when Singapore was kicked out of the Federation and found herself quite accidentally independent.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If someone tried to read the horoscope of Singapore at the moment of her birth, it would undoubtedly have looked a little bleak.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Resourceless, a hodge-podge of races, a country with few assets except for her people.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singaporeans, new members of a fledgling nation, like a newborn – a little fearful, looking vulnerable, defenseless, but also like any newborn, feisty, determined to be heard and with a natural instinct for survival.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We were expected by some to go grovelling back on their terms, but our destiny would not be like our Independence, it would not be accidental, but rather shaped by our own hands.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the words of our late founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew, he said, "The people understood what they were in for and were prepared to make sacrifices.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Page: 57 Mr Lee concluded early on that for Singapore to survive, it had to be extraordinary.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore had to be better, more organised and work even harder than those around us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But all this would have come to nought if the stars had their way and if not for the social compact forged between our early leaders and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Early generations of Singaporeans saw their lives improve over the decades; they were prepared to give their trust time and time again to the PAP Government to provide strong leadership in an uncertain world, to do the right thing for Singapore and by extension for them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We were literally plotting our way through violent stormed tossed seas of racialism, communism, communalism, and the Government was always prepared to tell it like it is – open about the harsh realities and multitude of challenges that Singapore faced.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet if we look to the skies again, that waxing crescent moon of our flag that "represents a young nation on the ascendant" has perhaps gotten a little fuller.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The generation that started with that waxing moon has walked with the Government and brought the light of the moon to its first quarter, shining just that little bit brighter on Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With the passing of Mr Lee last year, we mark perhaps a new chapter in the Singapore Story.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The next chapter needs new writers, new narrators, new publishers, new readers, new fans and no doubt critics too.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, perhaps, there is no better time than now to renew our social compact.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The past has brought us progress but where we have done well, we need to respond with a spirit of humbleness.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In these present days, soon after GE2015, where we need to do better, we need to respond with a spirit of openness.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And in looking forward, where we need to break new ground, we need to respond with a spirit of boldness.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A new generation of Singaporeans now live in different circumstances from the past.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Younger Singaporeans have perhaps everything going for them compared to others, they are now more educated, more discerning and some say, perhaps, a little more demanding.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You cannot reap only economic growth without the societal changes that come with it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, how do we boldly create, or more accurately, co-create and collaborate this new social compact?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I suggest that we once again look to the skies and be guided by the stars.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Not the stars like Gemini and Taurus, but the stars on our flag.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The same five ideals that correspond to the President's five key points in his Address.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have long passed the tumultuous days of 1964 and 1969 and perhaps it is time to look beyond convenient labels and start by seeing ourselves as Singaporeans first.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am factually Chinese, Catholic and male, but I see myself as a Singaporean-born, male Chinese, whose faith is Catholic.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Page: 58 To be truly equal in our sense would be for labels to disappear, where opportunities are available regardless and in spite of race, gender, language, origin or faith.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A softer, gentler meritocracy that we have talked about previously.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our country was built on the strength and equality of our laws and that cannot be replaced.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But justice should put on a different cloak as well, where justice extends to all who may be disadvantaged beyond laws.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Where we, Government and people, stand up against the injustice of poverty, the injustice of cruelty, the injustice towards animals, the environment, the unborn, the elderly, the disabled, the marginalised.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A new social compact needs us to respond with a more caring Singapore, one that takes care of its people through a more inclusive approach.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must remain prudent but can do more to maintain self-worth and dignity amongst the most vulnerable in our midst.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It used to be said that when the US sneezes, the rest of the world catches a cold.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Now, China's economic and financial woes seem to have the same chilling effect on the rest of us.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Progress needs to see us to grow socially.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Material wealth should not correspondingly lead to moral poverty.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just like equality, peace has been hard fought for Singapore and should not be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Religion can be a force for moral good but religion in deviant minds can be a potent force for destruction as we have seen in Indonesia, Syria, Iraq, France, Lebanon and beyond.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Peace needs to be defended but peace also needs to be communicated.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We cannot have peace simply by having the largest gun or the biggest stick.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That will give us security, but not peace.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Peace must also exist between people, that beyond the deviant views of terrorists, we must accept that, even us, we will differ amongst ourselves, even in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How we allow our differences to lead us – either to mutually assured destruction or constructive collaboration will be the mark of peace for the future Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some like to call it "illiberal", simply because it does not fit into any convenient political theory.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many political scientists have referred to us as a communitarian society with the community as the basis.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But whatever they call us, we have to acknowledge that we have a unique system that works.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What we need to also acknowledge at the same time is that this system has not stood stagnant, it has evolved and it has changed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What we have today is really quite different from our Independence and all this is part of an organic process of responding to the desires of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A maturing democracy needs, first, for us to play our part in shaping this new social compact and yet realising that everything we have is indeed fragile and can easily slip away from us if we are not careful.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My elder son just celebrated his second birthday.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The future Singapore belongs to them and their generation of younger Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By SG100, both will be in their 50s and hopefully they will, like all Singaporeans today, play their part to bring Singapore to SG150.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, we need to start that process now.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What we do today in forging a new social compact for Singapore, in setting the stage for Singapore's next lap will ensure that there is an SG150 to work towards.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not dependent on the stars or planets but hard work and careful planning.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the words of GA Nelson, former US Senator and the founder of Earth Day movement: "The ultimate test of a man's conscience may be his willingness to sacrifice something today for future generations whose words of thanks will not be heard".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We may not hear the thanks of future Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the onus is on us to build up on the goodwill afforded to us, with all humility and dedication.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We, Singaporeans, should share with the Government what we aspire to in this new social compact, offer constructive and innovative ideas and collaborate with the Government to create the kind of Singapore that we want in the next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Come forward to break new ground to create a better future for our children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is only apt that I end off by quoting the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew at this juncture: "For the young, let me tell you that the sky has turned brighter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There's a glorious rainbow that beckons those with the spirit of adventure.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And there are rich findings at the end of the rainbow.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To the young and to the not so old, I say, look to the rainbow, look to the horizon, follow that rainbow and ride it." Mdm Speaker, our parents rode that rainbow and were not disappointed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Now, it is up to us and our children to ride that rainbow to gather the promised rich pickings of democracy, peace, progress, justice, equality and a life in this great nation called Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Like many people, I was surprised at the strong results when the electorate gave such a strong mandate of 69.86% to the PAP.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: At the same time, I felt grateful and indeed humbled at the trust given by the residents to each of us to represent their concerns in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Even though the elections have been over for almost three months, I still receive congratulatory messages from residents.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And on many of such occasions, I can sense that the residents are placing their trust in us as their Members of Parliament to look after their interests and work to ensure that their lives can be improved upon.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is a heavy responsibility and, like all Page: 60 my other fellow colleagues in this House, I pledge to carry out these responsibilities to the best of my ability.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Singapore has had a good run for the last 50 years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We had made excellent progress from being a Third World nation to a successful nation which is well respected by many other countries.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our success is not just because we have a good Government but also dependent on the other natural resource which we have – the people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The next 50 years will be a huge challenge for the Government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: How can successive governments ensure that we have continued growth in the economy, that Singaporeans will have well-paying jobs, that we can enjoy good healthcare, convenient public transport and comfortable homes?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can we all continue to live the Singapore dream which the previous generation had lived?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Over the past few years, from the many conversations and dialogues held, I have concluded that Singaporeans will continue to support a government that listens to their views, address their concerns and look after them.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They want a government that will provide them with security for their future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Besides material needs, as we mature as a society, the people also want a gentler, kinder, compassionate and caring government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many residents also spoke to me about the rejection of confrontational politics.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They want a government that can work with different organisations that are committed to building Singapore to become a stronger and better nation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As we debate the Government's vision for the next five years, allow me to share what I hope to see in the Government's programmes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Currently, I still receive regular feedback that despite our excellent employment figures, many Singaporeans who have lost their jobs are unable to find another job readily even though they are willing to adjust their expectations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Second, ensure that costs of living remain affordable for the majority of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: One concern which I have is that as the years go by, costs of living will continue to rise beyond the average Singaporean's income.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For Singaporeans who are retiring, will the costs of living exceed the savings which they had accumulated over the years?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Will CPF savings be really sufficient for them if living expenses continue to escalate?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have many residents living in the private estates who are asset-rich but cash-poor.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many years ago, they had sought to improve their lives by buying their dream homes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Now that they are retired and have no income, they are unable to receive any form of social benefit or assistance just because they live in private estates.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is their only option to sell off the dream homes where they have lived all their lives?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In contrast, there are some Singaporeans who have higher income but are still living in HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They continue to receive the benefits of budget transfers or other social benefits from the Page: 61 Government just because they live in HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I hope that the Government will find ways to assist Singaporeans who are asset-rich but without income, so that they can live a meaningful life in their golden age.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Third, to ensure that healthcare costs are contained and remain affordable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Will it be affordable for older Singaporeans after 10 years or after 15 years?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the premiums sky rocket after several years, what will Singaporeans do?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can they afford the premiums for the insurance?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Fourth, continue to improve public transport and to keep public transport affordable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I believe our transport woes are well-known to all and I have full confidence that MOT will be able to tackle the issue of frequent train breakdowns.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Nevertheless, it is an area of great frustration to many train commuters and I urge the Government to spare no effort to solve the problem so that commuters' confidence in the reliability of our train system will be quickly restored.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Only when public transport becomes reliable, will it then be the public's choice mode of transport and, in which case, we can indeed have a "car-lite" city.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Fifth, I urge the Government to continue its focus on strengthening the family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We are living in a more stressful world today and family ties are subjected to frequent stress.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We need to find ways in which we can encourage Singaporeans to balance their lives and to look after their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Surely, we can review such policies and make appropriate adjustments.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The lives of ordinary people are constantly affected by government policies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, it is important for the Government to ensure that policies which affect its citizens are considered carefully before implementation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This change in policy has deep impact on many students who, for one reason or another, did not do as well in their PSLE.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the past, MOE's point to parents was that PSLE is only a placement exam.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Students who are well-rounded in their Co-Curricular Activities (CCAs) but, for some reason, fumble in the PSLE, may still appeal to a particular school for admission.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The rest of the student's performance seems to be less important.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I hope that the Government will not forget that Singaporeans have aspirations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is the role of Government to ensure that our policies are tweaked so as to benefit Singaporeans and never because it is administratively more convenient.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Page: 62 In conclusion, I urge the Government to remain humble, to be sincere in wanting to serve the people, to listen to their concerns and do whatever they can do to help Singaporeans lead a better life.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The President spelt out five key areas to be achieved in this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of these is to renew the economy so that Singapore will always be a place where our children can chase rainbows and fulfil their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a father of two, I too hope that my own children can fulfil their aspirations here in Singapore rather than abroad so that I can see them more often.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Committee on the Future Economy has been set up to develop strategies to ensure Singapore remains relevant and competitive and through SkillsFuture, we hope to prepare our workers for the jobs of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Today, I will be focusing on the slowing economy and the challenges faced by Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The General Election last September was the first since Independence which saw all seats being contested.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The people of Singapore turned out to vote and have given this Government a strong mandate, and that shows the confidence they have in us to steer the country through thick and thin.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These figures which I have quoted certainly post a gloomy outlook for Singapore in the year ahead.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While it is too early to determine if we are indeed facing a full blown recession, looking at the figures and also the sentiment on the ground, I think now is an appropriate time to make the necessary adjustments to help Singaporeans, especially our SMEs, tide over this uncertain and potentially difficult period.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many of them tell me about the rising cost of doing business over the past few years from rental costs to the cost of COEs for goods vehicles.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another common area of feedback I receive is the manpower shortage and that SME owners cannot find local employees to work for them.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have to recognise that some locals shun certain industries involving manual labour or shift duties outside normal office hours.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One resident, who is a small business owner in the construction industry, came to seek help at my Meet-the-People Session (MPS) as he is facing cash flow problems.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Business has become slower and his own customers are taking longer to pay him.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As such, his monthly foreign worker levy contributions have become an increasing strain on his operating cash flow.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Page: 63 To reduce Foreign Worker Dependency, we have been increasing foreign worker levies progressively over the past few years.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These are rates typically paid by sub-contractors who do not have Man-Year Entitlement.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Indeed, businesses, especially in the service sector, have responded by hiring more locals.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Anecdotally, nowadays, we are more likely to see locals rather than foreigners working in a variety of jobs, such as petrol pump attendants or in food courts.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our SMEs are certainly facing tough times and it is essential we help to keep them afloat in this testing period.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Levies were intended to equalise the wage levels between local hires and foreign workers, but under difficult conditions, can potentially jeopardise the very survival of these businesses.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I recognise that we cannot maintain a low-skill, labour-intensive economy in our next chapter of growth for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, if we do not help these SMEs weather the oncoming storm, they may no longer be around to tap on opportunities for growth when the economy recovers.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us not forget that every successful business was once small and I believe we should have the business environment to let a thousand flowers bloom.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we face a slowing economy, I would also like to urge the Government to review the quantum of foreign worker levies and hope to see some room for reduction.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will certainly allow more breathing space financially for our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the backdrop of such developments, I think it is timely that the Committee on the Future Economy has been set up to look into how we can continue to keep our economy competitive, so as to create good jobs and opportunities for our people.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope the Committee can also consider the struggles faced by SMEs during their review.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: SMEs by virtue of their smaller size are naturally less productive than bigger corporates and less likely to achieve productivity gains as they lack the economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But just like Singapore, small can be beautiful.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On this note, Mdm Speaker, I reaffirm my support for the Motion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Turkey and Paris suffered terror attacks, leaving scores of people dead and many more injured.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The threat of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) is spreading beyond the Middle East to Asia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Jakarta was attacked two weeks ago, leaving eight people dead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: India arrested four students with links to ISIS who were planning attacks within Delhi and, over the weekend, Malaysia arrested seven suspected ISIS militants who were planning attacks in several locations in Malaysia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our counterparts in Indonesia have identified Bahrun Naim, an Indonesian based in Syria, as the mastermind of the recent attacks in Jakarta.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In fact, militant extremist groups have voiced their ambitions to establish a "satellite caliphate" within the region, to become the unifying force for Islamic State supporters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The social fabric in our region faces the compounded challenges of returning Southeast Asian fighters, radical ideological narratives online and offline, and competing extremist groups for leadership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Scenarios like those attacks in Paris, Jakarta and others can happen in Singapore despite our strong security measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: These events highlight one salient point – the nature of threats we face has changed in important ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As a result of such pervasive social media outreach, as many as 1,000 Southeast Asians have travelled to join ISIS in Iraq and Syria since 2011, including two Singaporean families that joined ISIS since 2014.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Terrorism is closer to home than we think.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) had contributed to the counter-terrorism effort within our means and in niche areas of value to the coalition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The Minister for Defence will be speaking on the Singapore Armed Forces' (SAF's) contributions in greater detail.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) will continue to support MHA, the Singapore Police Force (SPF) and other social and security agencies in their counter-ISIS efforts and to strengthen Singapore's Total Defence, in the combat against extremism and terrorism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Internationally, our intelligence agencies will continue to work closely with their counterparts in the region to protect our borders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: However, a military solution alone will not be sufficient in the fight against radical ideologies and terrorism, which aims to exploit potential racial and religious fault lines and de-stabilise society by causing mistrust amongst different religions and races.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We need a whole-of-society response to this threat of radical ideologies and terrorism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Looking forward, MINDEF will continue to support MHA, SPF and other social and security agencies in their counter-ISIS efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In addition to what the Government must do, I would also like to highlight that each of us needs to pay special attention to strengthening our social and psychological defences, which are two of the five pillars in Total Defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Conceived over 30 years ago, Total Defence has enabled us to face and overcome national challenges, and will continue to do so in the years ahead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: But we will all need to continuously translate the ideas of Total Defence into effective actions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The fight against violent extremism will not be a quick or easy one.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is an ideological war against terrorists whose goal is social destruction through fear and mistrust and not only physical destruction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: To put it simply and directly, these terrorists are criminals who have exploited and misrepresented Islam and deceitfully portrayed themselves as practising and religious Muslims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Scholars and Islamic religious leaders have noted that terrorists who claim to be motivated by Islamic religious ideology often turn out to have little and incomplete understanding of Islam.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Unfortunately, such misrepresentation of Islam has caused anxiety and even fears in inter-group relations between Muslim and non-Muslim groups in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: But while this inter-group tension is understandable as a natural human reaction given the misinformation, if left unaddressed, it will surely – and not necessarily slowly – lead to suspicion and one group blaming the other.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
