text: Very soon, inter-group relations will deteriorate and tensions escalate, and everyone in Singapore will suffer when the social harmony we are used to, abruptly erodes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Hence, every group needs to make the effort to understand the other group, and act and react in constructive and adaptive ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Non-Muslims need to understand that terrorism is based on radical ideologies and teachings that are completely un-Muslim and unIslamic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: To believe that violent extremism is Islamic and that terrorists are religious Muslims, our society will fall into the terrorists' trap to sow discord.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: All non-Muslims in Singapore can help preserve social harmony by doing small but important things, such as correcting misconceptions or stereotypical and anti-Muslim remarks or actions by family members and friends, and also on social media.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our Muslim community must also act and act decisively – give the clear message and assurance that we denounce violence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: A Turkish Muslim scholar recently wrote in The Wall Street Journal that terrorists are committing grave sins in the name of Islam, and scholars studying the primary sources of the Quran and the teachings of Islam have all dispelled any claims terrorists make of religious justifications of their cause.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Muslims must, therefore, reject any forms of violence 	Page: 9 in the name of Islam.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The outgoing Ambassador of Indonesia to Singapore, Bapak Andri Hadi, informed me recently that the family members and fellow villagers of the terrorists killed in the recent Jakarta attacks refused to allow the bodies to be buried in their village, totally rejecting and disassociating themselves from the dead terrorists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Mufti Dr Fatris said, and I quote, "(the extremist groups) contradict the fundamental Islamic teaching of protecting the sanctity of human life and preserving peace and harmony at all times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The safety and peace of Singapore is of paramount interest to the Singapore Muslim community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We have a commendable tradition of living as inclusive and progressive Muslims within the context of Singapore's multi-ethnic and multi-religious landscape." Every terrorist act carried out in the name of Islam will significantly affect all Muslims, potentially alienating them from their fellow citizens and deepening the misunderstanding about Islam as a peaceful religion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We are fortunate that our painstaking effort for the past 50 years in building trust and maintaining social and religious harmony has brought us peace and stability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: However, this effort is even more critical now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our Muslim community needs leadership and guidance from our community and religious leaders and scholars to equip them with a moral and religious compass to help navigate the complex web of information in the borderless cyber world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This will equip our Muslim community with a deeper understanding of Islamic teachings and discern it from the misrepresentations of Islam and the multitude of alternative extremist views that are readily available on the Internet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It also benefits the larger non-Muslim communities who will have greater awareness of the true Islamic values and teachings, given our multiracial context, and be better able to understand and engage our Muslim community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For example, some of you may be aware of calls for Muslims to abstain from wishing Merry Christmas to Christians via SMS and WhatsApp messages that have gone viral.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For those who did not know better, they might be taken in and believe that it is, indeed, un-Islamic to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Habib Hassan said, and I quote, "The purpose of greetings is to make the recipient happy and feeling of delightfulness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In Islam, it is strongly encouraged to make friends, family members and people happy, regardless of race and religion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is not wrong in Islam when a person greets and gives well wishes to a friend or acquaintance who is not of the same faith, as the intention is to make the person happy".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Ustaz Hasbi Hassan, the President of Persatuan Ulama dan Guru-Guru Agama Islam Singapura (PERGAS), the Singapore Islamic Scholars and Religious Teachers Association, advises that the Muslim community must be discerning in adapting to their circumstances and context and, in this 	Page: 10 case, for a multi-racial society like Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This occurrence of expressing a festive greeting, if taken alone, may seem insignificant, but, if it were to occur every other day and if the Muslim community does not have the religious ballast to fight the ideological challenge, one can only imagine the religious fault lines it could create in our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We cannot underestimate how actions by the Muslims could cause non-Muslims to react.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is the natural process of human interaction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Similarly, actions and counter-actions of non-Muslims draw reactions from Muslims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As more attacks occur around our region, it is not unexpected for some non-Muslims to wonder if, indeed, our Muslims are becoming more religious and whether this means they have an increasing propensity for terrorism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: At the same time, we also need our non-Muslim leaders to speak up on how non-Muslims should and should not treat Muslims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Non-Muslims also look to the leaders in their various communities for guidance on what to do in such sensitive situations, be it religious or non-religious communities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Ultimately, it is about interacting and engaging constructively with the Muslim community as fellow Singaporeans, so that everyone in Singapore can continue to enjoy the social harmony and stability we have built together all these years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This action-reaction effect applies to both positive and negative actions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We need to focus on generating positive chain reactions to preserve social harmony and build social resilience so that we remain a strong society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For this to happen, we must commit ourselves to share mutual respect and wider ideological and social spaces to facilitate positive interaction and deepen understanding amongst one another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We must guard against external influences that constrict our common spaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As a society, we will only stand to lose if this happens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The common social spaces that we share are the cornerstone of our multiracial society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Islam teaches that God identifies learning from one another as the primary goal of diversity and that respecting each human being as a creation of God is respecting God.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Thus it is critical that the moral and religious compass presented to our community reflects our deep appreciation of this diversity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In short, we must continue building social and community resilience against the spread of extremism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Extremists will continue to exploit the misunderstanding of Islam and seek to divide us along racial and religious lines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is critical that, whether we are Muslims or non-Muslims, we all recognise that we have a major role to play in strengthening our social and psychological defences against radicalism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our social cohesion depends on all of us having a proper understanding and trust amongst the different races and religions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Without social cohesion and social resilience against the threat of radicalism, all it takes is one hit for terrorism to sow deep mistrust and create irreparable fault lines in our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: (In Malay):   Our Muslim community must act and act decisively in order to give the assurance that we also denounce violence, similar to the view of a Turkish Muslim scholar who wrote in The Wall Street Journal on 27 August last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: He felt that 	Page: 11 the terrorists are committing grave sins towards Islam.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: According to him, scholars and researchers of primary sources like the Al Quran and the Traditions and Sayings of the Prophet Muhammad have all dispelled any claims by the terrorists that their cause has religious justifications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Therefore, Muslims must reject strongly any forms of violence in the name of Islam.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The outgoing Ambassador of Indonesia to Singapore, Bapak Andri Hadi, told me that the family members and fellow villagers of the terrorists killed in the police counter-attacks in Jakarta recently have refused to allow their bodies to be buried in their village.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Essentially, they have disassociated themselves from the dead terrorists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The Mufti said, and I quote, "they (the extremist groups) contradict the fundamental Islamic teaching of protecting the sanctity of human life and preserving peace and harmony at all times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The safety and peace of Singapore is of paramount interest to the Singapore Muslim community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We have a commendable tradition of living as inclusive and progressive Muslims within the context of Singapore's multi-ethnic and multi-religious landscape".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Indeed, every terrorist act carried out in the name of Islam will significantly affect all Muslims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In fact, it will potentially alienate this group from their fellow citizens and also deepen the misunderstanding about Islam as a peaceful religion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We are fortunate that our painstaking efforts in the past 50 years in building trust and maintaining social and religious harmony have brought us peace and stability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We need to build up the resilience of our religious relations and our minds so that we are not vulnerable to the influence of the Internet and social media.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our Muslim community needs leadership and guidance from our religious leaders and our religious teachers, who will equip them with the moral and religious compass to help them navigate the complex web of information in the borderless cyber world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It will not only be useful to equip our Muslim community with a deeper understanding of Islam and its true teachings, and discern it from the misrepresentations of Islam and the multitude of alternative extremist views that are readily available on the Internet, it also benefits the larger non-Muslim communities who will have a greater awareness of the true Islamic values and teachings, given our multiracial context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: They will be better able to understand and engage our Muslim community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For example, some of you may still remember the call that tells Muslims to not wish "Merry Christmas" to Christians through SMS and WhatsApp.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our community knows that this view is inaccurate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: According to Habib Hasan, I quote, "the purpose of greetings is to make the recipient happy and feel delighted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It gives happiness to friends, families and acquaintances, regardless of race or religion, and this is encouraged in Islam".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: He stated that the Muslim community has to know how to adapt themselves to their context and situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The occurrence of expressing a festive greeting may seem insignificant if taken alone, but if it were to occur every other day, and if the Muslim community does not have the religious ballast to fight the ideological challenge, one can only imagine the religious fault lines that they could create in our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We cannot underestimate how actions by Muslims could cause non-Muslims to react.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This is the natural process of human interactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Similarly, actions and counter-actions of non-Muslims will also draw reactions from Muslims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: As more attacks occur around our region, it is not unexpected for some non-Muslims to wonder if, indeed, our Muslims are becoming more religious and whether this means that they have an increasing propensity for terrorism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: At the same time, we would also need our non-Muslim leaders to speak up on the best way for non-Muslims to continue their relations with Muslims today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: This action-reaction effect applies to both positive and negative actions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We need to focus on generating positive chain reactions in order to preserve social harmony and build social resilience so that we remain a strong society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For this to happen, we must commit ourselves to sharing common spaces in order to facilitate positive interactions and deepen understanding amongst one another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: We must be on guard against external influences that constrict our common spaces with other communities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Otherwise, as a community, we will stand to lose.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: These common social spaces that we share are the cornerstone of our multiracial society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Religious and community leaders, including returning religious scholars who may be exposed to and potentially be influenced by different societal structures, must be assisted to consciously reorientate their world view in order to be consistent with our societal values and the make-up of our country – for our Muslim community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It is one that supports the tenet that Islam embraces and respects diversity – diversity in terms of culture, social, religion and politics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Islam teaches us that we should learn from one another and this is the main aim of diversity; and respecting each human being as a creation of God is respecting God.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Thus, it is critical that the moral and religious compass that we present to our community reflects our deep appreciation of this diversity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: In short, we must continue to build social and community resilience against the spread of extremism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: The extremists will continue to exploit the misunderstanding of Islam and seek to divide us along racial and religious lines.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Hence, it is critical that, whether we are Muslims or non-Muslims, we must all recognise that we have a major role to play in strengthening our social and psychological defences against radicalism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our social cohesion depends on all of us having a proper understanding and trust among the different races and religions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: It will not only allow us to prevent an attack, but also prepare us to deal with the aftermath of such attacks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: Our commitment to fortifying our social and psychological resilience will make us much stronger and more resilient and bolstered by a renewed sense of conviction as we unite in the face of terrorism and violent extremism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: A strong sense of national identity and commitment to the values of our society will be the irreplaceable pillars for the years to come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: For now, we must continue to strengthen ourselves against untruths, fear and mistrust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Foreign Affairs (Dr Mohamad Maliki Bin Osman)
text: On that note, Mdm Speaker, I move to support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we are thankful for much that we have achieved and gone through in the last 50 years, the next 50 years will likely be more challenging.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We cannot rest on our experience of the last 50 years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the world becomes more complex and people more mobile, it is important that Singaporeans feel rooted and committed to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are many elements in nation-building and, for today, I would like to focus on just three points: social justice; rule of law and access to justice; and strengthening governance in our national institutions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The President talked about a caring society and treating one another with warmth and dignity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before we can move ahead together, we must continue to have a Singapore that looks after its people, regardless of their economic means.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ultimately, how we treat our people reflects very much on ourselves.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How we care about the less well-off and the less fortunate will speak very much about ourselves.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must have compassion and empathy for our fellow Singaporeans who are less privileged.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should desire to grow together as a nation and as a people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recently, I had a poignant conversation with an experienced social worker who shared her deep concerns about families she worked with, where both the parents and, subsequently, the grown-up children in the families continue to rely on state welfare assistance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, we have to take care of such Singaporeans when they are in need but, like the social worker, we must have 	Page: 14 empathy with even the most difficult of cases and, at the same time, we must not easily give up on trying to find ways to help needy Singaporeans get out of this financial spiral.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a small city-state like Singapore, we cannot afford to be a society where every man lives for himself.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is especially so in a place like Singapore where a large part of our population is made up of transient residents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like pilgrims on the same journey, we have to watch out for one another so that we can all arrive together.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rule of law is the lynchpin of developed nations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is the knowledge of the rule of law that informs citizens their rights: what to do, how to conduct themselves, how to lead happy, orderly and lawful lives.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The rule of law also helps the government of the day and our national institutions to manage and run the country in accordance with the laws of the land.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And rule of law must come with access to justice.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As Mr Thio puts it succinctly, and I quote, "Justice and fairness are served because it is that lawyer's job to advise the suspect to tell the truth, to articulate any defences that they may have, to cooperate with the Police, to advise if no defence is available, but also to advise on the privilege against self-incrimination".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He mentioned that, and I quote, "An accused may be detained for days or weeks without access to a lawyer", and "we need to re-evaluate whether this is fair or desirable".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In our legal system where the accused is innocent until proven guilty, we must give the accused an opportunity to have early access to legal counsel.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Until he is proven guilty, he has all rights as every other citizen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a democracy, we must value the rights of every Singaporean and guard them jealously.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These rights must include his rights to early legal advice in a situation where the end game is potential punishment by the Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just as the accused's failure to abide by the law shall have consequences, equally, we must give the accused an opportunity to understand his rights and defences at the onset.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moving to another point regarding access to justice, I would like to refer to the Attorney-General's (AG's) speech at the Opening of the Legal Year as well.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a step in the right direction for our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fair disclosure of evidence in criminal cases in common law countries are usually taken seriously.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Discovery of obligations under our civil procedure rules have been in place since time immemorial.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the AG said and I quote, "Disclosure may or may not affect the outcome of the case, but the fairness and openness of the process is important".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The accused is aware of the case he has to meet.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, in some cases, he may be advised from the disclosure made that he has a weak case, and he may be advised earlier to take a certain course of action.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Transparency in a criminal justice process will demonstrate to our citizens that evidence is taken seriously and that, in fact, evidence is submitted early and efficiently.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This knowledge will surely strengthen public confidence in our criminal justice system.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have to ensure that our legal system is readily accessible to all Singaporeans, regardless of their economic means.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is heartening to see the continuing increase in the number of cases that are handled by volunteer lawyers under the Law Society's Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, it is also heartening to see many lawyers volunteering at our community legal clinics all over Singapore, giving legal advice to many needy Singaporeans, and also lawyers volunteering their services to do pro bono legal work under various auspices, such as the Law Society, the Community Justice Centre and various non-government organisations (NGOs).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I think there is still a shortage of lawyers who are able to provide pro bono representation work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many lawyers in private practice are already doing pro bono work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: AGC has a big pool of lawyers who are called to the Bar.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will not only help to increase the assistance that can be rendered to Singaporeans who cannot afford legal assistance, it may also help Government lawyers, being public servants, to better understand the challenges that many needy Singaporeans requiring legal assistance may face.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I move on to strengthening governance in our national institutions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the next 50 years, we need to work towards further strengthening our national institutions, including our Civil Service and Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have a highly talented Civil Service which we have built over time and one which is known for its integrity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Until now, our Civil Service has only worked with one ruling party.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the next 50 years, we must ensure that our Civil Service will always remain one of the key stabilisers of our country, regardless of which political party is in power.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The President mentioned that the Government will work closely with the people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must remember that Singaporeans are the masters of our country.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this connection, Singaporeans must feel engaged in the country.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They have a right and a say in the governance of the country.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They must not feel resigned to being a digit in the country, helplessly dependent on those in authority to make all decisions for them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans must feel empowered about their future and in giving them a voice and a role in nation-building so that they will be engaged and vested in the country.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To this end, access to information is important for all.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is important because every citizen needs access to information in order to make informed decisions concerning matters around them which we need a comment and input in nation-building.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The engagement of Singaporeans does not stop at giving them a platform to speak.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They must be given the background and information so that they can make informed choices and give constructive input for nation-building.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Page: 16 Correspondingly, transparency is also one of the features of a good government.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such an office can review any allegations of wrongful decision-making, as well as to investigate any allegations of wrong-doing on the part of public servants.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a process may also avoid legal costs that may come with judicial review.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And on judicial review, although our laws provide for judicial review, this avenue remains under-developed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is important for us to develop this area such that people will have confidence that they are able to challenge any questionable decision-making process of any public authority.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As an eminent English Judge Lord Hoffmann puts it succinctly, "The principles of judicial review give effect to the rule of law".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To this end, it is also important that provision be made for sufficient legal aid to be extended to the applicants of the judicial review such that legal costs will not be a deterrent to Singaporeans who have a genuine case that he wishes to bring up.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans must be amply consulted and Singaporeans must be happy with such changes before any decision is made for their introduction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans must feel secure about our country and where we are going from here in the next 50 years and be confident of the governance and institutions of this country.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I support the Motion of Thanks.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: President Tan said that it is important for us to upgrade our economy to sustain growth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Of late, it is fashionable to focus more on the inclusive part of it, rather than the growth.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, just now in the House, there was talk about social justice.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But really, if we think about it, growth is a critical element and ingredient for inclusiveness.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Without growth, our society's wealth will be more commonly inherited and less commonly created.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Without opportunity, our society will be one of permanent class and stifling glass ceiling.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And without success, we will not be able to pay for an inclusive society, for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, in this fast-changing world, how can we make sure that Singapore remains relevant?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One, how we can grow our future economy by creating more businesses, especially those with disruptive innovation and models.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, how we can refresh our education system for the new economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Three, how we must retain our fighting spirit.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Before we talk about the "what" to do, it is important to understand where the global economy is at today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We still have a lot of surplus production capacity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To keep the world afloat, the central banks have flooded the world with money and, businesses and individuals fearing deflation and disinflation, are afraid to spend or expand.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Even China today is cutting back and is entering a low-demand period.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, on top of the supply challenge, we also have a demand challenge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The other emerging economies are also getting more competitive.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore Airlines (SIA) has to fight "tooth and nail" against Middle Eastern airlines, which are well-funded.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our shipyards have to contest against capable Korean counterparts.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Even our role in the region is also less certain moving forward.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the Western-dominated economic order, we have a distinct role in Singapore – as a finance and business hub in Asia.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But think about it: when China builds its One- Belt- One- Road initiative, a new world economic order, it is unclear how central our role will be in Asia.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And then, there is the disruptive effect of technology.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Multinational corporations (MNCs) that Singapore traditionally relied on are being disrupted by start ups, and start ups have much less to do with Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A case in point – Hewlett-Packard (HP) employs around 10,000 people in Singapore, while Google just have a few mere hundreds.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, what is the underlying theme to all these?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And let us not forget that Singapore is mainly designed to support this mainstream economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our mainstream economy is important, and will continue to be so, and I will share some of my thoughts about it in the Budget speech.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But for today, I would like to talk about how we can urgently grow the economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Let us ask ourselves: how many significant companies with disruptive models and disruptive technology has Singapore created in the last decade?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If we do not have a frank conversation about this today, and do not adjust, we will be in for a tough ride in the future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The Government's role is primarily to create a conducive environment for the new economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But in specific areas, such as finance, smart-nation, urban planning, where Singapore is boldly inventing the future, we should give ample opportunities for Singapore-based businesses and start ups to grow together with Singapore, and they can be global giants one day.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We usually equate the new economy with cutting-edge technology.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Case in point – Facebook, Instagram and Uber – these are combinations of existing technology, but not necessarily leading-edge ones.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, what matters is the combination and the recombination of ideas and technology and the ability to test and scale the innovations quickly in the global markets in weeks rather than months.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Page: 18 Our role as a Government is to build this environment for the new economy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One, our research efforts must be aggressively translated, first, into innovations and then into enterprises.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our research labs should get the ideas out quickly in an affordable and simple manner, preferably to Singapore-based companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Let us not forget that the circulation of the ideas is just as important as the ideas themselves.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We also do not have a real venture-focused bank like a famous Silicon Valley bank that looks at start-ups' viability beyond their balance sheet.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Three, crowd-sourcing platforms like Kickstarter are fast becoming the preferred way to test and scale innovations globally.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, we should entrench these players in Singapore and, as our start-ups secure commitments from such crowd-sourcing platforms, we can help them scale up their ideas in weeks, instead of months, by giving them access to capital by also connecting them with local manufacturers, contract manufacturers and partners.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Four, we should provide opportunity for start-ups to demonstrate their ideas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The finance industry is on the verge of being disrupted by financial technology companies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am confident that Singapore can invent the future and set the gold standard on how financial hubs should operate in the digital world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The important thing is this: while we invent the future, let us make sure that we bring our startups along to ride this wave.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After all, the United Kingdom is doing the same already for the finance industry.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: If Singapore startups can do it, our Government should provide more support.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many of our economic agencies are pro-business, but many regulations fall outside their purview.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Try putting a food truck on the side of any road in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After all, if the National Environment Agency has certified the food truck for safety, is it still necessary to have a location-based licence for every location?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: After all, do we not have solid rules on traffic obstruction?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But in most areas of the new economy, Singapore can strike a better balance between stability and opportunity, because it is hard to go against what the consumer wants.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Once Internet banking is invented, it is hard to uninvent it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is hard to protect our local banks by limiting the number of foreign banks' branches or automated teller machines (ATMs) because when you go to the Internet and use your smartphones, you will get past it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, therefore, our regulations should go with the type of consumer preference, which usually 	Page: 19 embraces the new economy and not against it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I think that we can go the extra mile by setting up an advisory centre for startups to assist them in regulatory and public sector matters.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The second part of my speech is about education.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The future of science fiction is almost upon us.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Fast forward 10 years, and we will live in a world of self-driving cars, computers detecting diseases, and robots doing routine tasks.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: History has shown that technology creates winners, especially in the long run.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But in the short run, it can create many losers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the last industrial revolution, it took 100 years before the steam engine was able to uplift somebody's life in Europe.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two centuries ago, the world's 10th best bricklayer was assured of a future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But today, an app developer working for the world's 10th best, let us say, music streaming app company has a questionable future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, the question is: are we preparing Singapore to thrive in such a future?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must prepare our children starting in their earliest years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, I urge the Ministry of Education (MOE) and SkillsFuture to critically examine our basic and continuing education system in two ways.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It means we should teach them how to innovate, how to communicate complex ideas, how to recognise macro patterns, how to connect ideas across different fields, sense the ground and tap on intuition.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: By that, I mean letting them learn the basic principles of computer programming, artificial intelligence and big data.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must prepare Singaporeans as if their future depends on it, because it does.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What I am saying is not for every kid, on top of their hefty curriculum, to be a top-notch programmer, an AI specialist and a big-data analyst.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What kind of childhood is that going to be, if it is all work and no fun?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: What I am saying is that we must teach them the broad principles through a general programme, so that when they graduate into tertiary education and beyond, they are able to specialise in some of these areas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore is in an excellent position to refresh our education system because we are excellent and nimble and we can plan 10 to 15 years ahead and adjust our curriculum quite quickly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Just look at the number of kids with iPads when you go out.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But we must go beyond being just consumers of technology to being co-creators of technology.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My first two points are about how the Government can help Singapore preserve our livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But no Government intervention is sufficient if our people are not hungry enough.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, the question is: how can we preserve our children's will to fight and win?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Education – be it history or social studies – is a key way we can pass down values from one generation to another.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To me, the real story of Singapore is in the first 20 years of our Independence.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is the Singapore exceptionalism Deputy Prime Minister Tharman spoke so eloquently about at the St Gallen Symposium.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is about how we turned our perpetual disadvantages into a determination to 	Page: 20 succeed and innovate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Out of nothing, we created a multiracial society, a contrarian growth strategy, an inclusive housing programme, a thriving metropolis well-defended by all.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, the story is not just about the Government.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Will our nation continue to defy the odds?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, I came across a quote by Richard Branson, the founder of Virgin Atlantic.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: He has this line, "Train our people well enough so that they can leave, but treat them well enough so that they do not want to".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Before I come to my main speech, I just want to add my comments to the two points which the hon Member Mr Dennis Tan spoke about just a couple of minutes ago.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, I think social mobility is something which this Government and, certainly, the People's Action Party (PAP), subscribes to and takes great pains to ensure this remains the case for every Singaporean, something which our Prime Minister, our Deputy Prime Ministers and many of our Ministers have mentioned several times, that we should leave no one behind, and that we should build a more caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The way many of our assistance schemes are designed is tilted to give more to those who have less.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is something which we continue to do over the years, not just the last few years, from Year 1 – SG1, to now, SG51.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am sure we will continue to go on that route.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For many of them, education is, indeed, the most important area we want to invest in.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is the best way for each and every Singaporean to break out and create a better life for themselves – which is why we always see MOE getting a large slice of the Budget, something which we all support.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The other point which Mr Dennis Tan made was about strengthening governance in national institutions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, strengthening governance is something that should take place in every organisation and we should all embrace it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If you are a public-listed 	Page: 21 company, it matters.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If you are a sports association, it matters.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A voluntary welfare organisation (VWO), a charity and, I dare say, also in the Town Councils, we all have a duty of care to all stakeholders in any organisation to make sure that governance is there.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Last year, I had a senior, although young, civil servant observing one of my Meet-the-People sessions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The combination of youth and seniority is sometimes an indicator for high flyers, but it can be an unpropitious mix.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This officer observed what we did that evening.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the end of the session, as we were sharing, he turned to one of my key volunteers, exasperated, and he asked, "Why do you keep writing us these letters to make exceptions?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: You do not waste time writing; we do not waste time replying".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And as a former Administrative Officer, I am very seldom at a loss for ideas.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But that night, I paused on both counts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On the one hand, this high flyer is right.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Some residents do sometimes ask me to write letters that are beyond the pale.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One resident lives in a landed property and owns three cars.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Unfortunately, her house is only big enough to have one car park lot.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: She expects the Government – that is me – to provide her with lots for her two other cars.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If not, she told me, the Government is lousy and she would vote against me in the next election.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My reply, given verbally, was quite a strong one.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: With hindsight, I was lucky that she did not video-tape me on her handphone.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) officer was not so lucky.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am sure you are all familiar with the incident that took place at the Social Service Office (SSO) at Boon Lay, where a man went to demand his monthly social assistance which was late for that month.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Even as the MSF officer was trying to explain this, the recipient, loud and hectoring, demanded "his money".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The whole exchange was put up on social media.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, the man seeking assistance intended to record everything because the recording started with his session.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, there is a strong sense of entitlement and the tone he took was that the officer, indeed, "owed" him the money.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Both sides were not right, but in this sense, my sympathies lie with the officer.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Judge and jury – the social media public.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On the flip side, I have also seen some very bad responses by civil servants, the very few which give the Government as a whole a bad name.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Some put on what they call an "EQ face" but their empathy quotient leaves much to be desired.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is not what we dream of becoming.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The President, in his Address, noted that many Singaporeans are willing to contribute and share a part of their lives with one another.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He invited all of us to participate in shaping our common future, to strengthen our bonds and deepen trust with one another.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And implicit in his speech is the tension I spoke about.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He said, "Our individual aspirations may differ, but we all 	Page: 22 realised that we must work together to create our common future.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This spirit was sustained through our SG50 celebrations, and profoundly deepened when we mourned the passing of our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They are the people who help those of us who cannot help ourselves.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We should have neither vigilante justice from the public or high-handed behaviour from the civil servants.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is not who we are as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But every week I walk around Braddell Heights, Marine Parade, Serangoon Central and, yes, Aljunied too, I can see our language is one kind.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our style – you do not mind I say – is other places cannot find.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Nasi lemak and roti prata, our yong tau foo got halal one.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I ask you, you just listen, can tell lah.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: By the way, I ask you, what is this "Eu-no-ia"?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I do know that our language is like us – we are Malay and Chinese and Indian – and we are "others", too.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We care too much to allow what makes us different to keep us apart.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our faiths, our race, our religions may be different, but these differences make us strong.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Sure, our country is young, especially compared to Greece, but in our names and in our lexicon, let us be proud and celebrate our own.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And to the students of Eunoia, be confident and make the name your own.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The history of your school is yet to be written, so co-create it and write it in your own words, with your own accent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is said that the Singaporean is pragmatic, which has often been mistaken for not caring enough; for not having a particular political philosophy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is what gives us meaning and hope, and this is how we define our shared future.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must keep our common space large and our country united.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What makes us Singaporean is invisible – the way we sound, the way we think, the way we reason and the way we make collective decisions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To continue to do this, to continue being Singaporean, we must remain together.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must not see people to be herded by rules that cannot be broken; at the same time, we must not see our collective good as largesse to be exploited, our public servants as servants to do our bidding, to bear our anger, to right our personal wrongs.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We, the people of Singapore, we are Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We are the Government and we are the people.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My starting point is the reaction to the results of the General Election 2015.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One key note quickly emerged from some quarters.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was said that the results showed that we were one united people.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It suggests that what unites us as Singaporeans is our support for one political party.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am sure that most Singaporeans believe that what unites us is not that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singing with one voice is neither proof of unity nor is it conducive to real unity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our bedrock as a nation should lie not only in the trust between the Government and the people.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will outlast any government and any party and is a firmer foundation on which to build our nation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To me, there is no more eloquent statement of what defines us than the Singapore pledge that our children recite every day at school.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no point in asking our children to do this if we do not fashion our institutions around the values that it enshrines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some say that the pledge enshrines abstract principles.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But are we a people who do not hew to any abstract principles?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are we a people who only recognise purchasing power as a touchstone of progress?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am sure everyone in this Chamber would agree.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first is a confident Singapore, and the second is what I call a big Singapore – a Singapore where not only the state is strong but non-state actors are strong and influential and steering our course as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, our economy faces major headwinds, as many Members here have noted.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such challenges are likely to recur in the 21st century.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is because we have already picked all the low-hanging fruit of economic growth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Future growth in the 21st century as a developed economy in an increasingly competitive and globalised world may not come from pursuing exactly the same economic development strategies that got us to where we are today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Confident citizens are not so worried about the cost of living, or 	Page: 24 their ability to retire, afford property or afford to have children, that they cannot take risks or make career choices with longer-term payouts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Confident citizens will dare to switch industries to start a business, to take time out from working to reskill or further their education.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Confident companies would not be so insecure about future business costs and rentals that they cannot invest in big bucks about the future or secure the funding to do so.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The confident citizenry and companies would drive productivity, innovation and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Confident Singaporeans will not only want to work for multi-national companies, but to found their own multinational companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should continually strengthen our risk-pooling of social safety nets and management of the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Insecurity about the risks and costs that lie in the future holds back risk-taking and breeds short-termism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should cherish social mobility, take steps to enhance it and measure it regularly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should do more to ensure retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If Singaporeans fear retirement, they will not make confident choices that a 21st century economy needs us to make.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should do more to groom our local companies to become world leaders and to form a strong third engine of economic growth, alongside multinational and Government-linked companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Workers' Party has called for a National Secretariat to bring a whole-of-Government approach to this critically important task for our nation's economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Together with a raft of other measures that not only provide Government support and help small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to manage costs, but also help to nudge SMEs towards greater productivity, a way of setting long-term productivity targets and enabling our SMEs to benchmark their own productivity performance within their industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, we should look at our education system when talking about a confident Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is our education geared to producing leaders, innovators and entrepreneurs?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or are our students focused more on content-mastery at the expense of cultivating soft skills like leadership, problem-solving, initiative, communication skills and confidence?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is said that, in Singapore, a child raises his or her hand only when he or she is 100% sure that he or she has the right answer, whereas in Silicon Valley, for example, a child would do so even if he or she was not completely sure.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are we nurturing Singaporeans who have enough sense of self-worth and self-esteem to make confident choices?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is a sunrise or a sunset industry will change, and change more frequently as the 21st century meanders on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Confident Singaporean citizens and companies will be able to seize opportunities in any new sectors that emerge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But when we talk about future-ready economic sectors, we should not forget those sectors where Singapore's small size and high population density force us to develop 	Page: 25 expertise.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We shall have more to say about these matters in future sessions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my grassroots work in East Coast Group Representation Constituency (GRC) and Aljunied GRC, I meet many residents who feel insecure and, in some cases, overwhelmed by the cost of living and the challenges of retirement and by fears about whether their children can afford housing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second theme that we should unite around, Mdm Speaker, is that of a big Singapore, a Singapore that is not dominated by a very strong state, but one where non-state actors are also strong, confident and influential.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Here, I refer to the private sector, civil society, alternative political parties and the citizens of Singapore themselves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How can we face the future as a developed country if we are dominated by a very powerful state that is, in turn, dominated by an entrenched, single political party?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This structure creates too much dependence on a small group of people.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When our leadership core comes overwhelmingly from one kind of career background – lifelong civil servants – the risk becomes greater.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But to have a core leadership that has very few with any other kind of career profile, that opens up the danger of groupthink, self-rationalisation and self-congratulation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is good, but we need more civil society bodies that take on the role of policy debate and advocacy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the General Election of 2015, it was said that voting for the Opposition went against human nature because it was human nature to thank a party for good policies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is something else that is more or less predictable about human nature.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my opinion, when too much power becomes entrenched in one party or group of persons or individuals, whoever they may be and from whatever party they may come from, inevitably, that power breeds complacency and a tendency to be self-serving.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is yet another argument about diversity and debate, Mdm Speaker.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If policy ideas are not tested in open and public debate, not only in Parliament but outside Parliament, there will be 	Page: 26 less public understanding and buy-in into the thinking that has gone into the policy making.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will make it harder for us, as a country, to truly move as one.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, Mdm Speaker, in the last election, we came close to having no elected Opposition Members of Parliament in this House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With a Parliamentary super majority for one party, what is the greatest danger facing Singapore's political landscape in the long term?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it that of gridlock, a word which we had frequently heard yesterday?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or is it that of the non-existence of any viable alternative party other than the ruling party?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This must start in our schools and carry forward into this Parliamentary Chamber and to all social spaces in between.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must celebrate debate and disagreement as the best way to test ideas.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must learn to agree to disagree without branding one who disagrees with us as our enemy or as someone who has disrespected us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is real unity; this is real respect.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us debate and disagree but remain united as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us not forget that in 2019, which is just another three years into the future, we face another anniversary – 200 years of Singapore's existence as a recognisably modern society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if we focus on that test of time, on the longer term, there is one way in which we, in Singapore, can be a beacon to the world; there is one purpose which can serve to focus our hearts and minds in the 21st century.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have done very well with a very high quality of civil service, government efficiency and urban planning.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can show the world how a country can be vibrant economically while having a vibrant political life and a deep sense of belonging.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a new Member, I am humbled to be given this opportunity to serve and be a voice for our constituents whom we care about a lot.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Despite overwhelming odds, our Pioneers had brought Singapore from Third World to First within a generation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore has experienced such remarkable growth that other nations are looking to us to share our experience.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A number of my residents told me that the recollections of our past during the SG50 celebrations last year have strengthened their resolve to protect our little red dot and preserve our 	Page: 27 way of life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Indeed, as the President has highlighted in his Address, we must, first and foremost, keep Singapore safe and secure to ensure our own sovereignty and livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Terrorist attacks had claimed many lives in the last few years, with the most recent in our neighbouring country Indonesia.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must be prepared and vigilant against potential attacks as well as the impact of incidents upon our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must maintain our neutrality and be careful not to get involved in foreign politics or religious movements which could disrupt our delicate social balance and erode the goodwill which has taken years to build.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The social harmony we are enjoying today has been hard-earned.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us continue our work to deepen mutual understanding, tolerance and respect among our diverse racial and religious groups.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The President's call to all Singaporeans to unite and to move ahead together is an important reminder for a young nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Whether we are fifth generation Singaporeans or new immigrants, we must always be mindful that we have pledged to stay united, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every one of us has an important role to play.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Social integration and assimilation are built one encounter, one day at a time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A kind word, a thoughtful gesture or a considerate act can make all the difference.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And occasionally, when we accidentally step upon one another's toes, let us always remind ourselves to take the high road for the greater good.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since our Independence, social integration and harmony have always been the Government's priorities, backed by innovative policies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I say "innovative" because these policies have no precedent elsewhere in the world and were even criticised as overly controlling and intrusive.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our political system, National Service, schools, HDB estates and even People's Association activities bear testimony to successful integration.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One of the ways is through our community bonding programmes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition to our usual inclusive festive seasons' activities, we should put in more effort to update our programme formats.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When I was working in the People's Association, there were activities to promote inter-generational bonding, such as parent-and-child, grandparent-and-grandchild, young-and-seniors singing/dancing contests.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can have similar formats to promote inter-racial bonding.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our community clubs can organise more activities which require participants of different races to team up and work together over a period of time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, cooking contests comprising several rounds so that participants have to practise and create several dishes over a few weeks.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Clan associations can also be encouraged to consider inviting non-Chinese to participate in more activities and events.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Similar initiatives by private companies should also be encouraged 	Page: 28 through Government funding or resource sponsorship.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another important platform where social interaction takes place is in cyberspace.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The importance of social media will only increase as our younger generations become more and more Internet-savvy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The anonymity provided by social media facilitates freedom of expression but this freedom can also be abused, trigger conflict and deepen divides along racial, religious and income lines.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have legislation in place which enables the Government to act against incendiary expressions in cyberspace or in print.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to step up on public education to set the parameters for acceptable expression and inculcate responsible behaviour online.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge the Government to continue taking the lead in creating, funding and supporting such public education programmes which should reach as many as possible – schools, housing estates, recreation centres, workplaces and more.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In his speech, the President talked about his hope that Singapore can build a caring society.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We say that, "One should look after the seniors the same way he treats his own parents".

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When we care for our own seniors, we should also care for and help the seniors around us.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Looking after the elderly is not just the responsibility of the children, family and Government; as long as it is within our means, we all have the responsibility to extend help to the elderly around us.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will streamline administration, improve service quality and ensure the long-term sustainability of the various programmes for seniors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The centres should have day care services and look after the seniors' needs in areas, such as medicine.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
