text: But we must ask ourselves these questions: how can we create a more conducive ecosystem for our entrepreneurs to thrive?

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Are there hindrances that we must remove to allow ideas to germinate and innovative start-ups to prosper?

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Will over-supportive policies stifle the fighting spirit and the desire to succeed, much like over-watering a plant would kill it?

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: How do we calibrate the relationship between Government and the industry to ensure that the optimal amount of intervention and creative-tension exist?

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Is this a case of "doing more is not doing better but may be doing more harm"?

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: How can we be more flexible in the way we render help to our small startups and SMEs to make impact where and when it matters most?

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As we move from SG50 towards SG100 and cast our thoughts on what our future economy entails, these are questions that we need to think carefully about.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The entrepreneurial spirit of our next generation, like the group which started ShopBack, will open new avenues through which we can create the economy of our next 50 years.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government must rethink how it supports our entrepreneurs and work closely with the entrepreneurial community to build a vibrant startup ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Page: 46 Today, we stand at a critical inflexion point in the journey of our nation-building.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Even as we celebrate the successes that we have achieved in the past 50 years, we also need to take the necessary steps to build the framework and the groundwork for our future generations from this position of strength.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The path forward does not promise to be easy.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With the business community, the Government and the people working hand-in-hand, I am confident that the next chapter of our economic story will transcend what had preceded before and bring about greater prosperity and opportunity for each and every Singaporean.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With this, Mdm Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: A critical question then is: how do we want our society to age?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How prepared are we to manage and deal with not just the economic consequences of a rapidly ageing population but, perhaps, more importantly, the social implications of a greying society?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In my conversations with my residents, dialogues with VWOs and also with healthcare professionals, a striking observation here is that our seniors often feel they are unable to integrate within the community post-retirement and has a tendency to be or to feel isolated.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Studies have also shown that many of our seniors wish to continue being a part of the community, actively involved in one way or another and, to some extent, the broader society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Understandably, this helps in improving their self-esteem and builds confidence even as they age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This being so, whether there are choices readily available to them is thus something we need to focus on.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The Government has also encouraged the tripartite partners to enhance job opportunities and employability for our mature workers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This could be attributed to a lag on the employers' mindset and also the general work culture that we have here.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We still do not easily associate having experienced older workers with a positive value.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: What then are the implications to those seniors who wish to but cannot be gainfully employed at a mature age?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: From their feedback, many of these seniors remain at home not to care for their grandchildren but because they have no alternatives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Many choose not to go out as they do not wish to spend much since they no longer have an active income.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Unfortunately, for some of our seniors, their ageing conditions also deteriorate after their spouses have passed on.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It may seem surprising, but surveys show that these lonely seniors are not living alone.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In fact, many of them actually live with their families.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, they feel isolated 	Page: 47 as they have little communication with their children who often work long hours or they do not have activities to be mentally and physically preoccupied with.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Over time, such isolation has detrimental effects on their health and, naturally, increases their healthcare costs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Given where we are today and a future with more seniors, what should we do to ensure that they have a meaningful life?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I believe that, first and foremost, we need to consider the needs and aspirations of our seniors and their caregivers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: I think many of them wish to continue to be active contributors of the society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some want to be part of the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Others actually require activities to have a regular routine.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some want to be active and positive contributors, for example, being volunteers or fulfilling dreams that they were not able to pursue previously, having no time for it.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They want to have a social network that provides mental and physical support, one that encourages communication and channels to seek assistance, and caregiving beyond just their family network.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They want to have awareness of their health conditions and being financially capable to seek the necessary medical treatment and with the discipline to follow through.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For their caregivers, they hope to have personal awareness leading to better preventive care for themselves and also how best to play the role of being a caregiver and having a larger community network to support caregiving – from volunteers, healthcare options and financial support – and for the support group to provide mutual sharing and learning.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To help see how this may work in practice, let me describe how a day would be like in an integrated social hub.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Presently, many of our Community Clubs are not extensively utilised during the weekdays.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: At the same time, we face space constraints in accommodating more facilities at the HDB void decks.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As the Community Clubs today are much better equipped with facilities and they already serve many functions, we could consider enhancing their functionality and leverage the infrastructure to serve as an integrated social hub.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The Community Club becomes an integrated social hub during the weekdays and continues with its usual outreach activities in the nights and on weekends.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Various services from the VWOs, like the day-care activities and training, the healthcare partners who manage elderly care centres and the Government agencies with their social service helpdesk will be co-located at this hub.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Additionally, the constituency office, together with the social enterprises, can coordinate the resources available within the community and can allocate these resources accordingly for employment, training and for volunteer work.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Mr Salleh is a former school teacher who retired about seven years ago and Mrs Salleh is a housewife.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They have three children − two sons who are married, while their daughter is single.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: One of their sons lives within walking distance from them and they 	Page: 48 have two children who are attending nursery with childcare.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Mr Goh, aged 50, is working odd jobs as he has some health issues requiring regular treatment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As he is single, he needs to continue working in order to afford his daily expenses and medical bills.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: After her spouse passed away about three years ago, she has been a little depressed and has not left home much until our volunteers engaged her and started bringing her to our Community Club activities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Mrs Soh is a stay-at-home mother who is a caregiver for her two school-going children and also her father-in-law.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Her father-in-law is still healthy and very mobile.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: He is very much interested in music and likes to interact with others during his younger days when he was working as a producer.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: So, below is an example of what their usual day is like within the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Mr and Mrs Salleh usually begin their morning by sending their grandchildren to the nursery at the void deck of their HDB block.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Like other volunteers, when first inducted to the care centre, the Sallehs are trained by the professionals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: They feel that they have personally benefitted, as these ongoing training sessions and practical experiences also help them raise awareness of how to better care for themselves as they age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With education and support from these healthcare professionals and volunteers, Mr Goh has been more disciplined going through and following through with his treatment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: She gets to socialise and learn more about what is taking place in other parts of Singapore and some of our policies through the explanation from the trained staff, our volunteers and also her local advisor.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Moving forward, being illiterate and unable to read the papers will not stop her from knowing and learning broadly.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But what excites her most is her newfound job, to become a part-time cook and to prepare nutritional food for the children at the nearby childcare centre.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Through the social enterprise, they also found a network of friends who have strong passion on some causes and continue to set up their own initiatives to support these causes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This, then, is how an integrated social hub for our seniors would work.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If properly executed, these hubs will help, first, to raise awareness of this stage of life and will effect a longer-term positive social impact.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Most in the middle-age working group today play the role of caregivers and will, in the next two decades, become seniors themselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Often, in their state of busy-ness, they will conveniently 	Page: 49 forget or ignore what lies ahead of them as they progress in their life stages.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, it is imperative for them to be aware at an early stage what it entails and be mentally prepared for life as a senior which involves, often times, discomfiting changes on various fronts − ranging from relationships with their families, preventive care and well-being both medically and socially, adaptations at the workplace and social acceptance in retirement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Second, leverage our social capital to maximise resources and strengthen our social fabric.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Diversity adds colour to a society, but it is the communal strength that defines us as a community and a nation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We do not, and should not, hope for unity to shine through only when we have difficult times.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As Singaporeans, we can and should aim to build solidarity at different levels within the society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This is possible if we aspire to be a part of nation-building and want to define community involvement at all ages and in varying forms.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Singapore will compete with other countries, like Japan, Germany and Italy, for external caregiving resources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Thus, the urgency and need for self-reliance and building resources that cater for the characteristics of our aged as they are strongly influenced by the culture within the country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Third, to help to supplement and provide support at the community level to state-level welfare initiatives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Increasingly, we have seen that it is a social and economic cost to our society when older people are shut out from mainstream life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Loss of income, status and a positive role in community life means a greater likelihood of dependence on the taxpayer.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In addition, the failure by society to use the experience of older people results in further costs to our communities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Older people are as heterogeneous as any group in society and reflect the social and cultural mix of any cross-section of the community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Similarly, they have needs and aspirations which differ from their individual circumstances.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For some, work has provided a sense of identity and recognition of their contribution to society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: A substitute thus must be established in retirement to maintain their individual self-esteem.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The stories mentioned earlier may seem to be a dream to many.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This year, we embark on our journey to SG100.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our first 50 years have not been easy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But our founding fathers and our Pioneer Generation had a "never say die" attitude.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They took on whatever challenges they faced with courage and determination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through hard work and innovation, they overcame many obstacles and brought Singapore to where we are today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As a newly independent nation, we faced many difficult issues for the first time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There were no templates and standard operating procedures to follow.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We had to chart our own destiny and find new paths as we go along.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We started National Service and built up our armed forces to defend ourselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also succeeded in many other areas, such as turning Singapore into a Garden City; creating a harmonious multiracial society and allowing many Singaporeans to become home owners through our public housing policies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: All these achievements did not happen by chance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They were due to the hard work and innovation of our Pioneers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On the education front, we have created new pathways for our students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I was fortunate to be part of the MOE team working on some of these initiatives, including the establishment of Northlight School and Assumption Pathway School, for students who are less academically-inclined.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These innovations in policy and implementation have benefitted Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And they either attributed this to Singaporeans not being confident enough, or tried to put the blame on our education system, schools and educators.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If we had not been innovative, could we have survived after 1965 and become one of the most admired and prosperous cities in the world?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Could we have improved our lives and transformed Singapore from Third World to First in one generation?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Mr Lee Kuan Yew said, "This is not administration doing a job.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is entrepreneurship on a political stage, on a national scale." The President has highlighted our key challenges in the coming years and how we must create Singapore's future together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Looking ahead, my worry is that we get trapped in the comfort zones of our current success and we start to lose our appetite to take risks and question the status quo.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Will we end up playing it too safe by staying well within existing boundaries?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Will we focus too much attention on complying with rules and procedures, instead of the outcomes we want to achieve?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is fine if we just want to cruise along in maintenance mode and make small, incremental improvements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But it is not good enough if we want to deal with difficult challenges and bring 	Page: 51 Singapore to the next higher level.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To do that, we need to embrace the enterprising spirit of our Pioneers and we need to innovate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are three important things we could do to encourage innovation and enterprise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, we must face our problems and challenges with a positive attitude.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We should view these as opportunities to develop new solutions and discover new breakthroughs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Innovation often involves bringing together ideas from different disciplines and sectors and also from other countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Existing ideas from adjacent sectors can be applied to new problems to achieve a better outcome.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We want to develop infrastructure and solutions that encourage active ageing and intergenerational bonding.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By combining ideas from different disciplines, such as healthcare, information technology, design and social behavioural research, we aim to provide better care and greater convenience for seniors in a home and community setting.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The learning points from this project can be applied to other estates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is a priority for Singapore as we need to be ready for an ageing population.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many of our older towns already have a higher proportion of seniors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I see this when I meet my residents during house visits and constituency events in Toa Payoh.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Some of my elderly residents are in good health and lead active lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I met this 100-year-old lady who stays with her family in Toa Payoh North.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: She exercises regularly and joins her friends for outings and activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: She is more fortunate than some of her neighbours who are non-ambulant and require frequent medical assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We need to come up with innovative solutions to provide a conducive living environment for these different groups of seniors, so that they can age well and age in place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides improving our quality of life, such innovations also allow our companies to realise commercial value from their products and services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By innovating and solving our problems, we will develop new ideas and create new value that can be exported overseas to grow our economy and provide good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Contestable consumers today can choose from many electricity retailers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These include independent retailers who offer innovative contracts, such as supply of electricity from renewable sources and energy management solutions like smart meters and demand response.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Previously, there were no independent retailers in Singapore because we did not have an electricity futures market for independent retailers to manage their risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Setting up the futures market was a complex and difficult task.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Earlier attempts had failed because power generation companies did not want independent retailers to enter the market and compete with their retail subsidiaries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But my colleagues and I did not give up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Together with the Singapore Exchange (SGX), we thought of different ways to overcome the obstacles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And after some initial setbacks and many months of hard work, we succeeded.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The second thing we could do to promote innovation is to encourage risk-taking and experimentation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We need an environment where people are willing to try new ideas and are not overly afraid of making mistakes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This spirit is a key success factor for British technology company Dyson, whose inventions include the bagless vacuum cleaner and the bladeless fan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Its founder, Mr James Dyson, said their engineers are not afraid of testing and failing, as that is part of getting to the final product.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When I was at the MTI, I visited Tan Seng Kee Foods (TSK).

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is now run by Mr Raymond Tan and his sister Annie.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: TSK manufactures noodles which they sell under the "Kang Kang" brand.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They are preservative-free, fresh noodles that can be kept for a month without refrigeration, far longer than conventional noodles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, how did TSK overcome the problem of fresh noodles having a shorter shelf life?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: TSK adapted this process – typically used in dairy products – to extend the shelf life of their noodles without affecting the taste and quality.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This makes it more convenient for their customers and allows TSK to export its noodles to overseas markets, opening the door to more business opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Like many who take the innovation route, TSK had to deal with risks, challenges and setbacks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They are building on their initial success to experiment with new ideas and products.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am proud of what TSK has achieved and wish Raymond, Annie and their colleagues continued success in their innovation journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As a society, we must not be intolerant of genuine mistakes and come down too hard on people who try and fail.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We should encourage new ideas and accept that some of these ideas will fail.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is part and parcel of learning what works and what does not, so that we can refine our solutions and make them even better.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At the individual level, we need people with the gumption to take calculated risks and to push the boundaries when pursuing their passion; Singaporeans with the determination to press on in the face of adversity and the resilience to bounce back when they fail.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This enterprising spirit is not only for startups and entrepreneurs, it also applies to other areas, such as how the Government formulates and implements new policies; how we improve our social services; and how we develop strong and caring communities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In Mandarin):  I believe that there are many people like me who patronise the heartland shops for daily necessities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These heartland shops have become part of our lives and they also contribute to the community by providing job opportunities for residents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In recent years, heartland shops have encountered many challenges, for example, rising costs and manpower shortages and so on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Most of these shops are small businesses which are unable to derive benefits from economies of scale and find it difficult to invest to improve productivity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Page: 53 Moreover, many proprietors of heartland shops are ageing and their children may not be keen to take over the business.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I am worried that with this trend, our communities will soon lose their vibrancy and this unique aspect of local culture will be lost.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I have discussed with the Federation of Merchants' Association on how to help heartland shops improve productivity and enhance their products and services to attract more customers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, how we can provide opportunities for young people to start their business within the community, to take the first step in becoming their own boss.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When I visited my constituency, I noticed that the vicinity near Toa Payoh West Market has attracted some young people to set up shop.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One of them is a successful ice-cream shop known as Creamier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This shop was started in 2011 by three Singaporeans in their 30s.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Their business is good and they have attracted many customers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They have subsequently expanded their business by opening a cafe named Sunday Folks at Chip Bee Gardens at Holland Village.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Recently, during a visit to the National Design Centre, I found out that the handmade ice-cream created and produced by Creamier has won recognition from the centre as a top-class locally created product.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This shows that their creativity and design are, indeed, outstanding.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Apart from cafes, we can also consider setting aside some heartland retail space to create an entrepreneurial hub, so that startups, entrepreneurs and investors can set up shop in the HDB heartlands.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, the heartland shops could also consider providing part-time or temporary job opportunities for residents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This would encourage more seniors to continue working and stay active.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It would also help some Singaporeans to return to the workforce on a part-time basis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In this way, they will be able to take care of their families and earn some income at the same time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must be bold in thinking of new ideas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Only with innovation and determination can we achieve the desired outcome for these schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When necessary, they should move with the times, improve existing policies and schemes to further support entrepreneurship and small businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, I will now conclude in English.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The third thing we need to do to promote innovation is that we must stay connected to the world and be open to different sources of ideas and talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes attracting overseas Singaporeans to return home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They bring useful perspectives and networks from abroad.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To be an innovative society, we also need to have a largeness of spirit to welcome and integrate international talent, especially in sectors where we are still growing our local talent pool.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Being open to international talent does not mean we dilute the focus on developing Singaporean talent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The two objectives are not mutually exclusive and can, in fact, reinforce each other.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ultimately, what we want is to strengthen Singapore to benefit Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Page: 54 When I met our local film producers and designers, they supported keeping Singapore open to international talent, so that our creative industries can remain vibrant and competitive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They also saw value in having young local talent work with these foreign experts, to broaden their perspectives, deepen their skills and build stronger networks that could lead to possible partnerships in future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have to manage our population growth carefully.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: That will hurt us as it will lead to slower economic growth, fewer jobs and a less vibrant society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I know this is a sensitive topic to raise in a maiden speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But I believe it is an important issue for Singapore's future, which we need to discuss and find the right balance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Earlier this month, there was an article in The Sunday Times by Leo Lewis entitled "Japan's deflated generation".

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It described how Japan's ageing population, deflation and slow economic growth over two decades have produced a new generation of young Japanese who are afraid of taking risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They do not dream big but look for small moments of happiness in their current situation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One of them, a fashion school student, said, "I often surprise myself.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: She lived in a time of war." When I read the article, I asked myself, will Singapore end up like that?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Or do we have the vision and courage to innovate and chart a different path?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One of our key success factors has been our ability to stay connected to the world and be open to new ideas and talent from abroad.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We must preserve these elements if we want to remain an innovative society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is not easy to achieve and there will be tensions, but we must find a way to strike a good balance between these objectives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If we simply do what is convenient and choose the path of least resistance, including pandering to populist sentiments or avoiding difficult topics, we are effectively short-changing our future generations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we will end up like the Japan which Leo Lewis talked about in his article.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: That is not the future which I want to see for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: That is not the kind of society which I want my children to inherit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The PAP Government believes in facing difficult issues with courage and determination and working closely with Singaporeans to tackle our challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government does not have all the answers and we cannot do everything on our own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We need to work with partners from the private and people sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I see more scope for such collaboration going forward as our challenges become increasingly complex and multifaceted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But it does not mean that we simply step back and do less.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Having a reduced role for Government does not necessarily mean other sectors will become more innovative and dynamic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: What we want is to grow the pie for all stakeholders, and for the Government to catalyse and enable stronger collaboration and innovation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: More importantly, we must have leaders in all sectors who walk the talk and who say what they mean and mean what they say.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: After all, we know that actions speak louder than words.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singaporeans are a pragmatic, resourceful and resilient people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are the descendants of lion-hearted Pioneers who built this country.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Together, we have come this far and built this place from scratch.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Together, we have created a country that we feel proud to call home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And, together, we will build a better Singapore for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have faith that the Singapore that we wish to see over the next 50 years will happen if the Government continues to take responsible actions with the next 50 years in mind.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The President's call "to develop a caring nation" and "renew our economy" resonates strongly with the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is within the Labour Movement's DNA to care for our workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, NTUC has been a strong voice to advocate changes for many groups of workers through all the various initiatives and help given by our support centres, such as U-Care Centre, Migrant Workers' Centre (MWC), U-PME, e2i, U-Family, U-Live and many others.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Centre for Domestic Employees (CDE) is the latest to join this spectrum.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through our Social Enterprises, NTUC has helped Singaporean workers and their families stretch their dollar and made essential goods and services more easily available.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These Social Enterprises brought together a platter of opportunities for work, live and play.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moving forward, our Social Enterprises will rethink, redesign and reinvent products and services to cater for the changing life-cycle needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore has changed remarkably over the past 50 years and the Labour Movement is presented with new challenges as we continue to grow.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Technological advancement, globalisation of jobs, shorter product cycles and future manufacturing demand that we think out of the box to ensure that the Singaporean workforce can adapt to these changes and our economy remains competitive.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workers are now better educated and have greater aspirations.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are choosing alternate career paths, such as freelance and contract jobs.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This re-emphasises the importance of the Labour Movement in reinventing itself, not only to remain relevant and continue to be the strongest voice of workers, 	Page: 56 but also to be part of Singapore's effort "to develop a caring nation".

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are facing a tight labour market and slowing workforce growth, coupled with structural unemployment and shortage of skilled labour.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are worrying trends that must be addressed as we renew our economy.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And in weathering these, my deepest concerns are on the widening income gaps that affect our workers in the lowest percentile of the economic pie.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The real income growth could have been worse for this group of workers if not for numerous interventions, such as providing Workfare Income Supplement, introducing mandatory Progressive Wage Models in low-wage sectors, making specific National Wages Council (NWC) recommendations for low-wage workers, and providing training to upgrade and deepen their skills.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must take bolder steps to address the widening income gap and, at the same time, ensure sustainability of our efforts and their outcomes.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I strongly call for more affirmative action to give a hand to our low-wage workers to cushion the oncoming impact.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are several areas that I would like to bring to the House's attention.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was a laudable move in 2012 when NWC made specific recommendations to help low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unfortunately, many workers in non-unionised companies and those working in outsourced industries still had not received the recommended dollar quantum increase.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is another aspect that can bring about better pay packets for our workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Government can play a greater role in encouraging their service providers with many low-wage workers to give annual increments (AI) and annual wage supplement (AWS).

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Government procurement officers can be more worker-centric by being more proactive to look into the welfare accorded to the outsourced workers by their potential service providers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: All these moves, with the Government taking the lead, will create a ripple effect, gradually evolving to become an industry norm.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Government has shown strong support for the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) in the three low-wage sectors.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond these three sectors, PWM should be introduced to other sectors to better the livelihoods of more low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: All Government-linked companies must be encouraged to be the catalysts to take the lead in implementing PWM by insisting that all major projects and tendering should incorporate PWM for the workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have moved from price-based outsourcing and have been advocating best sourcing over the past decade.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The nuances of this mechanism have allowed the stakeholders to take advantage of some loopholes.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The second big area that I would like to touch on is the President's call to "renew our economy".

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Renewing our economy will entail restructuring to improve productivity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC and its affiliated unions will give its strong support to companies to adopt technology and innovation in their work processes.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Government has invested heavily to encourage productivity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Management should leverage on this and spearhead the productivity drive within the company and build a culture that supports innovation at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Without doubt, the unions and our workers will do our part to support new ways of harnessing technology and innovation and by contributing ideas for improvement at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is to ensure such efforts gain momentum and sustainability in the long run.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When companies restructure, it would bring about a need for new skills to facilitate operations.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will demand that both companies and employees invest in continuous training and skills upgrading to ensure that the workforce remains competent and relevant to the changing needs of the industry and resilient at all times.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While employers may bring in new employees, this also presents an opportunity to strengthen our fort on the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There should be no compromises and our SkillsFuture initiative must achieve its key deliverables.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):  For the Malay/Muslim community, we must be prepared since Singapore's economy is expected to go through a challenging phase and this will affect many local workers here.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many training opportunities to enhance skills or perform new jobs are made available with the Government's assistance.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is important that these opportunities are used in order to help their employers make the necessary restructuring measures to improve their competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This can affect the ability of our Malay workers to get good jobs when Singapore's economy undergoes renewal.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Government should also take more aggressive steps to help workers, especially the low-wage workers, to overcome this challenge.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC would like the Government to give more focus and attention to low wage workers, since the income gap is becoming wider, compared to other workers.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, the tripartite partners must champion new approaches to improve productivity by reinventing business processes, rethinking creative use of robots and machines and redesign deployment of manpower.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We will face failures as we chart forward, but we should not be discouraged because every wrong attempt presents an opportunity to move a step forward more intelligently.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The difference 	Page: 58 between the impossible and possible in SG100 will depend on the determination of every Singaporean to make it happen.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With that, I support the Motion to thank the President for his Address.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The 13th Parliament commences at a time when Singapore is entering a new phase of its development.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: SG50 celebrations helped Singaporeans from all walks of life appreciate how far we have come as a nation, but, as the happy year drew to a close, the new one began on a rather grim note.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The President is right to recognise that the journey ahead will not be an easy one as we cope with the challenges posed by a slowing mature economy, an ageing population, greater social diversity and continuing threats of terrorism.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Amongst the five key aims that the President has laid out for this term of Government, I would like to focus my speech on how we may renew our economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is critically important that we transform our economy to meet the needs of the global marketplace of the next 50 years, for only then can we hope to provide for all that Singaporeans wish for, whether it be good jobs, security, housing, healthcare, transport or welfare for the less privileged.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The year 2016 has gotten off to a rocky start, with tumbling stock markets, slumping commodity prices and world news dominated by security incidents.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The International Monetary Fund rated China at the top of their list of concerns in 2016, and the impact of its reduced rate of growth will continue to reverberate through Asian economies, not least in Singapore, because of our open economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Help the more vulnerable amongst us to ride out the coming storms.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am particularly concerned about how certain segments, such as the older PMEs, will cope.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Once displaced, they often find it hard to rejoin the workforce.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Targeted Government interventions can help this group transition to new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I urge the Government to do more to systematically retrain career switchers, to provide mid-career Earn and Learn Programmes to help them secure new jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should explore how IE Singapore can tap the rich experience of older PMEs to help companies expand overseas, especially into emerging markets.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many of these are wizened and street-smart from years of hard knocks.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They could represent an invaluable resource for companies trying to internationalise.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In fact, mature PMEs, whose children have already grown up, may be raring to find their second wind in foreign lands, flying the flags of both their employer and of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have some suggestions for the committee to consider.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, despite the efforts of many in the past few years, productivity growth continues to elude us.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must now be prepared to make drastic changes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is time to do away with generic Government support schemes that served more as subsidy schemes to help businesses defray fixed and equipment costs, rather than to address their underlying lack of competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Future schemes should focus on helping firms create new, innovative and differentiated products and services that are truly competitive internationally.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Schemes should also be tailored at the sectoral level and streamlined for easy access.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must also make a concerted effort to invest in indigenous Singapore technology – innovations made in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In fact, developing globally competitive local firms was already listed as a key objective of the Economic Review Committee recommendation in 1998, yet we are still far from realising this ambition.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To achieve this, we need to take bold steps to create an ecosystem that enables targeted growth clusters to proliferate, multiply and develop depth in capabilities that are competitive internationally.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is much we can learn from South Korea on how the Government can enable growth of new clusters and build indigenous capabilities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Korean government rolled out a comprehensive strategy to build the movie, drama and music industry as a new cluster, after the Asian Financial Crisis.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As many K-Pop and soap opera addicts amongst us will attest, this has also promoted the Korean brand internationally.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Some of the more significant government initiatives include lowering entry barriers by providing artists access to many movie-making locations, government seed funding and assistance in market development with the Busan International Film Festival and the encouragement for chaebols, the large Korean groups, to enter the entertainment industry in order to provide the investment needed to produce blockbusters.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The government also played an active role to foster talent by promoting majors in entertainment, including pop singing, film making and acting, and even setting up top-quality master's degrees, such as the Hanyang Entertainment Master's degree, for the development of management and leadership skills in the entertainment industry.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Another innovative government initiative is the setting up of the Korea Technology Finance Corporation (KOTEC), a special purpose financial institution to provide funds to technology-innovative SMEs with weak collateral capabilities, in the form of credit guarantees for new technology.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, companies, large and small, can benefit from collaborating with one another when they 	Page: 60 venture overseas.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Large Singapore corporations which have secured overseas projects should be encouraged, perhaps through tax incentives, to bring along a whole collection of smaller Singapore suppliers as part of their expansion internationally.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This will help smaller SMEs kick-start their overseas ventures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Companies can also benefit greatly by collaborating in skills development, jointly uplifting talent for their industries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is the norm in some of the most competitive and innovative economies in the world, such as Switzerland and Sweden.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should explore incentives for companies to come together to set up shared training facilities and to co-develop training programmes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, Sweden has elegantly built training demand and employer support into the design of continuing education, and HVE programmes have achieved strong outcomes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I hope a similar approach can be adopted by Singapore industries and supported by the SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: SkillsFuture is a key initiative to sustain Singapore's competitiveness by raising the quality of our workforce and refresh our value proposition in the global marketplace with new skills and capabilities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I hope the setting up of a new Statutory Board, SkillsFuture Singapore, under MOE, will enable as robust and strong a sector in continuing education as is currently the case with our formative education sector.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: At this point, I wish to declare my interests as CEO of the Wealth Management Institute and Temasek Management Services Academy, in the interests of transparency.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government has announced sectoral manpower strategies to identify medium-term manpower and skills plans for each key sector in order to support industry growth and deepen expertise.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But for the sectoral manpower strategies to be successful, we need employers and employees to be fully on board.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The skills ladder identified must be owned by the industry, anchoring training efforts.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Career and pay prospects must also be commensurate with skill and competency levels.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Targeted training solutions should be readily available to enable individuals to advance their career by climbing the skills ladder in their area of interest.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have received feedback that many programmes in the continuing education sector are too generic and not targeted enough.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is an urgent need for training solutions to be aligned to the skills ladder, enabling individuals to achieve mastery and expertise in their jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To jump-start the sector, I strongly suggest that SkillsFuture Singapore consider the Swedish HVE model to bring industry and training providers together, in the way I had described earlier in my speech.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have all heard the saying, "What gets measured gets done".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should, therefore, develop a set of metrics to track the outcomes of our lifelong learning initiatives, with clear plans to achieve a certain goal or reach a certain level, within a specified time.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Furthermore, we need to leverage SkillsFuture to develop a strong Singaporean Core in the workplace, especially amongst PMEs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And the success of their EP applications and renewals should be influenced by the extent to which they 	Page: 61 fulfil their obligations to train and develop locals.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For innovation to thrive, people must be willing to experiment and explore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But the fear of failure drives Singaporeans to "play safe", rather than "play to win".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must foster a culture that is more tolerant of mistakes, where failure is less stigmatised and missteps are seen as merely learning opportunities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: No successful Silicon Valley entrepreneur is ashamed to tell you of his mistakes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Instead, they are proud to tell the tale of how they picked themselves up, dusted themselves off and bounced back from adversity.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They are willing to try again because failure is not a "bad word".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Beyond the willingness to take risks, most successful entrepreneurs also possess an infectious belief in the cause they pursue.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They have a strong sense of purpose and mission in life and will not be easily deterred from chasing their dreams.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many believe they are working for something bigger than themselves.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And it is this faith that will lead others to overcome obstacles and drive innovation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whether it is to find the cure for cancer, to be the biggest star on Youtube, or to save the planet, the dreams of Singaporeans will light the way to our tomorrows.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must nurture this precious spirit and inspire beliefs, arm Singaporeans with the fortitude to deal with adversity and infect them with the hope of success and then set them free to create and build a better life for others.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must teach them what it means to "play to win".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And come what may, we will always have one another.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: May this House lead the way, with the clear-eyed determination, courage and wisdom of our forebears.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree with the first line of the President's Address that "SG50 was a defining year for Singaporeans".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we now move into SG51, we are entering a new era.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many citizens whom I have spoken to, feel a sense of excitement and optimism.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, this is also tempered with some caution and concern, due to the new challenges that Singapore is facing.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Externally, we are dealing with an increasingly borderless world that military strategists would term as volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous, or "VUCA".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This VUCA world presents economic, security and environmental challenges to a small country like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At home, we have a more pluralistic Singaporean society defined by a greater multiplicity of voices, perspectives and opinions on what is best for the country.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The new generation of Singaporeans has to deal with education, transport, housing and healthcare landscapes that have evolved, and will continue to evolve, over the next few years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, we are not so much talking 	Page: 62 about a "new normal", but a "New Singapore".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would first elaborate on how we can develop the next generation of Singaporeans and imbue them with the resilience and the necessary life skills to navigate this increasingly complex global and social landscape.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, I would like to comment on how we can better strengthen our social fabric and community ties in this pluralistic society, so that we can tap on the collective wisdom of the crowd, while avoiding divisive forces that might segment our nation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our early leaders and Pioneers lived in a unique era where the exceptional circumstances that surrounded Singapore at that time produced tough and resilient men and women who were mature beyond their years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it is impossible to replicate the exact same political climate and social settings of that period, I believe that it is important for us to imbue our youths today with the spirit of resilience that kept our Pioneer Generation going when things got tough.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have heard "resilience" being mentioned quite a few times in this august Chamber in the past few days.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My "resilience" is defined by the American Psychological Association as "the ability to adapt well in the face of adversity, trauma, tragedy, threat or significant sources of stress." Contrary to what many people would think, resilience does not require extraordinary fortitude and strength.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, it is a concept that can be taught.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Renowned psychologist Dr Martin Seligman created the Penn Resilience Program at the University of Pennsylvania for young adults and children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This highly successful programme has been run in many schools ranging from those in the US suburbs and inner cities, to schools across China.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Youths and young adults who had undergone the programme were found to be more optimistic; they were more likely to interpret setbacks as temporary and regard them as learning opportunities; and they were less likely to display depression-like symptoms later in life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In short, they were more resilient than their peers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While training our youths in resilience will prepare them to ride the waves of change and challenges that will undoubtedly come their way, we also need to give them the tools that will allow them to master their own future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That brings me to my next point: creating the "I" shaped graduate.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Allow me, Sir, to speak more on this concept.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The horizontal bar at the top of the capital "I" is the breadth of knowledge that is embodied by the same horizontal bar that denotes the T-shaped education mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The vertical bar in the "I" is the depth of subject matter knowledge and technical skills that will help our students master the key competencies of the field of their choosing.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Page: 63 What I believe is important and is currently lacking, is the horizontal bar at the bottom of the "I".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that the bottom stroke on the "I" should be anchored by life skills.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While there is currently no one recognised universal standard of what might constitute a "life skill," Ellen Galinsky, co-founder of the Family and Work Institute in the US, gives us some insight.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The IB Learner Profile is designed to facilitate 21st century learning and aims to provide the platform for lifelong learning and to give its graduates all the characteristics that are necessary to succeed in a 21st century society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are skills that will allow our youths to not only move across different career stages and pathways, but also allow them to traverse the diverse and sometimes, uncomfortable scenarios that this VUCA world will throw at them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just as the base stroke of the capital "I‟ is what differentiates it from a "T‟, so, too, will these skills and attitudes strengthen and anchor the character of our youths.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The aim should be to go beyond broad and general statements in textbooks and to adopt a deep-rooted approach in building these skills into the whole learning experience.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this way, these skills will become second-nature to our youths by the time they reach adulthood.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will help us build a generation of confident Singaporeans who can rise above adversity and grasp their future, and Singapore's future, firmly in their hands.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has always prided itself as a multiracial and multi-religious society where no one is disadvantaged or discriminated against because of the colour of their skin or because of their faith.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we continue to work through various grassroots organisations and committees to ensure that Singapore remains a tolerant society, we also have to acknowledge that the communal mix of Singapore today has changed over the years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Among us are foreigners, Permanent Residents (PRs) and new citizens who have decided to sink their roots into our country, which highlights the social reality that the "New Singapore" is facing today.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This reality was acknowledged by the President in his Address when he commented on how we are becoming more diverse, and posed the question as to whether we will "remain a cohesive society, or will our differences pull us apart?" The oft-repeated message that Singapore has its roots as a migrant society and that immigrants need to be introduced in a calibrated manner to augment the low fertility rate is something that has been absorbed into the collective consciousness of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What we need to do, however, is to think about how we can better integrate these PRs and, especially new 	Page: 64 citizens, into our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At a community event welcoming new citizens last year, I observed that there were quite a few new citizens who had trouble communicating because of their inability to speak basic English.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Grassroots leaders have also provided feedback that some of the new citizens tend to not get involved in community activities, because they feel that they are not able to communicate with their fellow residents of different ethnicities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To respond to that, I would like to say, "I double confirm, agree, with what my brother says lah".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I would also like to add that English, specifically standard Singapore English, is possibly the most common language that is used in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is the main language of commerce, information and, more critically, of communication across the different ethnic groups.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is, in short, our lingua franca today.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would allow them to develop a deeper understanding of the wider community and society that they are in.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These measures would, undoubtedly, help new citizens assimilate and integrate better into our social and community fabric and that, in turn, would allow them to better contribute to Singapore's growth and development.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would also allow all Singaporeans to have what the President referred to as, "a shared understanding of what unites and binds us to one another." Sir, Singapore has achieved much in the last 50 years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the horizon is a "New Singapore" that faces a set of radically new challenges that are different from what we once encountered.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we will adapt and adjust to meet these new challenges, let us also continue to hold true to our unassailable principles of democracy, meritocracy and equality of ethnicities and religions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will ensure that Singapore will always be that special and unique place in the world that Singaporeans are proud to call home.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Together, we will navigate these uncharted waters with courage and look ahead to SG51 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On this note, Sir, I support the Motion of Thanks to the President.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In his speech earlier, Mr Dennis Tan raised a few points which really touched upon the work of the Ministry of Law and I thought it might be helpful if I responded to them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Page: 65 His two main points under the Legal Aid and the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme can be considered under the broad rubric of access to justice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Dennis Tan had called for a review of the $10,000 cap on the means test for legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I thought that I should share what has been done because, sometimes, the perception is that that parameter of the $10,000 cap is too strict.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
