text: In fact, what we have done over the last couple of years is to expand the coverage, even though the amount of $10,000 has not itself increased.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The net effect of the amendments was to expand the coverage of legal aid to include more vulnerable applicants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To qualify for legal aid, the individual must have an annual disposable income of $10,000 or below, and disposable capital of $10,000 or below.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, it is a double-barrelled test, meaning you have to meet both the income test and the capital test.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The thing about the income test is that most people have the impression that when we say $10,000 income, that means your gross income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They think that so long as you earn more than $10,000 per annum, that disqualifies you.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What we actually look at is disposable income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, you look at the gross income, minus off all the things which you can deduct, like the cost-of-living expenses and so on, and you see what remains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What remains is the disposable income, and, if that is $10,000 or less, then you would qualify.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, someone could have a gross income of $30,000, for example, but if after deducting all the items that are permitted to be deducted, your disposable income is, let us say, $9,000, then you would qualify.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What we did in 2013 was to increase the deductibles, so that more people would qualify.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This extended coverage does not even take into account the Legal Aid Director's discretion to depart from the general means test in certain circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Just to reiterate the point I made earlier – although we have not increased the $10,000 cap, we have, nevertheless, increased and expanded the coverage of legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I move on now to criminal legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Dennis Tan noted that more people had stepped up for pro bono work and called for others to step up as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I should say here that we are completely in agreement that more volunteer lawyers and others who are in a position to do so, should step up for pro bono legal work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What I want to do is to highlight what the Government has done in the last couple of years and to indicate that it is also our mission to encourage pro bono work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In May 2015, the Minister for Law Mr K Shanmugam launched the Enhanced Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Law Society is the organisation that runs the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The lawyers deal with the Pro Bono Services office of the Law Society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But the funding now comes directly from the Ministry of Law, given to the Law Society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The increased funding covers the honoraria, operational costs and disbursements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Page: 66 We should have a look at the contrast before and after the provision of funding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In 2014, there were 1,780 applications for criminal legal aid, out of which only 431 were granted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is not the same as market rate, but that honorarium goes some way towards defraying their legal fees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In effect, by providing the increased funding, my Ministry is supporting criminal legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I should also say that there is another aspect of access to justice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I talked about legal aid and criminal legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There is another category of cases where it may not actually be necessary to have a lawyer because of the nature of the claim, but you, nevertheless, want to have your dispute resolved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Two very good examples of this are the procedures under the Prevention from Harassment Act and the Community Dispute Resolution Act 2015.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Those two Acts were specifically designed to allow individuals to make their claims in person, and not to have to incur legal costs and expenses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If you take these three things that I have mentioned, you can see that, very slowly, what we have done is, we have been boosting and supporting legal aid, we have been boosting and supporting criminal legal aid, and at the same time, increasing access to justice by simplifying procedures and making it easier for individuals to have their disputes resolved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: What amounts to a reasonable time would, of course, depend on the circumstances of the case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think it has been explained in this Parliament before that we need to strike a balance between the right of the accused person to consult his legal counsel and the public interest in ensuring that the Police is able to effectively investigate each case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the end of the day, we have to carefully balance the needs of the accused person on the one hand and the public interest on the other hand, and that means to enable the Police to conduct complete and thorough investigations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Every country must find the right balance that suits its circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Our system is well-established; it has proven effective over the years to help keep Singapore safe and secure and our crime rates low.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We owe it to our children to keep the country strong and our economy vibrant so that they can also chase the rainbows and fulfil aspirations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That includes the tens of thousands fresh graduates that join the workforce each year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the last 50 years, we earned our prosperity largely by value adding and we are pretty good at that.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This strategy has enabled companies large and small to ride on the global economic cycles and thrive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Enter the value creating and innovative economy, a term that we have be hearing a lot in the last few months since the Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) was set up.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is the next logical step, and it is also time that we make bold moves to open up new growth frontiers and expand possibilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Any restructuring and any major re-positioning of the economy of this magnitude comes with its challenges and risks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There will be disruptions to existing businesses and jobs, and the outcomes are by no means guaranteed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fortunately for Singapore, we are in a position of strength.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our strong economic fundamentals, our solid financials and the adaptable workforce can help us weather the risks and to tackle the multiple challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our hard-earned political and social stability also give us the scope to think and act in the long-term interest of the country – in contrast with many of our regional competitors who are bogged down with their domestic political impasses or social disharmony.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For a small country with unchangeable physical constraints, further advances in digitisation and easier access to the global knowledge pool actually works better for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With smarter resource optimisation, greater technological adoption and enhanced global linkages, our smallness as a country can be less of a disadvantage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the future landscape, it may well be the case where the big no longer beats the small.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is the fast that beats the slow and the imaginative that will eat the lunches of the uninspired.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we need to be among the early movers and trendsetters, and to exploit the fast-expanding networked world to our advantage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The key is how we identify the future opportunities and how we could transform ourselves to seize those opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The CFE has that difficult task on their plate.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Finance, Trade and Industry looks forward to participating in discussions and engaging the CFE on the various suggestions and recommendations in the months ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this era of fast-paced technological changes and, as a result, shortened obsolescence cycle, it is increasingly very difficult to predict future product trends.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We may be none the wiser about what the next "Big Thing" would be – more than ever before.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, building hard infrastructure ahead of demand, something that the Government is very good at, may not be as straightforward in the future world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, the road ahead towards a value creating economy is more about developing soft infrastructures to become an innovative and entrepreneurial society – and thereby be able take advantage on a range of possible scenarios that comes our way.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore has been consistently recognised for its business-friendly environment and producing graduates excelling in mathematics and science.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We also have among the best legal framework for intellectual property (IP) protection rights in the world as well as the high availability of venture capital and research and development (R&D) funding.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, it was not the lack of support schemes for the businesses or the regulatory frameworks being less or not innovation-friendly enough, that is the impediment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The smart and hardworking officers of the various economic agencies are always on top of this and will continue to add new schemes, finesse existing schemes as well as to keep up with the best practices around the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I think we only need to look at the SPRING Singapore website to see the range of schemes available to help the start-ups.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am sure the CFE will further add more new ideas and new approaches in developing innovative capabilities for companies and to expand our market linkages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can debate that at a later date, while the new approaches that we should explore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But what I think we need do more, and what we are talking more about today, is the human dimension of innovation and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The human factor is the spirit and purpose of innovation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the economy of the future, having good subject-based knowledge is important but not good enough on its own.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to foster critical and creative thinking as well as develop behavioural and social skills.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It just stresses out everyone – the students, parents and teachers and even the Members of Parliament, when the parents come to see us to appeal for the scores and to get into the schools.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, it stresses out everybody with very little gain in return besides generating the national examinations scores to help us do the school postings.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, it risks producing an education system that dampens the innovative and entrepreneur spirit.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Students may score well in exams for those subjects, but they may have little passion or interest in that subject matter, which some recent international studies have shown.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How does stopping CCA during the PSLE year or O-level year help in developing the students that we want?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is just going to increase the tension and add more stress.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to develop students to be self-assured, confident and, for that matter, to be able to multi-task.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I agree with Minister Ong Ye Kung that we should not be too obsessed with numbers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Often, when I attend schools' annual award ceremonies, the Principal's speech and presentations sometimes really sound like a shareholder's Annual General Meeting (AGM).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There will be a lot of performance indicators being shown.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I do not think numbers are that important.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The speech should be about motivating the students and motivating the parents as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do believe that there exists a distribution of strengths and abilities for each cohort of students.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There will be some who may appear to do less well in a whole bell curve, but who, nevertheless, have the inclination to think out-of-the-box, and are perhaps less "conventional" than others in their learning attitude.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Perhaps, they have more of the "maverick-like" thinking.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are the people who may have street savviness to be entrepreneurial and to venture into uncharted waters.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These may those who may not do well in schools, very much like Jack Ma, Steve Jobs or George Quek of "BreadTalk".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the early years, they tend to daydream a lot – I agree with Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam that some of it is good.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, we should not dampen their natural curiosity, especially during their early formative years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Help them, open up to them and give them second chances and if not, third chances even if they have not done well academically in their early years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And that the learning institutions will help Singaporeans discover their strengths and interests and thereby cultivate passions and fulfil aspirations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am sure this is music to our ears.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are all necessary moves to become an innovative and entrepreneurial society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must not just say it or signal it, but also do it in every sense and every aspect.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another human aspect that is essential for a flourishing innovative and entrepreneurial scene is the existence of lively communities of innovators and the related stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are very much informal social structures that may involve the university alumni support groups, networks of overseas Singaporeans, mentors or serial entrepreneurs, among others, to create buzz, facilitate sharing and mentoring, and also to foster collaborations and partnerships.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to place-make of some sort to get the entrepreneurs and innovators to come together to participate in lively forums and to leverage on the value of interdependencies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Universities and polytechnics are among the suitable convenors for such social groups and should be encouraged to initiate such communities to form.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Continual learning and seeking new knowledge are the best response to the rapidly changing technological landscape and also equally fast changing business models.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must keep up and not be on the wrong part of the skills mismatch curve as the landscape changes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Coupled with the emergence of the so-called "gig economy" – something that Mr Ang Hin Kee has talked about with the freelancers – the concept of full-time employment or permanent employment may well be under threat.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have already seen how Uber has disrupted the traditional taxi business and the livelihood of taxi drivers, or how waves of digitisations by fintech companies are threatening traditional bank financing and bank intermediation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, we have to make learning continual, whether it is by seeking new knowledge or learning new skills a way of life and actually enjoy and be motivated by it.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, continuous learning should be made more accessible to all in ITEs, polytechnics and universities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can calibrate the right fee structure, but we should make it accessible to all.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should also ensure that it will not be at the expense of places set aside for each cohort of new undergraduates.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over time, we need to blur the lines between learning in schools and training during employment, and it should be a continuous journey.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Going forward, we literally have to think like a start-up in the way we respond to opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not just the businesses and individuals but the entire ecosystem including the educational institutions, social stakeholders, business associations and, crucially, the Government and regulators.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is very much part of the interdependencies needed for the ecosystem to flourish.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having a diverse range of talents will strengthen our position as an innovation hub.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we must remain open and not be averse to an innovator or entrepreneur from a foreign land coming here to innovate and venture.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is all a necessary part of the buzz and vibrancy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Staying open and staying plugged to the global network has strengthened our position as a key economic hub in the past.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to continue to stay open, to stay connected and to stay open to changes, and that way, we will give our local entrepreneurs and local innovators access to more opportunities, and it enhances our chances of succeeding as a value creating economy.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The next chapter, in the words of President Tony Tan, will "see Singapore progress as an exceptional nation with a thriving economy and a caring an inclusive society".

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is apt that the President has called on Singaporeans to renew our pledge at the half-century mark of our nationhood to build a better Singapore as one people, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But our pledge goes beyond calling on Singaporeans to merely unite as one people to build a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The frameworks of our pledge support good politics and espouse the values of justice and equality to be the foundation of our democracy so that our people as a nation can achieve happiness, prosperity and progress.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Although the President did not talk about justice and equality when he spoke on good politics, these values are non-negotiable if we want to get our politics right in the next chapter.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The President has reminded us that as Members of Parliament, we all have a responsibility to do our best for our people, regardless of our party affiliation.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: About 18 months into my first term as Member of Parliament for Hougang, a resident asked me if his child would be given the Edusave Bursary, will the child receive the award from me?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I believe all of you know the answer so I will dispense with that.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Nevertheless, I thank the President for the reminder, and I can assure the President that the Workers' Party (WP) will do its best for the people while we wait with bated breath the impending improvement to our political system, as mentioned in his Address.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Our way of life as we know and enjoy is now under threat.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These are indeed dangerous and uncertain times we are living in.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Thus, I fully support the President's call for Singaporeans to remain steadfast and united under these trying times, when misguided extremists are trying to tear this world apart through violence and fear.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The war on terrorism at our homefront is psychological as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We cannot influence the people beyond our shores, but we can surely remind our own to value and preserve the peace and harmony we have here.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The walk with terrorism probably begins with some form of self-radicalisation, and such activities are impossible to prevent and they usually go under the radar.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Self-radicalised individuals will probably pose one of the biggest threats to our security and the preservation of our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Our cultural and religious diversity is a testament to that.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Our work at achieving our unique interfaith, interracial and intersectoral harmony should be told to each successive generation to counter those dangerous and destructive ideologies propagated by radicals with misguided and violent intent.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I share Senior Minister of State Ong Ye Kung's observation that it is a sight to behold to see religious symbols of different faiths side by side and opposite each other in our HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: But behind the cold existence of these religious artefacts lie a whole lot of effort in exercising tolerance, consideration and good neighbourliness.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: These stories must be passed down from generation to generation in all forms and means.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We have to start young to sow the seeds of religious and racial tolerance in our classrooms, and hope for the best that our children will be able to discern dangerous ideologies online and reject them outright.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We all have a part to play in this – this Ministry, the schools and most important of all, the parents – to make Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Government has made many changes to our education system over the years, in search of a balanced approach to prep our young for a world that is constantly evolving.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The change the educator intends to make in the next chapter must stand the test of time because lives are at stake.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It must result in fostering a generation of thinking, self-motivated and innovative, and confident students.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We have to invest heavily in our human capital because it is our only hope at becoming an exceptional nation.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Prime Minister has shared that his biggest achievement as Head of Government was the emphasis he had placed on education when he first assumed office.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In his first National Day Rally, the Prime Minister talked briefly about the "Teach Less, Learn More" concept of getting the maximum benefit out of educating our students through quality teaching.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The "Teach Less, Learn More" model has found its way into schools in the past decade.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Can our educators say for sure that this model really works because our students continue to do well in high-stake examinations, despite being taught less in school?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Has the shift to focus on quality teaching instead of quantity teaching resulted in better desired outcomes of education?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Moving away from basic education, how far are we prepared to inspire our young to shoot for the stars in the pursuit of their interests at the tertiary level?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is the Government pull out all the stops to attract a Nobel Laureate to take up a research or teaching chair at one of the local universities so that the Laureate can inspire a student to dream big?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In the next chapter, it is my hope that Singapore will produce a Nobel Laureate of our own.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Almost 900 Nobel Laureates have been recognised since 1901.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Countries such as Azerbaijan, Cypress, Algeria, Guatemala, St Lucia, and Madagascar, to name a few, have all produced a Laureate or two each.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is this Government prepared likewise with the same vigour in our human capital outside of sports?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: A Nobel Laureate is recognised by his or her own country of birth, so we cannot engineer that by import.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Many American universities were intricately involved in the US Space programme from Project Mercury to Project Apollo and to the Space Shuttle programme.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I wish our young inventors well and hope that their inventions will go into commercial production someday.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The R&D Framework under the National Research Foundation cuts across many Ministries.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am unable to determine who gets the lion share of the R&D budget, but I do hope that our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) will be given ample opportunities to nurture our young Singaporeans into exceptional scientists and inventors if the future.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We all want a clean, effective and accountable Government, but not at the expense of less democracy, justice and equality.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I am also quietly confident that Singaporeans of all faiths will stand united to reject terrorism and attempts by misguided extremists to sow seeds of discord among the diverse and peace-loving people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And finally, Madam, we all know education is not all about classroom and examination.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: However, the values we impart to our young must stand the test of time.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I fully agree with the five key priorities of the Government as outlined by the President.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The devil, of course, is in the details.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Citizens who cannot add value enough are at risk of being left behind.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the words of Albert Einstein, "The significant problems we face today cannot be solved at the same level of thinking we were at when the problems were first created." Madam, let me first share a simple poem that shows the different levels that we can view and address the challenges we face in life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This poem by a Ms Portia Nelson is entitled "Autobiography in 5 Short Chapters".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a deep hole in the sidewalk.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It takes me forever to find a way out.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chapter II I walk down the same street.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a deep hole in the sidewalk.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I can't believe I am in the same place.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It still takes a long time to get out.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chapter III I walk down the same street.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a deep hole in the sidewalk.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I still fall in ... it's a habit.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chapter IV I walk down the same street.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a deep hole in the sidewalk.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Often, when it involves entrenched mindsets and structures, it will take more than patching up or just walking around them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We may have to walk down another street or make U-turns.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, in the space of Learning; next, in Caring and Doing.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: On Learning – the future of learning will be far from the teacher-directed, traditional classroom settings we are used to.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the future, learning can take place anytime, anywhere; not constrained by time or the physical dimensions of a school.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We can choose from a quiver of tools, devices and learning solutions that can be face-to-face, online or blended.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: If SkillsFuture were to succeed, then learners will come in all ages with all backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They will have to be self-driven lifelong learners – a habit that is not yet pervasive today.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many positive changes have taken place in the education landscape in Singapore in the last decades – learning support; online learning resources; special education; teacher recruitment and compensation; and, most recently, to me, a brilliant move of having MOE actively take on the SkillsFuture portfolio in Continual Education and Training (CET) for adult learners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our pre-occupation with academic scores is an outcome of years of conditioning, a choice borne out of a perceived lack of other better avenues of social mobility.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Academic rigour is a good thing, but it becomes an impairment when even academically stronger students start seeking extra help through tuition.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is hard to cultivate or inculcate a love for learning when all that matters to the majority is the score from a series of high-stake examinations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When the curiosity and love for learning is snuffed out when one is young, it will be hard to re-ignite it after one's formal school years when he leaves the school gate.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second unhealthy "P" of our education landscape is parentocracy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is commonly described as a phenomenon in which a child's education is shaped according to the wishes and opportunities that can be afforded by his parents.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As the stakes of academic scores become higher, parentocracy will further rear its ugly head.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Parentocracy restricts social mobility and can unfairly deprive those with lesser resources and networks, undermining the development of their potential.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the case of overseas exchange programmes or internships, the more affluent parents will be better able to put their children through.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to level the playing field as much as possible.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The third "P", physical segregation of our young during their school years especially.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We tend to promote a system where those who excel in the academics are placed in the top academic schools, those who excel in arts in School for the Arts (SOTA); those good at sports to the Singapore Sports School, and so on – a very efficient system that sorts and places our students in geographically different location, meeting occasionally at school-driven projects or events.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But, Madam, one of the most effective ways of keeping our country safe, secure and empathic is to forge relationships of acceptance and trust among citizens of different abilities, faiths, and socioeconomic status, during one's growing-up years, in natural settings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Trust and empathy cannot be built deeply when Singaporeans are physically segregated from young.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At times, it would take walking another path or making a U-turn, when tweaking and patching will not work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Suggestion one is to create an open architecture and invest in e-learning developers and curators to accelerate the sharing of best learning materials including lectures and self-driven learning modules.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is especially urgent across some 400 primary, secondary and special schools in order to level the playing field and empower more teachers, students and families.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Invest at the national level for learning management systems like Canvas or the like.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Make templates on these platforms available for easy development and sharing.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Reward those who share materials and pedagogy of good standard, lesson plans as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Create 21st century jobs of Curators and Coaches who can help sieve through the submissions and advise on usage.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Take reference from the smartphone apps platform where both developers and users can interact actively and put the power of learning content development into the hands of those beyond the Ministry as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is not the first time that I and other Members of the House have raised this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the age of 12, it is too early to sort.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Tweaking the assessment grading system will not remove the deeply entrenched mindsets of chasing the scores.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The problem is unlikely to disappear even if we replace PSLE T-scores with Banding – students will start scoring four "A"s, five "A"s and so forth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Re-think the concept of the  School of the Arts, the Singapore Sports School, Normal (Technical) schools, the Special Assistance Plans (SAP) schools, and the Special schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Think programmes, yes, even programmes for the gifted, and make these programmes available across more physical school campuses – so that students of different abilities and talents can grow up together under one roof.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is no better way to learn inclusion except to play, eat, interact and learn with others who are unlike yourself.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let those who are academically stronger learn via subject-banded classes, but design school campuses that allow diversity and vibrant social interactions for all groups.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Better still, make full use of these Education Villages to allow SkillsFuture learnings for adults to take place there too.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is no better time to consider taking another path in this aspect especially when enrolments are falling, and some physical capacity can be found.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am most concerned with the elderly, especially those who are lower skilled and those with special needs and disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Building a caring society is an aspiration expressed not only in the President's Address; it is the desire of many Singaporeans who participated in the "Our Singapore Conversations" led by Minister Heng Swee Keat.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government has made some excellent moves in ensuring the essentials of healthcare, housing and transport for the vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is time for us to consider taking bolder steps to entrench this value of Care into our system.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Do we have the courage to legislate the protection of their rights and welfare into our way of life?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The women have the Women's Charter; abandoned parents have the Maintenance of Parents Act; those who are mentally incapacitated have the Mental Capacity Act; even the animals have the Animals and Birds Act to protect their welfare.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We should do the same for the education, employment and care support for the elderly and the disabled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Should we aim for a way by which Civil Society and the Government can work more collaboratively to achieve their mission and shared values?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In this matter, I beg to differ from the WP's desire to have the Government out of the way as much as possible.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At times, getting the Government out of the way may not work when it is in the interest of the target community or the cause to have more of Government engagement and involvement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One is my journey as an advocate for the special needs community and the second, that of Member of Parliament Mr Louis Ng, an animal rights advocate.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We were both not Members of this House when we first began our work in the two causes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Separately, we decided at some stage, that the confrontational "name and shame" way of advocacy could only go that far.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We learnt that if we truly have the interest of the communities we care for at heart, then we need to be part of the solution, to persuade, to coax, to explain and dirty our hands, where necessary, and to engage those, including the Government, who can help us as partners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We do not all need to end up as parliamentarians, but we can lead, sponsor and/or run initiatives that can advance those whom we care for.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Sweep and clean up the school compound or the animal habitat, if necessary.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We learnt that we need to move beyond criticising, and initiate or join others and get involved in Care Projects ourselves.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The "Future of Us" is only as strong as our determination to stick our necks out for what we instinctively know is right and humane.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: By any definition – statutory, scientific, common sense – I am or will soon be in the "aged" category.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: That I suppose qualifies me to speak on this subject.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is not a new subject, but one that has exercised the minds and skills of policymakers for many years now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: And we welcome ground up innovative ideas including those suggested by Members Miss Cheryl Chan and Ms Joan Pereira yesterday.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The SCC will also provide home care services to surrounding residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are also planning for Active Ageing hubs in new HDB developments with both aged care and active ageing programmes together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We hope to work with more grassroots organisations to develop a range of active ageing and aged care programmes, using existing CCs and Residents’ Committees (RCs) as platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: SCCs, nursing homes, and other forms of long-term care facilities would be provided in places where we assessed that there are needs from the residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Just like Edusave awards which are awarded based on eligibility criteria, they will be awarded to students who qualify regardless of which constituency they stay in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I think these are very fair and objective assessments based on needs and merits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Indeed, we should not be consumed by what we see on one side of the coin – the fear of a silver tsunami, with all of its attendant problems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The other side of the coin is longevity, with the immense opportunities for Singapore and Singaporeans that come with a population living longer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I would urge all Singaporeans to be bold and positive about our ageing population, and not just look at the challenges this brings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Just as we have turned our water insecurity into path-breaking water technology solutions highly sought after even by other countries, we need to reframe our ageing problem as a platform for us to innovate and create new opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We need a new "philosophy of ageing" to guide our national narrative on ageing at the individual, community and national levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For individuals, ageing can be a positive force.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Longer life spans could open up new life choices, new learning, new careers and new experiences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To allow this to happen, we will need to provide the platform for seniors to keep their minds active and their spirits fulfilled by working for as long as feasible and providing them with opportunities to learn new skills and develop new interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For the community, ageing can become a powerful, unifying cause that rallies residents, students, community organisations, and grassroots organisations to create new programmes and develop new social networks to embrace our senior population as active and participating members of an inclusive Singapore society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: One aspect of this is promoting senior volunteerism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We can help them start the journey by matching volunteering opportunities to seniors with the appropriate backgrounds, and by providing the necessary tools to equip them to function more effectively as volunteers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This will be the proof of concept for an inter-generational volunteer movement to help and be helped by seniors in our community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At the national level, ageing can be an opportunity for businesses to create new products and services to tap the silver market, in the same way that millennials constitute a distinct market segment for smart phones, tablets, social media marketing and the like.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Whether it is gym facilities for those over 65 only or anti-ageing products – if you swear by them – or holiday packages for retirees, the opportunities are limited only by our imagination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Likewise, rather than fret over a declining workforce, or dependency ratios in some cases, we should instead seek to harness the productive and creative energies of more mature workers, many of whom bring a steady hand to help and guide the younger ones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Beyond the mere economics of a longer stream of income, productive work has many benefits such as bestowing on the elderly a sense of fulfilment and keeping their minds alert.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Minister Heng's Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) will also need to blend in the demographic inevitability of an ageing population into its deliberations and recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our seniors should not be taken out of the equation in the future of our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Based on our current demographic trends, they are part of the future of our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: So, instead of being overwhelmed by the prospect of a silver tsunami, let us ride on longevity to create a distinctive Nation for All Ages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: However, this is a future that can only be created by all of us working together as partners – Government, Community, Businesses, Grassroots organisations and individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We must have strong families that provide emotional support and are willing to love and care for older members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Some frail and older people can be forgetful and walk very slowly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They can become quite grouchy and difficult to get along, like Carl Fredrickson, the elderly widower in the 2013 Disney Pixar movie "Up".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But they are still family members with whom we have long ties of kinship and bonds of love.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I myself have also recently seen a few such instances of financial abuse at my Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: While we strengthen legislation to protect the vulnerable elderly, what is key is that every Singaporean parent must help to inculcate the right values of filial piety and care for our seniors in their own children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our young Singaporeans should not only learn about such values in schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Most importantly, they need to see how their own parents live out these values in caring for and loving their grandparents, in word and deed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: They will do the same when it is their turn to look after their parents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Businesses can unlock productivity and innovation in longevity for their own companies and for our economy as a whole.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But they can only do so if they see older workers as assets, and if they can create ageless workplaces to enable older workers not only to continue to work but also to thrive in their jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This human resource solutions specialist has tailor-made its working and remuneration arrangements to enable older workers to take on payroll processing and other jobs in the company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This need not be a rare exception and indeed it is not.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We can find other examples of such age-friendly companies but there can be many more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In fact, I believe it can be the norm if business leaders apply their minds and hearts to it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Government will continue to help both employers and workers to transit more seamlessly into this new regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: However, employers as well as HR and line managers must take ownership of this challenge to avoid unconscious ageist employment attitudes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Much work has been done over the years to encourage employers to hire older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As one The Straits Times reader, Loke Soo Heng, puts it in a Forum article dated 19 November 2015, re-employment legislation caters to older workers who are already recognised for their value in their current companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But older workers who leave their jobs due to restructuring may be perceived differently when they apply for jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Government will do its part to encourage and engender an ageless workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But ultimately, the business community must be convinced of the benefits of being age-blind and to hire purely on merit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We need neighbours and residents living within each community to look out for older residents among them and lend a hand in supporting them to age well in place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is even more pertinent as families are getting smaller and there is also increasing incidence of singlehood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: More fundamentally, we want to provide an environment where the elderly can age with dignity and be supported by family, friends and the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But the ecosystem for this to take place is multi-layered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Because of the immense strain that caregivers bear, they themselves also need support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have all read about the tragedy of caregivers in Japan going down a slippery slope after they quit their jobs to look after the elderly, only to find themselves unemployable after their loved ones pass away.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We ourselves may also know of friends and family who are triply strained by the stress of their day jobs, the pressure from looking after young children and caring for their ailing elderly parents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We need therefore to refresh and strengthen the support environment for caring for the elderly so that they can age in place in their own homes, in the community, among people who know and care for them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This will also help to strengthen family ties and the community spirit so essential to a cohesive society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: An example is the befriending programme that has sprouted in different communities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Various community organisations have taken the lead to recruit, train and deploy befrienders to visit and help frail seniors living in the neighbourhood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: So, there is now a kitchen in the void deck, where stay-alone seniors can come down, cook together, eat together and clean together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I am told that even the gentlemen themselves are learning to cook.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We hope to nurture and grow more of such movements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But challenges have never deterred us as Singaporeans from striving to build an exceptional nation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We can apply that to population ageing too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: With the same shared vision, many determined hands and many strong hearts, we can chart a positive path ahead for population ageing, one that will inspire not only Singaporeans, but hopefully even other ageing cities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But a key ingredient to creating such a Nation for All Ages as in tackling other national challenges is leadership and good politics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: President Tony Tan has also raised this subject in his address.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: How do we further strengthen the political system such that the right leaders – honest, selfless, capable, and committed – can surface?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: How do we sustain a robust political system that does not paralyse Government unnecessarily, but also does not stifle well-reasoned, cogently argued dissent?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: How can we assure alternative and minority voices a platform to be heard at the national stage?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Singapore has implemented various political innovations over the past few Parliaments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: One such innovation is the Non-Constituency Member of Parliament (NCMP).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The NCMP scheme was introduced some 32 years ago to allow for alternative party views to be aired in Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This was in recognition of Singaporeans' desire for alternative views and the value of contest of ideas and robust debates to sharpen policy making.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But while the People’s Action Party (PAP) has won a strong mandate from Singaporeans in the recent General Elections, the desire for alternative voices has not waned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is especially relevant as the challenges we face becomes even more complex and unpredictable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In fact, this would also affirm our desire to build a more inclusive society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Hence, it would be sensible to increase the number of NCMPs in this House.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But, regardless of the number of NCMPs admitted, what is most important, to ensure that our Parliament continues to have robust, well-informed and quality debate that will help shape and sharpen policies, is for Singaporeans to judge and scrutinise every Parliamentarian with the same lens and apply the same set of standards – whether it be of conduct or the substance of the argument.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Another political innovation has been the Elected Presidency (EP).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The EP is the custodian of our financial reserves against pilferage by irresponsible government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: He also safeguards the integrity of our public service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The EP is therefore to be above party politics and should play a unifying role.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The issue of the EP has drawn vigorous debate in the media recently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: One key issue is how to depoliticise the EP scheme, such that it is not an alternate power centre that keeps "checking" on the government of the day or offer presidential endorsement of everything the Government does.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Both actions would be contrary to the EP's role and lead to either policy paralysis or cause divisions in our society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The last presidential election was widely perceived as a kind of proxy contest between the PAP and the Opposition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As the 24 January 2016 Sunday Times lengthy feature on impending political changes has suggested, the qualifying criteria for candidates, which has remained unchanged for the last 25 years, should be raised to ensure that the candidate is up to the task given the greater complexity and demands of the EP's custodial roles in today's environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I would also support more public education so that Singaporeans have greater clarity on the role of the EP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Way before then, quite a number of us in this House, myself included will be in the aged or very aged category.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Hopefully, by then, through the inventions of science, and our efforts in living a healthy lifestyle, we will have many more years to life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health and the Environment and Water Resources (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But I also hope that our Nation for All Ages will be a shining reality, and that it will also add life to our years.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 3.55 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.35 pm until 3.55 pm.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The President had spoken passionately about the importance of building a caring society.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And as the hon Member Dr Amy Khor had mentioned earlier, a key characteristic of this society of ours is that an increasing proportion of it will comprise the elderly.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, for this speech, I will be focusing on strengthening the care of our seniors.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The numbers are familiar to all of us.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just five years ago, under 10% of our population was aged 65 and above.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While these statistics may sound alarming but, in fact, getting old is not necessarily bad news.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What we need do is to focus on functional age, not chronological age.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Healthy lifestyles and preventive health measures play a big part in ensuring that an older person remains as functional as possible, enabling him/her to lead an active and fulfilling life in his/her golden years.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Socially and economically active seniors will lessen concerns about the support or dependency ratios – 60 will be the new 40; 80 the new 60, and so on.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the Ministry of Health's (MOH) Addendum, one of its priorities is to intensify efforts to keep Singaporeans healthy, such as through plans to reduce obesity and smoking.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a society, we must work together to make ageing a positive experience for all.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And in my opinion, there are three important criteria for positive ageing.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, one must be healthy and stay connected to the community.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, in the event that one falls ill, I am glad to note that help for our elders has been significantly expanded.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, when the elderly need to be looked after, they should have a range of options to choose from.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This does not mean taking more medicine or going to see the doctor more often.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, over-medication or treatments could do more harm than good and is costly for both the patient and the country.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Recent studies suggest that reducing medication, a process that has been termed "de-intensification", has significant benefits in terms of both morbidity and mortality.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The other day, I wished a sprightly octogenarian lady the best of health, and she brightly replied that she was indeed in the pink of health, and whereupon to emphasise this point, she proceeded to show me a fistful of pills that she takes every day.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This led me to ask her, "Since you are so healthy, why is there a need to take so many pills?" She just smiled wistfully but did not have a reply.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singaporeans should take preventive measures, such as eating healthy and exercising regularly to slow biological ageing.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, we are embarking on community-wide longitudinal health screening in some parts of Singapore, more recently in the Mei Ling and Stirling estates in Queenstown.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have health programmes that are customised for mature workers in workplaces.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Keeping healthy is not just a matter of exercise but feeling involved and connected.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many elderly want to continue to lead active lives.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I know of examples of many nurses and other healthcare workers whom I work with, who continue employment way past the official retirement age and still continue to contribute significantly to the care of our sick and elderly.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The role of family and friends is very important.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our seniors should be able to live in a familiar environment surrounded by loved ones, friends and neighbours, not segregated from the rest of the community.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ageing-in-place is a principle that should be robustly defended.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of the elderly I spoke to speak of the joys of remaining part of the community, living in their own homes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For those living with family members, they benefit from the inter-generational bonds.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For those who are living on their own, ties with long-time neighbours and even shopkeepers keep them integrated within their communities.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I was delighted when the Ministry for National Development (MND) supported a programme to allow up to six neighbours to select their replacement flats together, as part of the en-bloc redevelopment of the historic precinct of Tanglin Halt.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We want to see as many Singaporeans grow old with dignity within the community where they have spent the better part of their lives.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe that this is one area in which this Government has done a lot, and I am sure that our seniors can be assured that the Government has invested significantly in building up capacity across the healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, medical bills have become more affordable through higher subsidies for Specialist Outpatient Care (SOC) and outpatient drugs, Flexi-Medisave, the Pioneer Generation Package, MediShield Life and Medifund has also been strengthened.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our elderly will get the care that they need, without unduly worrying about healthcare costs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Outside of healthcare, our elderly will get help with their daily living expenses through a variety of programmes such as CPF LIFE, the Silver Support Scheme, Enhanced and Additional GST Vouchers.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And they also receive assistance with housing matters through, for example, the Enhancement for Active Seniors (EASE) scheme which helps to put age-friendly improvements in the homes of seniors, studio apartments, the Lease Buyback Scheme, the Silver Housing Bonus, priority schemes and/or additional grants for children and parents to live close to one another, such as the recently announced Proximity Housing Grant.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Housing estates are also undergoing continuous improvements to make them as senior-friendly as possible, and even our traffic system and road networks are making the transition, for instance, outdoor lifts in housing estates and for overhead bridges, and the Silver Zone programme which has a suite of age-friendly traffic safety enhancements, the latest example of which was inaugurated in Lengkok Bahru just last weekend.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Moving on to long-term care needs, I think this is one area where we still face many challenges.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: About 3% of residents aged 55 years and above are non-ambulant and require physical assistance.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Long-term care needs can last for several years if disability strikes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This group of elderly require a lot more support from their families to care for them and their daily needs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many prefer to age-in-place, but strong family support is needed to make this happen.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They also need the support from services in the community, for example, like home nursing care.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I applaud MOH's efforts in expanding long-term care capacity, including nursing homes as well as home and centre-based senior care services, to ensure that the disabled elderly have access to the care that they need.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MOH has also worked on enhancing the quality of aged care services by introducing new licensing standards for nursing homes and new guidelines for home and community care services.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government has been increasing support for long-term care and more Medifund assistance has been made available.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, it is evident that much has been done, and yet it is timely to ask if we should consider other ideas to address nagging concerns among some Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One of these is the uncertainty over long-term care costs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many Singaporeans believe this to be large and required for an extended period.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They also worry that nursing homes may be their only option, when they prefer to age at home.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Quite a number of families are willing to have grandpa or grandma or their parents at home, if they have access to quality home care services.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another worry they have is being a burden to their families – financially, physically and emotionally – should they lose their independence with severe disability.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Naturally, they are apprehensive about long-term suffering if they were bedridden and needs various aids to survive.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have some suggestions for the Ministry's consideration.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, we should have a comprehensive action plan to help our seniors remain healthy and connected.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to accelerate the development of more alternatives to nursing homes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our seniors want to be with their families even when they become frail.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Family members want to be assured that they can rely on skilled help and nursing support when their parents or grandparents require it.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
