text: And for seniors without family, or when their families can no longer look after them, new models of care such as assisted living centres should be explored.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The level of care delivered by a traditional nursing home may be excessive for some residents.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Studies have shown that restoring the autonomy of nursing home residents, while theoretically putting them at higher risk of accidents, may actually have many positive effects on their well-being that more than offsets the potential risks.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And so, they have called for a move towards providing more individualised care for the elderly in nursing homes and also to allow them to retain some degree of independence.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not only is this good for the elderly, but it may also reduce the need for manpower in the long run, as earlier stated.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And so, perhaps a mix of both single and multiple bed setups can be considered for future subsidised nursing homes, so that we can explore both paradigms.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, we should have an ongoing public education campaign to sensitise our young and middle-aged to the need to plan ahead.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This means putting aside some savings for old age, not to over-commit in terms of property purchase and not to opt-out of ElderShield.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And if they do buy a larger flat, to consider downgrading after their children move out, for ease of upkeep and to release cash for post-retirement needs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have seen the recent advertisements on our television channels highlighting this issue, and I think this is a good start.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Japan is one of the leaders in this field and exoskeletons like those developed by Cyberdyne and interactive personal robots, such as Pepper, which was launched by SoftBank recently, provide us with an endearing view of the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The President and many Members of this House have spoken about the bracing challenges that we face in the future – terrorism, our economy, maintaining our social cohesion, among other things.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But as Members have emphasised, we have every reason to be confident that we can overcome them – one by one, together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The question is: how do we do that?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For Singapore to succeed, what must we do?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Members would have read the Addenda to the President's Address.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These comprehensive documents lay out the agenda for this term of Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Voters elect us to develop policies, to implement them, and to make things happen.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They want policies which respond to people's needs, like enhancing social safety nets, making housing more affordable and accessible, improving public transport, and managing the growth of foreign workers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They want to see policies that will enable our people to achieve their aspirations, for themselves and for their children: investing in education at all levels, for example, the SkillsFuture; implementing major projects which transform Singapore, like Changi Airport – building T4, putting up Project Jewel, planning for T5 – or Jurong Lake District or the Southern Waterfront City.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: One by one, brick by brick, building a better Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is what this Government has done for many years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Good politics make sure that we will elect governments who will develop good policies, who will expand our common space and strengthen our society for the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we have good politics, then we have the best chance of having our system continuing to work for us, instead of against us, over the long haul.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we are only concerned over the next five or 10 years, we do not have to make any changes in terms of politics because the system is working now and will continue to do so for the next 10 years, maybe a bit longer.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We know where the leaders are, we know the response function – you press this button, this will happen; you pull that lever, something else happens.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We know how to make it work today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But if we are thinking beyond this term and this team, about a new Prime Minister and a new Cabinet, and a new population, different electorate, then we will need to keep Singapore able to work well with them in charge and with them being the team that leads Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then, it is prudent for us to consider what possible adjustments may become necessary now, in good time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In theory, to get your politics right should not be such a very difficult problem for most countries because there is some sense of identity and unity, and leaders and your followers of different political persuasions should be able to come together and work for the common good.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It makes sense to work together; it is a lot of trouble if you are at odds with one another.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The executive and the legislative branches are controlled by different parties.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The government is stalemated on issues ranging from gun control to trade policy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Democrats run the Administration; the President is Democrat.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The two do not see eye-to-eye and are unable to compromise.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And last year they nearly had to shut down again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In President Obama's recent State of the Union address, this was the theme he took up right at the end of his speech – the most important thing which he felt he had not been able to achieve – to get American politics to work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He described how the founding fathers of the US – Washington, Jefferson, Madison – had distributed power between states and the branches of government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That means between the federal government and the different states; between the executive and the legislature and the judiciary; checks and balances.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And they expected people to argue over matters as they themselves did, but eventually to find common ground and be able to work something out.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But now, the basic bonds of trust between the major parties, between the Democrats and the Republicans, have totally broken down.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is rancour and suspicion, no willingness to compromise.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The system desperately needs to be fixed but no Congressman, no Senator, not even the President, is able on their own, to put it right.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is the US, the most powerful country in the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Other countries too have seen their national consensus fray.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many European countries were governed by stable, centralist coalitions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Sometimes, you have a centre-right coalition that will govern for a time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The mood changes, the country's priorities shift, a different balance emerges, and you have a centre-left coalition, perhaps even some of the same parties continue in the new coalition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You shift from one to the other within limits, never out of control.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But now, the economy has broken, the immigration and refugee crisis is presenting them with an insoluble problem and deep disenchantment has set in.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Extreme left and right groups are gaining ground.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In every country, the regular political parties are losing support, never mind whether you are left-wing or right-wing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is the extreme parties, the ones who just say, "To hell with it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Vote for me and I will show two fingers to the world." They are the ones who are getting support.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are now in government and having to make decisions which their supporters do not like at all.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have just had elections and Podemos won a significant number of seats.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Now they are having a lot of difficulty forming a new government – in Germany, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), an anti-immigration party; in France, the National Front; in Britain, UKIP – pushing anti-immigrant, anti-EU, anti-globalisation platforms.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Just expressing angst and anger, not propounding compromises and solutions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are reflecting public unhappiness, but they are also riling up the public, offering no coherent policies of viable alternatives.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In many Asian countries, whom you vote for depends on your race, depends on your religion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In some countries, it depends on what caste you belong to.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is not policies; it is not integrity but "Is he my guy?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Does he have the same caste name as me?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then, I know whether I can trust whether he will look after me." These are fundamental divides, divides which countries have tried to close but which remain deep and have sometimes even deepened decades after independence.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You may say, "Well, that is the problem of democracy", but even countries which do not have elections also have not such an easy time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a major challenge for the Chinese government, for President Xi Jinping, to keep his system clean, to keep his officials accountable and to keep his government with authority and legitimacy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Invariably, they ask to see our Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They come, they sit in, they watch our Members of Parliaments and Ministers take cases and they are deeply impressed at how the system works.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They go back and try to do the same.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Singapore, Members and Ministers are taking cases for their voters.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The person sitting in front of you votes for or against you come election time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In China, the officials may have a good heart and want to do good for their population, but they do not owe their positions to the votes of the people they are in charge of.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we look at other people's political problems, we do not feel any "schadenfreude", any sense of superiority or rejoicing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, we say, "There but for the grace of God go I", because what happens elsewhere can easily happen in Singapore too, if either we blindly copy other people's practices which do not work here, or we find our own way but take a wrong turn.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We can end up in such a situation also.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It means we have to keep evolving our system carefully, step by step, making sure that our Government works and the politics in Singapore serve our people's interests.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have to find our own way forward.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What kind of political system do we want in Singapore?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You have to be responsive to the people, able to look beyond the short term and keep us safe and successful.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because as a small country with no luxury of resources, with no domestic hinterland, excellence and integrity have been and always must be a crucial competitive advantage for Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we cannot ever afford to be paralysed, gridlocked or become dysfunctional like some other countries.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For Singapore, you go down, you are finished.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There has to be free and fair elections, and it must not be forbiddingly expensive for people to stand and contest elections.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, that is one of the greatest things we have done to keep our system open, to make sure that we keep money out of politics, and it does not cost a lot of money to contest elections.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, if you take last year's General Elections.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You compare that with the cost of the US elections.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Not cost the government to run it; cost the candidates to raise it and to spend it; US$7 billion divided by about 350 million Americans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That you may say is American-class, one of its own.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But look at the money politics that you see in many countries, including in our region.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The sums which are spoken about, which are necessary for elections, openly, not a secret, not even illegal or embarrassing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is an insoluble problem and ours must never become like that.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Thirdly, our political system must foster accountability so that the government is always kept on its toes and will always be motivated to look after the interests of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government's actions have to be scrutinised and debated in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If a Member of Parliament – whether it is an Opposition Member or a Government Member – argues a case against the Government's proposal, then either the Government has to be able to rebut it and explain convincingly what it is doing and why, or if the Member makes a good case, then you have to acknowledge that, and policies have to be changed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is what Members have seen happen in this House, not just with Opposition Members but with Government Members or Nominated Members of Parliament (NMPs) as well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: On the other side, if a Member makes a good proposal and advocates convincingly for it and persuades the Government, then I think the Government should support it, back it with resources and help to make it happen – as also has happened with PAP Members and Nominated Members, who have, from time to time, moved private Member's Bills and other times, have persuaded the Government that the bee in the bonnet is a justified bee in the bonnet and we should do what they are buzzing us loudly to carry out.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And I think we take Parliament seriously in Singapore on both sides of the House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a place where you have debates, where big issues have to come to be decided.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You can agree or disagree, and vigorously; and you ought to disagree, if you have strong views.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But you must take it seriously; it is not a place where you throw chairs, swing handbags or pour water on one another; or a place where you exchange clever put-downs but really avoid the serious issues concerning the Government and the future of the country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, our Parliament may not be as entertaining on television as many other parliaments which you watch on the news at night, but I think, in terms of quality and seriousness of purpose, we have it and we should keep it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Ultimately, of course, the Government is accountable not just to Parliament, but also to the electorate.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If it performs well, then it gets the support of voters again, and it can continue in office.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If it performs poorly, there is an electoral price to pay.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then, either the Government mends its ways and regains its support, or the electorate can vote it out and another party, another team, will have to take its place and try to do better.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we must have a system where the Government does not, over time, become complacent, go soft or even worse, become corrupt.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Multiracialism is fundamental to our identity as a nation because we have three major races in Singapore, we have all the world's major religions in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Race and religion will always be fundamental tectonic fault lines for us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has got to encourage political parties to seek broad-based, multiracial consensus and pursue moderate policies in the interests of all Singaporeans, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has to discourage parties from forming along racial or religious lines or championing the interests of one race or religion over others, whether it be a majority or minority group in our society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Minority Singaporeans must have the confidence that they will not ever be marginalised, or shut out, or discriminated against.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Every Singaporean must have the confidence that he has a place in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government has to be responsive to the will of the people, but at the same time, we also have to have safeguards, in case the country is swept off course by a transient public mood, or an erratic government, which can happen.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: By the time you change your mind and realise it is unwise, it is too late to come back.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, you need stabilisers to make sure that you respond to the mood, but you do not get carried too far and capsize the boat.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Most political systems have such stabilisers built in.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have an Upper House like the Senate in the US, the House of Lords in the UK, or especially in big countries, you have a division of powers between the city and regional governments and a national federal government on the other.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, no single point can cause the whole system to fail.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You clear the Lower House, you must go pass the Upper House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Elections may be different times, may have different rules.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You persuade one region to do something, but it is a big country and other regions have to go along.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You have to get the consensus, take some time, sleep it over, think carefully and perhaps think the better of it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are too small to have either an Upper House or to have a regional set of governments.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The most we can do are Town Councils.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have overlaid on top of them Mayors.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We call them Mayors, but actually if you compare them with the Mayor of London or the Mayor of New York, it is what they call, 小巫见大巫.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This happens in countries much richer than us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Ten years ago, under a basically conservative government, they built up significant amounts of reserves or surpluses.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They set up a pension fund for the future and said, "This is our sovereign wealth fund and this is to make sure that in future, you will be provided for with state pensions" and so on.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But then came elections and both parties, whether in government or out of government, because of the dynamics of the situation, they have no choice.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: One side offers something, the other side offers more, and back and forth.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Today, the funds for the future have disappeared.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It can happen to Australia with all that wealth and resources.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Think what can happen if it is Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The whole of our excellence in Government, the competence and the performance of the country depends on the integrity and the ability of the individuals in the key posts in the public service – judges, central bankers, the Accountant-General, the Commissioner of Police, the people who head our Statutory Boards, who sit on our key Statutory Boards, the people who manage our Reserves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Once corrupt persons get into key positions, it will be the end.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is not only the end because they take money and help themselves because we can stop that and put them in jail.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is the end because they subvert and corrupt the system and make it impossible to root out the cancer which then becomes entrenched throughout the system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono of Indonesia used to lament publicly about the problem he had with what he called the "judicial mafia".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He does not mean the mafia on the streets.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He means judges whom he could not trust for their integrity because they had become corrupt and had become part of the problem.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If you look at other countries where the police are in cahoots with the crooks, and if you have a problem, you are not sure whether you should go to the police station or run away from the police station.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Or you look at countries where those responsible for safeguarding state assets instead raid the bank.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As the Malay proverb goes, "Pagar makan padi".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You are the hedge but you are eating the rice which you are supposed to protect.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have evolved our system of politics over the years and it has served us well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our political and constitutional history is quite different from that of most other newly-independent countries, countries which were colonies and became independent after the war, in Asia, Africa and particularly in Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Most newly-independent countries start life anew, with a brand new fresh-minted Constitution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But when we became independent, we did not do that.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We decided to retain and tweak our existing Constitutional arrangements that had worked for Singapore when we were part of Malaysia, and that had been working before that, when we were a self-governing state before we joined Malaysia.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew felt that it was better for us to evolve our model gradually, learning from experience, rather than to strive for some unworkable perfection.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee said that his best teacher of the difference between political reality and constitutional theory was the Tunku.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Once, he wrote, I think this is in his memoirs, Mr Lee was in the Tunku's office and admiring a beautiful leather-bound green-covered volume.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was the Pakistani Constitution and was presented to the Tunku by Ayub Khan, who was at one time President of Pakistan.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee admired the book and the Tunku told him, "You know, Kuan Yew, they make very good constitutions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: With every leader, they have to make a new one." When we became independent, we cobbled together the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, which is what we have today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Part of the provisions from Singapore's State Constitution, part of the provisions from Malaysia's Federal Constitution which we adopted and incorporated, plus amendments which we made after Separation, for example, amendments to safeguard our sovereignty and to ensure that any decision to give up our sovereignty would have to be put to a referendum of all the voters in Singapore and not decided by the Legislature.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a messy document and such a messy document that in 1970, Mr Lee asked the British High Commissioner to get British Constitutional law experts to polish it up.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee thought that the British experts had done a first-rate job.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The idea was you look at the American Constitution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has lasted 200 something years and over these 200 something years, it has only had 20 plus amendments.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You get it precisely right, beautiful form of words, every school child knows it and that is what is going to guide the country for the next several hundred years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But, in the end, Mr Lee decided not to take that approach.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He used Thomas Jefferson's analogy of a suit.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He said, "From my experience, Constitutions have to be custom-made, tailored to suit the peculiarities of the person wearing the suit".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He changes the metaphor here but I think you will forgive him this mixed metaphor.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He said "Perhaps, like shoes, the older they are, the better they fit.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Stretch them, soften them, resole them, repair them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are always better than a brand new pair of shoes".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He said, "Our people have got used to and understand the present system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But most important of all, the Constitution works.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many countries have tried and gone through several Constitutions since Independence.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I believe it is better to stretch and ease an old shoe when we know that the different shape and fit of a younger generation requires a change." Like many of Mr Lee's speeches, this speech made in 1984 in the old Parliament House is still worth reading more than 30 years later.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I encourage you to read it, and I urge Members to read the full version in the Hansard.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Apart from talking about Singapore politics, he gave a tour of the horizon of how historically other countries – Britain, France, America – have each got their own histories and how the system evolved for them and how difficult it was.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He talked about France, and how as a young man in 1956, after attending a constitution conference in London, he took a side trip to Paris on the way home, and the taxi driver took him around, showed him the sights and brought him to the National Assembly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This was 1956, it was a democracy and the politicians could not agree.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The taxi driver pointed at the National Assembly and said to him, "wala, wala, wala"  , and he said that was an education for a young politician to the reality of politics.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Unfortunately, Hansard did not quite catch the nuance of this expression and the Hansard, I just recently noticed, transcribed it as "voilà" three times, and as a result of which, it makes no sense.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You will therefore not find this in The Sunday Times because The Sunday Times could not make sense of it and edited it out.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But it is a most vivid example of how things can go wrong in politics.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was a highly civilised nation, but the system did not work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the end, General de Gaulle had to come back out of retirement and changed the rules.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He took very stern measures and created the Fifth Republic.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But even de Gaulle must die and till today, the French, they also, like other countries, have political problems.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Today, in the newspapers, if you read The Straits Times, Paris is in upheaval, because there are strikes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Taxi drivers, air traffic controllers and for good measure, civil servants are on strike.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I think we have to understand the difference between the theory and the practice, and what looks good on paper and what we need really, truly in real life to do.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The approach which we have taken has been to evolve our political system as we go along.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee did this and we continue to do this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Learning from experience, stretching and easing the old shoe, and adapting it to our needs and dealing with problems as new problems emerge, as we understand the difficulties and weaknesses.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, we inherited the first-past-the-post parliamentary system, modelled on the British House of Commons in Westminster.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is why here we sit opposite one another – the Government and, in principle, the Opposition on the other side.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Each institution with a purpose, each one in line with our principles.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The first-past-the-post parliamentary system tends to produce clear election outcomes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You either win decisively or lose decisively, and especially in Singapore where every constituency is more or less the same composition and the same mood as every other constituency, all the more you tend to have a national swing and it goes across the board and so you end up with a clear majority in the House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: From then, Parliament was composed entirely of PAP Members.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the next four General Elections, the PAP won all the seats and as well as all the by-elections in between, the PAP won all of them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It had been, by then, 16 years since Separation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A new generation of voters was coming of age.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A new team of Members of Parliament and Ministers was preparing to take over.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee and his senior colleagues watched what happened in the House after Mr Jeyaretnam came in.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Opposition provided Mr Lee and his team the "foil" or a backdrop against which they could set out their ideas more clearly, in contrast to what was being presented on the other side.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Right against wrong, good ideas against better ones.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At first, this minimum was three Opposition Members – either elected or not elected NCMPs, or some combination.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The design of the NCMP scheme is unique but the concept of a parliament with members who have been elected in different ways is not at all unusual.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some Members are elected from constituencies; others are chosen from party lists – in other words, the proportional representation system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How many you take off the party lists depends on the proportion of the total vote that your party got.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: One reason that New Zealanders do this is because they want to ensure that there is Maori representation in parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Such a system, where you top up beyond what the first-past-the-post system gives you, will help to moderate the extreme outcomes of a first-past-the-post system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is why we did the NCMP system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We did not do the proportional representation way because we felt that it would be bad for Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It would result in political parties that are based on race or religion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It would encourage political leaders to champion the demands of their particular segment against the broader interests of Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It would divide us, rather than bring us together, because to win in a proportional representation system, you have got to have your base.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It can be Christians, it can be Buddhists, it can be Muslims, it can be Indians.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It can be a special interest group, maybe on gender issues.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Your interest will consolidate that base, take a hard position, demand as much as you can for your group.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You do not have to win seats, you just get a higher percentage, and you will get seats in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I think if you do that, you end up split, polarised and severely weakened.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: NCMPs are Opposition candidates who had the best results but did not quite win their seats.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, some NCMPs have higher percentage, if you look at it on a personal basis, than other people, Members elected in GRCs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If you just count their chunk of the GRC and how many votes they got and the percentage, the NCMP may have got more than the person from a GRC.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But the point is, he did well, he is one of the best losers and they come in, ensuring that Opposition voices are always represented in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have at least as much right to be in Parliament as Members who are elected on a party list under a proportional representation system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, arguably more, because on a party list under a proportional representation, no voter specifically chose you.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Your party boss puts you on the list in position number two or three or 20 and there is a cut-off, and you happen to make the cut.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Here, to be an NCMP, the voters in a constituency in which you contested have to have a sufficiently high regard of you to give you one of the highest votes amongst all losing candidates before you can come in.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, you have got people who are really, truly, personally voting for you.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I think that gives legitimacy as well as objectivity to the system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It depends on electoral contest and not just on the say-so of the party they belong to or the party bosses of the party they belong to.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, there is diversity, there is debate, and I think there is value.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The NCMP scheme is a good one which has achieved its purpose.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, Ms Sylvia Lim was first elected as an NCMP in 2006 and she acquitted herself in Parliament, impressed voters and became a Member of Parliament elected in Aljunied GRC in 2011.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the last term, we had three NCMPs: Mrs Lina Chiam, Mr Yee Jenn Jong and Mr Gerald Giam.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They all took up their seats and participated actively in Parliamentary debates.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This term, the WP's NCMPs have also taken up their seats.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have Mr Leon Perera, we have Mr Dennis Tan – they made their maiden speeches this week – except for Ms Lee Li Lian who has said that she will not take up her NCMP seat.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: She is not taking it up not out of any objections of principle but to give it to another WP candidate.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Whether that is in the spirit of the scheme, we can debate but we will wait for the Motion which I believe Mr Low will move to discuss the matter further.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Opposition, of course, would like to have it both ways – take up NCMP seats when they win them, but also protest that an NCMP is a second-class Member of Parliament, in order to persuade voters to cast their votes for them and make them constituency Members of Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, in reality, NCMPs have exactly the same opportunities to question, speak and debate in Parliament that constituency Members have.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They can file Parliamentary Questions (PQs), move Motions, speak in all debates, and they can show voters – past and future – what they can do.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is just one distinction between an NCMP and a constituency Member today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This was how the scheme was designed by Mr Lee Kuan Yew back in 1984, and he had his reasons which he explained in an exchange, because Mr Jeyaretnam was in Parliament and challenged him on this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I suppose this is an example of how Mr Jeyaretnam as the Opposition played a constructive role.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee was particularly concerned with one scenario: a split in the ruling party leading to a motion of no confidence in the House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He felt that in such a situation, NCMPs should not have a say in determining the Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In 1984, Mr Lee would still have fresh in his mind, the memory of what had happened in 1961, when the extreme left-wing split off from the PAP and formed the Barisan Sosialis, and the PAP hung on in the Legislative Assembly with a one-seat majority.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And then one Member of Parliament died and it was levelled – no seat majority.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I think Mr Lee must also have been conscious that even in 1984, within the PAP, there was opposition to the pace of leadership renewal, which could have led to a leadership challenge.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The general election was upcoming and took place in December 1984.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was a crucial General Election because many of the third-generation leaders entered politics in that election – Wong Kan Seng, Yeo Cheow Tong, Mah Bow Tan, Abdullah Tarmugi and myself.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There were very strong different views within the PAP on whether this was going too fast, and it was not to be ruled out that there could have been a challenge.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee felt, in that situation, NCMPs should not have a say.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But after 30 years, in a different phase of our political development, we should re-examine this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am not saying that we can now rule out the possibility of leadership challenge within the ruling party.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have a cohesive team but as Mr Lee said, "It is a real distinct possibility because strong men have strong views and they can collide." In other countries, it happens regularly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Australia, in the UK, it is marvellous theatre!

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Suddenly, you hear news there is going to be a spill.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A "spill" means somebody has mounted a challenge.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The leader then has to call his members in Parliament together to vote.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Ministers take positions, Members of Parliament take positions, furious to-ing and fro-ing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Next thing you know, there is a new Prime Minister, and I am writing a new letter of congratulations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has happened three or four times within the last five years in Australia.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And in Britain, leadership challenges are also dramatic events.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Tony Blair left because he knew if he did not leave, somebody would challenge him, and he would be pushed out.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we cannot rule out it happening in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They will be equal in powers, although not in responsibility and scope, to constituency Members of Parliament because they are non-constituency and they do not have specific voters to look after.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Given that in any election, at least 30% of voters will vote against the Government, ensuring a minimum of 12 Opposition Members of Parliament in the House of about 100 Members, I feel it is reasonable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Opposition often claims that they are unable to put up a stronger showing in Parliament because they have too few Members of Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I think this is an excuse because the Opposition's impact depends on the quality of Opposition Members of Parliament and arguments, far more than on their number.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But having more NCMPs will give the Opposition more opportunity to show what they can do.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if, in fact, the NCMPs are capable and effective, the exposure will win them recognition and help them win a constituency the next time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will also continue with the NMP scheme.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, together with the NCMPs, 12 plus 9, we will now have at least 21 non-ruling Members of Parliament in the House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In making these changes, I am by no means presuming that the Government will always have a strong majority in the House, although this has been the case for the last 50 years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Nor do I assume that the PAP will always form the Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That will depend on the performance of the PAP and the verdict of Singapore voters.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But regardless of election outcomes, the NCMP scheme ensures a stronger Opposition presence in Parliament, so that if the Government wins overwhelming, nationwide support, it will still have to argue for and defend its policies robustly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In effect we will be aiding the Opposition, giving their best losers more exposure, very possibly building them up for the next General Election.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But I believe that in this phase of our political development, this is good for the Government and good for Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: No ruling party or Government should ever be afraid of open argument.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The PAP never has been and ultimately, Singapore will benefit from a contest of ideas in the House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This would also encourage all political parties to pursue multiracial politics rather than sectarian politics.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Unlike a proportional representation system, which would also have led to minority Members in Parliament, but via racial political parties.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: With the GRC system, parties and Members of Parliament have to give weight to the interests of minorities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The GRCs have pushed parties to become more multiracial in their approach.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Opposition parties know that they have to win support from the minorities and that they have to field credible Malay and Indian candidates in their teams.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They make quite a big effort to go and do that.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It puts pressure on us in the PAP, but I think it is the right system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Opposition parties have to make that effort in order to put up a credible team.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They also know that if they play racial politics during elections, then whatever votes they may win from one group will be at the expense of votes which they will lose from the other groups, because in the multiracial team, with a multiracial electorate, you have always to strike that balance and internalise that balance within your team and amongst your voters.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Of course, this has not stopped candidates from being naughty from time to time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the 1997 General Election, you will remember Tang Liang Hong in Cheng San GRC.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He made provocative, chauvinist speeches to appeal to the Chinese majority vote – outrageous statements, but powerful.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The PAP exposed him, and the minorities swung solidly against Tang Liang Hong and his WP teammates.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the last elections, some Opposition candidates tried the opposite; tried to exploit Islam to collect Malay votes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some ostentatiously performed prayers in public before election rallies and posted photos of themselves doing so on the social media.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But beyond a point, they would have hurt their non-Malay fellow candidates in the GRC teams, and it would have cost them non-Malay votes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the end, their tactic failed and their teams lost.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The GRC scheme also has one bonus, which I think is important and that is, it works together with our system of Town Councils.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The constituency Members of Parliament have to run the Town Council.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have to manage Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC) collections.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have to receive, spend and account for Government subsidies.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have to maintain the estates to a proper standard.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have to administer rules and fines, and look after substantial sinking funds.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This makes sure that any party which aspires to form the Government of Singapore, first has a chance to demonstrate in a Town Council what it can or cannot do.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if it can do, that is a base from which it can build and persuade Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If it cannot do, it is as well that Singaporeans know this early and everybody is under no illusions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The GRC system is a good one, and I think we should keep it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How many big ones should we have, versus small ones?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: How many GRCs should we have, versus Single Member Constituencies (SMCs)?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A bigger GRC benefits from having an anchor Minister take care of their affairs and also benefits from having better economies of scale in running GRC-wide programmes and activities, and in running the Town Council.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But smaller GRCs create a closer connection between Members of Parliament and their residents.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: On the other hand, SMCs have their place in our system too, because they are not just easier to contest, but also give a Member of Parliament direct responsibility for everything that happens in his constituency.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we have to strike the right balance between GRCs, big and small, and between GRCs and SMCs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the last two elections, we have created smaller GRCs and more SMCs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Elected Presidency as an institution was a major innovation, again with no precedent anywhere else.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we spent a long time designing it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After extensive debate, we legislated it, operated it and have amended it over the years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In addition to exercising custodial powers, the President would also continue to be the Head of State.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He represents all Singaporeans, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He is a symbol of our sovereignty and of our nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But in the last Presidential Election, many people did not understand this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I suspect even now, quite a number of people still do not understand this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Regrettably, during the last Presidential Election, those who did not understand it included some candidates.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They campaigned for President as if they were going to form an alternate Government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But the President is neither the Government nor is he the Opposition.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The purpose is specified in the Constitution, and we have to operate by the Constitution, both to be complying with the law and to make sure the system works.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For the system to work, both candidates and voters have to understand this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Otherwise, if you have a President who thinks that he is the Government, competing with the Government, you have two power centres in the system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At the very least, you have confusion, you could have an impasse between the two and the democratically elected Government will be undermined.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As the Chinese phrase says: 天无二日,国无二君, which means that you have no two suns in the sky, you have no two governments in a country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There are one or two countries which have had two Prime Ministers simultaneously, and it was not a happy experiment.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the last 25 years, we have accumulated experience operating the institution of an Elected President.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have improved and updated it over time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have refined how the financial safeguards operate.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The details are complex, and we could only get them more correct after operating them and getting experience operating them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In the Global Financial Crisis in 2008, we exercised and put to the test the President's custodial power over Reserves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We ourselves watched the indicators with great alarm.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We needed to make sure we threw all that we had at the problem.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We briefed the then-President, President S R Nathan.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He consulted the CPA; the CPA supported him and he gave approval.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was a critical decision, instrumental in saving jobs and enabling us to bounce back quickly from a deep recession.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we had not done that, if we did not have the mechanism, both to lock up the money for ordinary times and to unlock the money during extraordinary times, we could have not have reacted.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we had not locked it up in ordinary times, and we had just helped ourselves from time to time from it for some good purpose or other, come a crisis, you would not have had the kitty.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we had not been able to unlock the kitty in a crisis and spend it when we needed it, we would not have come through the crisis the way we did so smoothly that many people did not even realise that we had gone through a near-death experience.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As Mr Lee Kuan Yew would have said, this is now a shoe that we have worn for 25 years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I hesitate to call it an old shoe, but it is 25 years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have mended and adjusted it from time to time and, generally, it has fitted well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Yet, we need to continue to review and adjust the scheme regularly to keep it functional and in good repair.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If the President is not elected, he will lack the mandate to wield his custodial powers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have read various op-eds in the newspapers which say we can go back to the old system; just do away with the Elected President and have Parliament elect the President, do not have a national election.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I think the WP has sometimes espoused this view, too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a difficult system to get right, but we have to adjust it and try and get it more right than wrong over a period of time, and not abandon the project altogether and leave ourselves naked and defenceless against all the difficulties which the Elected President enables us to avoid.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But I think it is timely for us to review specific aspects of the Elected President system, and I would like to set out three areas which merit further consideration.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Before I do that, I would like to state upfront that the Government has a very good and constructive working relationship with this President, President Tony Tan.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are not proposing this review because of any dissatisfaction with the present working arrangements or any difference of views between the Government and the President.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But we are doing this because any adjustments that may be necessary for the future should be made in good time, in order to give us time to think it over in a thoughtful, mature and unpressured way and in order to keep the Presidency a robust and effective institution in our political system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have shared the Government's thinking with President Tan so he knows what I am going to say today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He has noted it and, in due course, he will formally express his views when we have more definite proposals.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What are the three things which I think we should consider?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Elected President is elected to fulfil specific constitutional duties.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And to be capable and qualified in carrying out those duties, he needs to have that experience to be able to judge and to make decisions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, there are qualifying criteria spelt out in the Constitution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The person who is making those decisions must understand what those decisions are, what is involved in that job before he can decide whether a person is fit to do that job or not, and before he decides whether a spending proposal is right or wrong, justified or otherwise.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, the candidates are required, under the Constitution, to have held key appointments themselves, like Speaker, the Chief Justice, Judges, Ministers, or Permanent Secretaries.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Or, in the private sector, to have held Chairman or CEO posts running large and complex companies, like Singtel, or, at that time, we said, the Public Utilities Board (PUB), because PUB was one entity before we had broken it up.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The principle remains valid, but I think the details may need to be brought up to date.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These are big organisations and they have grown much bigger over the last 25 years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have prepared a table which shows this.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The table shows a list of items with their values in 1990 and their values today.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The first row shows the Consumer Price Index.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If we take 1990 as 100, today it is 158, which is what I have told the House.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If we look at our nominal GDP, in 1990, it was S$72 billion.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: CPF balances, members' money − S$41 billion to S$275 billion.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: MAS' Official Foreign Reserves − this is in US$ because these are foreign Reserves and we are holding them overseas − US$28 billion increased to US$248 billion.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Temasek, which is one of the companies on the Fifth Schedule protected by the President, in 1990, they were worth about S$10 billion.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Today, the Net Porfolio Value is about S$266 billion.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I also put in Singtel − which is one of the jobs which you would consider comparable and suitable as experience to become the President − I do not have the figure in 1990 because they had not yet been corporatised and listed.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In 1993, it was S$500 million of paid-up capital.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If you look at their Net Tangible Assets, it has gone from S$2.5 billion to S$25 billion.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: On the other hand, if you look at the qualifying criteria and how many companies qualify, that is, S$100 million paid-up capital − I do not have the 1990 number, but in 1993, it was 158.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: More and more people, on paper, are qualified to do this job.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: During the Presidential Election, there is the Presidential Elections Committee which vets candidates to make sure they are qualified, and it is chaired by the Chairman of the Public Service Commission (PSC), and in the last election, the Chairman was Mr Eddie Teo.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It has gone up further. "The criterion of $100 million in paid-up capital in Article 19(g)(2)(iii) of the Constitution was set more than 20 years ago.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: It is therefore unclear whether or not, with inflation, the threshold continues to reflect the original intent of the requirement.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The PEC noted that in the Report of the Select Committee on the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment No 3) Bill, the examples of PUB and Telecoms…", presumably the Telecommunications Authority of Singapore, "…were cited as benchmarks against which organisations should be compared to for size and complexity.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The second aspect of the Presidency that we should review is examining how we can build up the Council of Presidential Advisers (CPA) further.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The CPA is an integral part of the two-key mechanism.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The Council assists and advises the President in exercising his powers, so that the system does not solely rely on the judgement of a single person acting alone but, rather, on a President well advised by a team of wise and experienced men and women.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: As Emeritus Senior Minister Goh Chok Tong once described it, together, the President and the CPA would play the role of "a goalkeeper together with a team of defenders".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We have to strike a delicate balance because the President must have the right to exercise his veto powers, even against the advice of the CPA.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He should have the right to say "no".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But a veto which is supported by the CPA should carry more weight than a veto which the CPA disagrees with.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Whether or not the CPA agrees that something should be vetoed, the President should have the discretion to say, "I believe it is right, I want to veto".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But if the President says, "Veto", and the CPA says, "Yes, I agree", that is a heavy veto.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If the CPA says, "No, let it through", and the President says, "Regardless, I want to veto", the President's view must carry weight.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But the weight in this instance will be less than if the CPA had agreed with him.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In fact, some parts of the Constitution are drafted like that today.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: For example, decisions on supply bills or key appointments, the President has to consult the CPA.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The supply bill is the bill when we vote money for the Government to spend during the year.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If the CPA concurs with the President's view, the veto is final, that is the end of the matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The Government must redo its sums or put up a new candidate.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But, if the CPA disagrees with the President, then the President can still veto but Parliament, in this case, can override his veto with a two-thirds majority.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, if the veto is unilateral, the CPA thinks it is okay, the President says "no", the Government can come back to Parliament, make the argument, explain its position and try and get a two-thirds majority to pass it through.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The third aspect we should examine of the Elected President is how we can ensure that minorities will have a chance to be elected to the office of President.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The President is the Head of State, he represents all Singaporeans in our multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think it is important that minorities have a chance to be elected President, and that this happens regularly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: From 1999, we had an Indian President, Mr S R Nathan, who served for two terms with distinction.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But in future, when Presidential Elections are more likely to be contested, and even hotly contested, I believe it will become much harder for a minority President to get elected.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And then, depending on the Commission's recommendations and the Government's response to them, we will follow up to table any legislation which may be necessary within this year.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Despite unpromising conditions at Separation, we have developed a political system that has worked well for us and we have evolved it carefully along the way to suit our changing needs and circumstances, in the light of our growing experience.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But our responsibility is not only to keep our political system working today, but to make sure that it works for the longer term.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Nobody can predict the future or tell how our needs will change.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If our system is to serve future generations well, then it is our responsibility to keep it up to date – regularly recalibrated, adjusted and improved, while preserving the principles that it was built upon.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: At the beginning of this term after SG50, I am raising this issue now because my aim is to strengthen the system to make it more open and contestable, to keep it accountable to the people, to go into the next 50 years with the best chance of making a success of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We have to have a system where all the political parties, and especially the PAP, have to fight hard, stay lean and responsive to the people, and win the right to govern afresh at each election.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: A system where Parliament will always be the place to debate and decide important policies, where alternative views always have a place, the Opposition will never be shut out, and the Government will be held to account, so that the Government of the day – whoever that may be – is always kept on its toes.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We must not assume that future governments, whether it is PAP or a different party forming the Government, will never falter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In fact, it is not possible for any political system to guarantee a country political stability and prosperity forever.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But we can make such a happy outcome more likely if we design our system carefully and correctly around the core principles: ensure high-quality Government; keep our politics open and contestable; maintain accountability for the Government; uphold a multiracial society; and institute suitable stabilisers and checks-and-balances in the system.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In 50 years' time − SG100 − I think many of us will not be around.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We do not know what Singapore will be like or whether the PAP will still be in Government.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: But whatever the shape of Singapore 50 years from now, today, we can and must help Singapore build a political system that will give us the best shot at prosperity and progress over the next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: A system that is not set in stone, a system that is not fixed and unchangeable, but one that future generations can continue to improve and adapt in order to meet their future needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: On that particular day, Ms Ellen Lee, the contingent commander, was on the parade square.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It was one of our dress rehearsals and I was at the reserve form-up point with the other reserve commanders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The reserve form-up point was at the entrance to a tunnel through the stands.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Above us were the seats with thousands of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Around me were the medical teams, stretcher bearers, and other members from the community contingent – what was called by one observer – the "Aunty-Uncle" contingent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A little bit further behind was a group of warrant officers, the Enciks who had trained the various groups out marching on parade.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This was something they had done many times before.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Many of us were engrossed with our mobile phones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Just in front of me, to my left, were three young men – soldiers, also on reserve duty, ready to go out on the parade square, if needed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Their uniforms were white and starched, their boots shined to a mirror finish – the brass all buffed and polished.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I was reminded of my three sons, especially as those three in front of me were engaged in a very familiar mix of bravado, aggression and camaraderie that seems to strike any group of young men when they are away from the influence of their mothers, girlfriends and wives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They were joking and poking, pushing and shoving and enjoying each other's company.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The first few bars of "Majulah Singapura", we all turned to face the flag that we could not see.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ahead and above, and around us were the stands full of people who could not see us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We began to sing as we had done many times before.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Maybe it was the excitement of the dress rehearsal, or maybe it was just the sense of whimsy or foolishness on the part of one of those soldiers, but these three young soldiers on my left started to sing as loud as they could, pouring all their energy – not shouting – but putting every ounce of effort into singing, using every fibre of their being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You could hear all the passion and pride that they could muster.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Maybe they thought they would try and drown out the thousands of spectators that they could not see.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Whatever the reason, the aunties and uncles around me – I will include myself in that – would not be left behind.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We also raised our voices louder and louder and louder.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Although I could not turn around to check, in my mind's eye, the Enciks behind us were also singing louder, louder and louder.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If you have ever sung in a choir, there is a special feel in the air when everyone gets it right, and the timing is just perfect with everybody in step.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is the same feeling you get if you are rowing a boat, paddling for a dragon boat and, suddenly, all strokes fall into perfect time and the boat surges forward.
