speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The choir lifts their voices a little bit more, not because of any effort, but because everybody had fallen into step perfectly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The moment does not last long, but it feels special, almost magical.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, louder and louder we sang, until it was a roar – a roar full of pride and full of passion, unseen and, perhaps, unheard.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: When the last notes faded away, we all fell silent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We looked around, smiled, acknowledged with the combination of joy and awkwardness that you get when you share a public experience with strangers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But we all agreed that we had felt something special that afternoon.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As the night came to an end, we were in the multi-purpose hall in the HDB estate singing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I found myself standing on the floor in front of the stage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It was the last event, and the stage was filled with kids.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, as the Committee was getting ready to play the music, I turned around and found a small boy, just on the stage behind me, with his head just behind my ear.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I said, "We're going to sing Majulah Singapura.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Are you going to sing?" I asked him.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Yes, uncle." "Do you know the words?" I said. "Yes, yes, uncle, I know all the words!" he replied, full of excitement and energy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He did not know the words, not at all.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You could vaguely make out the tune, but that was about it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And his parents from the front row of the seats facing me, they began to have a worried look on their faces, looking like they wanted to do something or fix something.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I smiled at them and shrugged, it was okay, he was trying his best, he was doing his best, and everything was okay, a little child trying his best to sing our Majulah Singapura.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We all smiled, we all sang and throughout this song, we heard his little voice trying harder and harder to get it right.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Maybe he thought that if he sang a little bit louder, all the Aunties and Uncles would follow him.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: When we finished, we all laughed, we high-fived, we hugged.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: On my way back home, I was thinking about the two versions of the song: one in perfect time, synchronicity; one completely out of time, chaotic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But all sung with passion and pride, celebrating our National Day.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I have told the story many times, to family, to friends, to my students, to my residents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And after a while, I began to think about how people would respond to the story, how they were responding to my story, as I watched them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Their expressions, their emotions, what they said and, in particular, I wondered about what questions might be asked when someone heard my story.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And there was one question that occurred to me.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One particular question that would be very natural in many parts of the world, if you heard the story.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Maybe it would have been natural to ask this question 50 years ago in Singapore, maybe 10 years ago, maybe five years ago.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I began to look out for the story, telling the story deliberately waiting to see if someone was going to ask me, watching and waiting.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I have never been asked what race they were.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have a unity of purpose to build the Singapore we imagine.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our country is not a utopia and I am under no illusions about the reality of race relations in our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are difficulties, there are frictions, there are tensions and there are troubles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There remains much work to be done, but we all recognise the need to do the work together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We all want the same thing and we will deal with the problems together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This started as a simple but important story about our National Anthem, but by highlighting a question that was not asked, everything has changed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The words left unspoken have had a profound effect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: You can listen to the story, imagine these young men singing the "Majulah Singapura", imagine their pride at being part of the NDP, imagine the excitement of the little boy on the stage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They will be alive at SG100, the soldiers will be approaching 70, maybe thinking about the next generation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The little boy will be in his 50s, maybe thinking about his second career.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Between them, they will build the next 50 years of our country.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Listening, you embrace them as Singaporeans through and through.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We sing the same songs, we eat the same foods, wear the same uniforms, believe in the same values that drive our country.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We, together, will stand shoulder to the shoulder, face the future and all that the unknown may bring, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: What if one of them is gay or an atheist?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Or maybe he is someone who takes his religion very, very seriously?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Maybe he embraces a different set of political views or is very conservative?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Listening to my story, are you still convinced that he will stand beside you as a comrade and as a brother?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Will you stand beside him as a fellow citizen?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In those few words, six words, are captured thousands of years – race, language or religion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Thousands of years of history, hundreds of wars, conflicts of blood shed between our races, of fights between other countries and religions, places we are not a part of.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In those few words are described hundreds of millions of people outside our borders with whom we share history, heritage, ties of ethnicity and culture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We do not ignore all of this, we do not pretend it does not exist.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But we look through, we look ahead and imagine a future where we have unity regardless of our history.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: If we can do this for race, language and religion, why not for other fault lines, other divisions amongst us?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will always have differences among us and between us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I will not suggest we can pretend otherwise, nor should we.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Often, these things that I describe are facts that determine our personality, determine our world views.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need to embrace this, we need to work through this together.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Over the next 50 years, what will be the new fault lines?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: How will the old divisions of race, language and religion be interpreted?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And potentially, how will these basic differences be exploited by those seeking to sow strife and divide us?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For sometimes, the things that are not said have a deep impact.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To create a division, to create a proverbial line in the sand, is very easy, all it takes are a few words – them and us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is easy to separate people, all it takes are a few words and that line in the sand is drawn.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And every line in the sand is a problem, every line in the sand can become a gulf too large to cross if given enough words, enough malice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A wall is created and before, there was just space.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: All it takes are a few more words and then there is no going back.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It becomes impossible or difficult to forget and forgive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But every line in the sand, every potential division, is also an opportunity and a chance – a chance to reach across and offer the hand of friendship and to face another across the line and speak words of unity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Every difference amongst us is an opportunity to show the world and each other that our diversity is our strength.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Fifty years ago, our nation was founded in troubled circumstances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Events that highlighted an important principle that the founding generation took to heart, and used to write our pledge and build Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: And that will take work to ensure that we get it right now and prevent it from ever happening.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Whatever the future, we must hold to that idea.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Returning to my story, it began as a warm fuzzy tale about National Day and the Anthem and some very enthusiastic boys.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Then, it became an example of the extent of our racial integration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I spoke only a few more words and it became a platform for some difficult and contentious questions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But I hope we can return to that first chapter, the initial frame that with the right circumstances, with the right drive and passion, we can roar "Majulah Singapura" and that we must do so as one united people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is still much to be done and many challenges ahead, but we are a forward-facing purposeful people.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The President reminded us of the need to continue our hard work and commitment in making this nation succeed – be it in safety and security, renewing our economy, nurturing a caring and magnanimous society, rejuvenating our urban landscape, or strengthening our Government-and-people relations in nation-building.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my speech, I would like to address two related areas – that of opportunities and that of inclusivity and social cohesion.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am deeply heartened and grateful for the opportunities available to Singaporeans, particularly through the SkillsFuture initiatives.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   I am pleased to see more and more of our Malays who are now becoming entrepreneurs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This shows courage – in seeking opportunities and exploring uncharted territories.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many are also displaying the "never say die" spirit.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although faced with failures, they kept trying, and improving themselves and their skills.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that many amongst us will draw lessons from the experiences of these entrepreneurs, not just from their courage in becoming entrepreneurs, but also their bravery and their willingness to never give up.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that our community can seize this opportunity to know more about these schemes, and how their businesses and companies can be strengthened through these schemes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here, I would like to urge mothers, especially homemakers, to use their SkillsFuture Credits to gain new knowledge or skills, or to deepen them.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These knowledge and skills may come in useful if our homemakers would like to go back to work, or in their efforts to enhance their family income.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Further details about SkillsFuture Credit can be found in this brochure, which is being sent to every Singaporean aged 25 years and above.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, I would like to suggest that organisations like Mendaki Sense and the Singapore Muslim Women's Association (PPIS) to lead a combined effort where skills upgrading programmes and courses using SkillsFuture Credit can be planned and implemented to help mothers, especially homemakers or single mothers, gain new or deeper knowledge and skills.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With this, our mothers will not feel that they are alone in their efforts to enhance their knowledge and skills.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When we empower our mothers, we will secure the future of our community through our children.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The hand that rocks the cradle can change the world.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): With this, Mdm Speaker, please allow me to continue in English.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The main focus of SkillsFuture is to help Singaporeans obtain relevant skills and experience that will prepare them for the future workforce and economy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I laud this move to look beyond paper qualifications and consider skills, experience and abilities other than the academics.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are increasingly many opportunities to recognise and reward diverse abilities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In our education system, there are multiple pathways that our children can explore and venture forth in.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is good but it will still take time before we are able to look beyond academic achievements and paper qualifications.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here, I echo the Acting Minister Ong Ye Kung when he cautioned against excessively viewing ourselves in numerical terms – whether in scores or ranking.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since we are already allowing lateral transfers and greater flexibility for students to take subjects at different levels of intensity or difficulty based on their abilities, we should extend that to remove the labelling of students altogether, according to academic streams.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My concern is that pigeon-holing students into Express or Normal (Academic) or Normal (Technical) streams will create and entrench the self-limiting belief in each student that they are only as good as the academic stream they are in.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yes, it will be a lot messier not to have academic streams, but neatness or expedience cannot be the reason for creating a less than optimal environment – for abilities to flourish and full potential to be achieved without imposing artificial limits.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Government has taken the lead in recognising different peaks of excellence, as a society, we still have some way to go in accepting, recognising and rewarding different talents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, sometimes, opportunities come not so much because of abilities or prior experience, but because of inherent factors – be it age, sex, or even race.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Age, sex, or race are characteristics that we cannot quite change, but which, to a certain extent, have influence on employment opportunities or job promotion.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are older Singaporeans who are worried about being retrenched because of their age or because of competition from younger co-workers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A resident I know, Joseph, was retrenched from his job as a C-suite executive as a result of budget cuts and job restructuring in the company.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, he was convinced it was because of his age.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He was 58 years old when he lost his job.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In light of a slowing economy, these concerns are very real.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, I have met Indian and Malay Singaporeans who have expressed their worry that a slowing economy would mean either opportunities for employment or job promotion for members of our minority races, would be even more difficult.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This may simply be a perception, but the perception that is observed or heard often enough becomes entrenched as a reality.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although I have reassured them that our Tripartite Alliance for Fair Employment Practices (TAFEP) will not allow such race-based discrimination from happening in the workplace, their worry still exists.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is always the worry that because of how different you look, you can be denied of opportunities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important for us to see beyond our physical differences and see the person within.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to recognise that our abilities and potential come from what is in our hearts and minds, and are not determined by our physical appearance, by the colour of our skin or by what is covering our heads.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have spoken about this before, but it is important enough for me to say it again.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that those in positions of influence or power can show that these worries and concerns will remain unfounded.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is necessary for us to continue our efforts to enhance social cohesion and inclusivity in our common spaces, such as in the community, at our workplaces, and particularly in our education institutions and schools.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us be sensible and honest enough to discuss issues of discrimination, stereotypes, perceptions and social cohesion openly with our children.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will enrich the racial make-up of students in the SAP schools and create more opportunities for multi-racial interactions and learning, making it more authentic and representative of society at large.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a parent and educator, I believe that taking Chinese as a third language and exposure to the Chinese culture for more of our children will help to prepare them to venture into a big market in China and other Chinese-speaking economies for employment and entrepreneurial opportunities in future.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am not asking for the SAP schools to be abolished.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If it does not, then at least we have tried.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are no sacred cows in so far as enhancing our education system to benefit as many of our children as possible.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To me, this will be a significant move towards greater inclusivity in our schools and among our children as current strategies for social cohesion in SAP schools are, at best, intermittent and simulated.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we cannot continue to just be cautious or careful about these sensitivities at the expense of not making progress.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The President's address reminded us of the opportunities and potential we have ahead of us, amidst existing vulnerabilities and sensitivities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us work harder and together to minimise our vulnerabilities and at the same time, strengthen the social fabric that binds us as we move ahead to many more years of nation-building.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I support the President's call for all Singaporeans to work together to build a better Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As we progress as a sovereign country comprising Singaporeans of different races and religions, we must stay united as one people and work towards improving the quality of life for all Singaporeans and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the next 50 years, we must focus on making Singapore a holistic, healthy and happy city.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must introduce and encourage innovative technologies allowing Singaporeans to access information easily for lifelong learning of new skills.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must provide a safe living and working environment and protect the vulnerable, especially the elderly and children in our society.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must set up informative and alert systems that will further strengthen our emergency rescue and healthcare support services.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this way we will be able to provide Singaporeans a better environment for them to grow in and live in.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First review the planning concepts and norms for land use.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, many Singaporeans still have to travel long distances from their homes to their workplaces as well as for food and leisure.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To better fulfil the needs of our people, we need to review the planning concepts and norms so that residential areas, business clusters and leisure amenities can be planned and built at suitable locations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This involves redeveloping and upgrading of HDB towns into large high-rise and high-density residential clusters.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can locate or relocate leisure amenities near MRT stations for better accessibility.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, building mega hawker centres, sports complexes, shopping malls, seafood centres and parks near MRT stations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Next, enhancing "live, work and play" in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, we must build quality homes; second, we must provide good connectivity for Singaporeans to travel to work conveniently; and third, there must be accessible leisure facilities for Singaporeans and their families to enjoy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: With better designs for new flats and the upgrading of older flats, HDB has provided a high-quality living environment for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, by building neighbourhood town centres which provide a wide range of services, HDB and neighbouring private estate residents enjoy affordable products and services at great convenience.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, as HDB towns grow, more flats are built away from the neighbourhood centres.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a result, some neighbourhood centres have become less accessible to residents, especially the elderly who live further away.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This problem will be exacerbated as our residents age – travelling the distance to town centres may be challenging to these seniors.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Today, our road pavements are cluttered with road signage, electrical installations, dustbins, trees with roots uplifting pavements and many other installations that impede easy access for pedestrians, cyclists and wheelchair-bound users.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many of these installations built many to different Government agencies.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must align these agencies in order to build wider walkways and cycling paths promoting accessibility for all users.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will free up more surface land areas for gardens, paths, walkways and cycling paths.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It will provide more green lungs within our towns and reduce the heat island effects – that is the warming of our built environment.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must aim to make every HDB town into a town where people can live comfortably, access town amenities easily and have leisure facilities near their homes.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I support the Ministry of Transport’s (MOT) proposal to build the North-South Expressway and provide dedicated lanes for buses, cyclists and pedestrians.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should also consider adding capacity to our existing expressways by building two-tier expressways.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The upper tier can have dedicated lanes for express buses and cars while the lower tier expressways can have dedicated lanes for motorcycles and goods vehicles.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This segregation will ease the flow of traffic and may help to reduce accidents.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will encourage more people to take public transport as they spend the day out with their families on the weekends.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must implement the correct policies to build a sustainable environment.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Climate change and environmental pollution will have adverse effects on our people and economy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have to prepare and protect ourselves from such changes, in particular, flooding, global warming, haze, and air pollution.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, we should further encourage the use of solar energy in powering our building utilities.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I understand that HDB has piloted the use of solar energy for HDB blocks.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should maximise the solar energy potential in Singapore and install more solar panels at our roofs.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will not only reduce heat transfer into our buildings but also promote the use of "green" energy and reduce our reliance on less sustainable energy sources.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many flat owners are installing larger capacity air-conditioning systems, larger capacity refrigerators, shower heaters, and home entertainment systems, increasing the demand for energy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: To be sustainable, we need to focus on promoting Green Homes among Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: New technology has been introduced to make cities smarter.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These include sensors, CCTV, big data analytics and dashboard management systems.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must be careful and vigilant when adopting these technologies.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must first understand the present and future needs of our people and ensure that Singaporeans are ready to adopt and benefit from these smart city initiatives.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In order to implement Smart City systems in Singapore, we must first prioritise the needs of our people and businesses.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I would urge the Government to focus on three key areas to apply smart city initiatives.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the last few years, the town councils have been working closely with our Police to install CCTV at HDB void decks and common areas to enhance safety and security.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I wish to commend the Police for spearheading this project and their success in using the CCTV system to solve crimes.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In view of the ever-present threat of terrorism, I urge the Government to introduce this project to more areas, especially at high human traffic locations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Smart city systems can provide intelligent and alert systems and facilitate data collection to further strengthen our emergency and healthcare services.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Big data analytics can provide real-time monitoring of trends.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The information gathered will support preventive healthcare interventions and contribute towards developing response strategies in disease outbreak management.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the areas of town and facilities management, smart technologies can provide 24/7 monitoring of the functionality of buildings or facilities and send alerts for faster response by the maintenance team.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many Town Councils have also installed LED lightings with sensors to control lighting and save energy.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I would urge the HDB to play a more proactive role in introducing more smart city applications in HDB towns.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: I was indeed very impressed by the innovations and futuristic thinking of the Japanese researchers.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: They were already exploring construction techniques and materials to build vertical cities then.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These vertical cities consist of skyscrapers towering 1,000 metres or 300 storeys.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: They house residential, commercial, office and recreational facilities within the same building, enabling users to live, work and play with convenience.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Together, we can build a great future for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: As we are all aware, all grand narratives may include elements of hyperbole, and parts may require further interpretation.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: In the telling, we allow ourselves some artistic licence.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Members who have spoken before me have painted vivid pictures of how we need to evolve, with "faster legs" and hearts of lions.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Even as we do so, we need to be careful of the myths that have been perpetuated as part of our national narrative.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to look at the margins of this story, and see those who have not been included in our story so far.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Recently, I came across an academic paper and the title interests me – as a politician.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: The paper was called "Stupid Public Policies and Political Myths".

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: The writer, David Shultz, a professor at an American university, claimed that such political myths often appear to "capture the imagination of political elites." By "stupid public policies", he means policies that are repeatedly proposed, and which do not work, and which have been proven by social science research not to work. "Political myths", he said, are ideas which "seem to circulate everywhere, often repeated or held up as true," even though there is no hard evidence to support them.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: One "stupid policy" he cited was the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Act, which held the provision allowing states to deny higher benefits to recent migrants to their state.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: This was based on the idea that welfare recipients migrate to the state simply to seek higher benefits.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: In Minnesota, which is a high-benefit state, officials have claimed that "busloads of individuals in Chicago would travel monthly to their state, which is about 800 kilometres away, to collect their welfare checks, only to return for the duration of the month." This picture appears probable.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Research found that few recipients moved between states, and when they did do so, it was not a result of benefit levels.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Poor people move, of course, but it is largely for the same reasons as rich people.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: They move for job opportunities, family reasons, or a fresh start in life.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: The writer said: "Much of the myth of welfare migration is premised upon several questionable assumptions.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: First, it assumes that the poor are rational calculators who make cost/benefit lifestyle decisions.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, it assumes they have knowledge about different welfare benefit levels.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Third, the benefit differences are enough to outweigh the costs of travel." He lists other assumptions which are questionable.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Overall, the reality of migration is that it is the more affluent who move and who are mobile.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Wrong assumptions are easy mistakes to make – it is wrong to assume that people would make socially deviant decisions once welfare benefits are made available to them.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: These may be the same assumptions that may lead a policy of differential benefits for single mothers.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, we could assume that single mothers are rational calculators who will compute the cost and benefits of a divorce.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Calculations that, say, just because they are eligible for the Jubilee Marriage and Parenthood Package, these women will stay married.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, some may assume that the single mothers have knowledge about these differences in welfare levels.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: And third, some may assume that the benefit differentials are enough to outweigh their desire to separate from their abusive husbands, husbands 	to-be, or to reconcile irreconcilable differences.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: If we treat single mothers differently from divorced, widowed or married mothers, such a policy might be premised on the basis that the above assumptions were true.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: But social spending need not increase deviant behaviour.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: And we could, and should, treat single mothers as mothers, rather than singles.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: If our assumptions are false, I call on the Minister to consider making available to all mothers the same benefit across the board.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Our older workers are often perceived to be less productive, set in their ways, less healthy and cost more.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Thus, we make them cheaper so that they can be more employable.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Why should older workers be discriminated in terms of their age, and see them more as a cost and liability, instead of seeing them as assets with experience and loyalty?

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Another assumption relevant to our Singapore society is that if you supply the option for 18-year-olds to devote themselves to sports, and to defer their National Service, there will be a floodgate of higher physical adult young men clamouring for this privilege.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: This assumption ignores the fact that these are young men who are willing to spend many hours a day training in their sports, enduring injuries and pain, and with that special talent, the necessary financial and mental resources to enable them to do this throughout their growing up years.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Minister Tan Chuan-Jin, the SNOC's President, has said he would wish to "push the boundaries" with MINDEF to see how they can collectively take a step towards including more promising athletes into the band for consideration.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: How can we help spur more promising and deserving athletes to reach their full potential, to be considered?

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Whether you are termed as a single unwed mother or an Olympian athlete, you are exceptional to the policymaker because you do not fit policy rules.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Since I have been a Member, I have had a resident who has come to see me every week during my Meet-the-People Session.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: She looks perfectly well, but her family left her, she cannot hold a job, she cannot take care of herself, and yet, she has no one else.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: She insists on seeing me first, even though there is a queue of people in front of her.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: When she does not get her way, she will throw a tantrum.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Neighbours have problems with her too, contributing to both her and her neighbours' woes.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: As a fellow Singaporean, she deserves a place at the table too.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: But building a society for all is not the job of the Government – it is yours, and mine.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: The President said, "Ours should be a society where the bonds of kinship run deep and people look out for one another.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: A society where we extend our concern for immediate families and friends to the broader community.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: A society consisting of generous hearts that treat one another with warmth and dignity." These are not matters of policy or of budget.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: These are moral choices we make as individuals.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a choice especially true for the mentally ill.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: There are a few things we can and should do.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the mental health stigma remains strong in Singapore.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: This would also include better understanding the mental health needs of vulnerable populations as well, for those with disabilities, persons from disadvantaged backgrounds, and catering adequately for their unique needs.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Last, in terms of human resource, there needs to be a commitment to ensure there are sufficient psychiatrists, psychologists and other mental health professionals who cater to persons with mental health problems.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: We want to help but a long-term sustained solution is needed, and if I may add, a professional one.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: I am not a counsellor, and I do not know what a medical condition requires.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: For this particular resident of mine, I give her patience and a listening ear, keep working with the volunteer welfare organisation (VWO), the police and her neighbours.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: And over four years of trial and error, I have figured out a way to keep her steady – for another week.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: But Mdm Speaker, her life cannot be lived band-aided from week to week.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: The Singapore Story is one of continuous experimentation, to test what works and to look at data without an ideological lens.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: The Singapore Story at its birth was one of uncertainty and grim determination, of tight belts and hungry bellies.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, we write the Singapore Story from what appears to be a position of strength.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: But we are a chain of people, as strong as the weakest among us.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Even as we develop "faster legs and wiser minds", we are as weak as our fastest runner, as strong as the single mother, the mentally-ill.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: Whether rich or poor, Singapore is strong only if we stand together, strong only when no one stands at the margins, when we leave no one behind.

speaker: Mr David Ong (Bukit Batok)
text: This is our new Singapore Story, one which all of us must be proud to write.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As we enter SG51, the President, in his Address, has called for Singaporeans to renew our commitment to a better Singapore and write the next chapter together.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many Members have spoken at length about how Singapore remains very vulnerable to our external circumstances and our inherent limitations, such as land and population size.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are reminded, even as we stand from a position of strength today, that our survival depends on us continuing to be exceptional, in both our security and economy.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In my view, the need for a strong security umbrella is never in doubt.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I know the threats and dangers to our country quite well.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We all must be clear-minded that our basic vulnerability of being small has not changed and will not change.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A strong SAF is needed to deter potential adversaries and, together with our Home Team, safeguard Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is needed to enhance the peace so that our vital interests can be taken care of.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A secure environment is critical not just for our safety but for our economy, our businesses, our very livelihood, our rice bowls.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have faced them for the past 50 years and we will continue to face them in the next 50.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will have to continue to take a pragmatic approach, adapt and evolve our policies so that we can continue to succeed economically and protect ourselves.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But in a fast-changing world with growing diversities and forces that can pull our society apart, Singapore will need a source of inner strength to keep us united.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Singapore is commonly known for our "Head" because of our pragmatism.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are admired for our economic miracle with a well-run, efficient and well-organised city.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Page: 30 Unfortunately, this may be a double-edged sword because, on the downside, many questioned if we have traded off some of our soul and heart in the pursuit of efficiencies.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Those of us who are honest about it will probably admit to having asked ourselves if we are too cold, or whether there is a Singapore "Heart".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Yet, last year, when our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew passed on, we proved the world wrong when Singaporeans came together in solidarity.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I think we surprised even ourselves at how much heart and spirit we have in all of us.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We all remember our own experiences and the countless stories of how ordinary Singaporeans, together with their elderly parents and young children, came to queue patiently for hours to pay their last respects.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many were touched by the accounts of businesses and volunteers giving out food, drinks and umbrellas so that they could afford some creature comforts to fellow Singaporeans queuing in the blazing sun.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I was moved to see the hundreds of thousands lined up on that Sunday morning in the pouring rain, standing shoulder-to-shoulder to send Mr Lee off on a final journey across Singapore to the state funeral service.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Economist described this phenomenon as "an improbable patriotism".

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For once, others, looking in from the outside, saw what it meant to be Singaporean.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They witnessed the pride of our people, who are usually not very expressive with our emotions.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It was truly uplifting for me personally to witness a re-energised Singapore Heartbeat.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This continued beyond the week of March and into the SG50 celebrations throughout the year, especially on our National Day on 9 August.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To me, these are two dimensions of the Singapore Heartbeat.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The heart is the central powerhouse that pumps life-giving oxygen and nutrients to all parts of the body.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While others consider us exceptional because of our Head, we must never forget that the Heart is our source of inner strength, our inner core.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, today, I would like to talk about how we can keep the Singapore Heartbeat strong and steady beyond SG50 and into the next phase of nation-building.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: First, we must keep united in vision and purpose, with one heart.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The idea of the Singapore Heartbeat is that all of us are indispensable and complementary parts of a living system, our Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Just as the different organs in the body have to work together for the body to be healthy, we, too, must find a place for every Singaporean to be part of the nation's progress.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We must also ensure that every Singaporean has the opportunity to succeed and share in the nation's prosperity and progress, regardless of their starting point and background.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will create multiple pathways to success and do our very best to nurture each and every child so that they can reach the fullest of Page: 31 their potential, grounded on sound values and character.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many Members in this House have spoken on education.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is a good indication that all of us place significant emphasis on education in our country on our children.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: On the social front, we have made significant efforts and must continue to ensure social mobility and strengthen social safety nets.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: After all, the well-being of our society, like the body, is measured by the health of all our parts.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Similarly, the strength of our social fabric lies in the spirit of mutual support within our society.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To my mind, this is a wonderful example of a ground-up initiative that embodies the Singapore Heartbeat.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It brings together the expertise and energy of different segments of the society for a common good.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As our society matures, we should do more to encourage individuals and organisations to come forth and take collective ownership of the community they live in, for the Singapore that we all love.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Second, for a steady Singapore Heartbeat, we must also nurture deep bonds of kinship.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A heart is much more than just a muscle.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The heart is also where we hold the things we cherish the very most and where our passions spring forth.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Therefore, a strong Singapore Heartbeat is formed by deep bonds of kinship among our people and the pride of simply being Singaporean.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These come from shared experiences of studying in the same school, playing together, living in the same community and, for our men, having served National Service together.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are connected by our everyday things that make us uniquely Singaporean, including our Singlish, perhaps our favourite chicken rice and even "choping" our seat in the crowded hawker centres with our tissue papers.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The irony is, sometimes, it is only when we are away from home, away from Singapore, that we feel such a surge of pride when we bump into fellow Singaporeans overseas or when our overseas friends ask us about our country and the secret to our success.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But pride and love for our country and fellow Singaporeans should not be just feelings that arise only because of the occasion or the atmosphere.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: That type of sentiment is not bad, but it is not sufficient for the long haul and does not anchor a nation.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We do not want a racing, erratic heartbeat when we run a long-distance race.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: What we need is a steady and strong heartbeat that will take us forward in our journey.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It involves us demonstrating our love for the country and to care for our countrymen on an ordinary day and in ordinary ways.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A middle-aged taxi driver approached me recently for help to appeal to waive a parking fine.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: He told me he was driving a wheel-chair bound lady on an early morning shift.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: When they had arrived at her destination, at her flat, he left his car by the road so that he could personally wheel Page: 32 her all the way up to her high-rise flat, to her very doorstep.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I applaud his act of kindness, going out of his way to help, at a certain level of personal sacrifice and personal inconvenience.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Till now, I am not sure what has happened to his parking fine but I hope it got waived.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But the point is, I think, sometimes, we tend to look out for the big gestures and forget that an ordinary act of kindness, like what this taxi driver did, forms the basic rhythm of the Singapore Heartbeat.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Indeed, patriotism and love for our country are inseparable from caring and looking out for our fellow countrymen.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In a team of undercover journalists, they would go around the island with a hidden camera to capture everyday kindness and graciousness among Singaporeans.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Then, they would upload videos or stories online.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our Singapore Heartbeat is about such altruistic acts, but it is also much more than that.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We must build the Singapore Heartbeat to forge our collective core strength, collective resilience and cohesion.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Together with our economic strength and a safe and secure environment, the Singapore Heartbeat will propel us forward to the next lap.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In English, "Come, let us unite; In a new spirit; Let our voices soar as one." In the last five decades, our founding fathers and the generations before us have risen to this call – building a strong and free nation, a robust and prosperous economy and a peaceful and progressive society.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Now, let us refresh and re-energise ourselves with a new spirit – a Singapore Heartbeat – to carry ourselves forward to SG100 and beyond.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While we do face new and complex challenges ahead, we stand in a position of strength, compared to where we started off 50 years ago in 1965.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Education (Schools) and Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With this, Mdm Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It was how to make sure our small island state and our multiracial people survive an unforgiving and hostile world.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Our solution has been to discipline ourselves and to make sacrifices under a strong one-party top-down rule to guide the development of the economy and society.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: National institutions were built and tied closely to the PAP so that the leaders could steer the ship in the direction they thought best and everyone else was not to rock the boat.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We are now a globalised society with a well-educated people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We are now seeking to ensure our children will thrive, not just survive.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans are aspiring to set sail on their own to fulfil their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We need to be nimble and experiment as a country to search and seize the hidden opportunities in the next industrial revolution.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We cannot simply rely on a group of so-called super talents in Government steering society from high above.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: For Singapore to continue to shine as a red dot, the people of Singapore must shine, Singaporeans must shine if Singapore is to chart our own path.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The red dot will no longer be red if its people turn pale in the face of challenges or when faced with intimidation.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Government takes a step back and only provides counsellors to help those who want advice to help them decide.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Third, it does not measure value in the narrow terms of economic value-add and caters to people's passion and interests.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It has been said that one could even use the SkillsFuture credits to improve one's skills in calligraphy.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, it exemplifies what some analysts call a nudge policy instead of the usual carrot-and-stick approach favoured by the Government.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: A nudge policy is said to be more effective for today's modern citizens and does not mean less or weaker Government.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The credit is nudging Singaporeans to engage in lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Empowering Singaporeans' future is something the Workers' Party will fully agree with.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If we want to empower confident Singaporeans, this policy DNA – all-inclusive, trusting Singaporeans, seeing value broadly, nudging and empowering Singaporeans' future – should be applied to many other policy areas.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It should be applied to at least the schools and the SME sector.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: These two are important and also because they are related to SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If the graduates of our schools are not self-driven and Page: 34 unafraid to take risks to pursue their interests, then SkillsFuture will become meaningless over time.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It would also be a terrible waste of synergy if SkillsFuture helps Singaporeans to be more enterprising but the lack of funding and business opportunities, as well as high operating costs, continue to hamper the growth of the SME sector.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the schools, we need to nurture the thirst for learning and to revamp the syllabus and assessment methods so that we would not kill the natural curiosity of children.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the last few years, we have been discussing educational reforms in terms of reducing the stress on children.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I think we might have been wrong in focusing on the symptoms of the problem.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Empowering our students to think critically and creatively and to solve complex problems can also be stressful, but it will be a rewarding and fulfilling kind of stress.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We have also been emphasising too much on cohesion as a value in schools and have not appreciated the importance of diversity, differences and even dissent for cultivating critical thinking and creativity in schools.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Our curriculum and culture in schools should avoid influencing our students to think in narrow practical terms and not in relation to their interests and passion.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Graduates of our schools should have a strong sense of self-driven purpose with the right values of tolerance and respect for diversity and differences.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Although the ASPIRE Report is the correct road map, we have a long road ahead to redefine our long-ingrained notion of success from the focus on material gains and academic achievements to the pursuit of passion and happiness and the possession of different kinds of skills.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: But while empowering confident Singaporeans is the way for us to ensure our shining red dot stays brilliant, getting our politics right is the way for us to insure against bad government and the failure of governance.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The outcome of good politics is not just good policy and ensuring no gridlock.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: That would be a narrow technocratic view of politics.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The outcome of good politics is the fostering of a political system that is able to withstand shock and turbulence, including the unexpected collapse or slow corruption of the ruling party, to ensure the continuity of the nation as a united people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Such a resilient political system must be able to make adjustments in the face of adversity.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: How should we do good politics to ensure a resilient political system and a confident nation?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I believe the same principles making up the policy DNA for SkillsFuture are pertinent.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Government should recognise that there are many on-going and independent national conversations and should allow for differences in opinions to flourish without marking these conversations as disloyal and divisive.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Second, our politics must be nudging instead of censoring.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We should not be afraid of narrow interest-based politics, which I do not think we can avoid.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In fact, if we look at SkillsFuture, it leverages on the so-called narrow interests of individual Singaporeans to pursue the collective good.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Page: 35 Instead of rejecting narrow interest-based politics altogether, we need to nudge Singaporeans with narrow political interests to talk to each other.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We should take such discussion as an educational process for Singaporeans to learn and to discern what is politics for the collective good of the nation and society.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We should not design a system of shutting out discussion based on assumption that it is interest-based and narrow.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Third, our politics must trust Singaporeans to be independent, rational and wise social actors.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: For a while, they were tightly controlled for fear of their political influence.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: But since they were released and their autonomy protected, we can be proud of our Universities today for achieving world-class status.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Today, our academics could disagree and criticise the Government and a few have even joined alternative political parties to contribute to the national debate and in politics.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Our political system has not been destabilised as a result.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, our politics must see value in the broadest sense.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The outcome of good politics is not to ensure no gridlock.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We cannot expect a political party to transform itself into a credible alternative party overnight.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Political value must not be narrowly construed and concentrated in one political party.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: That is too dangerous for a small state such as ours.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In all this talk about the future, SkillsFuture, Right Politics for FutureSg, we must not forget our foundational ideals enshrined in our national pledge – to build a democratic society based on justice and equality so as to achieve happiness, prosperity and progress.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew said, I quote, "In 1966, my colleagues and I settled the words of our pledge.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We did not focus on our navel or we would have missed that rainbow in the sky." Madam, no other nation in Asia has such lofty and progressive ideals.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: And it would be an injustice to the memory of our Founding Leaders and Pioneer Generation if we do not chase this ideal and keep focusing on the PAP navel instead.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Singapore needs to choose and make our own destiny, but we cannot depend on one political party or the Government for charting and directing our path, if we are to be not just an exceptional, but an outstanding nation that is an example to all in Asia.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The President's Address was a rallying call to all Singaporeans to stand together in solidarity as we embark on the new chapter of nation-building.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The realities of today's world merit Page: 36 a word of caution for the path ahead and the President, in his Address, said that we cannot expect an easy journey.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He explained the challenges that lay ahead and put forth the question that was oft repeated in this House: how do we ensure that our island-nation remains a shining red dot so that our children and grandchildren can thrive?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: My short answer to this question is that we have to do whatever it takes whilst holding true to the values that define us as Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have to fiercely protect and preserve the gem of a nation that our forefathers have built over the years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Fight and strive we must, but I believe that it is of utmost importance that we abide by our values and principles.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The President, in his Address, said that we must also have a shared understanding of what unites and binds us to one another.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, what are some of these values, principles and shared understanding?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These shared values include: encouraging community support and respect for the individual; consensus, not conflict; and racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Over time, we have developed a set of values and principles that makes us Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Values guide us when we make our decisions for this country and, as each day unfolds with its multifaceted challenges, the expressions of these values will develop.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Today, I would like to add a further perspective to these expressions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the area of caring for the vulnerable and disadvantaged, I believe that in principle, our common understanding on this is clear.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We will shape policies to encourage social mobility.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The challenge often lies in executing the principles and the policies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Over the years, the Government has made major shifts in social policy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The community and the state took on greater responsibility for individuals and families who needed social support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This was welcomed and provided a reprieve to many who struggled to keep afloat in this ever-changing world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, the implementation of this provision of support is fraught with rules and dictates certain expectations of the recipients.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is fair and reasonable but becomes tricky and sensitive when the family members have their own financial problems and are unable to support the individual.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should, in such instances, exercise discretion and provide the necessary support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The early withdrawal of subsidies and assistance can easily bring a family back into financial difficulty, particularly when the family has had little opportunity to build up a reserve for the rainy Page: 37 day.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
