text: We should look into how our social support networks and the community networks can continue to provide support and look out for these families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should not leave them at the starting block of the track, but be there till they are able to sustain themselves.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As we tread through the challenges that lie ahead, we should not regress and limit the efforts on improving social policy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government will need to continue to be responsible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should not compromise on the social support that needs to be given to the individuals and families that require them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In fact, it is when times are hard that we need to be more compassionate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Having said that, I am aware that we are not sitting on a pot of gold which we can distribute at a whim.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Resources are limited and there is a need to identify the ones who truly deserve the assistance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: While the Government remains responsible to care for the people, the people, too, have a responsibility to take care of themselves.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We all need to work hard, continue to improve our skills and remain relevant.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: While the Government has the responsibility to navigate the country through this challenging period, Singaporeans, too, need to have a keen awareness of the bigger picture – that Singapore sits in competition with the rest of the world and some tough decisions have to be made.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Since the future is unknowable, adaptation requires nimbleness of thought and action; and thought and action based on a clinical – some would say cold-blooded – understanding of the world as it is and not as we think it ought to be." The changing world forces us to change and adapt.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And we need to do what is necessary for Singapore's survival.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I move on now to the point of diversity of views and discourse, clearly, a point that has been raised often in this House as well.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As we write the chapters for the next 50 years, we do need to look at how, as a mature society, we handle diversity of views.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think we can all agree that diversity can be a strength, if it can be synergised and used for the good of the people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, it is also a potential divisive factor that can tear our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also feel that the approach of encouraging diversity of views should be extended to the masses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I laud the Government's efforts in creating platforms and engaging various segments of the community, including the young.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is definitely important to engage the youth on matters that are important to them, especially since they would inherit the nation and should have a say in how the society develops.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Platforms, such as the SGfuture Engagements, are definitely useful to trigger the discourse.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Page: 38 But beyond creating the platforms and spaces, there needs to be real discourse and the exercise of not merely lip-service.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe there needs to be a push for more open debates and discussions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For instance, in the light of the increasing wave of terrorist attacks and influence globally, inevitably some attention is now placed on the Muslim community in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is a need to have very frank conversations about real issues facing the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These conversations may possibly be difficult but this is an effort that should be put in together by all in the community, not just the Singaporean Muslims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And I believe that the leadership has a role in encouraging these discussions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The reality is that some of these conversations are already happening on the online platform.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In certain instances, such discussions appear to be rather toxic.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, we should manage and encourage further respectful discussions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And there should be open dialogues as such conversations allow for better understanding of each other's concerns.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Yes, we need to preserve the sanctity of the harmonious co-existence of various races and religions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our forefathers had learnt to live together despite their differences and had managed to achieve a state of peaceful equilibrium.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But we should also continue to build on the bonds we have.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is a need for faith in the maturity of the Singapore people and a realisation that the preservation of our individual identities or practice of our respective religions does not necessarily mean that our common spaces are being encroached upon or that we are distancing ourselves from each other.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Perhaps, there is a need to redefine the common space.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Perhaps, there are new norms that Singaporeans can agree upon.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We must allow for such discussions to flourish and work towards achieving consensus.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   The Malay/Muslim community has certain traits that bring something important to the table for other Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This spirit is always visible; so much so that the gotong-royong concept has spread and been adapted by non-Malays in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our community has a highly-developed culture, a refined language and is well-mannered.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If we look at it, our vocabulary is filled with noble values.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our proverbs, poems (pantun) and metaphors reflect the sharp minds of the Malays.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I will give you some examples: "We depended on the fence, but the fence destroyed the paddy", meaning "the one you trust betrayed you" – a proverb used by our Prime Minister yesterday.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Another example, "We have to face difficulties before enjoying the good times" – a proverb that gives us a reminder and encourages hard work.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should be proud of our culture and language and continue to use and internalise their values in our daily lives.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Page: 39 All these values are important in our societal relations, especially in the current context, which includes a challenging economic situation and the spread of radicalism.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In Parliament, many have spoken about the spread of terrorism and the attacks around the world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, the reality is that the attention is now placed on the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think it is important for the Government to take steps to encourage open discussions on these issues so that any prejudices and misunderstandings can be eradicated immediately.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There should also be stern reminders to condemn and prevent actions that reek of Islamophobia.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a woman who wears tudung, I definitely hope that all women can pursue their career of choice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Hence, I hope this can be reviewed and flexibility be given where possible, so that there will not be too many barriers for women to choose their own careers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, when we ask for something from the Government, I hope that we, as a community, can be mature and discuss respectfully.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should know and understand that there are implications to whatever decisions that we wish for, in the context of a plural society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should use the opportunities available to improve relations with the other races so that there is a deep understanding about our culture and religion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We are part of a plural society in Singapore and we must always be mindful to maintain racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Malay/Muslim community also has aspirations and hopes to succeed and see Malays in all fields, including leadership.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are now mechanisms to ensure that the concerns of Malay/Muslim Singaporeans are looked after due to the existence of the GRC system which requires the representation of minorities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is important and needs to be maintained.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We do not want the selection to be a symbolic one only.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Hence, while I welcome the Government's concern for the minority communities, I also feel that the Malay/Muslim community must continue to work hard so that they can generate the next generation of leaders of a high calibre, who can not only compete in Singapore, but also in the international arena.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Just now, Acting Minister Ng Chee Meng spoke about a Malay song, that is, our National Anthem.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would also like to highlight another song that is written by the late Pak Zubir Said.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am not a good singer so I shall just read out some of the lyrics. "If you become a Singaporean, Page: 40 You must have a good heart and be courteous.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: You must be resilient, work hard, Be well-mannered and respectful to your elders.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Only then others will admire and respect us, Only then you can be called a Singaporean." In this song, the late Pak Zubir spoke about having good manners, courtesy, resilience, working hard, loyalty towards the country, our race and our religion and living together as a society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think this is very meaningful and it truly reflects the values that should be present in all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am sure that, with this spirit, we can face any challenges that may come.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, allow me to conclude in English.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Over the past few days, my colleagues in this House have shared their perspectives and proposals on how to move this country forward.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The breadth of issues raised and the variety of ideas shared are a testament to the diversity and dynamism of the Members of this House.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This, in turn, reflects the diversity of the Singaporeans whom the Members represent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I look forward to seeing more of the likes of Mr Leon Perera and Mr Dennis Tan who will add to the robust debate and change laws.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am, therefore, quite surprised that they were being compared to duckweeds, because nothing stops the NCMPs from going to the ground, do house visits, organise sessions to gather ground concerns.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In fact, I recall Mr Perera mentioning that he does grassroots work at East Coast and Aljunied and definitely can bring value to this House with the issues that he will collate from all these people that he has met.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These improvements will strengthen the NCMP's position and I think it is hard to argue otherwise.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In any case, the contest at elections remains open to all and it is still open for Singaporeans to choose the best party and people to be their elected Members of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We do not argue for the sake of argument and will always seek consensus and not conflict.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Whilst there is much fear and uncertainty about what the future brings, I feel a sense of excitement on the possibilities for this little red dot.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 4.05 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.46 pm until 4.05 pm.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As a new Member of Parliament, I feel the weight of my new responsibilities.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I see my role as a Member of the Thirteenth Parliament as contributing meaningfully to the debate of this House in two ways.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One, I will voice the hopes, worries and dreams of my constituents and, two, I will talk about issues that I feel strongly about.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our predecessors in previous Parliaments have set a high standard.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Now, it is our turn to build on their good work.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I know a young man, Adam, 31 years old, father of two.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He has Secondary school education, tried several jobs and, finally, decided that being a taxi driver suits him best.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He explained that it is hard for him to tap on SkillsFuture as he works long hours and has family commitments.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I worry about the current cohort of workers due to the confluence of developments in information technology (IT), artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Are we prepared in our education and training systems to ride the crest of this development wave?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The future is very exciting but it is also very challenging.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Increasingly, we will see more machines taking over dangerous occupations and relieving us of mundane, repetitive jobs, including household chores.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It also means that many jobs we know today will be eliminated, including some white-collars.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A Merrill Lynch report says, "The combination of AI, machine learning, deep learning and natural user interfaces, such as voice recognition, is making it possible to automate many knowledge worker tasks that were long regarded as impossible or impractical for machines to perform." What about us?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I recently visited the Future of Us exhibition with my branch volunteers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We got a glimpse of life in future Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For example, we could be moving Page: 42 around in driverless cars.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But then last week's Sunday Times asked this question: "In a driverless future, what happens to today's drivers?" With the advent of taxi applications, driverless cars and car-sharing schemes, the taxi and bus industries will be affected.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Will all these technology advancements make taxi drivers redundant in 10 years?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A mere 20 years ago, dial-up Internet was hardly seen in most homes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Today, high-speed Internet has permeated all aspects of our lives, so much so that we can hardly imagine going through a day without it.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The pace of innovation and technological development is relentless.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I will have to persuade him to take SkillsFuture seriously, to make use of the opportunities to pick up new skills.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In this way, he will be able to earn a living in future Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: All of us will be affected one way or another; it is not only the blue-collar jobs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: With cloud computing technologies, many companies will automate white-collar functions, such as HR, IT, customer service and accounting.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need to do two things to prepare ourselves for this.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One, we need a renewed focus in education on these new technologies, such as ITE courses on the technology involved in driverless cars, augmented reality in JCs, and industrial robotics in Polytechnics.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Two – and I repeat my earlier point on SkillsFuture – we need to ensure that our current workforce, people like Adam, can be trained in other areas and to remain relevant even as their jobs may change or eventually disappear.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The second issue I want to raise is on the better integration of our infrastructure for caregiving.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our infrastructure must take into account how to better integrate facilities and services to make life easier.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One initiative which caught my eye was the decision to co-locate eldercare and childcare facilities in 10 HDB BTO new projects.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I have a combined childcare, student care and eldercare facility in my Tampines constituency, which was initiated by my predecessor, Mr Mah Bow Tan, 20 years ago.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My centre takes care of 90 children, 70 students and 50 senior citizens.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: One of my constituents, Mdm Tan, was enrolled in our eldercare facility in this 3-in-1 centre and her granddaughter is in student care.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They live in separate homes but they get to see each other in this centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So, it is very convenient and also precious that grandma and granddaughter get to "hang out" with each other because of shared facilities and programmes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I have seen first-hand the benefits both groups receive from each other because of this facility.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We have two public facilities which, I think, can be better used for this purpose.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Taking a cue from my 3-in-1 centre, I would like to propose that our schools have integrated eldercare facilities.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our schools have safe open spaces with appropriate exercise facilities and areas suitable for the elderly.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The seniors can participate in the school's activities, whether passively like watching school performances, or actively in music and art classes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Let our more abled seniors help the less abled.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The children and elderly can exercise, take strolls and be with nature.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Community "urban farmers" can supervise and share their gardening expertise.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Most of us will live longer and well into our eighties and beyond.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This means providing many more opportunities for our neighbours and generations to come together, interact and encourage each other.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As we strive to be a Smart Nation, I hope we can also be a cosy and compassionate Home for Adam, Mdm Tan and all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It was an extraordinary year and one thing that stood out for me was that we were all reminded of how exceptional we are as a little red dot and how the responsibility of ensuring another 50 great years for Singapore now falls squarely on our shoulders.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This mission cannot be taken lightly and we must do our best to ensure that Singapore remains a land of opportunities and a home for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For me, this mission is more personal and poignant, now that my son is barely six months old and he would still, hopefully, be in his prime when the time SG100 comes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe I speak for all parents who have young children, when I say that I would like him to grow up in a safe and secure Page: 44 Singapore in which he can get great education, achieve his aspirations, as well as live in and contribute to a peaceful, harmonious society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In his speech, the President described five key aims that we ought to fulfil.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I whole-heartedly agree that these are critical and we must get them right.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ultimately, no matter how robust our economy, how strong our society or how advanced our technology may be, a strong nation has to draw strength from its people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But more than that, we must enable our elderly, so that life post-retirement is still exciting and promising.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We all aspire to lead a good life and a good life cannot be judged by the number of years lived.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It has to be based on qualitative measures, such as health, a sense of self-efficacy and self-esteem.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At home, shrinking family sizes and increasing numbers of singles will limit the scope of home care for our elderly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One way to deal with this would be to have the elderly institutionalised in a nursing or an elderly home.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But this is far from ideal because, given our rapidly ageing population, there is insufficient space to build enough nursing or elderly homes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As we move towards a "Smart Nation", this has to be given priority.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At work, our elderly should be encouraged to work for as long as they can and want to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, the additional "pocket money" from the income earned is welcomed.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our systems, our working environments and, especially our attitudes, have to change in preparation for this eventuality.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is also a need for a more concerted and stronger push for jobs to be redesigned to become more elderly-friendly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the community level, we need to continue our efforts to build a strong social network of support, as it helps to keep out loneliness and complement familial support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Such a network requires not only the participation of Government agencies and voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs), but neighbours can have a role to play as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Neighbours can help to keep an eye on an elderly, notice any irregularity and call for help immediately.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Neighbours can help to, for instance, bring an elderly to his/her medical appointment at the polyclinic nearby, explain schemes that are available for the elderly to benefit from, or encourage and assist the elderly to participate in community programmes and stay active.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Within the community, we should not only consider the elderly as being simply the recipients of care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They can also be enabled to contribute meaningfully as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At present, I am very heartened and encouraged to witness how our seniors in MacPherson have been actively serving our community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For instance, many are involved in the Pioneer Generation (PG) Ambassador Page: 45 programme, in which it involves them helping to explain to fellow Pioneers what the package entails and even help them to seek help with problems not covered by the package.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The PG Ambassadors receive good training and support and they feel empowered and proud to be able to help others.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we must continue to promote senior volunteerism and find ways to empower our elderly, as they are hidden gems in our communities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   In recent years, many of our speeches have inevitably been about the vision of a caring society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In my opinion, the measure of success in achieving this goal is how we treat our elderly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Based on my observations in the last few years, Singaporeans are compassionate about our elderly and the Government has actively implemented many measures and packages to look after our elderly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, there are still some people who are prejudiced against the elderly, seeing them as a burden to the family, workplace and society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And some of the elderly also see themselves as old and useless, passively counting down to the last day of their lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This means to enable them to live in ease and comfort in their golden years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should look after the elderly, satisfy their basic needs and preserve their dignity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Besides basic needs, such as food and clothing, we must also make sure they age in place.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By doing this, we can achieve our ideal of "ageing in place".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Beyond that, we should continue to engage and organise the community, encourage residents to work with the Government and VWOs to strengthen our social support network and maintain the community spirit of neighbours looking after one another.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This means to respect the seniors and not to look down on them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should encourage and support those who still want to work to do so, or support them to fulfil their unfulfilled dreams.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is because work can help them to stay active physically and mentally and maintain confidence in themselves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, when working in my constituency, I would have seniors sharing their woes with me every now and then about how difficult it is to get a job as they grew old.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, we need to put in more effort in improving our national system, work environment design and attitude towards the elderly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the saying goes, "An old horse knows its ways".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It means that the elderly are very experienced.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we must respect them and provide them with opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At least, we should not deny them the opportunity of taking that first step.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can an "old horse" not continue to gallop?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It means to appreciate and treasure our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The elderly, especially those who have retired, are our precious resource.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They have the time and experience and are able to continue to contribute to the country and the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In MacPherson, we have Page: 46 many seniors who are passionate about charity and volunteering in the community.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They often help out at community events and look after vulnerable neighbours.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Sometimes, they can even mobilise the aunties and uncles in the community to help.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Sometimes, they will voluntarily offer to solve problems for their neighbours.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If they are unable to do so, they will accompany troubled neighbours to come and see me.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, let us not lose these gems of ours!

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In English): Families have been the bedrock of our society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we must continue to support families in Singapore so that Singapore will continue to be strong.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Often, I receive pleas from young parents seeking help with childcare as they have to work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They feel stressed having to balance the needs of their families and careers, sometimes, at the expense of each other.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Young mothers also lament to me about how they are trying to heed the Government's call to have children, how they are trying to fulfil their duty to the nation but it is just very difficult to do so when they cannot get the support they need.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, why should young families be subjected to such a trade-off?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, supply is still chasing demand at present.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to look for alternatives so as to enhance accessibility of care and provide options for young parents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One, could we leverage more on homemakers with childcare experiences within the community?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the course of my constituency work, I have met many housewives who are experienced and willing to care for neighbours' children and whose children have grown up.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They love children and, of course, a little pocket money would not hurt.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At the same time, I have also just recently come across a young couple with two-year-old triplets who are in desperate need of support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The couple need to work, their parents have yet to retire and they could not find a reliable maid.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we are now looking to the "auntie-network" within the community to provide some interim childcare support in the meantime, especially with Chinese New Year nearing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can we expand such arrangements into a wider support scheme?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Their profiles and childcaring resumes can be consolidated into a directory which young families can refer to when considering childcare options.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And for quality assurance, the enrolled housewives can go through basic courses to update them on some of the latest developments, needs and standards.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thirdly, we need to continue to entrench the belief that mothers can continue to contribute and value-add in the workplace and society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need employers and colleagues to be understanding to mothers who go on maternity or childcare leave.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Once, a young mother wrote to me to share her woes about her employer who would make scathing remarks when she took maternity leave.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need fair appraisal systems that focus on the quality of work done and that do not mark down mothers simply because they are out of action for a few months.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Such behaviours – mean remarks and unfair appraisal systems – are manifestations of an underlying prejudice that mothers are liabilities at work, thereby negating the value that they can offer professionally and to our society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should work to improve the situation in Singapore so that women can thrive in both motherhood and career.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At this juncture, I would like to highlight that active citizenry runs through almost all the points that I have made.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Indeed, I believe that all Singaporeans have a shared responsibility in the many works of our nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A truly caring society is not one in which the caring is only done by the Government or a selected group of people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A great nation is not one in which its people care only about themselves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Thankfully, I would say that Singaporeans do care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From the time I served as a grassroots leader, which would have been about 11 years ago, I have witnessed how many Singaporeans are prepared to sacrifice their personal time, space and resources to help others.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am constantly touched by their concern for the less fortunate or more vulnerable and, even more so, when those who needed help in the first place are also helping others.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Such care and concern for our fellow men and women build trust, strengthen our community and keep us together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It inspires us to do better, to think about how our actions affect the others around us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, beyond policy debate or discussions of current affairs, we must continue to focus on building an active citizenry.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This has to happen at all levels – within the community, we should enlist Singaporeans to form a network of support; within the nation, we should encourage volunteerism and charitable causes and engage citizens to give ideas for Singapore and to participate in building a better future for ourselves and our children.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singaporeans sent us into Parliament because they trust us and hope that we can give voice to the challenges, worries, hopes and dreams that they have.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We, all of us in this House, including my hon Non-Constituency Member of Parliament colleagues, must do our best.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must cherish it and, hence, in this Thirteenth Parliament, we must continue to speak up actively and work hard together to fulfil the five aims that the President has shared with us.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: SG100 takes time to build, but it is not that distant a dream.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Let us continue to build on one another's strengths in fulfilling the vision of a safe, secure, caring and united Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As one Singapore, we rallied together, we reminisced, we rejoiced, we reflected.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And we also came together in one unbelievable moment in the outpouring of grief when our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew passed on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The range of emotions we shared served to bring Singaporeans closer together, like never before.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We are still only a fledgling nation, but we have had much to celebrate of our achievements over the last 50 years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is nothing short of a remarkable success story.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But at the same time, we must recognise that all of that is now firmly in the past.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We can live in the past, or we can move on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We can strive to build on our past successes, but we can never assume it to be a given that the next 50 years will be anything like the last 50.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: By all accounts, the litany of challenges for us on the horizon is, indeed, very daunting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: What we make of it and how we overcome them will define us as a people and successive generations will measure us by what we put in place and achieve today for the Singapore of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Over the last few days in this House, we have heard many suggestions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There have been many passionate calls for bold new directions, policy changes – as my hon colleague Ms Denise Phua said – redreaming and calling for the slaying of the sacred cow as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There is much richness in the broad canvas of these ideas but we have to find a way to tie them together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: At the very heart of our success has been the stability and cohesiveness which we have enjoyed as a society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But that has not come about by chance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Inclusion, mobility and opportunity delivered by a sound political system which is fair, transparent and stable, has allowed successive Governments to design and implement policies to benefit and uplift society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In my view, therefore, behind every successful society – and, indeed, as Acting Minister Ong said, if we want to achieve, "faster legs, stronger hearts and wiser minds" – we have to have a sound political system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Politics and political systems shape and drive social norms – it is a point I will come back to later – but politics is never very far away from the way we run our society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In his Opening Address, President Tan spoke of the "innovations" to our system which have served us well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We might have started with the British system, but our founding fathers had the foresight, political will and gumption to adapt and bespoke it to meet the specific needs of our society, our Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We have had to adapt and change the original system because we are a pluralistic, multiracial society; quite unlike the British, from whom we inherited the system; quite unlike almost every nation in the world.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So much so that if you went to google "multiracial society" now, you will find that two-thirds of the hits on the first page mention or are about Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Carefully nurtured and cultivated over the years of our history, multiracialism is now self-evident in almost every facet of our life – in our schools, our HDB flats, our common spaces, our Page: 49 food and our shared heritage.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And that has to be a strength, not a weakness, but that requires leadership and government being true to these principles." It is, indeed, a unique strength, but we must jealously guard it for it could so easily turn into a weakness – a fault line in our society to be exploited.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: When you look around the world today, some of the deepest fault lines in civil society are drawn precisely on racial or religious lines and we, in Singapore, are not necessarily immune to that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Our racial and religious harmony and the Government's role in maintaining this through good politics, can never be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, not very far away from us, in Malaysia, we see an example of a society fractured by their political and social lines being drawn precisely on racial differences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Two recent examples come to mind and you would have seen them in the press, both involving scuffles at an IT mall, one in July 2015 at a popular IT mall called Low Yat Plaza and another one in December 2015 at the Kota Raya.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Both involved Malays and Chinese clashing over unhappy business transactions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In themselves, the incidents were not necessarily remarkable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But what I found staggering was the Malaysian government's response.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Can we imagine for a moment that taking place in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But why has this happened just across our shores?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As I have mentioned, politics drive social norms and shape behaviour.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The origins of the recent racial tensions in Malaysia can, in some ways, be traced to the racial stratification that has been deeply entrenched in the Malaysian political system for many years, for decades.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The Barisan Nasional coalition is made up of the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) and Parti Pesaka Bumiputera Bersatu (PBB) and the Chinese-based Malaysia Chinese Association (MCA), as well as the Indian-based Malaysian Indian Congress.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Can we imagine any of these taking place in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: A racialised political system has resulted in significant lines of divide in Malaysia's society which still persist today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: That is why politics is not an abstract.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is not distinct from the policies we seek to make, or the type of society we seek to build.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Politics touch and affect the way we live in a very real and tangible way.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: That is why the GRC scheme, an "innovation" which we have introduced, must remain a very fundamental tenet of our political system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is the bedrock which safeguards multiracial representation in our Parliament and, ultimately, in our Government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: These objectives remain relevant, if not more relevant, today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I, therefore, support the continuation of the GRC scheme and I should add that this scheme is by no means a political tool to marginalise the prospects of success for Opposition candidates in an election.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, having taken Aljunied GRC on two previous occasions, I am surprised we still see the Workers' Party continuing to make such an argument.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, I also welcome the move to have smaller and, therefore, more GRCs and more Single Member Constituencies (SMCs) in the next election.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I think this makes for better options and choices for the electorate and the Workers' Party surely cannot complain about smaller GRCs!

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The question of economies of scale in the running of a Town Council can, I think, be easily overcomed by having more than one GRC make up a town, which is currently not the case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Another innovation we will re-look is the Elected Presidency, first mooted by then-Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew in 1984.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Two White Papers later, the Elected Presidency became a feature of our political landscape, as an additional check and balance on the Government of the day – an additional insurance for the people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The question is whether this office has outlived its relevance and should be abolished.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: These reserves, carefully accumulated over years of careful, considerate and conservative budgeting, need a strong second key to safeguard them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The President, therefore, fulfils more than just a ceremonial function.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Though his powers are reactive in nature, he is the custodian of Singapore's accumulated foreign reserves and acts as a check and balance on public service integrity and against possible excesses of power by the Executive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In order to achieve that, it is, therefore, necessary for him to act with a mandate and moral authority and that is why he is elected and not appointed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: However, the review of some key aspects of the office of the Elected Presidency is timely and appropriate and I will suggest two points.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: First, as a starting point, it can surely brook no dissent that only the very best, the most qualified, experienced, competent and honest persons of the highest calibre should even be considered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There can be absolutely no political agenda behind this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Yet, we have previously seen the Workers' Party complain bitterly about this programme – complained that the stringent prequalifications for Presidential candidacy has made it much harder for aspiring candidates to become nominated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Why should we feel apologetic about imposing the very most stringent conditions and criteria on a person who is to be carrying out heavy constitutional burdens to safeguard your reserves and mine?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Only the very best people should be the Head of State, not an inexperienced or under-qualified one and certainly not a populist one.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, I would suggest that we would need to strengthen the qualifying criteria from at least two perspectives.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But, second and, perhaps more fundamentally, I hope the Constitution Commission can look into this, Page: 51 that we look beyond just the numbers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Just because a candidate has been a CEO or a CFO of a company with $x million of paid-up capital or turnover does not necessarily make that person the right person or, indeed, a suitable or appropriate person to become the Elected President.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In my view, there is every reason to impose far more stringent qualifying criteria because this is not a popular contest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is serious business making sure that the constitutional duties are properly discharged.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: If the Elected President fails as the guardian, Singapore fails.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, if we elect either a populist or a partisan President, what kind of an effective second key can we expect?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Second, we should review the current make-up of the CPA which advises the President on a range of matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I think we can all agree that the members of the Advisory Committee should be well-qualified – they should be strong.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The question is: how should we select them and who should they comprise?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This ensures transparency and accountability and engenders public confidence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang said earlier good politics is not shaped or monopolised by the ruling party – alternative voices, dissenting opinions should be heard.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I heard the press quoting Mr Low last evening as saying that "the NCMP is still weak because he does not have roots, unlike elected MPs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: He is not grounded in a Town Council.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: He does not have a constituency to run." I think Mr Low has missed the point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The privilege to run a Town Council and to manage a constituency is one that can only be bestowed by the electorate of that constituency.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And if, in elections, the electorate does not choose the Workers' Party to run their Town Council, perhaps because they feel that the Workers' Party is not qualified to do so – that choice has to be respected.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The NCMP scheme does not, in any way, take away the ability or opportunity of any candidate to contest freely for the privilege to run a constituency or the Town Council.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: If you win your seat, then you run the Town Council.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Clearly, the NCMP Scheme has brought a more diverse range of views into Parliament and we heard that in the last Parliament.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, it has also served the Opposition well, even if they do protest a little loudly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: They have, in many instances over the years, taken advantage themselves of the NCMP seat Page: 52 precisely for the advancement of their own political agenda.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: A good example of this is the hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As the Prime Minister noted, she was first elected as an NCMP in 2006 before winning her seat as a Member of Parliament for Aljunied in 2011 and again in 2015.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I think even Ms Lim would agree that her presence in Parliament, as an NCMP, gave her the exposure and contributed greatly to her eventual success as an elected Member.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: More recently, we have seen the Workers' Party opting to re-assign their NCMP seat from Mr Gerald Giam to Mr Leon Perera, both of whom were members of one of the best losing teams on the East Coast GRC slate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This presumably was to allow the younger and newer members, such as Mr Perera, to gain experience and exposure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Clearly for increased exposure, for their own agenda, so that he would be better placed at the next elections.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, the fact of the matter is that the NCMP scheme not only introduces greater diversity and debate in Parliament, it helps Opposition Members gain exposure and recognition.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I, therefore, cannot see the basis on which the Workers' Party continues to mount this complaint.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I am heartened by the changes that the Prime Minister has announced.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: They not only improve the political landscape and make for a solid infrastructure in which to take Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Far from navel-gazing, as Mr Low has said, I see in these steps the hallmark of strong political will, great foresight and a determination to build for the future, not for this term, not for the next term even, but for the future.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And with the Sigmoid Curve theory, transformational changes have to be made before the peaks of success are achieved, to ensure that success continues uninterrupted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But it takes two hands to clap and good politics also means that Singaporeans, too, must remain engaged with the Government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Singaporeans, too, must continue to be proactive in active citizenry and play a part in shaping our country's destiny.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is a crucial partnership, as we head into SG51 and beyond, if we want to build on the legacy of our founding fathers and leave Singapore in a better shape for successive generations to come.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, in the words of someone recently made famous all over again: "Do or do not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am not sure whether I heard Mr Tong correctly, but was he trying to imply that the Workers' Party is arguing for NCMPs to be on equal standing with elected Members?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I was referring to Mr Low's point where he was suggesting that the NCMPs create duckweeds.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As the Member Ms Rahayu Mahzam mentioned earlier, you really make what you will of it yourself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You have the opportunity to make your house visits.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You have the opportunity to grow your roots in your own constituency, whether you are an elected Member or an NCMP.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And those were the issues I took issue with.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I said you can make what you will of it yourself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think the fact of the matter is that whenever we choose to run an event, we hold a show, we all get the necessary permission, even for myself.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Ms Lim, your last point is actually no longer a clarification.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: So, I think I will stop your clarification at this point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In the days of the Cold War, there was an East German person who braved the landmines and the machine gun fire in order to cross the border into West Germany to freedom.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, when he got to the other side, the Western media at that time were very interested to find out what happened – why this guy did this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The first one asked, "Why did you risk your life?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I mean, you risked your life to run from communism to freedom.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, what do you think of democracy and capitalism?" So, this man said, "I think democracy is chaotic and I think, in capitalism, men exploit men".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This was not the sort of answer that the reporters had expected because this guy braved the machine guns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Stunned, they asked again, "If that is what you thought of democracy and capitalism, then why did you risk your life coming here?" The man thought for a moment and he said, "Because I think that there is more bread here." Mdm Speaker, certainly, man does not live by bread alone, but I think bread is also important.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And before I go into my text for today, I just also wanted to reflect some of the things that Mr Low said just now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: He said the first 50 years – not his exact words, but that is what I understood to be what he was saying – that it was a journey where Singapore came out of very difficult circumstances, hostile environment, hostile neighbourhood to make it this far and that the next 50 years is different and, Page: 54 therefore, we have to change the model of our boat.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I would agree that the first 50 years is a journey fraught with difficulties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We came out of difficult circumstances, people did not expect us to go very far or to survive very long.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And we made it this far, taking those necessary and difficult decisions along the way, good leadership, good people working together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The next 50 years, totally different, we have arrived and it is just about aspirations – I do not think so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I think it is on top of these constraints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If anything, I think the world is becoming ever more complex, more difficult to deal with and, therefore, I say that the aspirations that we have, the values that we want to espouse, we build it on top of and never neglect that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, Mr Low says that as a result of that, one thing that we have to do is to buy insurance for our political system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I ask Singaporeans to consider: in this world, where all the original constraints continue to bind us and it is becoming ever more complex, think of what insurance to buy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Yesterday, the Prime Minister spent a good deal of his speech explaining to Singaporeans and this House how we should enhance our system, precisely because – and he recognised that – we need that diversity of views.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For one, for the NCMP system, he is expanding it not only in numbers but in the powers that they would have, voting in this House.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That is a practical example of a political party which understands what the people want and taking steps in order to ensure that their interest, what they want, is also reflected here.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I say, buying insurance is correct, but please know which insurance policy you are considering.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Indeed, these are important elements of a successful society and nation because they help us imagine the ideal collective spirit of the nation that we should commit ourselves to protecting, to co-creating for the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That said, it is equally important that we think clearly about what needs to be done to achieve those ends in practical terms and in practical ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For today, I would just limit what I want to say in the context of a maturing population and local workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The young will certainly be there to inherit the future – that is true.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But what is often assumed, perhaps not spoken, is that the older population has less of a part in that future because they are, willy-nilly, fading away, or that they are more there to be cared for than to contribute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And I think we must strenuously disabuse ourselves in Singapore of that notion and I would explain why.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, this is not a question of a possible black swan appearing on our horizon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The older population among us is not fading away.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Page: 55 So, does it really matter if the older population is an expanding segment?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is a core part of our social and economic defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And this has led some to say that the 60s are now the new 50s.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is an important notion, in my view, because if the condition of mature citizens today is equivalent to those much younger in days gone by and, with improved assistive technology and design that the physical disparities between the older and the younger could also be compensated for, then what does that mean?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It means that we can and we must retune our thinking and mindsets about what each age cohort is capable of doing, not only as individuals but within corporations and for this country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The whole idea of what constitutes that bracket called "Working Age population" is itself shifting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And for us to fail to take note of this as individuals, as companies, as HR and companies, I think it is for us to live in the past and to be guilty not only of mindless ageism and misjudgement, but, indeed, of wasting national resources, to our own detriment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, the old is, in a relative sense, getting younger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Interestingly, even as that is becoming clearer to us by the day, I think something quite the opposite is happening to those who are, by chronological age, younger.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We hear much about the ever-accelerating pace of change in science, technology and societal tastes and norms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We acknowledge that whatever content we may learn in school and University will very quickly become obsolete as a result of this relentless whirlwind of change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The young people emerging from our institutes of learning in their twenties will also find themselves falling behind the technology curve within, let us say, 10 years of graduating and be considered by companies to be outdated if they have not kept up with upgrading.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Thus, strangely, those younger in age are also feeling the pressure of obsolescence that we typically think are associated with people maybe 20, 30, 40 years their senior and the physical fitness that they have, conferred by youth, is not an antidote for that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I look at these trends with keen interest, because what do we make of them?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: My belief is that they do not necessarily bode ill for us, if we play our cards well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is because these trends actually help us focus and they help educate us that we must abandon the deep-seated assumptions and biases about this correlation between chronological age and one's potential and capabilities on the one hand; and on the other hand, it makes it crystal clear that all of us, regardless of age, the chances of being able to take up good jobs, of being able to be matched to good jobs when jobs are, perhaps, not as plentiful as before, rest upon continual broadening and deepening of capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Page: 56 The data also show us what our realistic options are in terms of our sources of manpower.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Foreign sources will not be easily available and have to continue to be tightly managed for social and security reasons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If companies and industries fail to intelligently tap and hold on to persons with such valuable assets and lose them, say, through unnecessary and premature retirement or short-sighted retrenchments, then when they need them, they cannot find them, they lose important institutional memory, knowledge and expertise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is, to my mind, the equivalent of inflicting upon themselves a form of corporate or industry dementia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In order to avert this lose-lose scenario, HR systems, policies and training opportunities must certainly adapt to the evolving realities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Investment in mature workers' training and development, done over a longer time span and runway, certainly, is not about tokenism.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is straightforwardly, in our case, about smart decision-making by those accountable for business continuity and competitiveness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If you have a mature worker, you may say, by way of analogy, that you have a saw.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If you do not keep that saw sharp, you neglect to sharpen it, then you will find that your sawing operation will be less efficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: At the same time, we must continue to innovate and enable options for more earning years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And with that, I think it sets the stage for us to, once again, think ahead to what may be possible beyond that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For example, can we conceive of giving workers the chance and the choice to work beyond 67 on a regular basis?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And, if so, what safeguards would be necessary and appropriate to put in place to address both the interests, as well as the fears, of workers and companies?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Can there be more scope for customisation of arrangements according to industry or job types?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: How about, where there are company groups, the whole concept of where do you re-employ people to?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Could it see a possible extension in a responsible way?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These are some of the issues that I think are good for the tripartite partners to begin thinking about and discussing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I think there is also room for Government policy to be reviewed to enable more earning years in a responsible way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In June 2014, at my Meet-the-People session, one of my residents from Whampoa, Mr Ng, came to see me.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Sixty-nine going on 70, he had a heavy vehicle licence and had been using that to drive heavy vehicles for a living for years and brought up a whole family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Problem was that the Page: 57 policy says that when you reach 70, you cannot renew that heavy vehicle licence which, to him, meant what was he going to earn a living with?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I looked at him, he looked very fit, very alert and he said to me, "Send me to any health test, eye test, reflex test, test me.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If I am no good, stop me." I thought that was reasonable, I appealed for him.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We must, of course, ensure safety for all road users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And I felt that appropriate tests, indeed, ought to be put in place to safeguard that aspect and then allow those who pass to continue earning a living.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, both he and I persisted in our appeals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This shows that enabling, giving a chance and a choice, is possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If you think about it, think about what is it that makes a person employable, is it fitness, is it attitude, is it skills?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There is also more that the tripartite partners can do to further bolster retirement adequacy provisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For example, various measures were implemented in last year's Budget to boost that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We should continue to consider what further steps could be put in place, at the appropriate times, to enhance retirement adequacy through both CPF and non-CPF pathways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There should also be a deeper study of the apportionment of CPF savings between the various uses, to ensure that the original and primary purpose of the CPF scheme to help strengthen retirement adequacy is sufficiently assured.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Anecdotal evidence suggests that people are still generally reluctant to sell or partly lease-back their property in order to derive cash in old age, for cultural reasons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, how then, if they have locked the money in there, can we help people make more rational allocations and monetisation?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And this is not just a question about programming and funding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Page: 58 It is about clear-headedness, effort, judgement, perseverance and, above all, an unwavering commitment to creating a better future for each and for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Our goal must be that every citizen is a stronger and more versatile person and that, together, we will build a more resilient and dynamic Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To this end, I wholeheartedly support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are critical ups and downs that I would like to bring to this House.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Indeed, a timely reminder to all of us of the pressing need to redouble our efforts to restructure and find breakthroughs, lest we run the risk of having many of our fellow workers, especially PMEs, left behind or, worse still, left in the lurch.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The data reflect a worrying trend that I have been seeing in the increasing cases of PMEs coming to the Labour Movement for help.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are PMEs entering the workforce who want to land a job or are looking to move up within their jobs; there are also female PMEs who have left the workforce to look after their family and now want to re-enter the workforce; and then there are the mature PMEs, many of whom are above 40 years of age, who may be out of job or are vulnerable to job loss or returned from an overseas job role and looking for jobs to move across or move into.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I personally know some of them and have spoken to those who visit our U PME Centre.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some are demoralised, some are resigned, some are fearful and some dejected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I strongly feel we can do more and do better in this area of jobs and job security for our fellow Singaporean PMEs because, if we do not, we will run the risk of more ups and downs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We run the risk of an increase in the unemployment of PMEs and PME redundancy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We are also likely to see a dip in employment creation and, subsequently, a drop in the hiring of locals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In short, in the next couple of years, the likely reality will be that workers and, in particular, PMEs, may need to brace themselves for redundancies, unemployment, slower employment growth and, possibly, under-employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: So, what can we do for our PMEs?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We must, first, recognise the three mismatches or challenges our PMEs face.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They are the mismatch of skills, mismatch of jobs and mismatch of expectations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I often hear complaints from some employers that our local PMEs lack the skills and experience for certain jobs and, therefore. they have to look elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some employers feel our workers lack the regional and global experience and so cannot promote them or Page: 59 fill them up with our local PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Then again, there are those who are over-skilled or over-qualified for the jobs, resulting in an under-employment situation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: My colleagues at our U PME Centre and e2i have highlighted that there are some PMEs who go to them with unrealistic expectations in terms of the type of jobs and conditions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Then, I also hear of employers who lament and do not hire mature PMEs because they claim many of them cannot change, they cannot adapt to the new requirements expected of them and a host of other ageist remarks.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are some PMEs who may not be able to keep pace with the new job demands.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are also companies which do not take proactive steps to re-design, re-create or re-size the jobs or manage the change.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our society, too, must recognise and expect that we have a growing ageing workforce and that there will be an ever-increasing number of PMEs, mature ones, in our midst.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are cases where PMEs are not well-matched with their current jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They do jobs which they have neither passion nor interest for.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
