text: Sometimes, the job size is too small or quality of the job is not good.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are those whose characters or personalities do not quite fit or match the kind of requirements the job entails.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: So, with these ups and downs and three mismatches, how can we help our future workforce of PMEs grapple with the Future Landscape and land themselves in Future Jobs?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Is there a way to help us overcome the challenges of the employment landscape in the months and years ahead?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Can we do more to minimise the gaps?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I strongly believe we can and we can do so through strengthening what I call the 3Cs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They are: (a) strengthening the Core – the Singaporean Core; (b) strengthening the Connection – the Connection between PMEs and jobs; and (c) strengthening Careers – the Careers of PMEs to ensure they stay future-ready.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: PMEs I speak to highlight the issue of nationality bias in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: One is where the entire workplace is filled with PMEs of a particular nationality.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The grouse is not with their presence but the excessive presence and stark visuals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, is where foreign PMEs take jobs which Singaporean PMEs can fill, such as hiring a foreign PME to handle our local SME market or doing support or administrative functions, including basic HR functions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, the test now is whether it has helped create a Singaporean Core in all sectors and all companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I still hear murmurings about certain sectors, the IT sector and the financial sector, in particular.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The feedback is that there are still companies in these two sectors where there is a weak Singaporean Core and a weak commitment to create a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We should and must take more resolute steps.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, it should not be a broad sweep.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We should target at specific sectors and companies which remain recalcitrant and show a disregard or weak commitment to forming a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Mr Cedric Foo and Ms Foo Mee Har had, on Tuesday, sounded the same concern.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am now putting forward two Page: 60 suggestions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We need to move not just from a manpower-led to manpower-lean economy, but a Singaporean PME-led and foreigner PME-lean economy for our locals to fully exploit the labour market and, yet, be able to fully realise their potential and skills.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As we have seen in recent weeks, certain sectors have started laying off PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, strengthening the connection of PMEs to jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Many of the PMEs who come to the U PME Centres are experienced, knowledgeable and skilled.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, they may not know that with their experience and skills, there are other jobs, other sectors, that they can move across to.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Hence, we need to strengthen the connection of jobs to our people and minimise the information gap.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We need to know where the in-demand jobs are and the gaps in supply.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We have the National Jobs Bank and other job portals where we can easily aggregate the job openings, mine the data and get a good sensing and greater insights.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our national programmes and agencies would be the best source of sussing out the demand and supply, particularly now, with SkillsFuture and the sectoral manpower plans and EDB/MOM data.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With all this information, we can strengthen our employment facilitation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are lots of analysis, synthesis, forecasting and analytics involved.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is hard work and it has to be a joint and collective effort by all, across agencies, tripartite partners and different stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the same vein, even as we recreate current jobs and create new jobs, we should provide diversity and variety so that we can marry aspirations, passions, skills with good jobs and quality jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: PMEs are increasingly more vulnerable to job losses and retrenchments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the uncertain economic outlook, I worry for them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I, therefore, recently revisited the idea of better protecting our PMEs through unemployment insurance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I do not think unemployment insurance is an impossibility, whether privately-run or publicly-run and universally administered, but it needs closer study and scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We have to ask ourselves some important questions, such as: who can, should or shall be on the scheme?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What if you are in an industry which is more vulnerable or, in the converse, one which is more secure?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: How much and for how long should the monthly payouts be?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the end of the day, it all boils down to whether we can ensure the livelihood of the individual.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Instead of a short-term and temporary fix like an unemployment insurance, why not give our PMEs the best insurance – that of a decent-paying job with a decent pay?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Many employers and PMEs I speak to are not aware of the Career Support Programme (CSP) which was rolled out on 1 October last year.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I urge all to take a closer look.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Whether in peacetime or in the event of a downturn, the CSP not just helps PMEs land a job through direct wage subsidy to their employers, it ensures all PMEs affected have a job, a monthly salary, for the longer term.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Better still, no premiums need to be paid.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The CSP must drive and alter the behaviour of our companies and businesses and the mindsets of employers to seriously consider our mature PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It will also provide our PMEs more options and opportunities in a challenging landscape.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We need to arm our people with the right skills, put them in the right jobs with the right experience and expectations so that they can embark on a right career.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As part of SkillsFuture, we must focus on the skills required for our PMEs to progress and prosper in a rapidly changing world.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the past, training was about imparting knowledge.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Today, it is about providing each individual with the tools to navigate an increasingly uncertain, volatile world.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: One answer would be promoting skills-oriented learning throughout workers' lives and integrate it into the workplace and outside the workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It has to be a continuum from Primary education to work and adult learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is not just to up-skill but to deep-skill, second-skill, to stay future-ready and future-proof themselves and also reskill if old jobs are gone and new jobs created.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Training and lifelong learning needs to be both employer-supported and individually initiated and will require the involvement of every sector of society, from tripartite partners to various stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: All said, the future will depend on individuals and their willingness to take advantage of the opportunities and invest in their own futures to stay future-ready.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To conclude, we can overcome the ups and the downs and better match the three mismatches by: strengthening the Singaporean Core; strengthening the connection to jobs; and strengthening the careers of every worker, especially PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On this note, I support the Motion of thanks to the President.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore, as a nation, has to find our way amidst the shifting sands of global economic, societal and political developments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as the economy and society evolve rapidly, Singaporeans are in an ongoing struggle to survive and thrive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Page: 62 As we continue to adapt and develop, we must go beyond merely acquiring skills to developing an outlook that is enlightened and progressive, being confident in ourselves and having the strength to welcome the participation of some non-locals into our workforce to complement and supplement us in areas where we lack resources.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But in the process, it is our deeply rooted Singaporean Core and sense of belonging which will inspire Singaporeans to continue to propel the nation forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the President pointed out in his Address, we must strive to leave no one behind, even as we create opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This assurance of representation in leadership contributes towards all races having a sense of belonging to this nation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And it is, of course, also the case that all Members of Parliament – regardless of our ethnicity – are required to prove ourselves in the course of our terms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must demonstrate our competence in our duties and that we represent and protect the interests of all Singaporeans, not just any particular race.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is what makes Singapore strong, that we all look out for one another, regardless of our various backgrounds, for the benefit of our nation as a whole.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are also justifiably proud of our system of meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But along with that, we must also work towards ensuring that all citizens have equal opportunities for social mobility.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As science and technology advance at an exponential rate, we may soon be confronted with many chasms – one of which could potentially be between those who are able to use technology and those who are left behind.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, a lag in skills catch-up could lead to technological or structural unemployment, making matters worse.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Programmes have already been put in place to help train all Singaporeans and narrow the skills gap.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, at this point, please allow me to speak in Malay.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   The Malay/Muslim community has made significant progress over the last 50 years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This improvement was the result of various programmes by the Government and Malay/Muslim bodies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, our community can achieve much more and we should also seize more opportunities in Singapore and the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs has outlined three challenges for the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of them is staying relevant in a rapidly-changing economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In a few decades, we will have the opportunity to Page: 63 build a larger middle class that is highly educated and successful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This group will become an important component of a strong Singaporean Core – as positive contributors who are essential to the nation in all areas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nonetheless, this opportunity can also be viewed as the biggest challenge to our community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we fail to harness the potential of our youths, it can turn into a major and great loss.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should also focus on efforts to encourage and channel our youths into sectors that have the potential for high growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These sectors can provide high salaries and the community should try to penetrate and take advantage of these sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These include new areas that are required by digital transformation, special production activities, applications and modern services, which we will see in our future economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must also maximise the potential of youths who do not have tertiary education.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: About 45% will go to ITE, while 20% will become post-secondary school students.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The other 30% have ITE or Polytechnic diplomas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If this trend continues and if economic recession takes place, it is very possible that this will have a cascading effect on the economic status of Malay/Muslim families.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the other end of the spectrum, initial findings from a study commissioned by MENDAKI about employment prospects, which was done on over 100 Malay/Muslim graduates, managed to give a peek into the situation involving our Malay/Muslim graduates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The study was done by Prof Tan Khee Giap titled "Longitudinal Study on Comparative Employability and Career Advancement Path for Tertiary Educated Malay/Muslim Singaporeans and Chinese Singaporeans".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over 70% of respondents showed a risk-averse attitude and cannot see themselves moving to another industry in the next five years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Almost 60%, for instance, are unaware of the latest SkillsFuture initiatives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More than 60% feel that they will need assistance to enable them to progress in their careers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If these findings are taken as an indicator, future PMETs from this cohort will be facing major challenges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, it is important to prepare our youths and younger workers to face future challenges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Workers without new skills or those who have lower qualifications and skills will be affected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The recent call about SkillsFuture is timely for our Malay/Muslim youths.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Recently, MENDAKI set up a Future Ready Committee that aims to play an important role in this issue in a more consistent manner for the long term.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also important to strengthen our sense of belonging, especially in the efforts to ensure racial harmony and also increase the confidence of the Malay/Muslim community, so that we can stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the other communities at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, I would like to stress the importance of improving fair practices in job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the current situation, where we face a landscape of a slowing economy in the future, tight labour Page: 64 market and disruptive technology, it is crucial that focus is given to overcoming the perception that the available opportunities are unequal and there is discrimination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is important in order to avoid potential social and security issues from emerging in this country in the long term.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore's economic challenges will impact everyone in Singapore and not just the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We may see a future scenario where current Malay/Muslim workers and those who will enter the job market must be ready to compete on an equal footing in the job market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sure that the Government will do its best to help those who are affected to find employment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, while no Singaporean will be denied the opportunities, it also means that no one will be given special treatment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I end with a poem stating that there are opportunities being made available for everyone equally and we should also ensure that we have a broad view of the entire situation. "A major lane outside the city Travelling by car in the evening Opportunities are available equitably We have to keep an open mind." (In English): Deputy Speaker, Sir, I shall now continue in English to discuss enhancements to our employment practices as well as the challenges that the PMETs face.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We all remember the bad old days of the job advertisements in our local newspapers which would boldly state, for example, only a certain race can apply.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Employers are proactively seeking out resources to hire previously-disadvantaged groups of people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is very encouraging, as it is a clear indication that outreach exercises have been helpful and more companies are developing into conducive workplaces on their own accord.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While TAFEP has been inspiring and supportive, greater enforcement is necessary to get passive employers on board.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Australian Government's Fair Work Ombudsman comes to mind as a model statutory agency that not only educates, but investigates and enforces.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If there is a serious breach of a workplace law, Government officials will conduct the relevant investigations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The offending employer can be taken to Court, depending on the outcome of the investigation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Australian Employment Act prohibits discrimination against employees based on race, religion, age, gender, physical or mental disability, marital status, family or carer's responsibilities and pregnancy, amongst other factors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Likewise, in Finland, Finnish employment law specifically prohibits discrimination against employees on the basis of a similar range of factors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Employers found guilty of discrimination can Page: 65 be fined or imprisoned, while victimised employees may claim compensation for illegal discrimination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The employment laws for both countries have essentially made discriminatory practices prosecutable by law, in order to emphasise the importance of equality.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, the TAFEP framework deserves to be equipped with more teeth to be more effective in weeding out discriminatory workplace practices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Tribunal will have the power to make orders for employers to reimburse employees for employment-related claims.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Parties who disagree with the decision of the Tribunal or with the quantum of the award made by the Tribunal, will have the right to appeal to the High Court to review the decision.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These enhancements will go a long way towards ensuring that all PMETs and non-PMETs are protected under the law.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, I propose that we take things a step further.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, these sanctions should be extended to cover incidences of discriminatory practices during the hiring process.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must ensure every person has the same opportunities, giving each citizen the same platform to excel by their own merits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is even more important in an economic environment where labour market competition runs high.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Meaningful sanctions will go some way to ensuring optimal employment practices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is an escalation of the trend which has been growing in the past few years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Within my own constituency, we have seen a slow increase in PMETs attending the Meet-the-People Sessions, requesting assistance because they have not been able to find new employment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One such constituent is a 56-year-old tower crane operator, who was working for an offshore oil and gas company.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Due to the downturn in the industry, his contract was not renewed and he had been searching unsuccessfully for employment in any industry for the past year and e2i is currently assisting him to obtain a Class 3 driving licence, so he will be able to find work as a driver.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another constituent is a 52-year-old IT Systems Director who, in his last job, earned in excess of a quarter of $1 million a year but was retrenched over a year ago and is still unable to find a new job.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, my great concern is that this is merely the tip of the iceberg, as Member Patrick Tay has mentioned, as many PMETs, because of embarrassment, perceived loss of face, or the belief that we would be unable to help, are reluctant to approach Members of Parliament for Page: 66 assistance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is hard to hold on to that sense of belonging, of being Singaporean, when you are not able to provide for yourself or your family in your own homeland.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The e2i's Employability Coaches in its Career Services Centre highlighted the following.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, mid-career jobseekers have to grapple with acquiring new skills and to accept lower salaries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, workers with long years of service without acquiring new skills or increasing their scope of responsibilities, find it challenging to find a similar job matching their last-drawn salaries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And, third, employers are unwilling to offer jobs with higher salaries to potential employees who have not built depth in their field of expertise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must also consider how to effectively redeploy the segment of workers mentioned above.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They do have specialised skills which are valuable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, employers need to be more open in recruiting older PMET workers who are likely able to pick up new skills faster due to their technical background.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One approach would be to match PMETs with our SMEs in a more structured way.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And as SMEs are currently facing three key business challenges, namely, high labour costs, manpower shortage and increasing competition, the channelling of displaced or retired PMETs into appropriate SMEs makes great sense.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To further help PMETs to adapt, we need more transparency at the macro level to examine where the demand is in terms of skills, so that Singaporeans can make timely informed choices in their skills accumulation to meet future demands.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The displaced PMET workforce remains a significant potential contributor to the economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we face ever-developing challenges, we, as parliamentarians and individuals, have a duty to our fellow citizens to continue to ensure that every Singaporean has the best possible opportunity to reach their fullest potential.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is how we strengthen our Singaporean Core and prepare ourselves for the next 50 years and beyond.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On that note, Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Motion of thanks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Alexander Fraser Tytler, born in 1747, was a History professor at the University of Edinburgh.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: He said the following about democracy more than 200 years ago: "A democracy is always temporary in nature; it simply cannot exist as a permanent form of government.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: A democracy will continue to exist up until the time that voters discover that they can vote themselves generous gifts from the public treasury.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: From that moment on, the majority always votes for the candidates who promise the most benefits from the public treasury, with the result that every democracy will finally collapse due to loose fiscal policy, which is always followed by a dictatorship." He further said that the world's greatest civilisations always progressed through the following sequence: Page: 67 "From bondage to spiritual faith; From spiritual faith to great courage; From courage to liberty; From liberty to abundance; From abundance to selfishness; From selfishness to complacency; From complacency to apathy; From apathy to dependence; From dependence back into bondage." Prof Joseph Olson of Hamline University School of Law in the United States was of the view that the US is now somewhere between the "apathy" and "complacency" phase, based on Prof Tytler's definition of democracy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I was concerned that Singapore could be on the brink of passing from abundance to selfishness after GE 2011.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, the milestone events in 2015, from the passing of our founding Prime Minister, followed by a series of SG50 events and GE 2015, appeared to have steered Singapore away from the phase of selfishness.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are fewer incidents of the likes of the Maplewoods residents' protest against the launch shaft site blocking the entrance of their condominium during the construction of Downtown Line 2.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are also fewer complaints about the building of an eldercare centre in the neighbourhood in general.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But, is Singapore immune from the downfall of a democratic nation, as mentioned by Prof Alexander?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Singapore has gone against the grain to thrive, moving from Third-World to First-World in one generation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Singapore is special, in the words of Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Singapore needs to remain special if we want to see a glorious SG100.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The NCMP scheme is another unique feature that makes us special and has strengthened our political system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The intention to increase the NCMP numbers entrenches the importance of the NCMP scheme; at the same time, it recognises the contributions of past NCMPs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The political parties of the best-performing losing Opposition candidates that have accepted the NCMP nomination have benefited from the system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, instead of calling names, let us all embrace the NCMP scheme as a unique feature of Singapore's political system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is also consistent with what President Dr Tony Tan has said, "to remain special, we must first resolve to move ahead together".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The President further said that "we strove to leave no one behind, even as we created opportunities for all".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Page: 68 Yes, no one should be left behind as we progress as a nation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: No one, including the persons with disability, or PWDs, should be left behind.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Singapore has made much progress thus far in educating and assisting PWDs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Enabling Master Plans I and II have significantly improved their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: On the employment front, however, the progress is painfully slow.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In reality, for every success story which is highlighted, there are far more PWDs who have taken a long time to secure a job, if at all.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This runs the gamut from the low-skilled disabled who lost the job of cleaning airline headphone sets to technology, to a hearing-impaired university degree holder who missed her employment opportunities, many a times, due to the fact that HR personnel failed to note that the job seeker can only respond to SMS messages and not telephone calls.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is a classic case of "the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We can pump resources into training and assistance for PWDs and we can try to encourage employers to hire PWDs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, we are still reliant on the goodwill of the employers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Perhaps, we could consider introducing legislation to compel large organisations with more than 500 staff to employ PWDs, with some effort to redesign jobs to suit the PWDs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Countries which have quota systems in place include Germany, Thailand and Japan.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In Japan, for example, private-sector organisations with at least 56 employees must ensure that at least 1.8% of their headcount comprises PWDs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If these quotas are not met, the organisation is usually required to pay a levy towards a fund used to promote the employment of PWDs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Alternatively, some countries like Australia, Canada and the US have introduced anti-discrimination laws.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is illegal for employers to discriminate against current and prospective employees on the basis of disability.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: China employs a hybrid of a quota system and anti-discrimination laws.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With the right training and set-up, PWDs can become self-reliant and contribute as much as their able-bodied peers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: PWDs are also a valuable addition to the diversity of the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We do not want PWDs to be left behind as an Annex as Singapore progresses, a phrase often used by fellow parliamentarian and Mayor Denise Phua.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, when the Government implements its policies, it is important to look after Singaporeans' needs in terms of food, clothing, housing and travelling.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Today, I would like to touch on the issue of travelling and hope that the Government can make public transport more user-friendly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Page: 69 In the Addendum to the President's Address issued by the Ministry of Transport (MOT), the Ministry states that its mission is to connect Singaporeans from their homes to schools and workplaces all over Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As the train network becomes more extensive, many are willing to take the train, which is comfortable and convenient, but they are hampered by the connectivity from their homes to the train station.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For residents staying within 800 metres of a train station, most abled people are willing to walk to the station.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Beyond that, residents typically ask for feeder bus services.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Unfortunately, the authorities often cite resource constraints and cannot meet the residents' demand for more feeder services.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If resource is, indeed, a constraint, perhaps LTA could consider boldly reorganising bus routes, especially long distance cross-island routes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Imagine how many Singaporeans will be willing to take the bus instead of MRT to work or school!

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In fact, along the route of Bus 51, there are a number of MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Residents also use Bus 51 from the nearby estates to the MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For example, many residents at Ayer Rajah rely on service 51 to bring them to Jurong East MRT Station.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: How reliable can service 51 be when it has to travel about 30 kilometres before reaching Ayer Rajah?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: No wonder our fellow Parliamentarian, Ms Foo Mee Har, has been complaining about the reliability of service 51 when it serves as a pseudo feeder service for her Ayer Rajah residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Does it make sense to continue with such cross-island bus services?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: That is 14 long trunk services for 40 new feeder services.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These 40 new feeder bus services will go a long way towards improving the first- and last-mile connectivity and persuade more Singaporeans to switch to public transport and help achieve the goal of a car-lite society envisioned by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, on the economy, the President said that "we cannot predict the future, but we must adapt as the world changes".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The future of Singapore lies in encouraging innovation and creating value.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: People and businesses need to adapt and change.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While the Government has provided funding to people and businesses to explore new ideas which will benefit the society, the Government also has to constantly review existing rules.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some rules and regulations which might have been necessary previously are now harmful and not beneficial to value creation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is particularly relevant now, given the rise of the "sharing" economy in which people rent beds, rooms, cars and other assets directly from one another through the Internet and mobile phone apps.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These sites allow a growing global community of people to rent out personal spaces to travellers and transient tourists.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Since 2008, over 60 million people have used Airbnb to book accommodation in over 190 countries, but Singapore is not one of these countries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At least, not yet in a big way.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Nonetheless, we could still find more than 300 listings in the Airbnb Singapore website.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The owners who let out their units or room through Airbnb may be fined or jailed if caught.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In a study done in San Francisco in 2012, it was found that Airbnb travellers spent US$56 million in a year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: About US$12.7 million went to the hosts and US$43.1 million to San Francisco's businesses.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But beyond the money, what Airbnb travellers relish most is the novel experience of staying in an affordable and unique local space which could be someone's home and seeing the "authentic" side of a country.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In Singapore's context, this could be a HDB flat, a condominium or a shophouse.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There is much value in terms of local Singapore charm and a dash of real Singaporean hospitality, which could be offered to visitors and keep them coming back.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are concerns over rampant profiteering and neighbours may be uncomfortable with a constant flow of foreigners staying next to their apartments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, rules can be modified to make sure that there is compliance with local laws.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Similarly, car-sharing apps like Uber and Grabcar have been popular among commuters but have also created uproars as taxi-drivers all over the world decry the unfair competition.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Unlike home-sharing, car-sharing has already taken off in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many taxi companies complained that Uber taxi drivers do not have to obtain a taxi driver's vocational licence, unlike licensed taxi drivers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Uber cars also need not go through the stringent safety checks, as compared to existing players, thereby compromising the safety of commuters.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Otherwise, it is like tying the hands of the traditional brick-and-mortar companies and having them compete with online companies on a 100-metre tight race.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Change is never comfortable, especially when livelihoods are threatened.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If Singapore is to remain competitive and future-centric, we have to edit the rules to support value creation and innovation and not stifle them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At the same time, we all need to do our part to help the vulnerable, the disabled and those who are sometimes forgotten, so that Singapore can continue to march towards SG100 with no one left behind.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: President Tan said in his Address that "good policies and good politics go together".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We are known around the world for having an effective and honest Government that comes up with good policies, but there are also areas in which we did not do well enough.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The first one is not planning for the long term.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many of the commuters, including my residents at Khatib MRT station, were greatly inconvenienced.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The problem lies in engineering issues which were not properly addressed from the early days of the MRT system.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We did not train a pool of engineers and technicians to specialise in maintaining the rail system.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Having in-house expertise is very different from using subcontractors.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot be always using economic benefit as the sole yardstick in making decisions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now, Minister Khaw Boon Wan and his team have the unenviable task of completing a major overhaul while maintaining normal services.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Then, we have the grass pitch issue at the Sports Hub.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The pitch was not ready for many sports, the roof leaked and even the sound system got complaints from many concert-goers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We have to accept that the Government could have done better, expertise from our National Parks Board could have anticipated the problems and exercised more oversight over the project execution, especially with all the public money invested in the project.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, the Government had drawn the line too fine, too clearly and washed their hands too early.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The second is not keeping in mind how things are for the man-on-the-street.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One example is MOE's naming of a new JC − Eunoia JC.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The word was chosen for its meaning, but did anybody think whether the man-on-the-street can pronounce it easily?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Would an English, Chinese, Malay or even Tamil word have been easier for the common man-on-the-street to pronounce and relate to?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now, MOE is faced with unnecessary flak and even petitions to change the name.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And I certainly hope that the new hawker centre in Yishun will not have this kind of rental for the stalls.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, I was involved in trying to provide a covered linkway from the nearest HDB block to the nearest bus-stop in my new BTO, Acacia Breeze.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For many months, HDB and LTA could not resolve their differences.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I was trying to call a meeting for both parties to sit down to seek a solution.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, even our Deputy Prime Ministers have pointed out these issues recently.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Tharman said at a public service leadership dinner that we need to develop the habit of Page: 72 looking at issues through the eyes of ordinary citizens and bringing policies from different agencies together to serve their needs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean also said at a Civil Service award ceremony that the public service needs to stay connected with the people they serve.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I quote: "…to listen deeply and better understand aspirations and concerns and to work together with Singaporeans to make Singapore a better home for all of us".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I must emphasise that I am not here to point fingers or to make anyone uncomfortable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am bringing this up because I hope that the Government can do even better than before.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To do this, we need to look beyond the near term, beyond our individual agency responsibilities, at how we can maximise benefits for the man-on-the-street.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need people at all levels to be more than just carrying out the formulation and execution of policies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need people who are committed, trustworthy and serve with heart.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I know that in many instances, the civil servants are doing their best, but they are stretched as the public gets more vocal and they have to balance the different demands.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, we should pay more attention to the quality of the officers, their career path, training and the motivation for them to excel, innovate and give their best.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are three areas in which we need even more dedication and foresight from the Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They are the environment, housing and the economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore is famous for being clean.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, if you walk around the HDB neighbourhood at 4.00 am in the morning, you will realise that this cleanliness is, in fact, an illusion created by our cleaners.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In comparison, Japan and Taiwan have fewer cleaners than us but their environment is cleaner than ours.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I started the "No Cleaners Day" project in Nee Soon South.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I noticed that when we have to pick up the litter ourselves, we tend not to litter and we will also remind others not to do so.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can we expand the "No Cleaners Day" scheme and let our children clean their campus themselves, like Taiwan and Japan, so that the young will see a clean environment as their own responsibility?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I read a Straits Times report a few days ago.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It looks like not only our SMEs need to innovate; NEA also needs to be more creative in dealing with litter-bugs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How can we ensure a smoke-free environment and that non-smokers do not have to inhale second-hand smoke?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would urge the Government to consider making the Designated Smoking Point scheme a national policy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am delighted to hear from the President that the Government will continue to create a caring home for Singaporeans by building more affordable and comfortable HDB flats, higher quality infrastructure and convenient public transportation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope these plans can be implemented more smoothly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We do not want to see the situation again whereby new estates do not have enough childcare and transportation facilities even after the residents have moved in.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I also hope that the singles and the divorced people, especially those with children, can have their Page: 73 own flat as soon as possible.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This year and next year, Singapore will continue to face challenges, such as a shrinking manufacturing industry and China's slow economic growth.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe many Members, just like me, would have met many residents who came to seek help because they cannot find a job.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are many unpredictable factors when it comes to the economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Government have plans to deal with a slow economy and unemployment?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Early this month, a resident came to seek help from me.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He is a crane operator at a construction site.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He said that his company, starting from last year, would lay off one crane operator every month and it just so happened that, each time, it was a Singaporean who was laid off.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: My resident, who has diligently worked for the company for more than 10 years, was also laid off at the end of last year.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Another resident of mine works in the IT industry.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He told me that he was under a lot of pressure lately.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because his company has brought in a foreign talent, who is his boss now.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Soon after, this foreign talent brought in his own countrymen and asked this resident to teach them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He is under a lot of pressure and does not know when he will be laid off himself.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He said, "In Singapore, to have someone laid off is not difficult.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: You just need to cite the reason of the company restructuring." And his company has restructured many times.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I guess, after the Chinese New Year, there will be even more companies which will undergo "restructuring".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we will do even better in the next 50 years.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I support the Motion to thank the President.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She mentioned that to retrench one Singaporean, the company must cut one Work Permit.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because in Singapore, it depends on the sector and there is a dependency ratio.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the services sector, the ratio is one is to five, if I am not mistaken.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, it should be proportionate to this dependency ratio, then, it would be fair.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I wish to support the Motion to thank the President for his Address.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last year was a watershed year for us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The founding father of modern Singapore, Minister Mentor Lee, passed away.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Twenty sixteen is the first year of the post-Lee Kuan Yew era.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The world is watching us, as they have been for the past 50 years.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Well, we have proven to ourselves and the world, over and over again, yes, we can.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We sing lots of patriotic National Day songs every year.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Page: 74 In particular, one song "We are Singapore" expresses best for me what I want to say today: "There was a time when people said that Singapore won't make it, but we did.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There was a time when troubles seemed too much for us to take, but we did.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We built a nation, strong and free, reaching out together for peace and harmony." We have overcome lack of resources, lack of water, a few rounds of recessions, the Asian financial crisis, SARS, Lehman crisis.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Time and again, we have emerged stronger and more resilient.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the last General Elections, we witnessed a show of unity.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We demonstrated our determination to carry on the Singapore spirit, to forge ahead like our forefathers did.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We had nothing and now, we have everything.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We did not have water; we now have four national taps, including NEWater.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We do not have oil, but we process oil and is the hub for the fuel trade in Asia.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We may be small but we have a big impact.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In September 2011, a fire broke out at Pulau Bukom refinery.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It was Shell's largest refinery in the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This incident caused the premium of October oil gas swaps over November to increase to the highest for an inter-month spread in three years in anticipation of an oil shortage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We may be a little red dot, but whatever happens here also can move the markets in the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Minister Mentor Lee studied until he passed on.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He showed us the true meaning of lifelong learning 活到老, 学到老, 甚至学到死.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We upgraded our new skills, we are equipping Singaporeans to be multi-skilled and versatile so that they would qualify for fulfilling future jobs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When one is in a vocation one loves, then a job becomes fun and satisfying.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: People who work at jobs they love are usually good at them because they are motivated and naturally inclined to put in their best.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With Singapore's natural constraints, our workers have to be among the best for Singapore to survive.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not by providing them with fish but teaching them to fish for themselves.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Its many modules offer training across a wide range of sectors and levels of mastery.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A new mindset towards broad-based and lifelong learning is important.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have to go beyond the paper chase and broaden the definitions of success in our society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It enables skills acquisitions and constant improvement in a fast-changing environment where the lifespan of a know-how may be increasingly shorter.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Page: 75 May I suggest that for SkillsFuture, the Government raise awareness of its benefits through public education, similar to the efforts CPF has been making to get Singaporeans to start planning their finances for the future early?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will strengthen the Singaporean Core as we will be less reliant on foreigners in highly skilled and niche areas where fulfilling and better paying jobs will be available.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree with the President that in the face of a very competitive global environment and with our limited resources, we have to restructure our economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singaporeans must stay resilient and united and forge ahead as our forefathers did.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We cannot afford to shut our doors in this competitive world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am excited by the opportunities these sunrise sectors will be offering us as a nation and for our people.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To meet the requirements of these industries, we have to equip Singaporeans with the knowledge and skills and update technology regularly to take on these new challenges.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Otherwise, our prospects will diminish if our competitors make it with the same skillsets and lower wages.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Shielding Singaporeans from the reality of competition from other countries and their people will prevent us from improving.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the meantime, we will not be updated on a timely basis of how much advance the competition has made.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is better that we recognise and face up to the challenges and overcome them together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rising manpower, rental and compliance costs and foreign worker levies are a burden on our companies in a slowing global economy.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For smaller firms which are struggling to make ends meet, the combination of high costs and slowing demand could deal an irreparable blow which they will not be able to recover from.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I appeal to the Ministry to consider reducing the levies to lighten the load on our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To incentivise our SMEs to become more productive from mechanisation and technology, the Government had implemented measures, such as the Productivity and Innovation Credit (PIC) Scheme.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government will continue to provide tax breaks and cash incentives to our SMEs so that the drive to move to more productive technologies will be maintained.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Constant renewal and updating of technology should become a culture of our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Page: 76 It would be good if our SMEs can link up with our tertiary and research institutions to work on productive advancements jointly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would be at a level which many of our SMEs will find very useful, as manpower is one of the key components of their business costs, especially when our population is ageing.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nine hundred thousand Singaporeans will turn 65 years old in 14 years' time in 2030 and, probably, we will be only left with two working adults to support an aged Singaporean if nothing is done.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To support our ambitious plans for the future, we have to tackle the root of the problem of our manpower shortage which is our low fertility rate.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are implications for our economy, security and defence if we do not have enough Singaporeans from our next generation to replace us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our total fertility rate (TFR) has grown slowly from 1.15 in 2010 to 1.25 in 2014.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government has provided many incentives to encourage couples to have more babies, but the response has not been as good as we would like it to be.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my view, one of the most effective measures so far has been the easier access to accommodation and flat ownership.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The correlation between the availability of accommodation and fertility has been very encouraging.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry will continue to ensure a good supply of flats.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, the Ministry could consider maintaining a year's worth of BTO flat supply ahead at any point of time, for example, between 10,000 and 15,000 units.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With shortened waiting times, our couples will find it much easier to plan for their families.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to suggest that we build more affordable, bigger flats to encourage families to have more children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These flats will be different from the usual 5-room HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They may have four or five bedrooms built over 1,600 square feet with absolute priority given to families with four children or more.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such flats can be built in both mature and new estates and buyers can choose between leases of 99 years or the shorter leases of 60 years, which may be more affordable to them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, I would like to voice my support for the Fresh Start Housing Scheme which will help public rental households to own homes again.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope this scheme can be extended to include third timer families.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are third-timer families which had tapped upon housing subsidies or grants twice, sold their flats and have become public rental tenants.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of them had sold their flats due to poor planning or very difficult personal circumstances or unfortunate circumstances.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, they now want to have their own homes again.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To ensure affordability, the BTO flats under the scheme will be smaller – 2-room – with shorter leases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also need to put in place conditions to ensure that the scheme is not abused, such as restricting them to only reselling their flats to HDB.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of my concerns with the families involved is that they face multiple problems – financial, relationship and at work, or the lack thereof.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government would have to assist them beyond their accommodation needs and provide longer term counselling, especially if there are children in Page: 77 the families.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must help prevent their children from getting caught in the vicious cycle of low education, poverty and unemployment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another worry I have is that a number of these families have more children and may also have elderly members living with them, so the living conditions will be cramped.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there any way we can help these families cope by offering them some form of advice on how to maximise their interior layout and living arrangements?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   The success of Singapore's public housing policy and Home Ownership Scheme is universally recognised.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many foreigners are envious that Singaporeans can own their own flats and hope to learn from our experience in public housing.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Several new public housing schemes introduced during the term of the previous Government were well-received by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These good policies stabilised prices and assured Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the previous term, I spoke on the state of housing prices and resale flats at that time.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I felt that the strong demand was, to a certain extent, a panic reaction to the rising property prices.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is similar to stock market reactions: when the stock market is hot, investors will chase after the market; once the bear market emerges, investors become hesitant and stay on the sidelines.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To a certain degree, this also reflects the state of the property market today.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Those who need to sell their existing private property or HDB flats now, find that there are not many buyers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is in stark contrast to the flurry of activities seen previously.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, it will provide a relatively stable environment that allows Singaporeans to make long-term plans to upgrade and work towards achieving their dreams.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Gan, you have run out of time, half a minute.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: This will prevent single flat owners from facing the difficulties of living alone.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, it is better to teach our people to fish rather than to feed them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We have to strive to give every Singaporean lifelong opportunities to not only pursue one's interests but also do well and be the best, if not the best of the best.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: This will ensure Singapore will continue to attract quality investments that provide quality jobs for Singaporean entrepreneurs and workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: (In Mandarin):   In the General Elections last year, Singaporeans sent a very clear signal: Singaporeans want a stable, safe, prosperous, caring and harmonious society, a Singapore that is fair and just, where all are treated equally, regardless of race and language.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: They want a responsible, efficient, clean and good Government that is willing to serve the country and the nation, to create a beautiful home together with the people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am humbled to be given this opportunity to help shape policies and programmes and help make Singapore even better and improve the lives of Singaporeans significantly as we move towards SG100.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am here to speak my mind, to speak up constructively, to help ensure that we have the best policies in place for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am here to help ensure that we become an even more caring and compassionate society but still remain the economic powerhouse in this region and the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have talked and debated a lot about the hardware of this nation, about the software as well but I hope we place or continue to place equal emphasis on the heartware of this nation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is not something new but something I hope we can focus more on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Acting Minister Ong Ye Kung had earlier cautioned against excessively viewing ourselves in numeric terms and I wholeheartedly agree with him.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While numbers are important as we debate on issues, my sincere hope is that this is not just a numbers game.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we progress as a nation, we have achieved a lot in the past 50 years, we have made significant economic progress, but we must continue to place moral and ethical progress on par with economic progress.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to ensure that Singapore is not run as a Singapore Incorporated and that economic growth is not the only measure of success in our country.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Numbers and dollars and cents are part of the equation, in fact, very important parts of the equation in this complex world we live in, but there is more to it and it has to be more to it in order for us to progress.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My fellow Member of this House, Mr Seah Kian Peng, said in Parliament almost a decade ago, and I quote, "Minister Mentor speaks of how we want to be in the first half of the First World.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can only truly do that, join the ranks of the civilised countries, not just by cranking up our economy, churning ever brighter students, but by caring for those who cannot speak and are 100% dependent on us for their quality of lives – animals." And when we talk about animals, let us not talk about them as purely numbers, numbers of animals we trap and cull, but talk about them as sentient beings who live amongst us in the community and who share this island with us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no doubt that we have to do something to address the conflicts but, at the same time, we need to ensure that what we do addresses the root of the problem, not the symptoms of the problem but the root of the problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to ensure our policies are humane.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Several Members of this House have used quotes from Einstein and, so, I will also share one of his quotes which reads, "Our task must be to free ourselves by widening our circle of compassion to embrace all living creatures and the whole of nature and its beauty." Members of this House know me as a strong activist for the past 15 years, in particular, a strong champion for animal welfare and environmental causes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lately, I am known as the guy hunting the cat killers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Through monthly townhall and dialogue sessions, I will also be championing other concerns of fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Through my monthly work experiences, I will learn more about different professions and help champion improvements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have been a healthcare worker, a driver and, Page: 80 earlier this month, a cleaner, and it truly has been a worthwhile journey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are jobs which are important in the progress of our country but where the workers receive too little appreciation at times and should receive more recognition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am also a new parent of a 2-year-old daughter and having a child has been one of the most rewarding journeys of our lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My daughter lights up our lives and seeing her grow up, seeing her smile and laugh, hearing her start to talk have been an amazing experience and always puts a smile on our faces.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She is also a beaming activist already, having launched her first campaign, which is to end my 17-year habit of smoking.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am delighted to say that she has succeeded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her copy-and-paste function has also now begun and so she has made me a much better person as she now scrutinises and copies every single word we say and do, and all my bad habits are very quickly gone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, any bad habit she has is clearly not from me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And to make sure I do not sleep on the couch tonight, any bad habit she has is also clearly not from my wife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I worry about the Total Fertility Rate (TFR).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure we all know that it is a worrying trend.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But as we talk about the TFR, we also need to make sure that this is not just a numbers game again.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The maternity and paternity leaves have been useful as well even though we heard that fathers are not taking up the paternity leave, but I did.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I hope we can do more to promote parenthood, the positive aspects of parenthood and to share positive stories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to inspire people to have kids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our policies need to focus on making sure we have time to have kids, to look after our kids and bond with them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to focus more attention perhaps on flexi-working hours for parents without compromising productivity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we can do more to help those who have kids to have more kids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do not think I have all the answers to the million-dollar question of how we can increase our TFR, but I have ideas and suggestions I hope we can try out and see if they will work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have stories to share about the journey my wife and I have embarked on and, personally, I will walk the talk.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will help increase the TFR by having another child soon, I hope.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There really is no greater reward than having a child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another area that concerns me is an overarching one and, that is, how we can mobilise our most important and valuable resource in this country – our people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can mobilise them so we continue this journey, the Singapore story together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How can we mobilise everyone to step forward to volunteer, to serve and to make a difference?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we succeed in this, then this will help in a lot of the issues we will discuss in this House.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Page: 81 This will help the lower income families where we need to do more than provide financial assistance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having this strong community spirit is vital in times of crisis, be it a terrorist attack or an economic downturn.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is this community spirit, this caring society where we look out for one another, that will keep Singapore going and allow us to recover quickly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To mobilise people and get the active citizenry we want, we need to make sure people are engaged, empowered and inspired.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Engaged, empowered and inspired so that we have a nation committed to helping, giving and sharing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this also cannot just be a numbers game.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not just about sharing the total number of volunteers we have or the number of volunteer hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To engage people, we need to listen more, listen more than we speak.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I quote, "The most basic of all human needs is the need to understand and be understood.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The best way to understand people is to listen to them." So, we are not just there to explain policies to people, to throw them with facts and figures but we are there to truly listen and understand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Our Singapore Conversation and The Future of Us dialogue are fine examples of engagement and they have been impactful.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And I urge the Government to conduct more of such dialogues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to make sure that the debate on policies, programmes and legislation takes place beyond these four walls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I think the most important work Members of this House do is beyond these four walls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to ensure that the views of people are not just sought, but worked on, developed and presented in this House.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to ensure that the debate we have in this House is started outside these four walls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to ensure people feel and are empowered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The robust debate we have in the public arena is crucial and will ensure that we truly understand what the ground concerns are, the various ideas out there are and the different solutions available.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Because, ultimately, we do not have all the answers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us also empower by setting up committees comprising people on the ground, a committee of people who are not like-minded but who will come together to argue, to debate and to find common ground.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To move forward, it is committees like these, like the Animal Welfare Legislation Review Committee, where I feel we will get the best policies drafted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Empowering is vital and we need to empower our constituents and ensure that they have a voice in this House and a role to play in shaping Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And we need to inspire them with positive stories of the Singapore story, of the amazing Singapore story and how, with their help, their views and their partnership, it can continue to be and, perhaps, be an even more remarkable story.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Page: 82 We are, indeed, the island of possibilities, the island of the impossible, the island where miracles can happen, have happened and will continue to happen, if we continue to believe, if we continue to fight passionately and continue to be determined for a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we pass our 50th year mark, it cannot be business as usual.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, we cannot run this nation as a business.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And as far as my medical checks have shown, I believe, and I hope, I will be here for SG100.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
