text: We can make Singapore the caring society and continue to be the shining red dot our President spoke about.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In his Address, the President highlighted the need for the Government to partner citizens to shape our common future.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: He also urged all Members to work closely with the people to write the next chapter together.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We also heard calls for a more fulfilling pace of life, where we can pursue other aspirations outside of work.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: There was also interest among many to forge a stronger sense of a national identity and these are all important, and have guided the Government's work in the last few years.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But we need to adapt how we, as Singaporeans, want Singapore to be run, with the new challenges we face.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: And as it is evolving quicker than ever, we need everyone to chip in, to make it work for all of us.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It is an opportunity for Singaporeans to come forward to share their views and suggestions on how to build a better future for Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These are focused engagement sessions, aimed at looking into specific topics, including the arts, sports, volunteerism, environment and even hawker food culture.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These are not just discussions, but brainstorm sessions to establish the next steps on matters that concern us.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I attended one of the sessions last Thursday with over 70 youths.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Ideas came fast and furious, on ways to help other segments of society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For instance, one participant had the idea of building public gyms for people with special needs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Another suggested having retro disco parties for the elderly in the void decks of housing blocks.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: There are all ideas worth pursuing, so I encouraged them to take it further and, if necessary, consider how they can partner the relevant Government agencies and other organisations to turn these ideas into reality.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But there is a role for the audience to play in deciding who gets to go, who gets to stay and who finally wins the contest.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Hence, we should not sit passively to watch the Singapore Story unfold.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Take part in one of the SGfuture sessions, or get involved in other forums that exist.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We should take an interest in following the developments and better still, play a part in shaping the Singapore we want for our future generations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have all seen the power and effectiveness of collective wisdom.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Crowd-sourcing and crowd-funding, for instance, are concepts that have fuelled opportunities for many people and businesses.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The run-away successes of Kickstarter, Uber and AirBnB for instance are not solely because of the technology or the products they offer.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They manage to effectively match demand with supply and vice versa.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Their apps bring people together for a mutually-beneficial outcome and their apps make it easy for people to see what is out there, seize it and achieve a better outcome for themselves.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In the same way, SGfuture harnesses the wisdom of crowds.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This idea of co-creating with the people is not entirely new.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This also means within the Government, public agencies will need to reorganise ourselves, in order to effectively involve and engage Singaporeans.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: As Members of the House, we also need to do more engagement with our residents, whether is it to decide on what to build and where to build in estate upgrading projects.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They are vocal, energetic and teeming with ideas.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I know many of them want to be involved in shaping the Singapore they hope to live in.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I have been hearing from more of them since taking up my appointment at MCCY.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Recently, I spent a day at Outward Bound Singapore on Pulau Ubin kayaking and abseiling with students from Bartley Secondary School and Tanjong Katong Girls' School.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: As I think about the time we spent together that day, I was encouraged by the display of teamwork and resilience in our youths.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I hope to be able to catch up with more young Singaporeans in the coming months.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I want to hear about what moves them and what they want for Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I hope to share with more of them that they are in a good position to make a difference for Singapore and that the future is theirs to own.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I hope to do so through more informal ways, including more kayaking or abseiling, if necessary.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Over the last few years, as a Member of Parliament, I have found it useful to create such relatively informal channels to reach out to Singaporeans, through face-to-face conversations, social media and even exercising.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It is a way to connect with my residents in Tampines and the public at large.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: During these informal sessions, my residents raise questions as well as give feedback on improvements for the constituency.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We also talk about ways to manage issues, from noisy neighbours to national topics like whether there should be free parking at national parks, which the Senior Minister of State talked about just now.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But from these regular check-ins with my residents, and even some non-residents, I get a good sense of what concerns them.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: What I have observed, over the last few years of such engagements is that Singaporeans are moving away from just giving feedback or complaints.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: At the same time, I am also getting requests to help with their causes, for instance, in promoting a giving culture, better road manners and even attending their baby shower parties.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This is encouraging and affirms, too, that the approach we are taking as a Government, starting with the SGfuture citizen engagement, is timely and a step in the right direction.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Regularly, I would post an open invitation on social media, for anyone to join me in my runs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These sessions, which I call "Run with BYK", allow me to meet more people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: As we jog around places like Marina Bay or Tampines EcoGreen, we chat and learn more about one another.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These groups are not large; in fact, often, there are just about two, at most six people.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But what makes it different is that it is also very conducive to hear from one another because every new person I speak with is a new opportunity to learn about them, to gather feedback and to look at how we can improve the way we do things in Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I think this is the mentality we should adopt when we talk about engaging the public, that there are no "right" platforms.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We just need to recognise the many opportunities around us to engage with one another, to enlarge the common space to collaborate and to co-exist.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: And "Run with BYK" is all the more meaningful too now that I am with MCCY, where together with Sport Singapore, we are promoting better living through sport.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: During each small group run, we enjoy our conversations as well as the beautiful sights and green spaces of Singapore along the way.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: So, if you are keen, you can look out for the next run through hashtag #runwithBYK.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Well, this is my personal exercise regime which I do anyway.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I am just opening it up for others to join me.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Likewise, public engagement should be and will be in the Government's DNA.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These channels will augment the other established channels that the Government already has, from the REACH platforms, to the hotlines and Facebook pages that almost all agencies have.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Our Singapore Conversation and the SGfuture engagements are the most recent efforts to reach out.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These are not one-off efforts, but they are a continuum in the Government's plans to reach out to Singaporeans over the years.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: And with SGfuture, we also want Singaporeans to take up projects, to seed a change and to shape our future.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Many views will emerge, as well as ideas to take Singapore forward.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Importantly, we want people to take these ideas and views further, to translate them into action.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The Government cannot do it alone or unilaterally, more so as our society becomes more diverse and the demands more diffused.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But the Government can and will partner people in making Singapore a better home for all.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Mr Perera spoke about an op-ed piece by Arts Engage on the Government's role in funding the arts.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In Singapore, funding of the arts is a partnership between the state, corporates and individuals, which reflects the spirit of shared responsibility and co-creation that I talked about earlier on.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This approach acknowledges the role that the Government plays in supporting the development of the arts sector.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This is because the Government sees the importance of the arts and culture in meeting the aspirations of the people and in building a sense of national identity.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But as the custodian of public funds, the Government is also accountable to the public in the application of funds towards achieving our social objectives.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The need to maintain a wide common space among communities and ensure social harmony in our multi-racial and multi-religious society has been expounded by many speakers before me.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The public expects the Government and public agencies to uphold these values in our policies, including our funding guidelines for the arts.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: At the same time, there is funding from the private sector: corporates and individuals.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They do not necessarily carry the same social objectives and are not bound by our arts funding guidelines.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, one can expect conditions to be similarly imposed by these private donors and individuals.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The conditions may vary from meeting brand attributes to audience size, but the point is that there will be conditions.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It is therefore not realistic to expect any public funds to be given out unconditionally.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The public expects us as custodian to discharge our responsibility with care and to good effect.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But rest assured, as an advocate of the arts, NAC will continue to focus on arts excellence and continue to make the case for enlarging the space for our artists and arts groups to grow.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: And when there are broader interests of society that may be at odds with this role, we will try to bridge the differences.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: At the very least, we seek to help all parties see the other points of view.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: After all, there should be better and deeper engagement.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: She questioned the need for Members of Parliament to take up leadership roles in NSAs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Members of Parliament who are holding NSA leadership positions have to earn their stripes and gain the respect of the members of the associations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They bring along with them experience and expertise in their own right.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: At the same time, the vast majority of NSAs, in fact, 55 out of the 63 NSAs, do not have Members of Parliament as their leaders, for example: Singapore Swimming Association, Singapore Sailing Federation, Singapore Bowling Federation, Singapore Rugby Union, Fencing Singapore, Singapore Silat Federation and many others; and these are very good NSAs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In fact, leaders from NSAs have joined us in the Chamber as Nominated Members of Parliament.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have Jessie Phua, Nicholas Fang and Dr Benedict Tan.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: There is a group of Permanent Residents or PRs in Singapore who have been calling Singapore home for decades but they do not enjoy the privilege of having our red passport or pink IC.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Many of them live through the years when Singapore and Malaysia were both British colonies, when Singapore joined and subsequently separated from Malaysia.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Typically, they will fall in such a profile: with little or no education, about 60 years old and above and have raised a family of children who are Singapore Citizens.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Usually, only they themselves or sometimes with their spouses, still hold Malaysian passports.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I have seen enough appeals for citizenships and permanent residency to speculate that ICA look at the following key factors in assessing the application: applicants' educational level, income status, age and how well they have integrated into the Singapore community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This group I am speaking up for today, most probably or most definitely, would fail the first three criteria miserably.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They would also fail the minimum English Language standard for new citizens as proposed by Member Darryl David.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, they would be able to strike a good conversation with many of our Pioneer Generation members in Mandarin, dialects, Malay, Tamil; and Mr Seah Kian Peng would be happy to hear, probably Singlish, too.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: After living in Singapore for the most part, and some, all of their life, they are as Singaporean as can anyone can be in their experiences, lifestyles, attitudes and social habits.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Some of these PRs tried applying for citizenship in the past but did not succeed.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Others did not even try, for two reasons: either they did not think they stood a chance, or they did not see the need then.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To be fair to them, Singapore only started to make a bigger distinction between citizens and PRs in the last five to 10 years.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For a long time, PRs were treated no differently from citizens.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Hence, many of them did not bother with the hassle of going through the paperwork.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But now, there is a huge difference between subsidies for PRs and citizens especially in education and healthcare, for very good and valid reasons.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: While education may not be the top priority for this group of residents at this phase of their life, healthcare cost is.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: So, do we begrudge them that they are now seemingly only re-aligning their loyalty or allegiance for selfish interests?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Yes, indeed, they may now realise that by not being citizens in Singapore, they would face higher medical expenses.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But it is probably their Singaporean children who have to shoulder the heavier burden.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: What matters to them too is that after all these years in Singapore, they hope to able to travel with their children without having to apply for visas.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They hope to queue in the same line when they are at the Singapore immigration counters, or simply to rest in peace as Singaporeans.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: While these people may not be well-qualified in education, may not earn a high income, they have contributed to Singapore, even as a housewife, taking care of children, raising a family of children.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But, of course, he brought up the bigger point about leadership in other sports associations and he pointed out that many of them who are led by non-politicians are actually doing very well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wonder if the Government thinks it is actually better for politicians to refrain from going into contest in these sports associations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After all, we have enough talent in the sporting fraternity and I am not doubting the sincerity of the PAP Members who have gone into certain sports associations, but the bigger point is: is it not better to build a stronger sporting leadership and for politicians actually to sort of step back and let others take the lead and they can always support in other ways?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I was the President of the Volleyball Association for eight years.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Honestly, I do not know a lot about volleyball.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: But the Association had benefited from various Presidents coming from Parliament through our networks, through our grassroots experience and they have continued to request for us to continue and for other Members to succeed when our term ends.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, it is really up to NSAs to decide and to elect their president, their leadership as they deem fit, that is, in the best interest of the NSA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would just like to put a clarification question to the hon Parliamentary Secretary Mr Baey Yam Keng.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Baey referred to my speech when I quoted from an op-ed piece by some of our artists.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, here, I am quoting from the op-ed piece by Mr Tan Tarn How and Mr T Sasitharan.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr T Sasitharan, as you know, if I am not wrong, is a Cultural Medallion recipient.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In any case, he is a very prominent local artist speaking on behalf of the Arts Engage network of Singapore which involves a number of local artists.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The view that he expressed was, and I quote verbatim here, "Our website also documents cases of works censored to protect the Government from embarrassment rather than for society's good.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps it is fitting to remember here that arts funding is not the Government's but the people's money." So, I would like to ask the hon Member does he agree with that view; and if not, why not?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, there was a difference in what was submitted earlier.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: There was also some of this to and fro that happened.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Among the many applications and support that NAC has given to the many arts groups and artists in Singapore, these are a minute minority of cases which the group has pointed out.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: As I said in my speech, in MCCY and NAC, our role is to advocate the arts.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We will stand on the side of the artists in their pursuit of artistic excellence.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We hope to create and develop a bigger common space so that Singaporeans and the community-at-large can enjoy the works of our very talented artists in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Much of the attention surrounding the President's speech at the Opening of Parliament concerns the upcoming changes of the political system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The President's speech intermitted that an inclusive Singapore is a clear objective of the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will speak on one aspect of the political system that I believe can play a very significant role to improve both politics and policies in Singapore and that is through Parliament and the institutions it offers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It goes on to say "the Select Committee members have been able to acquire significant levels of expertise in the specific areas for which that committee is responsible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This, together, with the resources available to them have reinforced the authority of their reports".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is my view that the processes afforded to Select Committees are helpful because the testimony of witnesses, who could be private sector individuals, civil servants or implementing agents on the ground, would lead to greater information sharing and the acquisition of greater knowledge on specific policies by all Singaporeans, not just parliamentarians.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, an appreciation of the trade-offs in a more complex Singapore and a more complex international environment beyond SG51 would, in my own estimation, significantly mature our political discourse, level up knowledge and serve to unify our people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would also encourage Singaporeans not just to look at an issue more deeply, but to understand why what may be a solution to some, has to be balanced with other demands, all of which must confront the question of financing, a question that a small country with no natural resources can ill avoid.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The depth of knowledge of policies and their trade-offs enabled by Select Committee hearings and reports can also be a strong insurance against the danger of retail politics and political aspirants who irresponsibly make policies in the hopes of winning votes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fast forward to the next 50 years, any conversation with Singaporeans cannot only be about seeking feedback and brainstorming sessions from the people before policy-crafting and implementation, which is important in its own way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But instead, it has to involve Singaporeans along every step of the way, including during execution, so that mid-course corrections, reviews and assessments can be made together.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In September last year, as Members of this House were busy at the election hustings, the UK House of Commons' Select Committee on Business Innovation and Skills received evidence on the UK government's productivity plan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This plan sought to address the main causes of low productivity in the UK.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Select Committee sought to determine whether the government's policies were likely to achieve their desired results.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ordinary citizens were able to submit their evidence to the committee through the UK parliamentary website.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There was also the prospect of giving oral evidence at hearings that are open to members of the public and companies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As an example, some of the companies that gave evidence at the productivity inquiry included Rolls Royce and Virgin Atlantic, hence, providing a lot of scope for a deeper understanding of the problems of the day surrounding productivity from a wide canvas of citizenry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even Hong Kong's Legislative Council carries out significant policy work behind the scenes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These panels also examine important issues of wide public concern as referred by the Council or raised by the panels themselves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These include the development of elderly care services, retirement schemes, studies into free kindergarten education, animal welfare and cruelty to animals and even hawker policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In practice, Mdm Speaker, our Parliament does not need to mirror the UK system, Hong Kong system, or any other system in its entirety, nor do we need to establish an excessive amount of Select Committees for the sake of it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, there is a number of issues that would clearly keep the Government and the Opposition occupied in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the longer experience and size of the UK, they host an extensive A to Z of Select Committees.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our Parliament, on the other hand, can establish Select Committees for key issues of the day as determined by Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It will have an attendant impact not just on our healthcare system, but on families too with more children having to take time off to look after their parents to see that they age well and gracefully.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An Active Ageing Select Committee would be helpful in this regard to understand what gaps need to be plugged, in addition to where the deficiencies continue to exist in the system, the reasons for their existence and how they can be overcome.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his speech, the President clearly emphasised the importance of SkillsFuture to the economy, how important it is for SkillsFuture to be a success and how it must to be a national movement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are many dimensions to SkillsFuture: PMETs, career guidance, sectoral manpower plans, Earn and Learn credits, individual learning portfolios, amongst others, across the age spectrum.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As I noted in my Budget Debate speech last year, the National Productivity Council has now come under the purview of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For many advanced economies including Singapore, improving productivity is a serious matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The presence of Select Committee Members from all parties would not just be symbolic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, it will be in step not just with the wishes of many voters, but it would mirror the inclusive Singapore the President spoke about and the Singapore we all desire.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, it would operationalise what the President meant when he said, "Individual aspirations may defer, but we have to work together to create a common future".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This proposal to establish a SkillsFuture Select Committee can be read in two ways.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The more cynical view is that Select Committees could be used to secure information not in the public domain on Government processes and decision-making, and to embarrass the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But there is another long-term perspective to be considered.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And that is the in-depth granularity offered by Select Committees on vital issues affecting Singaporeans which would contribute significantly to create a culture of mastery and excellence; and for Singaporeans to take a deep interest in policies and to understand the trade-offs surrounding policymaking.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This theme of excellence and mastery, not just competence, was covered in the Finance Minister's Budget speech 2014 and that is exactly what SkillsFuture is about.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Parliament is in a privileged position to re-configure the relationship between the public and the Government as we march towards SG100.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A more public role for Parliament and more time spent in it by Members of Parliament, offers greater scope to better our political system so that it governs effectively in the interests of all.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I rise in support of the Motion to thank the President for his Address at the Opening of the first session of this Parliament.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: President Tan reminded us that we are a small country with no natural resources and our strength is our people.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This improbable nation, Singapore, is the result of the people who came before us.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Their conviction, courage and hard work brought us to where we are today.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many Members have discussed in the last few days in terms of ensuring that Singapore continues to be a special place for all Singaporeans, young and old, to realise their aspirations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We all have aspirations to provide for a better life for ourselves and our families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To enable Singaporeans, no matter where our starting point, to continue to improve our lives, I believe that Singapore must be able to give Singaporeans fulfilling jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe that to have meaningful work gives confidence to our people to not only make a living but also to feel included and, hence, a sense of belonging and commitment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This point was so nicely said in a movie that I recently watched titled "The Intern".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Robert De Niro, who plays a 70-year-old retiree, decided to apply for a job as an intern in an online fashion site, a work environment very different from what he knew.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He spoke about why he was doing so and I thought was so apt.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He said that he wants "the connections, the excitement, I want the challenges and I guess I want to be needed." With evolving business models, our economic changes, technological and social changes, the kind of work and the "workplace" is changing rapidly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many of today's top jobs did not exist a few years ago and even how work is organised is changing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There is no longer a place for people to go to work, with more people being able to work from anywhere.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am both somewhat optimistic of the new opportunities that will be created, as well as concerned of the impact and disruption on Singaporeans that these changes will bring.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Although anecdotal, I am hearing residents' concerns about losing their jobs and the anxiety of not being able to get another job given the slower economic growth or taking longer to get another job, given what businesses are going through in terms of the changes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This readiness goes beyond just the hard skills and knowledge and will involve greater adaptability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given these employment trends and feedback from businesses that it is taking them longer to find the right persons to fill the roles they are hiring for, I believe that there is urgency to ensure that we adapt to this changing employment landscape.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are fears that these changes will displace jobs and routine work would be automated or business models would change and make certain jobs go away.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These changes can also create new jobs or greater job scope and opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While both these views are valid, if we want to be future-ready and if we want to future-ready our workforce, we must advocate a mind-set of learning and curiosity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will enable us to adapt and embrace these changes so that we can take advantage of these opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We will have to acquire new skills on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And this ability to continue to learn and to build a portfolio of skills and experience will affect everyone regardless of whether we are young and just entering the workforce, or an older person, or whether we are a lower skilled worker or PMET.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Technology is pervasive and is impacting many aspects of our work and life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Today, with the ability to use search on even, what many of us have in our pockets, a smartphone, you will have quick access to information, to knowledge, even on a subject that you know nothing about.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And with this, you can ask, "Is that good?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Is that bad?" I think it is a good thing in the sense that it enables us to do work more quickly and more efficiently.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But it is also important that we understand the information that is coming towards us and what to do with that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: That is what we have to equip our people to be doing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But if we are not careful and we do not apply it, then that becomes a challenge.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With technology, relationships are also becoming more networked rather than hierarchical, so hence, being able to use these technologies will enable us to have faster and more effective communications and connections.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But it is important to prevent an opportunity divide.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must ensure that all people at all levels and ages are comfortable and able to leverage the use of technology.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need to better equip our people and we must invest in developing strong communication skills so that people can communicate their ideas better and connect and share these ideas.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Some fear that the lower skilled jobs will disappear with technology and that these roles will be displaced.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think that it is true but it could also create new and better jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Without having to do extra work, if we put sensors in the areas being cleaned, one person could probably be able to monitor a larger space and then go to the places where there are more people and where more cleaning is required.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And you can do that without having to make that person work extra hard.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To differentiate our workforce, as many have said in this House, we must have a mastery of skills and innovation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the rapid changes that we are experiencing, while knowledge is easily obtained and probably computers can handle information better than a human being, I still think that the person has a very important role to play and if we know how to leverage this knowledge, we would be able to leapfrog on innovation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe you cannot replace a good teacher, a good nurse or even a good salesperson.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But with the use of the right business processes and technology, you can provide them with the ability to do what they do best and improve the experience for the student, the patient or the customer.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One area that I must emphasise that we must never lose, is our desire to improve and a mind-set of resilience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I want to share a story of a young boy whom I met many years ago in my first term as a Member of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He and his mother had come to see me because this boy felt that he was being singled out by his teacher.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: When he came to see me he was suspended for some incident in school and he felt that he was being singled out.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And he said to me, "I have been unfairly singled out by a teacher." Then, I asked him why, and he said, "Yes, because he does not think I am capable." I said, "Okay, if he does not think you are capable, do you think you are capable?" He says "Yes!" I said, "Then, the best way to win your teacher over is to show him that." And I did not see this boy after that, but one day when I was in a school at a Book Prize Award ceremony.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This lady came up to me smiling away and I was trying to figure out where I had seen her.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: She said, "I am here because my son is getting an award and recognition." And guess what, it is the same boy, in the same school, a year or so later, being recognised for his capabilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While circumstances can affect us, we have to have that mindset of resilience and we must have that confidence and that belief.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Another area that I feel needs attention is the Human Resource (HR) function.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we talk about all these changes, businesses will need the HR function to be a lot stronger because not only will your talent base come from within your company, you will need to source available freelance talents somewhere else; you have to go into partnerships; you have to plan for that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And in order to do that, you need a very strong HR function.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do not think we are doing enough in Singapore to develop this competence and capability and I hope that we can do more.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because with the rapid changes in the workforce, regardless of whether you are a large or a small organisation, it is difficult for your talent to keep up to reskill and upskill fast enough that there would not be skills gaps.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Businesses would find it difficult to find the exact skill they will require and, so, if you do not take proactive actions to develop them, then it is not going to be possible.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Member Pritam Singh talked about SkillsFuture, PMETs, all these programmes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do implore companies, because this is not about companies doing what is right or what is good.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: You have access to a talent base in Singapore that is highly educated, very, very highly educated, both men and women.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My point is, for companies, you have a very strong base to tap on; why ignore that base?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Yes, you have to put some investment into it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But you have the backing of funding for the programmes and at the same time, you also have the educational institutions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If you are a small company, you have the educational institutions working with you and with that talent over a period of time, to actually help you with the skills development and skills match.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is a win-win for all and the individual as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I would say, go in with the right mind set.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Go watch this programme that I talked about, "The Intern" and you will know what I mean.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If I can quote President Tan in his speech, "To remain special, we must first resolve to move ahead together".

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Incidentally, I have made a mental note to watch "The Intern" this weekend.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   Singapore's ability to thrive and survive as a prosperous nation with a plural society depended upon several fundamental principles, which did not come about by accident.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is an ongoing effort that includes good and credible governance that corresponds with current and future needs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just look at the ever-changing global situation, whether in terms of the economy, politics, social and security, it will affect and impact us greatly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The harmony in society is one of the most valuable assets that we must look after.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I truly welcome the review of Singapore's political system in order to secure the future of the nation for the long term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The changes proposed take various aspects into consideration, among others, ensuring good policymaking through good politics.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many people are still unclear, including some candidates, about the actual role of the Elected President and they may even confuse the voters.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the move to form a commission to analyse the qualification criteria for Presidential candidates because it is important that we get male or female candidates of a high calibre and who are suitable and can represent us inside and outside the country.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The proposed changes will further strengthen the institution of the Elected President that is already robust.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although it is too early for us to understand how this will be implemented, nonetheless, in terms of concept and principle, it is something that is gladly welcomed by the minorities.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will certainly fulfil the aspirations of the Malay/Muslim community, who have longed for a Malay President.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We still remember the vast contributions of Encik Yusof Ishak, the people's President.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It has been a source of great pride for the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If the community is proud to have had President Yusof Ishak performing that role – he represented all races outstandingly – surely, there will always be a Malay of a suitable calibre and can fulfil the qualifying criteria.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But it will be unfortunate if our qualified Malays do not have this opportunity just because of the voting pattern.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another important issue is how the provision is implemented.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It must be done by ensuring that there are no perceptions that this is an affirmative action; and it must ensure that the candidate is presented on the basis of merit, and can fulfil the qualifying criteria.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, what is important is that we must ensure diversity, without compromising the issue of merit and without affecting the quality of candidates.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can see more of our Malays in key positions and there have been no questions on their abilities or qualifications.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The GRC system is a concept that looks after and protects the interests of minorities in the landscape of a plural society in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we plan for more Single Member Constituencies, the Government must also ensure that minority representation continues to be safeguarded.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a community, the Malays support this concept and this can even help us contribute more at the constituency and national levels.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The increase in the number of Non-Constituency Members of Parliament (NCMPs) also allows more Opposition representation in Parliament, which will ensure more diverse views and opinions, and may also give more opportunities for Malay opposition candidates to enter Parliament through this scheme.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I support the intent of these changes, in terms of providing diversity in this House and also because the Government is trying to fulfil the aspirations of the younger generation, who desires diversity in the Parliament of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, as President Tony Tan mentioned in his Address at the Opening session of Parliament, we need to keep our politics and our governance updated.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, Prime Minister's speech on Wednesday was a timely reminder of how our political system had evolved since Independence and why we need to continue to evolve our political system to prepare Singapore for the future, from the NCMP and GRC schemes to the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The NCMP and Nominated Member of Parliament (NMP) schemes both came about as a response to have more diverse views in Parliament – one partisan and the other one not.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Elected Presidency came about 25 years ago as a custodian and a checking mechanism to protect Singapore's national reserves and the integrity of the civil service.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In doing so, the President would help to deliver long-term stability for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we have seen in the last Presidential Election in 2011, this function of the President can no longer be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To be a stabilising force, the President has to be above party politics and play a stabilising role for Singapore, even if there was a change in the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since the last election for the President, there are concerns that the election process was seemingly politicised and threatened to divide a nation, rather than stabilise it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And I agree with the Prime Minister that the process and the elected position remains objective and non-political, supported by a capable and wise Council of Presidential Advisers (CPA).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, it is important that we find men or even women of calibre, of excellent standing who can represent us here and on the international stage.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the weightage in qualifying criteria cannot just be heavily weighted on one's ability to manage high-value companies or based on the limited number of key public sector appointments.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is an important criterion as a proxy to one's ability to fulfil the role of Presidency, but we must also ensure that this does not reduce the number of potential candidates, especially those from the private sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the proposal to have the CPA's advice to the President to be given greater weight, it is therefore, just as important that the selection process and the merits of the selection of the CPA be made more transparent to the public.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Also, if they had provided advice contrary to the President and a vote needed from Parliament, there must also be greater transparency on why this is so.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But, we also want Presidents who can represent the diversity of Singapore's society, especially when we want to project the accurate image of Singapore's meritocracy and multi-culturalism to the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The announcement by Prime Minister is thus welcomed by the minority races as it will go a long way in strengthening multi-culturalism in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the early years, our nominated presidential system ensured we had minorities like Mr Yusof Ishak and Mr Benjamin Sheares.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We were also fortunate to have Mr SR Nathan as an Elected President but his term came at a time when elections were uncontested.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the current climate and competitive nature of the last Presidential Election, I wonder when another minority can be expected to be elected to the office in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Here, I also note the concerns from the ground as to whether the intervention to ensure a minority President is elected then becomes a form of affirmative action and against the principles of a free election of the President.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Personally, I do not believe that we should revert to the old system of the appointed President.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But as a guiding principle, any mechanism that is chosen, the minority candidate must first and foremost, meet the qualifying criteria of any Presidential candidate, so that the merit of his or her abilities and character will not come under question.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But perhaps, one proposal to catalyse a minority in the office of the Head of State is to consider the concept of a Vice President, where President and Vice President candidates are elected as a team and either one should be a minority.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This may set the path for a minority Vice President to build his credentials and stand in good stead for the Presidency in subsequent elections in the event that we are unable to elect a minority President in the role directly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While we keep a view on ensuring diversity, what is important, ultimately, is that merit is not compromised and that the quality of the representation is not compromised.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must find men and women of good standing to safeguard the nation's and people's interests.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On Prime Minister's announcement on tweaks to the NCMP scheme, I am supportive, in order to promote greater diversity in Parliament in terms of voices.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To the outside world, this may sound a bit strange as the PAP is seemingly diluting its hold in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But I support this move, to increase the number of NCMPs and allow them equal voting rights with constituency Members of Parliament, to assure Singaporeans and Singapore that the Government respects the need for diversity, though it was not what the electorate expressed through the results of the last General Election.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a constituency Member of Parliament, if elected, you are expected to serve the five-year term.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Any Opposition candidate who stands for elections knows the system.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Once you stand for elections, you must then be ready to serve if you are called upon as an NCMP.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: You cannot just have a myopic view of being "a duckweed in a pond that cannot sink roots" and not give the NCMP position any dignity and "suka-suka" swap candidates.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a privilege enshrined in the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We do not want political parties playing the system to provide parliamentary exposure to whoever they like.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All of these also mean that there is a new normal in governance and society in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That is, the increase of religiosity and issues concerning religion and how the Government will manage this going forward.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are many such examples in recent times.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Like dealing with the sensitivities in the City Harvest case or the changes made to the rules for Thaipusam.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Or even addressing issues on radicalisation or extremism and learning how we need to deal with the hijab.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All of these things are fast becoming a norm and the Government has to understand and work out how it should manage this "new normal".

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For one, the Government may need to review how it engages all the different racial and religious groups.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, today, the Government uses a hub-and-spoke model, where it is at the epicentre governing the different groups.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such a model will also foster collaboration between the different groups and have more ground-up initiatives without the Government always having to play the role of catalyst.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such a roundtable will also not just mean involving the leadership of all faiths but also to engage them at their congregation level and that will help to gather their views on tough questions affecting the community.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This not only helps to promote greater understanding, it also allows us to reach a new calibration, that is, what we are each prepared to accommodate as Singaporeans in our respective common spaces.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Otherwise, the Government may be behind on where this "new normal" of acceptance is.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Religious leaders may also try to second guess the Government in what it is prepared to accept.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, this roundtable multi-way dialogue should become an important feature of Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In building this new construct, let us also not forget the atheists as I have also received feedback on whether they have a say and if policymakers understand their perspectives, too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, social cohesion today becomes more difficult as you try to figure out friend from foe.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And I fear most when this manifests, where opportunities and progression become more limited due to fear in our workplaces, schools and social environment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, our policies and how we manage increased religiosity must also take into account the "new normal".

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, Muslims here are not consciously distancing themselves from the mainstream.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, the majority of Muslims I spoke to recently do not take any issue in respecting other people's religions and practices as well, or in greeting them during their religious holidays.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, how the Government handles issues concerning Muslims and inter-faith must evolve, including the use of hijabs in civilian spaces.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand the limitations of the uniformed services and schools, but the trends have also changed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If you look the consumer groups today, hijab wear is big online.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Even global brands, such as Dolce & Gabbana and H&M, which are mainstream brands, have shifted to embrace hijab fashion as the mainstream.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think you would probably have seen them, quite common, with many of the young ladies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Maybe, Madam, you also want to consider this.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is Dolce & Gabbana, by the way, with nice handbags and nice shoes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That is the "new normal", it is not just about religion but, really, how it has come to mainstream as a fashion statement and how people dress.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I agree that any threat from any religion that may threaten our social cohesion among the religious and race groups must be curtailed.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And for the Muslim community, the Muslim identity in Singapore must also be strengthened, due to the many interpretations and influences given our open borders and the age of the Internet.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Simple things even, like altars, altar fixtures outside your HDB flats, for example.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While religion and faith cannot be ignored in our policies to maintain religious harmony, to preserve our secular nature of politics, we also need to be vigilant that we do not go the way of other countries by having religious-based politics.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With wise, calibrated and relevant political reform, and with the Government reviewing terms to manage the "new normal" in handling religious harmony, our social fabric will be strengthened.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I encourage all Members, new and old, to continue to speak from the heart, as Mdm Speaker has advised, and I would add, with heart, on the things that matter to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Members have spoken about the "whys", the "whats" and the "hows" of our way forward.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The "why" is the world has changed and we ourselves have changed in the last 50 years.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The "what" is the kind of good policies and good politics that we need to navigate this changed world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And the "how" is the way, throughout the changes to come, we remain as one dynamic, cohesive, caring people.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Today, I wish to speak about the "so what" and "what for".

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is the first Parliament without our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Throughout this week, his words have come up repeatedly in Members' speeches.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In this time, one word of Mr Lee kept sounding in my head.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: You could say that was his favourite word.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When I worked for Mr Lee; this is now more than 15 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He liked to ask, "So?" Say, I would report some facts to him.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He would say, "So?" I would talk about the implications of those facts and he would say again, "So?" And it would go on like that until we got to, "So, what does this mean for Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, what must we do differently to ensure the success of Singapore and Singaporeans?" All that, in one word: "So?" Members spoke about profound changes taking place around us: in the global economy, in security, in society.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, what does this mean for Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, what must we do to ensure the success of Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And I would like to suggest, the "so what" is this.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We can continue to do this by staying open, innovative and adaptive to change.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must create value for the world and ourselves, so as to achieve a society based on justice and equality.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is how we can enable every Singaporean to reach our dreams.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore will have a place in the world, if we are of value to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Throughout our history, that was what we did, by being of use to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For hundreds of years, we were a key node on the Maritime Silk Route.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We welcomed traders from all over the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Just outside these Chambers, on the Singapore River, traders exchanged a wealth of not only goods, but also ideas, cultures, friendship.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our streets remember that trading emporium history today in name: Arab Street, Armenian Street, Muscat Street.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our spirit retains that same trading emporium history in our openness to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the last 50 years since Independence, we have found new ways to be of value to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: During the wave of globalisation in the 1960s and 1970s, we welcomed MNCs, and differentiated ourselves as a first-world oasis in a third-world region.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the 1980s and 1990s, as the region grew, we regionalised and grew an external wing.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the 2000s, as the knowledge revolution took off, we made the shift to a knowledge-intensive economy.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The global economy goes through waves of changes.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Each time, we have been able to catch the wave, we have asked, "So, what does this coming wave mean?" And, each time, we unlock how we can be of value.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some are calling it the Fourth Industrial Revolution.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It will bring disruptive changes in connectivity and extreme automation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Already, we are facing an explosion of data and information.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is like each household in the world having around 300 iPhones!

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are more and more connected: humans to humans, machines to machines and humans to machines.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A more connected world can be a more dangerous world, as the recent well-orchestrated terrorist attacks show.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Terrorists are using social media to radicalise and recruit new members.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But a more connected world is also a world of new possibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Alibaba and Amazon are more valued by some investors than Wal-Mart.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Wal-Mart has a more extensive physical infrastructure, has a longer history, but the e-commerce giants are better connected and more nimble.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, what does this mean for Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We may be at the beginning of a major structural transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To succeed, we must remain at the forefront, not just of having new ideas but, more importantly, to have the capacity to turn ideas into useful products, services and business models.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must create value, by being a place where good ideas for the world can be realised; where people can come together to create value, to make an impact.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If we can be a place to help solve a fraction of the world's challenges, we will create value, we will have our place in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am optimistic that we can be a place where good ideas for the world can be realised.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have to solve many of our own pressing challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We created the water technology to overcome this.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will find a way to make that a source of new life in our society.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is most striking that so many Members this week, when speaking on ageing, viewed it not as a problem, but as an opportunity.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu said, "80 is the new 60 and 60 the new 40".

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We want Singapore to be a place where we can age with opportunity, dignity and vitality.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In fact, we have heard many good ideas in this House just over the last few days.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have been investing in R&D, in knowledge creation, in connecting with the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Just two weeks ago, I hosted 21 Nobel Laureates and eminent technologists from all over the world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Imagine 21 Nobel Laureates and the Millennium Prize winners, the Technology Prize winners, all congregating in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They were inspired by what we are doing and they want to come here to inspire our young people in Singapore and the region so that they can go out and make an impact.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Last week, we saw the first-ever Southeast Asia Venture Capital Summit.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There is a great deal of energy around how Singapore can serve as a base for good ideas from around the world and how we can deploy good ideas from Science, Tech, Engineering and Math (STEM) domains, especially in Asia, to uplift lives.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Third, there is no limit to our imagination.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We may not realise this, but we are a people with a habit of innovation and a habit of applying innovation in every aspect of our life.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Just earlier this week, the Prime Minister spoke at length on the innovations in our political institutions over the years and the changes that the Prime Minister is proposing will serve Singapore well in the long run.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In fact, some academics have said that our social policy innovations are most remarkable.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Of course we can be a place where good ideas for the world can be realised.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We also see innovation in many areas of life.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is manned entirely by a team of volunteers!

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Everyday Singaporeans who care about our libraries enough to make a difference.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The readers return the books to the right shelves.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
